Notwithstanding, the biggest hammer of them all fell on the price of oil where on the back of plummeting energy demands and inconsistent policies and announcements of potential sanctions amidst Russian aggression against Ukraine saw futures plummet by 1.6% down to USD 58.29/barrel. Local steel plate prices also seem to be taking quite a hit as flatlining seems to be theme of the week across most sub-continent ship recycling markets and even China, where steel trade seems to have certainly taken a hit causing steel prices to freeze.

On the various ship recycling fronts, a shaky last few weeks finally settled this week with news that NOCs (No Objection Certificates) on incoming vessels in Bangladesh were finally being granted after a month-long hiatus whilst inspections from various government departments were being conducted to ensure that ongoing HKC yard upgrades reported by recyclers were in fact on track. Aside from the 7 HKC yards now approved in Chattogram, there is a list of about 20 yards waiting to gain HKC accreditation and these yards are reportedly at disproportionate stages of their own upgrades, which drove this market into a state of stasis whilst ongoing inspections and approvals worked themselves out, resulting in minimal sales and deliveries into Bangladesh of late, as a descending lull on activity shifted focus of ship owners / cash buyers on to competing markets in Pakistan and India. However, with political tensions now on the rise between Pakistan and India on the back of a terrorist attack in Kashmir’s Pahalgam city that resulted in the unfortunate death of 26 souls and has resulted in an increased military buildup along the border between each country, amidst a dangerous escalation in rhetoric that seems to be heading towards an armed conflict / war.

Overall, as tonnage scarcities & shaky fundamentals result in ship recycling activity being dragged through a bumbling backseat across sub-continent backroads for another week, particularly as global markets struggle to recover (and negotiate) following the sharp shock of the Trump’s tariff reforms, is keeping shipping markets propped up depriving recyclers of viable candidates for another week. Prices and demand, however, remain relatively unchanged from last week, other than a heightened sense of caution amongst ship recyclers who are still on the lookout for tonnage.

headline: FAR FROM GREAT!
highlights: Month of May. | Unexpectedly poor. | Financial pinch. | Skin in the game.
body_text:
Ongoing steel volatility over the last month or so has seen India enter May on a weaker overall footing despite many expecting the market to fire up pre-monsoon, especially with Chattogram out of the fray due to ongoing HKC upgrades and stalling government permissions on extensions to complete minimum HKC upgrade requirements, resulting in a slowdown of fixtures into Bangladesh over recent weeks. However, even with Trump’s tariff tantrums appearing to settle down and reciprocal trade agreements due to be enforced between the US and India, sentiments in Alang have been far from great of late during this time, especially in the face of ongoing attempts at maintaining bilateral trade relations between the countries, which continues to take centre stage.

Yet, Alang recyclers remain nervous despite taking in the most tonnage as evidenced by India’s port report for the week on the back of a healthier (than competing neighbours) collection of sales being concluded over recent times (be it smaller LDT tonnage) and that too at decent levels despite a noticeable lack of favoured or workable tonnage changing hands for recycling at present. In addition to a slacking supply, domestic fundamentals continue to react to the menacing volatility that has been subjected onto international markets as on the one hand, local steel plate prices fell USD 4/Ton early in the week, only to jump USD 8/Ton and the week on an overall positive note. The Rupee however reported the strongest surges of the week firming an entire percentage point against the U.S. Dollar and closed out at a healthy Rs. 84.53 – a much needed boost to recycling sentiments as a firming Rupee makes vessel purchases that much more cost effective.

Meanwhile, the focus of the country revolves around the recent terrorist attack in the North as protests against Pakistan rage across the nation and push PM Modi to take an affirmative stance against cross-border terrorism, as he reportedly re-positions a massive arrangement of troops to the frontlines, resulting in an escalation of a words between the leaders of both countries. With most international nations (especially the U.S.) standing back at this juncture, leaving free reign for PM Modi take a decisive posture against the unrelenting decades long terrorist attacks on Indians. Should an armed conflict unfurl, the financial pinch to both nations would be concerning, especially for Pakistan whose treasury reserves are far lower than that of neighbouring India. Moreover, this could result in blockages of movement of tonnage around WC Indian / Pakistani waters and further affect ship recycling and even shipping on the whole.

Whatever comes of it, the state of ship recycling will remain suspended in suspense as 2025 brings with it, its own share of political turmoil to the shores of India. With the current state of affairs, perhaps a break from the mundane might be just what the recyclers need. For now, like competing markets, India remains subjected to supply, geography, and a competing Pakistan that still seems like it’s got some skin in the game.

headline: TENSIONS RISING!
highlights: International pressures. | Tit for tat. | Aiming for aid. | Slow Q2
body_text:
Cross border tensions with India have been grabbing most of the headlines in Pakistan of late, and even though a few international bodies are urging calm lest the situation escalates further between the two nuclear nations, the situation at present doesn’t seem to bode well for peace. Reciprocal moves banning Indian flagged ships from Pakistan and vice versa have hit shipping sectors and there is no telling how far each country will go in this needless game of one upmanship. And as stated above, Pakistan’s precarious financial position may not be able to accommodate an armed conflict with its much larger neighbor, which in itself could cause a maddening shortage of funds to the populous and domestic businesses at large as an escalation could mean authorities curtailing communications within the nation for security reasons, causing the economy to slow overall, just as we have seen during earlier riots and protests when cell services were also suspended.

And slow it certainly has been. As vessel prices dip and demand from recyclers curtails over recent weeks, Pakistan spent a second week devoid of any sales and ended the 2nd week with no fresh arrivals to report at local anchorage. Even the Pakistan Rupee lost 4 basis points and closed the week at a diminished PKR 281.11 against the U.S. Dollar, as local steel plate prices that are now flatlining USD 10/Ton lower at USD 614/Ton, leaving the advantage of much wider margins for Gadani recyclers to exploit on their recycling purchases, seemingly eroding as despite depreciating USD 50/Ton in the last 6 weeks, Pakistan plate prices still hold a decent USD 150/Ton margin over competing sub-continent neighbors, yet, ended the week with an empty port position.

The economy more than likely take a hit as India bans all imports from Pakistan and as the fallout from the terrorist attack continues, India is now approaching the IMF, ADB, and other financial agencies asking them to reassess all current and future loan applications from Pakistan, furthering the rift between the nations as it considers presenting an opposition to IMF’s planned USD 1.3 Billion aid package intended for review on May 9th, thereby compelling these governmental agencies to pressurize Pakistan into ceasing its activities.

What becomes of this terrorist tragedy remains to be seen. For now, Pakistani ship recycling activity has remained sidelined and will likely remain in the shadows over the month of May amidst the ongoing fallout, especially at a time when finances are in dire need by the domestic ship recycling community to upgrade local yards to HKC standards whilst the government preps for the possibility of war. This could result in Pakistan falling entirely out of recycling game by June, especially if funds become a scarcity and domestic ship recycling yards fail to meet their HKC goals.

headline: DIRE TIMES!
highlights: Regional sales.
body_text:
A quiet week saw Turkey recede into the background amidst collapsing local steel plate prices over recent weeks that finally settled this week, vessel offerings that have hit a recent new low, and a Lira that refuses to slow its maddening descent against the U.S. Dollar, which saw it collapse another 40 basis points down to TRY 38.57 this week, on its merry way to TRY 40.

As it stands, there has not been much to report from Aliaga as sentiments are clearly in a dismal state, and like the rest of the industry, market tonnage remains amiss for the most part – save for the steady inflow of small LDT tonnage from the region that is keeping the local ship recycling scraping through on the barest of minimums, and sadly, the situation doesn’t look like it will get better any time soon for this market. Expect another quiet onset of summer from this market.

headline: HKC … OR BUST!
highlights: NOC struggles. | HKC ONLY! | Slip to 2nd? | Global cosplay.
body_text:
After a backlog of ships piling up at OPL Chattogram over recent weeks on the back of missing No Objection Certificates (NOCs) from local authorities that would otherwise have permitted these units committed to non-HKC facilities enter port limits, this week, an exemption was made for just those units already outside whose respective facilities had also managed to secure their HKC SoC accreditations and approvals from the Bangladeshi government, resulting in a healthy collection of local arrivals at Chattogram’s anchorage. It also came as quite the zinger to see the recently formed ship recycling board announce that no further permissions / NOCs on any incoming vessel(s) or any further extension(s) would be granted to non-certified yards, and ship owners therefore need to be aware that any upcoming / future sale(s) into Chattogram will have to be to an HKC only yard, as units fixed to non-HKC facilities will simply NOT receive an NOC.

At present, there are only 7 ship recycling yards with full HKC SoC accreditations in hand and another +20 yards are at various stages of their own HKC infrastructure upgrades, some of whom are reportedly closer to getting their approvals within the coming week(s). Continued audits will take place in Chattogram to ensure yards are matching the required rate of improvements needed to achieve their independent HKC certifications. One thing is now for sure, the Hong Kong Convention has cemented its permanence in Bangladesh!

The situation with NOC restrictions has sadly also seen HKC accredited yards start to exploit the unfolding situation by talking down the market this week and arbitrarily presenting indications / offers on units that are clearly below last week’s levels. As being the only facilities to receive NOCs on incoming / future vessels now presents these yard owners with newfound leverage to import vessels at a lower price - as indications have certainly started showing a downward trend by the time the week ended. The onset of Monsoon and increasing stress of yard upgrades further offers the likelihood of prices slipping from Bangladesh in the coming weeks, which would then see Pakistan or even India retake the mantle from Bangladesh in the price rankings within May.

As the pre-monsoon madness starts to push prices down, coupled with an upcoming budget that has garnered little positive news thus far far, and domestic fundamentals that have conjointly done little to elevate local sentiments this week, saw the Taka make a mere 3 basis point increase against the U.S. Dollar and end the week at BDT 121.49, while local steel plate prices remained dead on the floor at USD 477/Ton – a level that remains dangerously close to breakeven on certain premium units. At the macro end, domestic investors remain weary of international tariffs as reportedly, a formal trade agreement between the U.S. and Bangladesh has yet to enter into force and the added uncertainty on Chinese tariffs is also making domestic manufacturers nervous how their source- pricing on raw materials might eventually affect their manufacturing costs. In the interim, the economic global cosplay saw Bangladesh’s GDP through the month of April.

Seems like Bangladesh is headed for a quieter end to May.

headline: TESTY TIMES!
highlights: Ceasefires. | HKC rules. | Bangla surprise. | Pak woes. | Pronto.
body_text:
In the meantime, Team Trump continues to steamroll the U.S. Economy and global trade volumes as reportedly on Friday, not a single cargo ship had departed Chinese ports for the U.S. markets, in troubling signs of what is about to unfold as this is the first time the U.S. has encountered such a situation since the worst days of Covid-19 closures. As ongoing volumes of international trade start to dissolve, the Baltic Exchange Dry Index reported a 1.3% drop with both Capes & Panamax indices falling 2.5% & 0.7% respectively, in clear signs that tariff infected products are rapidly running of out of supply chains. Surprisingly, despite trade volumes faltering and demand for bunkers starting to slip, oil futures made a healthy 1.8% jump this week and ended at USD 61/barrel on the back of the news that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was due to meet with Chinese officials this week, in an effort to iron out US – Chinese trade agreements, in addition to the news of a separate US - UK trade agreement that still leaves a 10% tariff on U.K. products exported to the U.S.

As a result, sub-continent recycling markets too have been on a negative spiral of late, especially as we head into the quieter monsoon season and Pakistani & Bangladeshi recyclers need to speed up their readiness and ensure yard compliance with the Hong Kong Convention by June 26th. While nearly all Indian yards are certified, the focus shifts to neighboring Pakistan and Bangladesh to get their facilities up to speed - and do it soon. NOCs on ships have meanwhile been granted as an exemption just this time, resulting in a busy anchorage not only in Bangladesh, but also in India, all whilst Pakistan remains stranded for a 3rd week with no fresh arrivals. Flatlining / declining steel plate prices including mixed performances by currencies (even Turkey) also didn’t help move the pricing needle at any recycling destination, especially given that the overall number of candidates has simply disappeared from the bidding tables of late, and ship owners collectively wait to see the eventual outcome of trade negotiations in the coming weeks before evaluating freight rates and deciding whether to continue trading their older assets at reasonable / above opex levels, or a trip down recycling lanes is on the charts. Certainly, a hot cup of testy times is on the menu for May.

headline: WAR … AND RECYCLING!
highlights: Underperforming. | Conflict reigns. | INR struggles. | Go to market? | Interesting month for India.
body_text:
Overall, a crazy week of armed conflict with its perennial rival Pakistan saw the attention of the entire nation glued to their respective sources of media watching the unfolding of PM Modi’s decisive action against terrorist factions across Eastern Pakistan. As India decimated vital army and air force targets across Pakistan striking the deepest the country has ever struck Pakistan in the last 50 years, the sudden cease-fire saw the populous voicing their collective disappointment that the recent terrorist attack from Pakistan did not meet with a firm enough counteraction, which would more than likely see Pakistani terrorists attack at a future date.

And while Pakistani officials certainly seem to have gotten the message given the close proximity Indian missiles hit Pakistani nuclear command and control centres, it remains to be seen just how long this newfound “peace” between the nations persists. The Indian Foreign Minister meanwhile voiced India’s strong opposition to IMF’s USD 1.3 billion loan package to Pakistan on account of Pakistani mismanagement of funds from the prior tranche that remains under IMF investigations, and there are no securities from Pakistan’s side as to just where this money will be eventually diverted to or if it will even be spent on future terrorist acts.

While on the one hand, the conflict kept Alang recyclers distracted throughout the week, on the other hand, it may have well been a good thing given that another woeful week of underperformance from Alang recyclers saw India sink to the bottom of the sub-continent pricing board – and not for the first time this year either! Fundamentals are certainly playing their respective parts given that not only have local steel plate prices declined by about USD 4/Ton this week, but the Indian Rupee lost nearly 1% as it plummeted back towards Rs. 86 midweek, only to end it at Rs. 85.30.

Moreover, both Indian and Pakistani stock markets surged on the back of the ceasefire, yet Indian sentiments remain cautions given just how fragile the current ceasefire is. Tariff talks too have reportedly been positive between Indian and U.S. officials as news of a mutually beneficial bilateral trade agreement is nearing conclusion. Yet, domestic economists fear that the tariffs that do go into effect, will eventually affect the nation’s GDP by 0.5% for the rest of the year.

For now, however, recyclers remain on the lookout for tonnage as surprisingly, a decent LDT tanker at Alang’s anchorage coupled with a collection of smaller sized units helped near India’s total LDT for the week over 26K LDT this week. Moreover, with tariff uncertainties abound and HKC taking front and centre at neighbouring competitors, India could stand to become the market to go to for the time being - even in the face of lower pricing, once Pakistani and Bangladeshi recyclers initiate the process of upgrading their facilities and divert their collective attentions towards HKC accreditations over vessel negotiations.

headline: SIDELINED!
highlights: Radar. | Declining India | Conservative? | Lucky.
body_text:
Pakistan has barely been on the ship recycling radar over recent years – struggling to compete (pricewise) on the back of an ailing economy and a drastically collapsed currency that resulted in a crushing lack of financing and available L/Cs for domestic ship recyclers. However, across 2025, Gadani recyclers have thankfully managed to get by on scarce and small LDT, geographically positioned tonnage that eventually raised hopes within the cash buying community of a resurgent Pakistan, given that a growing number of enquiries and aggression to buy emerged across March and April. However, Pakistan once again slipped back down and has been relegated to the last few weeks of an empty port position, with its competitively weaker levels.

Luckily for Gadani recyclers, a (once again) declining India has thrust the Pakistani market back into 2nd place in the market rankings this week, even though local offerings haven’t changed much for some time now, which remains puzzling. Despite the Pakistani Rupee depreciating of late, it has all but depreciated less than 2% in recent months as it ended the week 12 basis points firmer against the U.S. Dollar this week at PKR 281.20, all while Pakistani steel plate prices remain over USD 100/Ton higher than its sub-continent competition offering more than a healthy buffer to local recyclers at current offer levels.

Moreover, the approval of IMF’s USD 1.3 billion loan package will certainly ease any financial burdens the country or even local recyclers may have as they too approach the HKC deadline of June 26th. Unfortunately for Gadani recyclers, they remain lagging far behind the competition on the yard upgrades front and this may see Pakistani ship recyclers disappear from the bidding table all together once the HKC formally enters into effect. We can only hope that a sense of professional urgency prevails, and the incoming aid is put to good use for the future of this vital sector of the nation.

The conflict with India too sucked most of the country’s collective focus away from daily activities and this saw no market sales being confirmed into Pakistan this week. However, the aftershocks of the conflict will likely be felt for some time as the nation recovers from India’s deepest attacks into Pakistan over the last 5 decades and an overall sense of insecurity in the economy could also see local recyclers take an increasingly conservative stance in their pricing strategies and deliver Pakistan a short stint at the #2 spot.

Time will tell. Fow now, Pakistan may likely get lucky with the off-chance, smaller LDT geographically suited unit and keep a yard (or two) operating in the interim. What happens in the long run may end up surprising everyone.

headline: IT’S SILENT, SLICK!
highlights: Blended.
body_text: Other than the guaranteed depreciation of the Turkish Lira, which fell 30 basis points against the U.S. Dollar down to TRY 38.71 as the week ended, there is nothing to report from Turkey this week. The absence of tonnage blended with weakened prices has certainly seen this market take a vacation of late and like Pakistan, Aliaga recyclers remain on the hunt for small LDT tonnage from regional waters.

headline: REGULATORY RED TAPE!
highlights: 7 yards so far. | Audits underway. | Difficult destination. | Quieter May / June.
body_text:
With only 7 HKC certified yards open and currently buying vessels in Bangladesh, local offerings have conveniently cooled over the last couple of weeks as owners of the only operating yards with HKC approvals start to exploit the unfolding situation, resulting in recently proposed units for sale increasingly focusing on neighboring Indian and Pakistani markets. A few more local yards have reportedly completed their second audits with IRS class and are expected to receive their respective HKC certifications within the next few week(s). However, it seems destined to be a longer wait for a handful of yards that currently lag behind the necessary rate of infrastructure upgrades required ahead of yard visits from local authorities, and for their subsequent HKC certifications to come through. As it therefore stands, regulatory red tape will increasingly holding up local deliveries and fixtures and until these new regulations are ironed out and in force until more yards are approved, Bangladesh will be a difficult delivery destination for owners and cash buyers alike.

And the situation for non-HKC ship recyclers who are unable to import tonnage may ironically be well-timed given the performance of current fundamentals as not only are competing local HKC recyclers lowering their offers in the face of firming steel plate prices that jumped nearly USD 90/Ton over recent weeks and remain flatlined in the face of missing trade between Bangladeshi steel mills and local recycling yards given that recycling tonnage itself has been missing for the last 6 weeks, but the Bangladeshi Taka also fell nearly 30 basis points to end the week at BDT 121.82 against the U.S. Dollar, all while the Central Bank of Bangladesh announced its decision to let the market determine the rate of the U.S. Dollar, as required by the terms of the current IMF loan agreement and this could result in further volatility from the Taka, as well as deterioration of local sentiment.

DOmestic banks are also becoming increasingly stringent as a growing series of new demands from authorities whilst transacting L/Cs is causing a fresh batch of frustrations for local recyclers, local agents, cash buyers, and ship owners, as new-fangled documentary requirements are causing delays in inward clearing vessels, releasing L/Cs, and onto their eventual deliveries that is resulting in further unexpected expenses. Adding to local frustrations has also been a diminished level of demand from domestic steel mills that is likely to get worse once the rains come pouring down.

Finally, as the interim government announces a few ambitious projects this week, these have come far too little too late and much to the disappointment of the general public given that the optimism and idealism initially displayed by the interim government is slowly disappearing and the same old formula of corruption through mega projects is reportedly rearing its head again. Until the new budget is announced and fresh elections earmark political stability in the region once again, Bangladesh is likely to spend a quieter May / June than previously anticipated.

headline: SUDDEN SPEED?!?
highlights: Backlog beaching. | Only HKC. | Yard shortage. | 2nd half supply. | One month away.
body_text:
All while President Trump visits the Middle East and accepts planes as gifts while complaining to senior staff about Congressional restrictions blocking such favors, world economies are meanwhile having a hell of a rollercoaster ride with freight markets surging 6% by close of Friday and were essentially propelled by higher rates across all trading segments. The 90-day tariff truce between China and the U.S. also saw crude futures climb 1.4% and end the week at USD 62.5/barrel, as global trade starts to stabilize to global post-tariff conundrums despite lingering uncertainties around the Iran Nuclear deal, which, if successful, could see an additional 200,000 barrels of oil enter the market, placing further uncertainty on oil markets and trade planning.

Shifting from global economic chains to the ship recycling markets also saw the U.S. Dollar surge against nearly all ship recycling nation currencies (except China) this week, whilst steel plate prices firm / decline / flatline in a series of confusing signals to ship recyclers and the industry at large. The recent trimming of tonnage at the bidding tables also seems to be easing as local port positions in both India and Bangladesh reported a healthy collection of arrivals and deliveries this week. In Bangladesh, the recent backlog of vessels idling outside, awaiting their respective NOCs that built up across April also saw several deliveries ensue this week as exemptions came through from the ministry to recently approved HKC yards, all while a series of units committed to non-certified yards still remain stranded outside port limits.

Pending HKC upgrades aside, markets overall feel like the they have been cornered as diminished pricing and confusing fundamentals have left sentiments uncertain and demand anemic. With HKC hurdles shifting the recent focus of vessels to the more active Indian (or non-HKC Pakistani) markets, unfolding economic constraints stand to pressure prices down even as freight markets start to settle, charter rates start to climb, and the supply of candidates may start to increase through the second half of the year despite a traditionally slower and quieter monsoon season, thanks to trading opportunities for increasingly overaged units finally starting to disappear and these units should start truckling to recycling facilities at their end of their charters, after what has been a few years of buoyant freight markets across the board.

headline: TENSIONS COOL!
highlights: Ceasefire. | Refocus. | WTO threat. | Busy Monsoon?
body_text:
The fragile ceasefire between India and Pakistan this week has seen tensions cool between the two nuclear nations even though sporadic instances of small arms fire at the Line of Control has continued. Moreover, as the nation as a whole remains disappointed at the restricted response from the Indian army after decades of terrorist attacks, PM Modi re-assured the nation that Operation Sindoor has merely been paused but is not completed. What this means for the future of the conflict remains to be seen, especially as Indian Special Forces reportedly took out senior terrorist leaders in various locations in Pakistan occupied Kashmir (PoK) this week, which could well see the conflict be inflamed in the near future once again.

As such, focus has understandably been diverted away from recycling markets in recent times with the armed-conflict between the perennially warring neighbours taking centre stage for the nation at large. But armed conflict isn’t India’s only issue as tariffs and trade wars have seen the Rupee start to plummet once again as it fell nearly 35 basis points to end the week at Rs. 85.66, but even local steel plate prices dropped by about USD 2/Ton as the week ended, placing further downward pressures on an already feeble sentiment that has seen local offerings retreat and move India into 3rd place on the market rankings. Ironically however, Alang’s waterfront reported far more arrivals and deliveries than Gadani this week as 6 ships and nearly 33K LDT had arrived / was delivered to local recyclers, including a large(r) LDT Pax vessel.

At the macro end of India’s economic overview, its performance was just as mixed as India’s ship recycling sector as on the one hand, India’s forex reserves continue to increase as they surged past USD 690 billion this week on the back of firming domestic auto sales, the U.N. unfortunately downgraded India’s FY 2025 GDP growth outlook as unemployment remains stagnant and wholesale price index hit a 13-month low last month. Moreover, as the U.S. – India tariff situation remains precarious, the possibility of an incoming hike in tariff rates saw India threaten the WTO with retaliatory tariffs against the U.S., which only means further instability for India’s economy.

Notwithstanding, there remains some respite for Alang recyclers as a constricted number of available buyers in Chattogram coupled with the tense army situation in Pakistan has left India a far safer alternative for incoming vessels and departing international crew. Indian recyclers also remain more active at the bidding tables than their Paksitani counterparts, further shrinking any price competitive advantage India may have lost over recent weeks.

Unlike its counterparts, India may have a far busier monsoon in comparison.

headline: MISSING A TRICK!
highlights: Minimal deals. | Lagging on HKC. | Excuses reign. | Far behind.
body_text:
Pakistan has had an opportunity to acquire India’s share of vessels over the last few weeks as Bangladesh deliveries and fixtures have been stranded on account of the ongoing NOC restrictions and India has likewise suffered with declining sentiments and prices due to tariff confusions and volatility in its fundamentals. The Hong Kong Convention also does not come into force until June 26th so there remains a small window of opportunity for Gadani buyers to make the most out of the present and purchase a majority of the available tonnage before the landscape entirely changes.

However, it remains the same mix of excuses and confusion emanating from Pakistani recyclers as they unexpectedly find themselves higher up in the market rankings all while no positive changes to Pakistani fundamentals have been reported while the Indian Rupee continues to yoyo against the U.S. Dollar. Confusion over Alang’s recent diminished vessel offerings has also left Gadani buyer’s perplexed as to whether to maintain their currently higher pricing, or re-adjust down to match those from India.

And Pakistani fundamentals have all the tell tale signs behind why lower offers from Gadani in the near future are more than likely. Not only are local plate prices now within arm’s length of Bangladeshi plate prices as they drop to USD 610/Ton (vs. the impressive jump to USD 577/ton in Bangladesh) and remain flatlined, but the Paksitani Rupee also depreciated 32 basis points and closed the week out at a whopping PKR 282.12.

Economically as well, the nation continues to hemorrhage cash as despite incoming IMF funds to support the economy, national exports during the month of April plummeted an extravagant 17.65%, further afflicting the nation’s ability to recover on its own accord. The lingering conflict with India has also seen the army impose restrictions and movements along the Eastern front, in addition to the longstanding conflict in Balochistan where Baloch rebels hammered a Pakistani army convoy with IEDs killing several army personnel resulting in further blockades and closures.

The resulting uncertainty has left Pakistan suspended in the present times, accounting for the lack of any (market or private) deals to Gadani recyclers as a result. Highlighting the tonnage drought has been Gadani’s waterfront that has now ended a month with no arrivals. While all local yards desperately need to initiate infrastructure upgrades to their facilities so as to continue operating in a post HKC world, regrettably, not a single yard in Pakistan is anywhere near attaining these standards and remain far behind the competition at this stage.

headline: DOWN…AGAIN!
highlights: Repeat.
body_text: Aliaga recyclers continue to face unrelenting pressure from their fundamentals given that not only have local steel plate prices made a marginal USD 10/MT improvement over the last couple of weeks (having plummeted over weeks prior), but the Lira too has fallen another 30 basis points to end the week at TRY 38.80 against the U.S. Dollar, a whiff away from TRY 39. Market supply remains abysmal and there has been no meaningful delivery of units into Turkey for much of this year - sand it’s likely to be another repeat of 2024 all over again.

headline: TIK TOK TAK(A)!
highlights: Taka tumbles. | Backlog delivering. | Docs needed, delays | ensue. | Interesting June.
body_text:
Last week, the Bangladeshi government decided to let market forces dictate the value of the Taka, a move officiated by the terms and conditions of the current IMF Loan. This has seen the Taka fall 80 basis points and head nearly vertically towards BDT 122 (as the week ended) once again, ending it pennies short at BDT 121.80. And while the Taka suffocates Bangladesh’s ship recycling fraternity on the one hand, local steel plate prices on the other flatlined at levels region $475/ton post-Eid - pre-market / NOC closures in April and levels steel levels opened nearly USD 100/Ton higher at about USD 577/Ton, whereafter, in keeping with the depreciation of the Taka also saw steel plate prices lose a whopping USD 21/Ton this week. As a result, the movement of the overall economy has been increasingly spelling out disaster for the interim government that has finally committed to a June 30th date for General Elections to be held, as overall faith and confidence in the current administration loses further points among the domestic populous.

Notwithstanding the decline in plate prices, their current levels have certainly provided local recyclers with more than a buffer to present reasonable offers on available units under the present circumstances. However, with the HKC on the horizon, not as many local buyers have been able to bid on tonnage on account of missing HKC accreditations / inability to obtain No Objection Certificates (NoCs) on their incoming acquisitions until a certain rate of development has been confirmed by yard owners, as mandated by the recently formed Ship Recycling Board. And while several HKC yards have been approved over recent weeks - taking the total number of approved yards up to 9 – there are reportedly over 20 yards that are presently undergoing their inspections / approvals ahead of being able to get their respective NOCs once again.

This inability to obtain NOCs saw a healthy backlog of vessels build up outside port limits across April and even May whilst yard inspections took place, causing severe delays for ship owners and cash buyers alike. And given just how busy Bangladesh’s waterfront has been this week compared to its regional competition (8 ships and nearly 54K LDT), this market is certainly pushing the pedal to the floor with its acquisitions and even yard upgrades. But with all these regulatory changes come additional documentary requirements as now, a Ship Recycling Facility Plan (SRFPs), Ship Recycling Plan (SRPs), and even an Inventory of Hazardous Materials (IHMs) needs to be provided to, and approved by the ministry before NOCs can be granted, further highlighting that delays are all but guaranteed when getting vessels cleared inward, paid for, and eventually delivered.

With only 9 yards currently able to bid on tonnage being introduced for sale at the bidding tables and many in Chattogram having filled their yards over the last couple of weeks, a bare minimum number of open buyers are not pursuing fresh units aggressively in the face of pending approvals, which has seen prices from Bangladesh start to cool as the focus falls on neighboring markets to pick up the slack. The onset of rains isn’t helping local steel trade either as demand from steel mills itself remains curtailed, coupled with upcoming elections and a budget for the next FY leaves the potential for an interesting June lying in wait for this market.

headline: GMS PODCASTS!
highlights: People on the move. | Tariffs again??? | Markets react. | Freight cool. | HKC delays.
body_text:
Out of the digital realm and into the real one, a new tariff session of testing international economies has once again reared its ugly head with Trump specifically targeting India’s retaliatory tariffs with the WTO causing a mixed reaction in the sub-continent ship recycling destinations as the US. Dollar plummeted against the Indian Rupee this week and gained ground against Bangladeshi, Pakistani, and (of course) Turkish currencies by the time the week ended. But the tariff-high didn’t end there as Trump once again announced 50% tariffs on the EU this week, showing just how unpredictable and volatile the global business atmosphere will remain under his administration for the news 3 years, 8 months, 1 week...

Global stock markets, ship recycling nation currencies, and commodity prices collectively took hits as a result of Trump’s actions causing freight markets to cool even further this week, as smaller trading sectors failed the most and dragged the overall Baltic Exchange Dry Index down about 0.1% despite the larger dry sector making marginal gains, while containers and certain tanker segments also start to see declines of their own, further indicating what may be a busier inflow of tonnage over the second half of 2025. On the back of faltering global trade, oil futures too continue their retreat resulting in the barrel declining across the week, to register a minor improvement by the end of the week and still end at an overall lower level of USD 61.50/barrel.

On the ship recycling front, sub-continent markets are gradually entering the monsoon season on a weaker note, having faced political, regulatory, and currency issues, a war, and evolving tariff woes that continue to see prices recycling prices significantly cool since the peaks closer to USD 500/LDT witnessed earlier in the year. Bangladesh continues to endure delays and teething problems after the announcement that only HKC yards would be allowed to import vessels as currently only 9 yards are HKC certified and can obtain NOCs to import and at least 20 more trying to improve their infrastructure before the convention comes into force on June 26th. Pakistan meanwhile remains lagging behind with not a single yard HKC approved and all of this pressure building up at a time when Gadani remains empty, buyers struggle to remain price-competitive, and Gadani remains 2nd

headline: ALWAYS AVAILABLE!
highlights: Falling steel. | LNGs sold. | HKC ready.
body_text:
Despite declining vessel prices in Bangladesh and the recently established fragile peace with Pakistan holding ground for the time-being, Alang buyers have persisted in the market, able to secure any unit at prevailing rates and even pick up some of the slack from a recently slowing Bangladeshi market. Such a case saw several Hyundai-controlled MOSS type LNGs sold into India this week as the larger LDT HYUNDAI AQUAPIA (34,066 LDT) and HYUNDAI TECHNOPIA (34,046 LDT) were both fixed for a decent enbloc price basis an ‘as is’ Korea / Batam delivery respectively – in what is earmarking some of the freshest sales of the market. And given their pedigree and green requirements, these units are more than likely destined to end up in India, with Bangladesh’s ongoing delays in having vessels cleared locally and a minimum number of currently open (Bangladeshi) recyclers.

India’s economy, meanwhile, remains much stronger than its neighbouring competition and its fundamentals continue to take the opportunity to inflate and simultaneously deflate local sentiments as on the one hand, the Indian Rupee firmed an impressive 60 basis points to end the week at Rs. 85.06 against the U.S. Dollar, while on the other hand, local steel plate prices remain the lowest in the Indian sub-continent, plummeting a whopping USD 11/Ton this week alone, ensuring that tonnage hungry Alang prices will likely remain stagnated (for now). Alang also did not report a single fresh arrival this week and to make matters worse, there is reportedly not a single vessel idling outside awaiting entry. Certainly, a surprising week for Alang’s anchorage given just how busy last week was in comparison.

Yet, India remains comfortably in the lead with over 100 HKC approved yards, leaving the country a far more open and available market for owners and cash byers alike, albeit at lower levels than their competitors. India’s economy also continues to flourish as a nation as it displaces Japan for the 4th place in global rankings of the world’s largest economies, and forecasts have also set the rate of GDP growth at 7% when FY25 winds up, driving up national economic sentiment and firming the INR. Notwithstanding, despite an overall depreciated currency, declining steel plate prices, and ongoing global tariff concerns affecting the nation, Alang remains the go to destination for straightforward and prompt deliveries, far from the self-induced and ongoing delays being currently witnessed in Bangladesh.

If India steel plate prices make a small jump in the coming weeks, Alang recyclers would be in an incredible position take in a majority of the tonnage that is likely to come available prior to June 26th and even thereafter, if Pakistan doesn’t step up its HKC updates. Plate issues.

headline: TOO LITTLE, TOO LATE!
highlights: Greater demand. | Inadequate. | Need to improve. | 2023 again?
body_text:
Some greater demand, pricing, and sense of urgency to acquire tonnage seems to be emerging from Pakistan given that there remains just about a month to go until the Hong Kong Convention comes into force on June 26th.

Unfortunately, these moves to acquire seem to be too little too late with undervalued (in Pakistan) LNGs make the rounds this week while yard infrastructure / HKC upgrades remain woefully uninitiated at a healthy majority of domestic ship recycling yards, which itself is likely to take many more months to even get to anywhere near HKC standards, far from even achieving their respective accreditations thereafter; meaning Pakistan is likely to be excluded in the short term (perhaps even the long term if HKC development doesn’t pick up pace asap) from being proposed any units for recycling.

Meanwhile, the ongoing ceasefire has kept domestic tensions high and domestic fundamentals deviated from their performances over recent weeks whereby local steel plate prices managed to miraculously firm up by about USD 4/Ton this week, all while the Pakistani Rupee appreciated notably towards the end of the week and still lost about 11 basis points overall, to clock out at PKR 281.84 against the U.S. Dollar with a high that breached PKR 283 mid-week.

At the Macro end of the nation’s economic state, the IMF’s recent tranche has certainly helped stabilize the Pakistani economy for the interim, whilst the Pakistani Prime Minister assured various chambers of commerce that steps are being taken to ensure easier access to business and financial loans and instruments. While this should certainly assist local recyclers with potential negotiations on active tonnage, it should provide further assistance to yard owners and help them fast track the necessary improvements needed at their respective yards.

With the nation’s upcoming budget for FY 2025 – 2026 due on June 2nd, 2026, hopefully some much- needed attention is heeded to one of the most capital-intensive and vital sectors of the nation and if any units are to destined head to Pakistan before the HKC comes into force, prices will need to improve much more so as to divert Far East tonnage away from Bangladesh, and even some of the dry bulk sales, or even take a bite out of the less preferred larger LDT LNGs from India. Sadly, for the Gadani market, their efforts at acquiring tonnage remain far from fruitful as Pakistan’s recycling anchorage registers a 5th week of no arrivals.

headline: SURPRISE!
body_text:
As both India and Pakistan suffer dithering anchorages this week and tonnage fixtures remain non- existent for the Turkish market, this week, news of the Greek (ferry) giant Attica reportedly diverted another Ropax to Aliaga as the 1979 built Kriti I (about 12,850 MT) was towed to a Turkish recycler at a price of about USD 280/MT. Being EU-based and subject to the regulations of the EUSRR meant that the owners were compelled to commit the vessel at nearly USD 175/Ton below that of competing Indian. Certainly, a large value on a vessel this size.

Steel plate prices meanwhile remain relatively unchanged from those of last week, all whilst the grease on the soles of Turkish Lira continue to help its unabated slide as it fell nearly 50 basis points and closed the week out at a whopping TRY 39.02 against the U.S. Dollar. Although vessel prices have held for the time being, there is no telling where they will be when the Lira finally breaches past the dreaded psychological TRY 40 limit.

headline: GETTING TIGHT!
highlights: Upgrades continue. | Yards filled. | LNGs sold? | Flavors of June.
body_text:
Despite upgrade works continuing at pace in Bangladesh in an effort to get all local ship recycling yards approved to HKC standards prior to the June 26th deadline when the convention officially enters into force, realistically it seems as though only an additional 2 or 3 yards will be approved in the next few weeks, with the rest then playing catch up and unable to buy / import any vessels until their facilities are developed to the required standards and approved thereafter. Presently, of the nine domestic yards with HKC approvals, several have opted to remain inactive and are not negotiating vessels and a majority of the rest are filling up rapidly with leftovers from cash buyers’ unsold inventories that were delivered across recent weeks. It is therefore expected that the next batch of sales will likely be diverted to competing markets, due to the increasingly limited capacity of open HKC buyers in Chattogram. This has also seen prices start to cool as a satiated market diverts its attention towards recycling its recent deliveries in line with the HKCs requirements.

Local fundamentals meanwhile continue to demonstrate increasing volatility, especially after the interim government’s move to let market forces dictate the value of the Taka as required by the terms of the current IMF loan agreement, one that has seen the currency collapse from region BDT 106 against the U.S. Dollar from about a year ago, down to a massive BDT 122.16 on the back of a 33-basis point drop this week alone. Local steel plate prices also have been restrictively supportive of ongoing offers from local buyers as after Pakistan, Bangladeshi recyclers have the best margins in the industry with steel retreating a mere USD 1/Ton down to close at USD 555/Ton this week. This has certainly helped this market set the bar for the impressive volume of ongoing weekly deliveries into Chattogram (save for a few close calls) as HKC approved buyers welcomed at least 2 more units into port limits this week, more than both its competing neighbors combined.

Moreover, with four LNG vessels that were recently sold for recycling from the Korean market, which included two Moss and two Membrane types, the richer in non-ferrous Moss types usually end up in Alang given India’s propensity to beat recycling industry average offers on rich / non- ferrous loaded units, and the comparatively less rich might even see a diversion to a local HKC yard. The remaining yards will have a way to step away from the bidding tables until they get their infrastructure in place and audits concluded, meaning many will not be fully ready by June 26th

when the Convention finally enters into force.

Domestically, the political situation continues to present challenges in the face of upcoming budget and even elections, given that boycotts and strikes by government employees at the Secretariat Office in Dhaka is presenting its own challenges and ensuing delays in getting any pending matters resolved in timely manner will contribute to delays in grants and approvals on incoming vessels and yards upgrades. The rains have meanwhile soaked everything down for everyone to take a breather as domestic movements too have slowed, an expected return to life in the wet lane.

June will undoubtedly have its share of excitement for this market, just depends on if it’s your flavor.

headline: JUNE JITTERS!
highlights: New Season. | Liquid Gold. | Ping-Pong. | Milkshake? | Pak far behind.
body_text: On the receiving end of the mental economic milkshake is the sub-continent ship recycling sector, which, in addition to the above, has also seen subjected to unpredictable tonnage availability across much of 2025, along with a fresh batch of monsoon rains that ingloriously kicked-off across the sub- continent markets this week. And as has been case for sub-continent recycling markets, the rains will deliver the conventional decline in demand and pricing, regardless of availability of tonnage at the bidding tables over the next quarter or so. Currencies too continue to take a beating as nearly all of the major ship recycling destinations reported declines against the U.S. Dollar, except Pakistan, which also (surprisingly) reported more arrivals this week, than neighboring India has over the last 2. Indian recyclers have clearly endured another difficult week following the fragile cessation of an armed conflict with Pakistan, as Indian offers on tonnage have notably retreated by over 5% since the peaks seen of early May.

headline: PRECARIOUS LEVELS!
highlights: 5% down. | Diversions? | Perhaps busier. | Funny how that is.
body_text:
Disastrously declining Indian steel plate prices and a currency that is backtracking its recent progress has seen the Indian market fall to precarious levels over the last month. While the U.S. Dollar made a 55-basis point gain against the Indian Rupee and ended the week at Rs. 85.57, it was Indian steel plate prices that the made the most stunning of manoeuvres as they sky dived USD 12/Ton, down to a lowly USD 441/Ton and left local recyclers increasingly likely to take a hit on incoming deliveries - especially on the large LDT Stainless Steel units that are heading to Alang and generally take longer to recycle, which will spell trouble in the face of declining fundamentals, incoming steel tariffs, and a perennially nervy sentiment that will, like Bangladesh, present a muddy milkshake of its own flavour through the rains.

Alang offerings have meanwhile registered a downward correction of about 5% through May, on the back of the incredible and ongoing volatility that remains ready 24/7 and a certain degree of panic begins to increasingly permeate Alang buyers in the face of a growing possibility that an increasing amount of tonnage would be forcibly diverted to Indian shores, given the overall lack of any HKC infrastructure upgrades in Pakistan so far, along with the fact that many Bangladeshi yards are still undergoing upgrades and those that were recently upgraded aren’t negotiating fresh units for the time being. Making matters worse is that June 26th stands a mere 4 weeks away and with tariff uncertainty still ahead of the Supreme Court of the United States, it could be a messy end of Q2 and perhaps largely Q3.

Although Alang recyclers like their Bangladeshi counterparts, have managed to take in tonnage that is not only geographically better suited for an Alang re-delivery, but even specialist (non-ferrous rich / SS units) and HKC units designated for an India only resale, a majority of these have gone missing of late and resulted in tonnage disappearing from Alang shores over recent weeks as not a single new vessel has arrived Alang’s OPL over the last 2 weeks, and the only vessels currently idling outside have done so over the same time frame. Notwithstanding, there remains a lingering expectation that at least two of the recently sold LNGs (MOSS types in particular), will likely head to Alang and alleviate the ongoing state of recycling affairs.

On the broader economic front, India and the U.S. continue to duke out the tariff debates with the WTO and it seems as though things might end on a positive note for the Indian administration after all, given that the country is now the 4th largest economy in the world - even surpassing Japan. This certainly presents a negotiating edge for the Indian economy across recent and troubling times and has helped keep the nation’s economic trajectory on the right path, with an inflation rate of about 3.15% and is nearly to that of pre-pandemic times. Coupled with the lack of any HKC upgrade needs and despite facing immense pressure on offers at the bidding tables, India might ironically become the go to market for June. Funny how that is.

headline: RUDIMENTARY!
highlights: Upgrades needed. | Renewed aggression. | Too late? | Silent end.
body_text:
Rudimentary and basic upgrade work has reportedly commenced at a few ship recycling yards in Gadani who realize that their time may well be on the clock without the relevant investment and approvals, as the HKC inches ever closer to enforcement on June 26th. But at the current rate of progress, things aren’t looking good for this market despite a recently renewed interest and aggression to buy, which has seen Pakistani buyers reportedly secure a few geographically suitable, small(er) LDT units of late, the arrival of one of which broke Pakistan’s dry anchorage spell that lasted over 4 weeks, even beating India out for the number of arrivals this week.

Yet, the overall state of Gadani yards reports a bleaker overall picture for the nation’s critical sector and local buyers certainly have more than some ways to go before they get even starting to initiate infrastructure upgrades, let alone get anywhere near filling that many empty yards that have been empty for a majority of time over the last 2 quarters.

Pakistan’s economic fortunes, meanwhile, have certainly turned onto a better path with the recent release of IMF’s USD 1.3 billion bailout package that saw Pakistani fundamentals conjointly registering their individual shares of improvements across the week. While the Pakistan Rupee strengthened 26 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and ended the week (below PKR 282 again) at PKR 281.77, local steel plate prices themselves registered a modest USD 4/Ton jump as the week closed out, further keeping local sentiments balanced.

Pakistan’s upcoming budget is scheduled on or around June 10th and is expected to address items in line with the IMF that further require the Pakistani government to focus on domestic anti- terrorism activities. This tranche from the IMF along with a sensible budget should help local recyclers speed up development works so as to stay relevant in a post June 26th world, as all the financial stability in the world would amount to nothing if no owners or cash buyers are willing / able to diver their tonnage towards non-HKC yards along Gadani’s shoreline.

Overall, while the chances of securing any (if at all) tonnage until June 26th remains minimal, one thing is for certain. In the face of rising freight rates, prospective recycling tonnage disappearing from the bidding tables once again, and most units that will come for sale will likely be an HKC only unit, feels like we might bid adieu to Gadani for the time being.

A sad silent end to Gadani’s 2025 performance seems imminent.

headline: WHOOSH!
body_text:
And just like that, Turkey’s disappeared from the bidding tables as market tonnage availability returns to zero, and the Lira continues to drag local sentiments down without mercy as it loses 42 basis points this week and ends it at TRY 39.16 against the U.S. Dollar.

Import and local steel plate prices too have remained relatively unchanged since last week and with that, we’ll see you all next week.

headline: BUYING…NO MORE!
highlights: Demand drop. | HKC progress. | VLOC sold. | Unique challenge
body_text:
Given that there have been a number of high profile, large(r) LDT units committed to Bangladeshi recyclers over the last couple of weeks, including several LNGs and even a VLOC that was offered for a recycling sale to a recently compliant HKC yard, local demand has essentially tanked from Chattogram this week. The number of open yards that are also HKC approved remains at 9, with no fresh approvals being reported this week. In essence, the local market has gone from about 35 domestic ship recycling yards down to only 9 HKC approved facilities and even those have been stuffed with the recent ambush of tonnage fixtures and deliveries across recent weeks including this one, which has unexpectedly reported a single smaller sized unit arrive at the waterfront.

Impressively however, the big sale of the week that certainly captured the market’s attention was that of the Berge Bulk controlled VLOC BERGE FUJI (37,379 LDT) receiving USD 440/LT LDT, in the largest dry bulk recycling sale to have taken place in 2025 thus far. As evident from this fixture, levels are certainly on the retreat with local demand now full and restrictions for the rest, coupled with domestic fundamentals and ongoing economic instabilities that continue to rattle the nations day-to-day operations.

Eid celebrations and time off for the populous with family also commenced across Bangladesh this week, which also saw local steel plate prices fall another USD 7/Ton down to about USD 548/Ton, a drop totaling nearly USD 30/Ton over the last month or so. Yet, any transaction concluded in line with current levels should remain in the green for all parties involved. The incredibly depreciated state of the Bangladeshi Taka also saw some reprieve this week as it registered a minor 26 basis point improvement against the U.S. Dollar, still ending the week at a disastrous BDT 122.57.

Meanwhile, the announcement of the Bangladeshi budget for FY 2025 – 2026 mid-week saw some significant and material changes that are set to adversely impact the nation’s ship recycling sector via increases in import tax structures and duties that are expected to affect vessel values to the tune of about USD 5/LDT lower moving forward, adding to the festering negativity surrounding pricing while being simultaneously drenched in the torrential rains of 2025. As election fever continues, reports of opposition members staging potential riots and continued closure post-Eid, which is expected to last for the next 10 days, will likely see ship recycling activities including post-recycling sales to steel mills, being marred by protests and business closures.

What happens with local fixtures post July 1st as more and more yards attain certification amidst the ongoing burp of tonnage availability, remains to be seen. One thing is certain, the next 3 weeks of concluding units to a local buyer will be a unique challenge, both pre- and post-fixture.

headline: DEMAND GETS RAINED!
highlights: Out of the blue. | Tawdry tariffs. | Bangla delays. | Capacity limited. | Pak HKC change.
body_text:
While the lingering tariffs on steel imports into the U.S. hang in the balance, steel plate prices across the Indian sub-continent meanwhile continued to display their respective shares of volatility, all as the U.S. Dollar ended the week with a mixed bag of performances against various recycling nation currencies including Turkey, where it ended the week on a surprisingly even note. While charter rates in the dry segments certainly impressed, a recent influx of large(r) LDT wet tonnage (four LNGs) and even a VLOC that was recently sold for recycling certainly captured the attention of the ship recycling fraternity, despite the deteriorating levels due to the ongoing global economic turmoil and ensuing market volatility that has culminated on the back of inconsistent U.S. policies.

And with the aforementioned tariffs on steel imports still looming large, the ship recycling industry can almost certainly expect a knock-on effect on recycling offers in the coming weeks, with India being the market to react most negatively to the news and compounding the already destitute state of offerings from Alang recyclers, which have fallen about 5% over the last month or so, as local steel plate prices maintain an overall downward trajectory over recent weeks. The situation in Bangladesh is trotting along in a similar fashion as HKC yard upgrades now take centerstage and continue at pace. However, with local capacity diminishing along with the number of open and HKC-approved Chattogram recyclers disappearing from the bidding tables, demand and prices from Bangladesh, just like India, have started to rapidly dampen.

Pakistan meanwhile has been tragically lagging behind on their HKC schedule, which also saw a healthy collection of confused local recyclers hesitant to place offers as uncertainties surrounding the imminent enforcement date of the HKC on June 26th draws ever closer. Of note, local authorities are now being requested by various ministries to ensure future incoming recycling units have recent and valid IHMs on board, with the same being presented at the time of tendering the Notice of readiness, in what is clearly a landmark moment for Pakistan’s ship recycling sector. Finally, Turkey at the far end posted mixed performances in the face of fundamentals that have essentially been ‘absent parents’, which has clearly left Aliaga recyclers starving for some tonnage attention.

headline: SINKING LOWER!
highlights: Rough weeks. | Tariff Tango | Outbid. | Likely unlikely.
body_text:
Following the cessation of a potentially lethal conflict with its nuclear neighbour Pakistan, India’s fundamentals have endured a torrid few weeks on the back of both declining steel plate prices and a Rupee that is running up the totem pole of depreciation as it heads towards Rs. 86. once again.

To start with, Indian steel prices not only opened at levels lower than those registered close of last week, but they also proceeded to lose another USD 2/Ton this week totalling a nearly USD 18/Ton decline over the last couple of weeks alone. Trump’s Tariff Tango is meanwhile compelling the Rupee to weaken as it slips another 28 basis points and closes the week out at Rs. 85.90 against the U.S. Dollar, as pending tariff negotiations frustrate the Indian market and leaves a lot of uncertainty, especially for Alang recyclers who are operating in such a capital-intensive industry to boot.

The clear and cumulative effect of the weakening state of fundamentals has also seen about 5% knocked off vessel values from Alang over the month of May. And if fundamentals continue to slide at this rate, the ongoing drop in prices will more than likely continue across June as prospective ship owners stand on the precipice of chasing down markets once again - especially now that Bangladeshi yards are stuffed, and Pakistani authorities will likely not be granting permissions for local yards to get stuffed post June 26th. India has therefore sunk to the bottom of the sub-continent pricing board with even the seemingly confused Pakistani market outbidding Alang buyers on some of the tonnage offerings that are scheduled to arrive before the June 26th deadline, which could prohibit them from importing any more units into Pakistan (and until HKC certifications are handed out), and the HKC advantage for nearly all of Alang yards will also come under threat in a post HKC world.

Notwithstanding, the drop in prices and the seeming doom and gloom brewing in Alang amidst the pouring rains, a silver lining via lack of / limited options in Bangladesh and even a confused Pakistan has mercifully seen the volume of incoming units at Alang’s anchorage skyrocket (in comparison to its neighbours) this week as not only will Alang recyclers imminently take deliveries of over 31K LDT of tonnage, the amount of tonnage at Alang rivals both of its sub-continent neighbours combined. While the country’s economic trajectory remains in good standing through the first week of June and inflation drops to 3.1% beating domestic expectations, the government is also reportedly inducing tax savings and bank schemes to further boost domestic industries, as India’s treasury remains healthy at just short of USD 700 Billion.

Overall, for June, other than the rocky fundamentals and likely lower pricing, should the volume of tonnage continue to flow at ongoing levels, Alang’s anchorage will likely have an unlikely healthy start to its Monsoon season, especially as its competition remains shackled by governance.

headline: DECISIVE STEPS?
highlights: IHMs needed. | Little work so far. | Pricing on point.
body_text:
According to our local offices, Pakistan authorities are now demanding that vessels arriving Gadani for recycling need to include a valid IHM on board upon the unit’s arrival at Gadani – the first in what will potentially be decisive steps towards ensuring that Pakistan’s ship recycling industry becomes HKC compliant. Logically, it is still a step too small given that a bare minimum number of infrastructure development projects have been initiated until now and this still leaves much to be desired, with the Hong Kong Convention coming into force on June 26th and Gadani recyclers stand miss out on a majority of the tonnage until they can get their collective acts together and get their yards upgraded soon.

Meanwhile, despite news of a couple of eager local buyers looking to stack their yards before the end of the month, prices have certainly moved ahead and are nearly on point with Bangladesh, clearly moving past their Indian competitors this week. But this seems to be without much effect as the lonely vessel still outside Gadani has been there for the last 3 weeks and there have been no fresh arrivals outside Pakistan ever since.

Post-IMF funding has also seen Pakistan’s economy take a turn for the better over the last couple of weeks as not only have local steel plate prices remained flatlined at a comparatively healthier USD 611/Ton, but the Pakistan Rupee was the only recycling nation currency to register a 12-basis point improvement against the U.S. Dollar and closing the week out at PKR 282.18. This, coupled with the lack of any meaningful deliveries of late has motivated local buyers to act decisively before the shackles of HKC prohibit them from July on, and offer firmer levels.

And like Bangladesh, rumors surrounding possible increases in certain taxes between the local provinces for the upcoming FY budget for 2025 – 2026 may have a direct / indirect effect on local offerings once the budget is announced. Mixed in with a lack of locally developed yards and Pakistani recyclers may find themselves in a blender of pickles as Q3 kicks in.

What happens in July remains to be seen. For June, other than the occasional arrival of a unit before the end of the month is likely the only action we anticipate to report from Pakistan over the coming weeks.

headline: DEAD AGAIN!
body_text: No change from Turkey to report other than the usual i.e. Lira weakened marginally by just 2 basis points, inflation down a whole 3% points through May, and a return to the visuals of an empty Aliaga anchorage all over again.

headline: CERTIFYING AT PACE!
highlights: 2 weeks away. | Upgrades in progress. | Occupied. | Clockwork.
body_text:
Upgrade works continue at pace in Bangladesh as several more ship recycling yards received their HKC accreditations ahead of the official entry of the Convention into force in less than 2 weeks. Sadly, the crippling restrictions on NOC issuances have had a disastrous effect on the rate of vessel imports into the country as no fresh units have arrived Chattogram over the last 2 weeks and a lonely small LDT RoRo cargo vessel has been idling outside during this time. Reports of previously concluded deals to non-HKC approved yards that have arrived outside port limits and are still awaiting their respective permissions to enter once yards receive their HKC accreditations and the business of recycling can resume as usual.

The Bangladeshi budget has meanwhile delivered with it, a few surprises last week that included a marginal increase in taxes on the industry that are expected to affect vessel pricing by about USD 5/LDT moving forward, adding further pressure on local sentiments that are already seeing vessel prices retreating in the face of falling fundamentals through the heavy rains. Not only have local steel plate prices fallen by about USD 7/Ton to end the week at about USD 548/Ton, but the Bangladeshi Taka also fell 19 basis points to end the week at BDT 122.10 against the U.S. Dollar, while barely grazing BDT 122.95 late in the week.

The country also remains soaked through ongoing Eid holidays that are expected to conclude next week, and local trade has come to a virtual standstill while local businesses and industries remain closed. Moreover, on the back of a recently concluded ‘green’ deal to an HKC yard at a discounted price, lower overall offers have been emanating from local recyclers across the span of the week. Yet, inflation keeps falling as the domestic rate fell to 9.05% through May, down from 9.17% in April and in conjunction with the recent budget, this should hopefully see thing improve towards the end of the monsoon season in Q3.

In the interim, tonnage continues to be clearly redirected towards WC India shores on account of no open yards in Bangladesh and Chattogram recyclers already lowering their prices, which will leave more time for local yards to continue upgrades as much work lies ahead – including installation of concrete cutting surfaces, installation of hazardous waste disposal facilities, and finally, conducting of work safety, and equipment and training programs for yard workers and supervisors alike.

Overall, despite several larger LDT sales taking place into Chattogram over recent weeks and many of these newly certified HKC yards are now satisfied and occupied with tonnage, we are, like clockwork, witnessing demand and pricing take a hit as we firmly enter the traditionally quieter summer / monsoon months.

headline: GMS CELEBRATES HKC!
highlights: 3-part HKC | Global dramas. | Shadow moves. | HKC due. | Trickle persists.
body_text: In other worldwide news, the unending volatility that the world is barely getting used to through 2025, skyrocketed this week not only did Israel strike Iranian nuclear sites, arms facilities, and oil depots across the country, but Trump also revived the tariff wars once again asking for all nations to present renewed offers and barter fresh trade negotiations that saw economic volatility return with a vengeance this week. To start with, as Israel struck several sites across Iran over 50 straight hours including major oil refineries, oil futures surged by over 7.2% in a matter of a couple of days that saw oil futures settle at USD 73 / barrel, as further waves of attacks near the Gulf of Hormuz spark fears of oil export disruptions. Freight rates meanwhile tailed along with an overall 3.4% jump reported by the Baltic Exchange Dry Index, with Capes and Panamax sectors reporting 4.7% and 1.9% jumps respectively, reaching their highest levels in 2 months. The resulting chaos saw the U.S. Dollar surging against all major ship recycling nations while local steel plate prices fell sharply in India, Bangladesh, and even China.

headline: ALARM BELLS?
highlights: Not stabilising. | Cheap steel repeat? | Currency woes. | Best suited?
body_text:
The alarming price declines witnessed from India over the last month have hardly shown signs of abating or even stabilising as yet, with levels in the low USD 400s/LDT for bulkers (some reportedly even seeing indications in the high USD 390s/LDT) that has now placed India as the lowest of all sub- continent markets for another week. As the country recovers from Operation Sindoor back in May, local steel prices have unrelentingly softened off the back of ongoing tariff dramas emanating from the U.S. and the recent 50% tariffs on steel exports from various countries (including China) has already had a knock on effect in Alang across recent weeks, as Indian recyclers remain fearful of a repeat of the dumping of cheaper steel into the domestic markets that has caused so much trouble for vessel offers over previous years (despite India’s own punitive tariffs on same).

And while local steel plate prices fell about USD 5/Ton across the week, the overall decline has been about USD 30/Ton over the last months or so. The Indian Rupee too has been taking a beating once again as it declined 42 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and closed the week out at levels Rs. 86.14. And although India remains the financially strongest of all of the major international ship recycling markets, things might even out across Q2 / early Q3 as reports of ongoing discussions with the Trump administration seem to be making fruitful progress and possible news of potential trade deals being successfully reached are making the rounds.

However, domestically the situation could change very soon given India has been a major importer of Iranian oil on account of healthy relations between the two nations and given that the IDF is targeting oil refineries and oil installations across Iran, could see fuel and gas hikes across the nation causing inflation to potentially rise again despite retail inflation hitting a 6 year low at 2.82%, as the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) decidedly cut interest rates in an effort to fuel local businesses.

Alang’s ship recycling sector meanwhile continues on despite being lowest placed on the market rankings on account of Bangladeshi recyclers completely bowing out at the bidding tables and with the HKC now entering into effect a mere 10 days away, most ship owners and cash buyers are unwilling to take a chance on a non-HKC Pakistan and this has seen Alang’s waterfront balloon with tonnage arrivals this week, given that nearly 55K LDT and 7 vessels - including two large LDT tankers arrived the nation’s recycling anchorage this week.

Overall, and compared to the regional competition, Alang is certainly best positioned at the current time to take in tonnage without any hiccups (HKC or otherwise), just maybe not at a price that is matching ship owners intended expectations of “last done” as the market is clearly on the drop.

headline: WORK ONGOING!
highlights: Forging on. | Authorities move. | Playing catch up. | Slow Q3
body_text:
As Bangladesh forges on to complete HKC upgrades at all ship recycling yards in Chattogram and remains keen to continue buying recycling tonnage ahead of a much busier next few years ahead, it is now Pakistan’s time to shine with rapid upgrades of their own! Authorities in the country have recently taken encouraging steps by mandating that all future recycling vessels that are arriving Gadani, have valid IHMs on board in order to allow entry and beaching. However, far more investment guarantees are needed at Gadani yards, in order to stay relevant and in the game in a post June 26th world.

Nonetheless, given the devastating shortfall of infrastructure advancements and despite being placed above India on the pricing chart, only one 10K LDT vessel managed to arrive locally while competing India took in several units during the same time. Domestically as well, fundamentals aren’t doing this market any favors as local steel prices remain flatlined across Eid holidays and remained steady at an industry leading USD 616/Ton, in addition to the Pakistani Rupee that also declined 27 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and ended the week at PKR 282.90, inching ever closer to PKR 283.

The Iran-Israel war has also affected local fuel and gas prices as local reports confirm fuel hikes through the week. Pakistan’s FY 2025 – 2026 too was announced this week with reports that a 20% increase in defense spending is being appropriated after the recent conflict with India, while a potential 2% tax cut on scrap imports is being reported as further details are expected next week. In addition to the recent IMF loan and the sudden realization of local authorities that the HKC will come into force in less than two weeks, it may sadly remain too little too late for Pakistani recyclers, despite recent efforts and favorable vessel offerings, leaving them to playing catch up with the rest of the competition for the remainder of the year, and fall in line once HKC certifications start getting doled out locally.

Overall, as forecasted last week, despite a fragile demand and stronger pricing, Gadani recyclers will be chasing prompt vessels and ship owners will likely continue to chase Indian levels down in order to recycle at an HKC yard.

headline: SILENT HILL!
body_text: Turkey returns to a silent market as no interesting reports surfaced from this market this week other than the Lira sinking another 33 basis points and merrily on its way to TRY 40 against the U.S. Dollar as it winds the week down at TRY 39.38.

headline: ONE WEEK TO GO!
highlights: Upgrades continue. | Filling plots. | Negative pricing. | Writing on the wall?
body_text:
With only a week to go until the official entry of the Hong Kong Convention into force, upgrades continue at a furious pace at Chattogram yards in order to get more facilities certified by various classification societies in order to conform to incoming HKC standards that will ensure Bangladeshi recyclers can continue recycling vessels and operate in a post-June 26th era of ship recycling. As of now, 10 recycling yards have successfully obtained their HKC accreditations and with about 25 more yards still in the process of upgrades, these (yards) will remain incapable to receive NOCs that would have otherwise afforded them the freedom to negotiate at the bidding table, as there have been several units, including large(r) LDT vessels (LNGS and a VLOC), recently sold to Indian recyclers, despite the expectedly quieter monsoon months are firmly upon us.

With a brand-new conflict in Iran emerging and fundamentals expected to go on a roller-coaster in the coming week(s), we have already seen the starting signs as the Bangladeshi Taka, which had already lost 27 basis points by Friday against the U.S. Dollar, reduced the decline to only 7 basis points but at the time of writing and ended at BDT 122.15.
