Local steel plate prices have also resumed flatlining at USD 551/Ton (same as last week) that saw local offerings retreat, leaving the domestic steel market in a dull state at a time the nation is dealing with torrential rains that has delivered a restricted state of recycling, steel processing, and onward sales from local chop shops to domestic steel mills for further use. The disparaging state of unrelenting rains have also started to diminish domestic development and manufacturing works as demand for finished products is expected to remain low during this time.

At the macro end, although the country’s inflation has fallen to 9.05% across May, June has seen GDP slow despite the interim government reportedly implementing reform initiatives in the hopes of reversing the economic downturn that hasn’t let off the gas pedal since June 2024. Elections too are expected towards the end of the month and with a USD 5/Ton drop expected on vessel prices due to changes in tax structures announced in the recent FY 2025 – 2026 budget, the expectation is that vessel offerings at the bidding tables will continue to maintain a downward course, just as they have been over the last month or so. The resurging absence of tonnage at the bidding tables is also likely to keep the true price-gauge on potential vessels uncertain at this time even though ongoing indications have helped Bangladesh maintain the top spot on the market price rankings chart.

Overall, with the world of ship recycling set to change forever this week and a majority of local recyclers still in the process of obtaining their accreditations, the short-term flow of recycling tonnage across Chattogram’s waterfront is expected to remain anemic in the weeks ahead, just as it has been across the last few weeks including this one, with no fresh arrivals and a lone delivery of a unit stranded at anchorage since May. Is the writing on the wall already?

headline: LANDMARK WEEK…AHEAD!
highlights: Markets creak. | Weekend at | Dramas dominate. | Regulation bites. | HKC webinar.
body_text:
And while these seismic shifts are not without reverberations that have already been felt all over the Indian sub-continent ship recycling sector, the upcoming enforcement of the HKC exacted a self- imposed, yet much-needed set of restrictions to ensure that the business of recycling endures at key locations. Price declines that started recently will also continue across an already creaky Indian sub- continent ship recycling sector, which itself is going through a tonnage drought on the back of recently firming freight rates despite recycling markets suffering through one of the worst supplies of recycling tonnage in 2024 in over a decade, all while global ship recyclers were bracing (hoping?) for a healthy inflow of vessels in 2025. Much of this backlogged tonnage is still expected to come for recycling as owners have delayed the sale of some really overaged units as these vessels continue to earn decent rates amidst disastrous geopolitical events that continue to strike the global economy and keep freight markets, more than buoyant.

As tonnage remains absent from the bidding tables, for anxious ship recyclers, Trump’s incessant hopscotching over tariffs and changing trade policies now blended with a fresh new conflict in the Middle East will make it difficult to predict which way the winds will blow (where currencies and local steel plate prices are concerned) and just where subsequent offers will end – tea leaves anyone? One thing seems certain, as regulatory requirements stand to kick in as the HKC is due to finally come into force next week amidst requisite yard upgrades being fully underway in Bangladesh and some report of works beginning even in Pakistan, the convention stands to make significant improvements to a much-maligned industry and firmly places it in line with a global set of approved environmental and operational standards. To follow further developments, please join us for an in-depth discussion of the Hong Kong Convention and its ramifications on ship recycling with our dedicated webinar series on Junte 25th and June 26th.

headline: FALLING, YET BUSY!
highlights: Struggle to secure. | Lowest in sub cont. | No advantage. | Sunshine in the rains
body_text:
The Indian market has certainly fallen behind their sub-continent competitors over the last couple of months and as such, has missed out on much of the pre-HKC restriction tonnage that was recently sold into Bangladesh and even Pakistan, as Gadani recyclers geared up at the same time and tempted a few ship owners with geographically better-suited units for a Pakistan redelivery, helping owners eke a better price on their units and also help the Gadani gang get their hands on some much-needed decent LDT units (bulkers) away from Indian ship recycling hands.

However, subsequent HKC-restrictions imposed in Bangladesh then saw market tonnage, regardless of its geographic location, chart recycling routes towards WC India / Pakistani shores, isolating non- HKC yards in Bangladesh that had their NOCs tied to their accreditations. And as Pakistani offerings were firming, it was Indian steel plate prices and the Indian Rupee that decided to shake up Indian sentiments across 2025 that saw the Indian Rupee break historical records around region Rs. 88, then firm back up to region Rs 85, and resume a fresh ride down the depression chute of late as it was the only sub-continent recycling destination to suffer the largest decline against the U.S. Dollar this week, at 37 basis points and ended the week at Rs. 86.47. Local steel plate prices too were quick to join in during the same time, falling to the lows of USD 43X/Ton, then rising all the way to USD 47X/Ton, and are now back down to USD 428.31/Ton after having declined about USD 3/Ton this week.

Given the generally jittery nature of Alang recycler sentiments, the natural order of Indian vessel pricing is to follow the direction of domestic fundamentals that have yoyoed unrelentingly, leaving Alang recyclers at the bottom of the Indian sub-continent pricing chart more often than not. And with the unfolding uncertainty around the recent Iran attack yet to be fully grasped, in addition to oil jitters that are likely expected to send the barrel skywards in the coming week(s), the onset of inflation could take a healthy bite out of India’s current economic direction and simply make the business of ship recycling, an unsustainable affair in the interim. Notwithstanding, Alang buyers certainly remained busy taking in the most deliveries of the week as 5 vessels and nearly 67K LDT, including a 20K LDT tanker and a 32K LDT LNG, is awaiting at Alang’s anchorage or has already been delivered to its final owner,

With HKC now standing the global doorstep of the ship recycling world, India will no longer be able to use their acclaimed ‘Ace Card’ as being the only and fully HKC certified destination, especially as Bangladeshi yards are well on their way to becoming HKC compliant and Pakistani yards are also finally commencing upgrades of their own. Until all of the pending yards obtain their independent certifications, Alang recyclers will continue to rake in a majority of the market tonnage that is unable / unwilling to go a non-HKC destination.

Just how long this constantly narrowing HKC gap permits Alang to maintain their offerz at current levels remains to be seen. For now, let’s just let Alang recyclers enjoy some sunshine in the rains.

headline: ROOOOOM TO IMPROVE!
highlights: Positive steps. | Rather late. | Tankers? | Jarred July.
body_text:
Pakistan has finally made some positive moves over the last couple of weeks with most Gadani recyclers increasingly displaying a willingness to improve their respective ship recycling facilities and fall in line with HKC requirements, in order to continue to acquire recycling vessels from July. But, with less than a week to go before the convention enters fully into force, one does feel that their (Gadani recyclers) recent efforts may unfortunately be too little too late and that this work should in fact have commenced months ago. Moreover, at the given rate of yard improvements, it is evident that much of, if not the the rest of this year (and probably well into next), will likely be expended in bringing all Gadani ship recycling facilities up to speed.

And although the lack of infrastructure has helped Gadani recyclers acquire a few non-HKC units over the recent months, the urgency surrounding importing vessels under the upcoming rules of the convention and the timing of tonnage that is once again diminishing at the bidding tables, may offer local recyclers the psychological boost that not much is happening outside of yard upgrades that they are missing out on.

Moreover, Pakistani fundamentals, like neighboring India, have been functioning in a state of disarray as the Pakistani Rupee resumes its decline against the U.S. Dollar with a 32-basis point drop this week, ending it at PKR 283.52, all while Pakistani steel plate prices also resumed flatlining at a far healthier USD 611/ton despite maintaining the widest margins for Gadani recyclers (when compared to their neighbors) on their recycling acquisitions since last October (at least).

Meanwhile, all the HKC drama in addition to the ambiguity surrounding U.S. tariffs against Pakistan will likely pale in comparison to the unfolding events that will affect the nation now that the Iranian Parliament has voted to close to Straits of Hormuz. With over 20% of the world’s oil output departing Iranian waters including Pakistan that imports nearly all of its oil from Iran, the nation has an extremely rocky road ahead for its economy. Furthermore, with a greater inflow of (likely wet) tonnage that is expected to make it onto the bidding tables in the near future should the expected closure come through, just how the Gadani authorities handle incoming permissions for recycling vessels, especially tankers, remains to be seen.

It is however being reported that Paksitani authorities may consider issuing an extremely limited number of approvals and that too on a case-by-case basis, driven primarily by the level of upgrades completed at the importing yard. Will this be enough to convince ship owners to take the bait for a few USD/ton more and divert their vessels away from Indian shores, is a surprise waiting to happen. What is a certainty is that unlike any of its sub-continent ship recycling competition, a jarred July doesn’t seem likely to be one to go easy on the Gadani gang.

headline: NADA!
highlights: Real taste.
body_text: Lira fell a staggering 79 basis points and ended the week at TRY 39.72 against the U.S. Dollar. Aliaga steel pricing and thereby, vessel pricing, remains irrelevant given that there is no market tonnage to bid on. Price ideas remain but the real taste comes when you get bite into it hot. For now, there’s nada happening here.

headline: NEW DAWN!
highlights: Collapse. | HKC buyers taken. | Hard work realised. | Printing.
body_text:
The Bangladeshi market has (unsurprisingly?) slumped to the bottom of the sub-continent pricing board for the first time in months, with some abysmal levels and demand emanating from the few local buyers who are available to bid on tonnage at the tables. Yet, desperate owners and cash buyers are biting the bullet and committing units to open yards as Chattogram anchorage reported nearly 86K LDT including a large Ore carrier, contradicting the true state of the market while representing the real state of present-day recycling.

Most of the recently HKC approved buyers have filled their plots with some of the larger units recently sold (such as a VLOC and several LNGs) so their collective appetites have certainly been satiated for the time being. These ongoing deliveries are likely to those who are on the path to getting their HKC accreditations and received NOCs on the vessel’s idling outside. The entry of the Hong Kong Convention into force is finally the realization of much hard work on behalf of all stakeholders across the industry in Bangladesh, and whilst yard upgrades and infrastructure works are still underway for a number of yards, the next quarter (and beyond) will be a brand-new dawn for the forward thinking in the Bangladeshi ship recycling market.

Fundamentals have been the prime movers of local offerings and current depth of demand given that local steel plate prices fell by about USD 8/Ton, further diminishing local margins, but the Bangladeshi Taka also declined and ended the week at BDT 122.30 against the U.S. Dollar while having declined even further (at the time of writing) towards BDT 122.60. Moreover, with prices collapsing, reports of offers below USD 400/Ton are also coming forth as end-of-life values of these aging assets continue to collapse under the weight of global economic turmoil that has been aggravated by declining local demand and the implementation of HKC regulations as cutting becomes slower, while costs are simultaneously expected to increase at the same time due to slower recycling processes and mounting L/C interest charges.

With not much going on other than rains and barely any steel sales to steel mills amidst declining plate levels, July looks like it’s already printing itself on the wall.

headline: HKC IN FORCE!
highlights: Finally here. | Positive news. | Transition. | Certification. | Price slump.
body_text:
Of course, in the short term, there is likely to be a testy period of transition whilst everyone in the industry gets accustomed to the changing regulations, inward formality procedures, and additional documents required when a vessel is being transacted for HKC recycling from here on. Of note, documentation and procedures might change as the initial phase in period settles. In the interim however, owners / cash buyers seeking to deliver units into the Indian sub-continent ship recycling markets will now have to include IHM reports part I, II and III, along with a ‘Ready for Recycling’ certificate from the relevant flag state, all gift wrapped in the yard specific HKC and ISO certification by various classes. Owners now need to ensure these formalities are timed well with the arrival of the vessel in order to avoid unintended delays and potentially miss beaching tides.

At the Macro end of the spectrum, we continue to see the fallout from the recent attacks in Iran as oil has been the biggest beneficiary of global sufferance as it tumbled over 11% just last week, ending it at about USD 66/barrel. The U.S. Dollar is similarly getting hammered as it reported barely any negative changes against any of the recycling nation currencies (except Turkey). The supply of tonnage at the bidding table on the other hand, seems to be gearing up again as some older units continues to slip into the recycling stream (as confirmed by Bangladesh’s and even India’s waterfronts this week), as freight rates declined over 2.1% and the Cape index declining the most last week at 5.3%. Trade wars continue, major ports return to turning empty for the most part, and economies are bracing for the next thoughtless policy out of the White House.

Meanwhile, prices and demand have slumped over the last couple of months and continue to do so, in the lead up to the HKC even though we have seen few private sales realized through it all, it’s clear that both owners and cash buyers are chasing down a market and will likely continue to. Local steel plate prices are declining at the most convenient locations while flatlining in others and port reports in key locations (except Bangladesh) are turning sour through the rains. As tariff ping pong continues, Trump surprisingly confirmed trade deals being done with India, which should help this market in the near future given the incessant spiral state its plate and currency has been in.

Turkey, we just have nothing left to add other than the same ole’ bad news.

headline: BEEN THERE, DONE THAT!
highlights: Others catch up. | Unable to absorb. | Below 400/LDT.
body_text:
As the industry leaders in the safe and responsible HKC recycling of ships, India has certainly been a showstopper of late, with a magnanimous sense of ‘been there done that’ whilst Bangladesh and Pakistan desperately try to catch up as the HKC entered into force this week. Alang buyers have certainly been trying to absorb much of the excess tonnage that has been unable to head to Chattogram or Gadani of late, primarily due to ongoing HKC delays and increased regulations / certifications required.

But prices in the sub-continent and India in particular, have indeed been subdued over these quieter monsoon months, and as with Bangladesh, there is the danger of sinking below 400/LDT on certain poor condition, less favoured units including bulkers given that Bangladeshi recyclers are already dropping indications in the high USD 39X/Ton this week, surprising everyone in the industry and displacing India for 2nd place on the market rankings.

Local port position, meanwhile, continues to take in tonnage as an impressive number (under current times) of vessels made it to anchorage as nearly 50K tons (including a bunch of tankers) of recyclable units are waiting to get delivered to their respective recyclers, and have been impressively doing so week after week.

India’s successful negotiations with the Whie House also seem to be bearing fruit this week as Trump officially announced India as being a partner to ongoing tariff negotiations, which should ease some of the erratic stresses that Alang recyclers are currently battling The Indian Rupee too, skyrocketed against the U.S. Dollar climbing over 1.2% against the Dollar as it ended the week at Rs 85.49, while local steel plate prices continued to do the opposite for the local mindset and decline again, closing the week out at USD 426.30/Ton.

With the number of tankers coming in, it sure does seem like the Iranian war has had some effect as these rare Gas Free for Hot Works gems coming into India during the HKC transition, is certainly impressive at this early stage.

India seems to be heading into a busier July than most expected despite Bangladesh making strides towards environmentally friendly recycling, yet, with the outlook on respective anchorages this week, this rainy summer seems to be going rather well for Inia.

headline: RIGHTING THE WRONGS!
highlights: Underway. | DASR certs. | Firmest placed. | Firmest
body_text:
The Pakistani budget and various announcements made by the government and PSBA in recent weeks have finally left a positive impression on the domestic ship recycling community after years of unintended neglect. Indeed, IHMs will have to be issued for any incoming vessel deliveries and provisional DASR certificates showing that select yards have begun upgrade works to an acceptable level, will always remain at the discretion of the PSBA and ministry of affairs, on any incoming sales / vessels.

As it stands, Pakistan is now the firmest market in the sub-continent for any new vessel sales (first time in many months) – but there is still some uncertainty / ambiguity over how long it will take to get various ministry permissions in this new regulatory HKC landscape the shipping industry has to operate in now. This effect has certainly played itself out at the waterfront given that there have been no new arrivals in Gadani over the last couple of weeks and the sole idling member of the waterfront is finally on the beach this week.

Meanwhile, fundamentals continue to rock the already degraded state of local recyclers mindsets as the PKR continues to decline week after week, ending this one, at Rs, 85.45 against the U.S. Dollar while local steel plate prices remained flatlined at USD 616/Ton – the highest of margins for recyclers in the industry today. The negative trajectory of the PKR is certainly worrisome for local recyclers as after the budget and a reported tax on local recycling imports, the weakening currency will continue to make it that much more expensive for recyclers in the short run, resulting in misplaced deliveries.

Moreover, with HKC rules currently in place and with no direction or ability to garner the true status of domestic yard upgrades, deliveries will certainly face problems across July and perhaps bleeding into the next quarter as not a single yard thus far has been certified. So, if you break it, you buy it, at the currently declining levels from this market that has unexpectedly found itself atop the market rankings at a time the HKC has entered into force and this destination is unable to import any.

Overall, neighboring India seems geared up for a wet summer more than Pakistan – and with tonnage already flowing in, including tankers, Pakistan seems to be sidelined from most ship owners and cash buyers for the time-being. At least until confidence in this market’s ability to effectively import ships, matures in the weeks ahead.

headline: ZILCH!
highlights: Cash buyers.
body_text: Other than the falling Lira and local recyclers forming independent Cash Buying entities to directly negotiate units with potential EU owners, there is nothing we can report from this market for this week.

headline: LOW SHE GOES!
highlights: Below 400. | Interim failures. | Diverting tonnage. | Universe ordered.
body_text:
For the first time this year, as the lowest placed Indian sub-continent ship recycling market, Bangladesh remains worthy of avoiding for any owners or cash buyers with geographically better suited / Far East positioned units that are considering a recycling sale at this time. Prices and demand from Chattogram have been so low of late that any potential recycling vessels are being introduced with the intention of being diverted towards competing Pakistani and Indian markets further East, despite the higher delivery costs on hand, and the fact that there are simply no offers from Bangladeshi shores at this time. Local authorities have been the primary drivers behind drastically reducing the number of available buyers as at the time of writing, only about 12 yards are HKC approved and these have already taken in a batch of recent deliveries. An additional 10 yards are reportedly still interested to remain in the game and are working towards upgrades of their own at this time.

On the back of rapidly receding offers from Chattogram recyclers and as confirmed in the market commentary above, local port position is once again starting to trim in numbers as no new arrivals were reported this week, save for a couple of final deliveries. One of the key reasons behind the collapsing level of local offerings has been the inability of local yards to sell recycled ship’s steel / recycled product of late given that not only have local steel plate prices declined over recent weeks, but this week, they practically fell off a cliff on account of maddening monsoons and local holidays / strikes that halted any domestic trade. Adding to the fluency of the situation is the inability of the interim government to stimulate any building / infrastructure projects since June of last year, and this has led to the gradually exacerbating situation of growing stockpiles of material at local yards, which in is now diminishing demand and dampening local offerings.

Yet, a local buyer surprised the industry this week with the private sale of a poorer condition Handymax bulker in the USD 390s/LDT, the first sale that registered below USD 400/LDT in quite some time in the industry. Making matters worse is the fact that domestic steel mills have reportedly booked cheaper imported steel products at levels region USD 330/Ton, which has further earmarked Chattogram to remain on an extended period on the sidelines and away from the bidding tables, unless the Bangladeshi government is able to implement restrictive measures to economically protect the country, or become the latest victim of the seemingly never-ending Indian sub-continent ‘cheaper steel import’ tariff war.

Overall, the only market sale of the week into Bangladesh wasn’t also the only silver-lining for this market as the Bangladeshi Taka firmed nearly 20 basis points against the U.S. Dollar this week, withdrawing from the dreaded BDT 123 territory and back towards BDT 121, as it ended the week at BDT 122.45. Moreover, with pending yard upgrades, new recycling routines, and backed up inventory, all taking a swim in the deep end of 2025s monsoon season, perhaps a quieter may just be what the universe ordered.

headline: WILEY JULY!
highlights: 90 in 90. | Oil drops | Tonnage deprived. | Regulatory delays. | HKC era begin.
body_text: This has continued to deliver an absence of recycling tonnage for the markets at the bidding tables, which has represented itself rather well at this week’s anchorages. And speaking of anchorages, recycling destinations have continued to go through a volley of market sentiments amidst their own disjointed market disorders that saw their currencies and steel plate prices dance around. HKC troubles for 1/3rd of the sub-continent recycling destinations has also left ship owners and cash buyers with minimal options to consider, especially as Pakistani authorities have stated that only those yards who have committed to HKC upgrades will be issued provisional DASR certificates to import vessels for recycling in addition to mandatory IHMs, as Bangladeshi HKC recyclers are not only taking the time to get accustomed to the ‘new’ way of recycling, but also digest recently delivered tonnage at a pace and in accordance with the HKC. Indian recyclers, meanwhile, were the only ones to have some positivity with at least one fresh arrival and some positive movement in local steel plate prices. An abundance of HKC ready Alang yards also means that owners looking to take make a quick sale, still do have the option to. But, as the HKC firmly enters into force, recycling markets overall remain on a glum and uncertain footing as demand and prices have slumped alarmingly over preceding weeks and the trajectory doesn’t seem much too different at this time. While recycling tonnage is seeing far lower levels, some exploitative levels have once again been making the rounds as end buyers test the waters to see what might just bite.

headline: SURFING THE RAINS!
highlights: Odd place to be in. | Teething expected. | Price subdued. | Mama drama.
body_text:
Alang recyclers find themselves in a comfortable, yet soaking wet predicament as on the one hand, they are battling not only their local fundamentals, but also the ongoing shortage of tonnage amidst the rains; yet on the other hand, all non-HKC yards in Bangladesh and Pakistan are tapped-out while those remaining (in Bangladesh) have just returned from the tonnage buffet – essentially leaving no one at the bidding tables other than Alang recyclers, who now find themselves as the only game in town despite being 2nd on the price rankings. Whether they can benefit off this unique position as tonnage shortage continues on, or even how long they will benefit off of it if it ever gets to it, remains to be another 2025 surprise. For now, Alang buyers are certainly one-up on the regional competition with at least one fresh arrival this week.

Currently, with well over 100 fully HKC certified, long operational yards in Alang, it does seem rather eye-opening as we consider the fact there are only 12 recently HKC certified yards outside of India in the entire Indian sub-continent. Moreover, even this recent rush to finalise upgrades in neighbouring Chattogram and Gadani has regrettably come at the very last moment as the Hong Kong Convention finally entered into force last week, which will see some teething issues before the remainder of recycling yards become fully HKC-certified, and owners and cash buyers fully come to grips with the new realities, regulations, and documentation that are, and will be additionally required at all locations as the process streamlines over time, in order to continue importing vessels into this HKC only world of ship recycling.

In keeping Alang’s position tempered on the market rankings is their perennial love triangle with the U.S. Dollar and local steel plate prices, which continues to keep the Indian market alert on caffeine as this was probably the first week where despite crazy jitters, local steel plate actually ended USD 2/ton higher than that of last, ending the week at USD 427.35. Even the Indian Rupee that has yoyo-ed unrelentingly since the start of the year between Rs. 84 – Rs 88, thankfully saw a week where the Rupee practically ended where it started, at about Rs. 85.45 against the U.S. Dollar. At the Macro end of things, while the week started with more positive news between Indian and American authorities in coming closer to a trade agreement, the week ended with trade negotiations reportedly souring and Indian authorities once again turning to imposing counter-tariffs on American imports, stalling the process once again.

Overall, prices are expected to hold at current levels for the time-being, but if what is happening in Bangladesh with their domestic steel industry where cheaper steel import fixtures recently undercut the price of processed recycled ship’s steel, should that bleed into India as well (just as it has in the past), we may as well bid goodbye to USD 400/Ton, just as the markets bid goodbye to USD 500/Ton not over a quarter ago, and fundamentals continue to deliver some ‘baby mama drama’ for Alang throughout the year including this week.

headline: ROLL CALL!
highlights: Breakthrough! | Highest levels. | New certs. | Work cut out.
body_text:
The ship recycling industry in Pakistan finally achieved a breakthrough of sorts this week, as a select group of about 10-yard owners have committed to upgrading their respective facilities up to HKC standards, in order to continue operating and keep the nation relevant in the international ship recycling arena. Unfortunately for Gadani recyclers, their decision to appear for roll-call has come at a time when several deals have already been committed to end buyers at competing destinations across all of June, given the yet to be upgraded / non-HKC-certified state of all Gadani ship recycling yards despite having the best levels on show in the world for the last couple of weeks at least.

And although it will be good to have Pakistan along for the ride when local yards finally get up to speed, their absence from the bidding tables and their offerings (competitive or otherwise) will remain irrelevant in the interim! Thus far, we understand that the various authorities and the PSBA will allow for vessels to be imported and issue provisional DASR certs to the yards that have committed to HKC upgrades and begun their infrastructure work to an acceptable standard, along with the inclusion of mandatory IHMs parts I, II and III that are now required to be onboard for entry to all recycling locations, including Pakistan.

Of little consequence are local steel plate prices or the Pakistani Rupee, which has flatlined at USD 616/Ton – the highest in the industry – while the Pakistani Rupee fell 24 basis points against the U.S. Dollar edging ever closer to PKR 285 as it closed the week out at about PKR 284.20. If cheaper Chinese steel imports that are currently hovering under USD 300/Ton flood the international markets as the excess steel continues to float around and just as it has done so in Bangladesh this week, the overall specter of retreating recycling prices will likely continue through Q3 as well, earmarking 2025 for another tragic year in the Pakistani ship recycling industry – just as 2024 and even 2023 was for the Gadani recycling gang when only 16 ships were delivered into this market throughout 2024.

Gadani certainly has its work cut out for itself ahead as at least a month (if not two) of yard upgrades will be required before Pakistani ship recyclers return to the scene during which time, neighboring India will be the only choice in the interim.

headline: TRAGIC WEEK!
highlights: Common sense.
body_text:
The Turkish business of ship recycling that is more a marriage of rules and restrictions than objective ship recycling, continues subjecting ship owner, cash buyers, and even ship recyclers to lengthy and process intensive rules and documentary requirements stemming from exporting countries to flag state requirements to IHM evidences – a process that is more dissuasive for international players or even affords asset owners a cost-effective recycling alternative for that matter.

And to top if all off, accidents can and will continue to happen despite all the red-tape and incorrectly applied regulations designed to control an industry and detract the natural flow off commerce (where global ship recycling is concerned), as demonstrated in Aliaga this week were a large ore carrier caught fire at an Aliaga recycling yard. While thankfully no injuries or casualties have been reported, it is poignant to note that this vessel could’ve easily been redirected towards an India re- delivery during her negotiations, but political plays had her destiny charted out to Aliaga instead.

headline: STUCK IN THE MUCK!
highlights: Lowest for year. | Below 400/LDT. | Interim failures. | Oopsies.
body_text:
Amidst the incredible torrent of rains, the Bangladeshi market remains stuck in the muck at the bottom of the market rankings as both demand and pricing on prospective tonnage turn miserable and fall to the lowest level they have been since January of 2024, when a container vessel was sold at a massive price of USD 600/Ton to a local recycler. And while there have been deals concluded below the USD 400/LDT mark, for the time being at least, it seems that a healthy majority (if not all) of the tonnage being introduced for a recycling sale that is / can be a Chattogram candidate, is being introduced with the intention of being diverted to competing sub-continent markets with their higher levels on show, even if the unit is opening up in the Far East or is geographically better- suited for a Bangladesh redelivery.

A big part of the problem remains with the fact that there are very few yards actively negotiating for tonnage as only 12 have thus far managed to get their HKC affairs in order and have already taken in a bevy of deliveries over the last month. A remaining 10 are still scrambling to get their certifications in order before local authorities start dishing out NOCs on future units destined to these yet-to-be certified yards. Rising confusion on the new regulations has not only exacerbated ship owners, cash buyers, and ship recyclers alike, but it turns out that even local authorities are seeming to “cope” with the additional changes themselves as reportedly, the newly formed Ship Recycling Board ended up issuing an NOC in favor of an uncertified yard this week, further causing confusion amongst those recyclers still working towards their HKC goals.

Further shortcomings lie with the interim government that has meanwhile failed to stimulate the domestic economy ever since they took office after the collapse of ex-PM Sheikh Hasina and her regime in June of 2024. The nation has struggled with infrastructure projects ever since, causing local steel inventories to continue stockpiling at local yards due to clearly high local steel plate prices, which was made worse by the shocking news that local steel mills had reportedly booked imported steel at region USD 330/Ton just last week.

Rather surprisingly, local steel plate prices resumed trading once again mid-week and even opened about USD 3/Ton higher than last at about USD 552/Ton, where they flatlined till close of Friday. But the biggest boost to the local mindset is the massive jump in the Bangladeshi Taka that firmed an impressive 1.27% against the U.S. Dollar, closing the week out at BDT 121.40, after hitting an impressive low of BDT 120.62 mid-week. Adding to the silver-linings is the fact that another large LNG arrived local anchorage, bumping the total LDT at Chattogram to over 42K this week.

Overall, amidst the shaky offerings, bottom of the market levels, reported renegotiations at the waterfront, unpredictable fundamentals, and oopsies from local authorities certainly leave much to be desired for, from a market that was the recycling leader for a majority of the year and is now struggling to merely maintain balance amidst a serious “list” in its Q3 2025 performance.

headline: SUMMER SUFFERANCE!
highlights: Terminal tariffs. | Regulations bite. | Rising reticence. | Weaker time. | Gov impacts.
body_text:
Trump’s twisted tariff tantrums went terminal this week after his self-imposed July 1st deadline to major U.S. trade partners on presenting potential proposals to offset his tariffs saw no response from trading nations that were in his crosshairs. As a result, a new deadline of August 1st, 2025, has been put forth as the final date to respond, all while tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on nations from Bangladesh to Brazil are reportedly set to automatically kick into gear by the end of this month. Expectedly, stock markets went haywire in the early hours of Friday trading and sent virtually every major index into a tailspin, defying their collective performances across recent weeks. And while U.S. inflation continues to rise, the U.S. Dollar yoyoed against all of the major ship recycling nation currencies, even seeing the Turkish Lira finally breach the dreaded TRY 40 mark this week. Local steel plate prices also surprised everyone the industry as all ship recycling destinations (even China) saw levels climb in unison this week. And while the news certainly seems positive for upcoming vessel pricing, recycling tonnage remains amiss at the bidding tables as the Baltic Exchange reported a 13.5% jump in the freight index this week, primarily on the back of the Cape index that jumped a whopping 26.4%, whilst the Panamax and Supramax indices added 8% and 2% respectively.

In the interim, international ship recycling markets continue suffering over these summer / monsoon months as prices fall and an overall temperament of diminishing demand settles in on the back of volatile fundamentals, a Hong Kong Convention that finally came into effect on June 26th, a rising reticence amongst recyclers from offering firm on potential units, and ship owners and cash buyers who remain hesitant to test the higher priced offerings from the yet-to-be certified HKC yards in Pakistan, simply on the basis on an interim DASR certificate issued to the yard. Increased regulatory and documentary demands also continue to cause confusion / consternation writ large, and this is likely adding to the reduced number of candidates on show. While several large(r) LDT units such as LNGs and even a VLOC have been recycled over the last few months, it has remained a trickle in the supply of tonnage throughout the year, against the backdrop of an expectedly busier 2025. Surprisingly however, this week has seen the number of units and (especially) the volume of LDT at certain destinations improve, and markedly at that.

headline: MIS-FIRING!
highlights: Mixed results. | No specialist. | Steel down. | Into 1st.
body_text:
While Bangladesh and Pakistan’s efforts at the bidding tables have been arrested for one reason or another, India has struggled, yet managed to pick up some of the slack with mixed results thus far. And while both of its competing neighbours (yes, even Pakistan) managed to get at least one unit each, India remained the leader of the pack with nearly 70K LDT of larger LDT tonnage arrivals and deliveries just this week, bumping the total number of vessels and tonnage at Alang anchorage to 6 and nearly 104K LDT respectively. Certainly, an impressive number given that the number of market offerings over the last month have been greatly diminished due to fluctuating international trade policies from a White House that has once again aggravated a miscalculated trade war, whereby a potential 35% tariffs would likely be applied against Indian imports.

Although this did see the Indian Rupee drop 42 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and end the week at Rs. 85.80, local steel plate prices were the ones that climbed another (nearly) USD 3/Ton through the week, closing it out at nearly USD 430/Ton and shifting potential upcoming fixtures further into the green. India’s exports and overall GDP also continues to strengthen as the Reserve Bank of India reported U.S. Dollar reserves to have increased to over USD 702 Billion this week, further cementing the nation’s financial independence and ability to fund domestic projects, as the country’s economic trajectory (and growth) continues along the right path under PM Modi.

On the ship recycling front as well, having 10 times the number of approved yards in the Indian sub- continent than its competing neighbours, Alang recyclers remain well equipped to handle the inflow of tonnage no matter the volume. And while the single major caveat has been price, which itself has been on the drop for a few weeks now, recent HKC changes / requirements have seen both owners and cash buyers unwilling to accept even higher offers from Pakistan or geographically cheaper / more profitable deals into Bangladesh - as has been evident from ongoing fixtures / arrivals at both competing locations. Non-ferrous vessels (including Moss type LNGs and stainless-steel tankers) and specialist units (reefers, passenger vessels etc) have also been heading to Alang this year, but as has been the sign of the times, these too have started to dry up of late.

Overall, with fundamentals (especially steel plate prices) demonstrating some return / positivity over recent weeks (having firmed nearly USD 6/Ton) and the Indian Rupee also seeming to be stable despite being shaky in the Rs. 85 - Rs. 86 region, it might not be too long before India squeezes past Pakistan into first place. Either on account of India’s firming fundamentals or Pakistan’s weakening Rupee that could compel Gadani recyclers to pull back their levels and inadvertently slide themselves into 2nd. Whatever remains the case, Indian still remains the go-to destination for ship recycling today.

headline: BACKING IT UP?
highlights: Snafus. | Leading the way. | HKC moves. | Streamlined process.
body_text:
Although market tonnage has been hit-or-miss of late, on the back of several private units proposed and being the highest placed sub-continent market at present, Pakistani recyclers have reportedly been busy negotiating units as news came forth on several dry bulk units (including Panamax and Handymax bulkers) being reportedly fixed locally, on the basis of local authorities confirming provisional DASR certificates to the relevant negotiating yards that have demonstrated that HKC upgrades are ongoing and presently under way. And while the delivery of these upcoming fixtures will certainly be interesting when the time comes (given that Chattogram authorities have themselves been committing snafus over the new regulations), it will be just as interesting to keep an eye out on upcoming deliveries at Gadani’s waterfront, for the types and sizes of units that will make it here and how this market struggles to catch up to HKC standards.

Speaking of the waterfront, the markets were surprised to witness a smallish nearly 6K LDT Bulk Carrier make it to Gadani’s waterfront front this week, likely to one of the ship recyclers who has demonstrated a degree of improvement to his ship recycling yard, as the timeline of her final delivery to the end buyer remains key at this time given that the vessel is still idling outside.

As local offerings continue holding up above the psychological USD 400/LDT mark while offers on various vessels in both India and Bangladesh have been below that level, it may not be long before Pakistan’s offerings follow the trail of the gang – as they have historically done so when determining where local levels should stand. And if the case of the recent fixtures stands true, we certainly encourage ship owners to grab this window of opportunity and fix at the currently higher level from Pakistan before fundamentals drag local offerings down, just like their neighboring competition has been suffering through of late.

The Pakistani Rupee has become a bone of contention for the domestic ship recycling fraternity as it has consistently declined over the last 5 weeks, falling another 15 basis points this week and closing at PKR 283.40 against the U.S. Dollar, whilst briefly spiking above PKR 285 on more than one occasion through the week. Local steel plate prices however, cushioned some of the Rupee- induced fear that saw steel climb nearly USD 4/Ton and close the week out at nearly USD 619/Ton – still the highest in the industry. And thankfully something local recyclers of impending deliveries should be able to enjoy the fruits of as long as cheap Chinese steel doesn’t flood this market.

Overall, the Pakistani remains a market of concern, not only because this destination is more prone to delivery hiccups than the market has been providing its own; adding additional formalities into a market where neither the importer nor the imposer of the law knows exactly how to abide by it, makes it a hit-or-miss market until a few deliveries have streamlined the process.

headline: SURPRISE WEEK!
highlights: Natural evolution.
body_text:
The Turkish ship-recycling fraternity has managed to surprise once again as not only has the Lira finally passed the point of no return, collapsing 82 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and closing the week out at TRY 40.20, but an approximately 3K LDT General Cargo vessel has reportedly been concluded to a local recycler at levels region USD 260/MT.

This is impressive for 2 reasons as firstly, the dearth of tonnage has driven Aliaga recyclers out of their offices and into international markets, directly attempting to locate and negotiate tonnage for their yards, but secondly, their attempts at doing so have helped them establish relations that are further driving them to become pseudo cash buyers for others in the local fraternity, which likely resulted in the above mentioned private sale.

Certainly, pleasing to see the natural evolution of ship recycling.

headline: STAGNATED HICCUPS!
highlights: Perking up. | Grappling with docs. | No new sales. | In the spotlight.
body_text:
Bangladesh remains the lowest placed of all Indian sub-continent ship recycling markets since the advent of the customarily slower monsoon / summer months that have been greeted by a myriad of self-induced problems, which are driving prices mercilessly down and resulting in a staggered state of sales into Chattogram as port reports nearly dry up some weekends, while perking up on others such as this one, where 5 ships and nearly 66K LDT, including 2 large LNGS, arrived the nation’s waterfront this week, being delivered to HKC recyclers with yard space opening up.

And although the increase in tonnage is certainly a welcome surprise, both end buyers and local authorities continue grappling with the new realities of now having the HKC in force, as they continue working on getting the remainder of local yards approved after inspections are being conducted in conjunction with various class societies (such as Class NK, Rina, IR, BV etc.), requiring IHM parts I, II and III to now be a mandatory part of inward formalities for recycling vessels entering Chattogram’s port limits, as are SRPs (Ship Recycling Plans) SRFPs (Ship Recycling Facility Plans) and ‘Ready for Recycling’ certificates that are to be issued by the relevant flag on the select unit that is headed for recycling. And it is this inundation of local activities is also seeing delays in ward clearance of vessels as authorities scramble with multiple hats on at the same time.

While the inflow of tonnage this week was a welcome change from Bangladesh’s ongoing struggles, these will remain a hit or miss as local offerings come under pressure from domestic fundamentals once again as not only did local steel plate prices resume flatlining at region USD 552.58/Ton (a bad sign in light of local steel mills fixing steel imports at nearly half that), but even the recently stronger Bangladeshi Taka found itself in the crosshairs of depreciation as it fell nearly 70 basis points to break past BDT 121 again, ending the week at BDT 121.63 against the U.S. Dollar.

On the domestic front, there is still no news about the intended elections that were to be held at the end of June as the interim government continues to struggle getting key economic factors under control, including the incessant volatility of the Bangladeshi Taka. Trump’s recent announcement of levying 30% tariffs on Bangladesh has so far not hit the domestic ship recycling industry as it is primarily targeted towards the ‘Ready Made Garments’ (RMG) and textile and spinning Mills. Notwithstanding, an impact on the overall economy is expected and will likely only get worse, unless preventive economic measures are not formulated by the finance deparment as the country’s Government meanwhile tries to diffuse the situation working with the U.S. and find a reasonable solution to ongoing trade.

Overall, other than having the misfortune of opening in the Far East at a time Chattogram levels are the lowest in the sub-continent (and will likely remain there for the time being), owners of relevant units find themselves likely taking hits on their units, as the state of the Bangladeshi market conveniently delivers WC India / Pakistan into 2025’s monsoon recycling spotlight.

headline: SLOWDOWN SURPRISE!
highlights: Activity drags. | Below 400. | Pak top. | Slow deliveries. | LNG sales.
body_text:
The ongoing tariffs conundrum that has brought on the recent and ongoing global instability, has also seen ship recycling markets reacting in confusion for over 2 months now (perhaps even longer). As global trade and even trade route disruptions are being reported once again (on account of the Houthi’s recently sinking a couple of merchant ships in the Red Sea), inflation has started to rear its head again, rising in the U.S. to 2.7% in June (up from 2.4% in May). The U.S. Dollar has meanwhile found itself firming against all ship recycling destinations once again this week while oil futures find themselves on the opposite side, sliding 0.3% down to USD 67.3/barrel as both Trump and the EU threaten additional sanctions against ongoing Russian aggression in Ukraine, including those specifically targeting Russian energy exports. Topping it all off is perhaps the most critical of all essentials is the state of the Baltic Exchange’s Dry Index that found itself rising about 1.1% this week and reaching its highest level since September 2024, placing even more pressure on the supply of tonnage, which has made a surprisingly mild return over the last couple of weeks and as highlighted by the state of the various sub-continent waterfronts this week (including even in Pakistan).

As we filter down to the ship recycling end of things, the last few months of diminished activity across sub-continent recycling markets has shown few signs of abating while sentiments and pricing remain muted overall, whilst key markets grapple with recently imposed HKC realities that have resulted in the industry getting increasingly comfortable at tabling offers below the USD 400/LDT mark on certain tonnage, particularly as both Alang and Chattogram face pressures of their own. There have also been few (market) sales being done at these lower levels even though Pakistani offerings remain well above the USD 400/Ton mark and have been the top placed market for about a month now. During this time, the Gadani gang has even managed to secure a few dry bulk vessels in recent times as both Panamax and Handymax units have been heading to local recyclers who are able to provide provisional DASR certificates for inward permissions. Bangladeshi NOCs are still proving challenging as delays on vessels arriving here are now becoming customary as government departments and ministries take time on granting approvals, while local banks simultaneously prolong the approval and opening of L/Cs. Yet, there have been several larger LNG sales and ongoing negotiations in recent weeks, in what has been the most active sector of the ship recycling markets of late. India meanwhile remains close on its heels with a healthy batch of acquisitions of its own, as owners unwilling to test Pakistani DASRs are willing to take a hit on the lower, yet safer offerings from neighboring Alang.

headline: FLUMMOXED!
highlights: Marginal gains. | LNGs talk. | HKC ready. | Throuple
body_text:
As tariff dilemmas get kicked further down the road with various deadlines now looming large, ship recycling prices in Alang have shown marginal improvements over the course of last week, on the back of recently firming local steel plate prices and the Indian Rupee, which firmed to Rs. 84.9X against the U.S. Dollar in recent times. Yet, Alang recyclers were left flummoxed this week as both local steel plate prices and the Indian Rupee registered declines as steel levels fell about USD 2/Ton back into USD 428/Ton territory, while the Indian Rupee faced a 37-basis point penalty against the U.S. Dollar, backtracking its way to Rs. 86.15 as the week ended.

Notwithstanding, despite some of subdued supply of vessels starting to bite, Alang recyclers have managed to surprise of late and even this week as they took in over 42K LDT, including a couple of decent LDT units. Moreover, as some larger MOSS type LNGs (rich in non-ferrous) have been under negotiations over recent weeks, this has seen several eager Alang recyclers step up to the bidding tables in an effort to fill dormant plots once again, barely missing the mark against their Bangladeshi competition.

Meanwhile, given the current recycling state of the neighbouring competition, Alang’s anchorage might be the one to come out on top, at least until the rains are nearing an end / are over as HKC hurdles continue to fracture the ability of both Bangladeshi and Pakistani recyclers from freely negotiating on any available unit(s), restricting them to cherry pick on only the right unit instead and make their HKC efforts worth the unit at the given price. India on the other hand, faces no such restriction(s) having over 100 HKC certified yards in operation, some that have been certified for nearly a decade now. But with fundamentals acting funny again and mixed news on the tariffs front forthcoming week after week, Indian bids might see a displacement on the market rankings, sooner rather than later.

In the interim, however, Alang remains the safest bet at this time and levels aren’t expected to shake too far below recent offerings, always subject to the condition of some of the newly introduced aging old ‘rusties’ making it to local anchorages that have seen renegotiations on the rise once again. A safe price with a reliable cash buyer always makes for a safe delivery, especially in current times when rules regulations and fundamentals form an unlikely throuple that has seen hiccups arise across recent deliveries.

headline: SHAPING UP!
highlights: Top placed. | Dry bulk mostly. | Taking seriously.
body_text:
Invariably finding themselves placed atop the global ship recycling rankings seems to have pushed Pakistani buyers into a renewed sense of aggression to negotiate on (and even acquire) some of the slim pickings of vessels that have been making the rounds of late (primarily, locally preferred dry bulk vessels). And this has manifested itself impressively at Gadani’s waterfront this week as currently 2 vessels are idling outside, including another decent LDT arrival this week, both of whom are awaiting their DASR formalities and a fresh set of permissions before making it on to their final deliveries at the respective recyclers yards.

As it has been evident by the type of deliveries at neighboring destinations, Gadani recyclers do not have a sophisticated local non-ferrous market that has resulted in this location consistently undervaluing high value non-ferrous assets. Moreover, for Gadani yards that have initiated HKC infrastructure upgrades and have received provisional DASR certs from the ministries in Pakistan, a growing demand has been emerging amongst these buyers over recent weeks.

Surprisingly so, given that not only have local steel plate prices resumed flatlining at USD 615/Ton, but even the Pakistani Rupee continues its Lira-styled nose-dive as it dropped another 14 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and ended the week at PKR 284.73, on its way to likely breaching PKR 285 and giving another reason for local recyclers to justify lower offers.

Yet, economic problems continue on the domestic front as reportedly, tax withholding on services has been raised form 9% to 15%, which could indirectly increase variable costs for the country’s ship recycling industry, as industry pundits call the government’s recent move, an act of economic- sabotage. How this will help Pakistan maintain top spot in the rankings remains to be seen.

For now, as the Gadani gang gets back to business of filling idle plots and with a few provisional DASRs still reportedly available for some local recyclers who are looking for units, it is good to finally see Pakistan take the imposition of the HKC seriously, as for a period of time it looked as though the market there may have been becoming redundant, they were so far competing India and Bangladesh where their own yard upgrades stood.

We maybe witnessing an exciting end of July / early August for Pakistan after a long time.

headline: ON THE DL!
highlights: Natural evolution.
body_text:
Aliaga’s ship recycling sector seems poised for a price correction as the Lira continues to collapse without mercy, falling another 50 basis points this week ,closing it out at nearly USD 40.40 against the U.S. Dollar, all while local steel plate prices remain subdued at their recently declined levels and offering very little motivation for local recyclers to maintain current offerings, despite many having expected a decline much sooner.

How ongoing tariffs and the declining Lira will affect Turkey’s ship recycling turned cash buying community, remains to be seen. For now, Aliaga buyers ended the week on an empty note and with no fresh vessels having arrived the nation’s recycling front.

headline: REALITY BITES!
highlights: Hurdles. | Fundamentals funk. | Bypassed. | One-off sales?
body_text:
The Bangladeshi market still seems to be struggling with the adoption of the HKC and the resulting yard upgrades, yard inspections, class ratifications, ministry approvals, and ensuing documentary requirements seem to be collectively presenting a much large hurdle for ship owners, cash buyers, and ship recyclers far more than previously anticipated. As such, most local recyclers who have imported tonnage pre-HKC adoption seem to have temporarily satisfied their demand. Meanwhile, recycled ship’s steel / steel product is still struggling to move from local recycling yards to domestic steel mills due to failure to initiate building / infrastructure projects by the frustratingly slow and lethargic interim government that has been in control for over a year now. And as the remainder of the marginal number of units at anchorage were delivered to their respective buyers this week, no fresh units have arrived locally, a forecasted reality for this market, especially in the short run.

Interestingly, most of the recent recycling sales including large LDT LNGs and even dry bulk units have bypassed Bangladeshi shores over the last month or so, onto the far more HKC-stable Indian market where prices remain ahead of Chattogram’s offerings, which don’t look like they have any potential to mark any improvements anytime soon. The Bangladeshi Taka has meanwhile resumed its fall against the U.S. Dollar once again, as it declined 65-basis points this week down to BDT 122.18. Even local steel plate prices were not spared from the brunt of recent steel fixtures by domestic steel mills at region USD 330/Ton, resulting in plate prices retreating nearly USD 2/Ton this week.

Is this a sign of times for Bangladeshi vessel offerings through August as it has been through June thus far, with competing markets overshadowing the performance of Chattogram Choppers? It would certainly seem that way given that previous high-priced purchases are still languishing at local yards as local authorities have reportedly caused unexpected delays in granting cutting permissions amidst all of the new HKC requirements and ensuing red-tape between the various government departments.

The resulting delays in cutting / recycling of vessels and ensuing inability to resell recycled steel will stand to stimy the ability of local ship recyclers to even hold a chair at the bidding tables if this trend continues. And the aforementioned decline in the Taka was enough for the central bank to step in and stall the decline through monetary means. Just how long these controls hold remains to be seen given that growth projections for the country remain weak despite domestic inflation falling to 8.48% in June (down from nearly 11% at the start of the year), but could likely start to rise on the back of looming tariffs that stand to disrupt the economy overall as the year progresses

Overall, other than one off sale of a juicy unit to an HKC approved yard, we do not anticipate much from Bangladesh in the coming week(s).

headline: GLIMMER OF LIFE?
highlights: LNGs again. | Bottom out? | Glimmers? | HKC rules. | Busier times await.
body_text:
As we stand on the eve of Week 31 this 2025, global market turmoil continues unimpeded as wars rage, freight markets firm, economies flutter, and oil, currencies, and steel prices all fluctuate in a wavering tandem, delivering headaches along the way for all on this ride. While Trump announces further deals with Japan and the EU late on Sunday, his sketchy past is what keeps hammering this administration down, which itself is scrambling to do damage control vs. attempting to fix the state of the U.S. economy that has seen the U.S. Dollar weakening against key global competitors, whilst strengthening against virtually all recycling destinations. U.S. inflation meanwhile climbs from 2.4% to 2.7% in June as Turkey, India, Bangladesh, and even Pakistan all report declines in their respective inflations. Oil futures also declined 1.3% to settle at USD 65.2 / barrel on the back of said U.S. trade deals, in addition to concerns of an oversupply of oil as Trump announces the possibility of easing sanctions against Venezuela that could add a reported 200,00 barrels of oil to global supply-chain. The Baltic Exchange’s main sea freight index meanwhile reported another improvement this week with the Cape index surging 1% of its total annual value via a 24% gain just this week, all while the Panamax and Supramax indices confoundingly fell 2.3% & 0.3% respectively.

Notwithstanding, glimmers of life seem to be emerging from the Indian sub-continent ship recycling markets as offers on the large(r) LDT LNGs making the rounds (including various other types of tonnage) surpassed most expectations this week. But what remained the most impressive (and as forecasted in weeks prior), Alang recyclers have been the ones to take in virtually all of the market (and private) fixtures as Alang’s anchorage was ‘fully loaded’ this week. This may be a sign that the markets have likely bottomed out, but the situation may remain in a state of statis until the end of next week before any movements can be expected from any of the sub-continent markets, especially after the recent and significant decline of about USD 60/LDT in residual values from the highs of USD 400s/LDT seen at the start of the year, including the massive USD 600/LDT seen just 12 months prior. Moreover, we have also seen prices decline below USD 400/LDT during the historically slower monsoon / summer months as several deals are still being fixed at those levels in 2025 as well.

headline: LNG KINGS!
highlights: Modicum of form. | ADNOC sales. | Aspirin.
body_text:
After a series of Moss type LNG sales confirmed to local recyclers, it could be comfortably considered that India is at least getting back to a modicum of form this week, after what has been an extremely lacklustre few months of price declines and lethargic financial inertia that has seen this market at the 2nd and 3rd place on the market rankings a lot more than as historically has been the case.

And this week’s activity was certainly a welcome surprise given that two large LDT LNG carriers were successfully committed to Alang buyers as ADNOC controlled GHASHA (33,406 LDT) and AL KHAZNAH (33,456 LDT) were both fixed on an en bloc basis, for an extremely firm USD 42.9 million (about USD 641.50/LDT) basis an ‘as is’ Malaysia delivery – the strong price being attributed to the large quantities of non-ferrous (including significant aluminium) on board these Moss type LNGS. India has certainly been the most sophisticated non-ferrous metals markets to trade with, even when they are lower placed against both their Pakistani and Bangladeshi competitors, making them the go- to market for stainless steel tankers, Moss type LNGs, and similar other non-ferrous rich units.

And this return to form was also hard to be missed as Alang’s waterfront remained a sight to behold this week, with 11 vessels (including a large LDT tanker) and over 107,000 tons of recycling tonnage having arrived the waterfront and a majority being delivered to their final owners. And this trend is likely expected to continue as Pakistani yards are still grappling with yard upgrades across the board and there has not been much positive news from the remainder of the Bangladeshi non-HKC yards that still have their works ongoing.

Local fundamentals too offer some hope as despite the Indian Rupee reacting like its sub-continent brethren against U.S. Dollar that saw it falling 40 basis points to Rs. 86.48, it was local steel plate prices that offered some Aspirin to local sentiments as levels reported firmed nearly USD 4/Ton this week and back to USD 432, offering an increased buffer on margins, especially on some of these recent and expensive deliveries. Moreover, with trade projections expected to grow in excess of 6.5% in 2025 on the back of increased domestic investments backed by trade deals concluded with the U.K. and a 2nd round of FTA talks with New Zealand that look increasingly promising, India could be in the limelight for the remainder of the year. Finally, Trump’s growing assertions of reaching an agreement with India could also further the overall trajectory of the nation’s economy.

Overall, India will likely remain the go-to ship recycling destination through early August, perhaps all of it, making it a promising month for owners looking for prompt and hassle-free recycling-relief. Promising August.

headline: SECURING SALES?
highlights: Best placed. | Bulkers sold. | Marooned. | Quick dry unit?
body_text:
The Pakistani ship recycling market remains the best placed for yet another week and was even able to secure of series of bulkers this week, reportedly with significant quantities of bunkers remaining on board at the time of arrival. These sales are particularly interesting given that Gadani recyclers have traditionally been a selective group who tend not to veer too far left from the types of tonnage they have historically been comfortable recycling – and non-ferrous, Moss type LNGs, LPGs, and the likes have not made the cut for local recyclers, more often than not. Accordingly, markets witnessed both the RISING FALCON (5,694 LDT) and the RISING EAGLE (5,440 LDT) fixed en bloc to cash buyers` basis a likely Pakistan redelivery, at a decent USD 446/LT LDT including about 250 - 300 Tons of bunkers onboard at the time of delivery, contributing to almost USD 20/LDT to the purchase price of the vessel.

With an increasing number of candidates expected to enter the markets in the fourth quarter of the year (sounds like 2024 wishes all over again) and as government bodies and end buyers finally start taking their respective HKC infrastructure upgrades seriously (including authorities issuing provisional DASR certificates to those yards that have committed to, and made notable progress at upgrade works to their yards), it is certainly a pleasure to have a competing Pakistan back at the bidding tables – albeit, like their Bangladeshi counterparts, restricted to a limited a number of local recyclers.

Domestic fundamentals aren’t doing this market any favors at this time either as on the one hand, local steel plate prices stay marooned at region USD 615/Ton (still the highest in the industry), with no major market sales (of late) to take advantage of these impressive margins, while on the other hand, the Pakistani Rupee made a surprise bounce, firming about 55 basis points and end the week at PKR 283.20 against the U.S. Dollar. While certainly not a return to the saner days under PKR 280, it is hopefully firm motivation enough for the rest of the recycling community to join in their HKC efforts. And while Pakistan’s economy and domestic stock exchange has faced increasing volatility over the recent past post-operation Sindoor, most businesses and even the government are wary of the way ahead with neighboring India.

Notwithstanding, Gadani is certainly a destination to keep an eye out on, especially for owners looking to retire a dry unit quick in August.

headline: UNCHANGED?
highlights: Weekly badgering.
body_text:
While on the one hand, Aliaga’s anchorages have been comparatively deserted for the most part of 2025 leaving the country’s domestic ship recycling sector in “Airplane mode”, on the other hand, the ongoing decline in Turkey’s inflation rate has seen a drop from 42.12% back in January down to 35.15% back in June, which has reportedly resulted in the Turkish central bank favorably re-adjusting national interest / lending rates – a promising sign for domestic businesses in the short run.

But it has been the Lira that has been unable to escape its weekly badgering as it was reportedly subjected to another 50-basis point decline this week as well, ending it at TRY 40.56 against the U.S. Dollar. Import and local steel plate prices aren’t doing very well either as they remain relatively unchanged and subdued over recent weeks.

Mercifully, the benchmark interest rate saw a 300-basis point reduction to 43% and might hopefully fuel the purchase of some of the cheaper, smaller, and regional end-of-life ships.

headline: BACKLOGS BITE!
highlights: Lowest still. | Frustrations abound. | HKC underway. | Tariff tricks.
body_text:
The Bangladeshi ship recycling market remains the lowest placed of all sub-continent destinations for yet another week / month and as such, has been unable to partake in much (if at all) of the activity at the bidding tables of late. And this level of pervading disinterest to be competitive has seen the waterfront suffer over the last 3 weeks with minimal arrivals and deliveries ensuing, including this one, where just a lonesome albeit decent LDT tanker arrived the nations recycling waterfront this week, and remains idling (likely) awaiting its tide.

Meanwhile, the incessant rains in the face of reported global warming wrapped in the threat of impending tariffs saw fundamentals hammering the purchasing mindset of local buyers as despite the Bangladeshi Taka displaying a degree of stability and even firming 30 basis points against the U.S. Dollar to end the week at BDT 21.52 (thanks to the central bank’s reported intervention last week), it was steel plate prices that fell another USD 2/Ton as recycled steel fails to move from yards to domestic steel mills. And with the recently reported trade deal between steel mills and steel importers at levels far lower than current rates, there has been a growing frustration at the lack of constructive movement from the interim government to help move the domestic steel industry forward or even announce any government-backed or subsidized infrastructure projects to help the nation’s economy for over 12 months now, which is leading to a reduced overall demand for steel - and ships.

As such, much of the growing steel inventory at local yards that was previously concluded at much higher prices (than today), is now starting to backlog post recycling and this is creating even more frustrations for recyclers that are now starting to extend beyond merely financial. The ongoing shortage of a monsoon induced worker shortage at Chattogram recycling yards is also not doing anyone locally any favors, which may have its own silver-lining in that, a slowdown in recycling of recently delivered units stands to extend the overall process, likely beyond the monsoons and into late September during which time, there may hopefully be some economic reprieve.

Notwithstanding, HKC developments have reportedly continued at pace at the remainder of yards with works is ongoing, in order to get all local yards up to HKC standards and continue operating as the number of disinterested Bangladeshi recyclers at the bidding tables is clearly starting to affect Chattogram’s anchorage. Moreover, with inflation reducing in June and July hopefully following the trend (awaiting official July numbers), the Central Bank may hopefully re-adjust lending rates thereby helping local recyclers on future vessel purchases. Bangladesh’s stock exchange has also rallied since last year as it climbed a whopping 6.9% in July and over 46.45% during the same time 12 months ago.

But with tariffs against Bangladesh now reportedly in effect, the nation’s growing GDP is expected to take a notable hit across Q3 – and likely beyond. Just how this will affect the nation’s ship recycling waterfront remains to be seen. For now, we don’t expect any meaningful transactions to take place until August likely comes to pass.

headline: ROCKY MOVES!
highlights: ‘Two Weeks’. | Russian sanctions? | Volatility. | Market improves? | Bangla lags.
body_text:
As the shipping and ship-recycling worlds seemingly collide going down a rabbit hole of this thoughtlessly induced global economic turmoil bought on by a blind surgeon, we can undoubtedly expect to see further issues arising in the coming weeks (unless immediate countermeasures aren’t enacted) as president “two weeks” finally approved a wave of tariffs (infamously declared on April 4th as Liberation Day) against U.S. imports from dozens of countries, including Canada, Taiwan, India, and surprisingly, even Russia as in a show of force against Putin’s unrelenting and truly unabated aggression in Ukraine, this week Trump reportedly instructed CentCom to strategically re-position two nuclear submarines at undisclosed locations off of Russian shores. This move, in addition to the sanctioning of not only Russian oil, but also those trading Russian oil, is reportedly expected to see over 1,000 vessels enter the dreaded OFAC list, leaving their futures in disarray.

And the inevitably of his actions is already starting to (sort of) bear fruit for the ship recycling sector as a gradual inflow of tankers into India and bulkers into Pakistan over recent weeks (including this one), has seen fresh arrivals at both locations this week. The Baltic Exchange dry index also reported a 0.75% overall jump brought on by the Cape and Supramax indices that firmed 1.8% and 0.1% respectively this week, all while the Panamax index fell nearly 1% of its total value, an over 10% drop in weekly trading. Unsuspiciously, both wet and small-to-medium size dry units are expected to continue sailing into the Indian sub-continent ship recycling markets through August, given that the sanctions have already seen oil futures in turmoil as they declined an unpopular (well any negative number is unpopular) 2.7% this week, closing it out at USD 67.30/barrel.

Fundamentals at ship recycling destinations also displayed results similar to a darts contest at a blind congregation, all over the board this week (just as they have been over the recent past) despite ‘some’ price stability and even improvements being registered, resulting in a growing collection of fixtures into the sub-continent recycling markets of late – most notably were the two larger LDT LNGs into India and even two bulkers into a resurgent Pakistan, with reports of slow but ongoing improvements to local yards coming forth.

headline: ROSIER GLOW?
highlights: Competitive. | Non-ferrous desires. | HKC ready. | Tough call.
body_text:
Recent LNG sales into India have given this market, a rosier glow than they perhaps would otherwise have expected bearing in mind, the incessant volatility in local steel plate prices has seen them go through a bit of a roller coaster ride this week as they started and end the week at the same level. And this volatility in steel that has seen far more declines through Q3, was also joined by ongoing currency woes that saw the Rupee fall a drastic 93 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and end the week at Rs. 87.37, leaving Alang resting in 2nd and even 3rd place on the market rankings for a majority of 2025.

Logically, given that India remains a specialist in non-ferrous trade, has certainly helped this market keep the final destinations of most LNGs routed to Alang’s shores where demand for non-ferrous and non-ferrous vessel remains high, thanks to the above average quantities of aluminium and stainless steel onboard these units that has helped them achieve prices far in excess of prevailing averages, thanks to these vessels being particularly high in demand here.

Meanwhile, domestic yard capacity and HKC infrastructure upgrades were at the forefront of Alang ship recyclers since 2014, invariably helping key local recyclers snag high-profile vessels from the fleets of blue-chip owners. This fundamental shift in the global mentality from the ship owning fraternity saw a better quality and grade of maintained vessels arriving Alang, much to the envy of non-HKC neighbouring yard owners who then went on to pursue HKC certifications of their own, gradually planting the initial seeds for further progress across Alang’s landscape. 12 years later, this process has snowballed to where nearly every ship recycling yard is HKC SoC approved and the only thing needed for the local community and governmental agencies was to modify NOR documents at the time of arrival in a post June 26th / HKC world.

The result of which, continues to be a busy anchorage for Alang’s ship recycling community that has struggled with tonnage availability for well over a year now, and recyclers here have been the busiest in the sub-continent, taking in a breadth of types and volumes of tonnage over recent weeks including this one, where a couple of new tankers arrived locally, in addition to a few final deliveries. Clearly, the number of open and available local buyers over these stagnating monsoon months has survived behind the scenes, who have been monitoring tonnage movements and decidedly picking up units now that prices have bottomed out and global tumult gradually starts to drive tonnage towards retirement. Tariffs imposed this week are certainly on the minds of Indian businesses and these are expected to keep recycling vessel prices in check, at least in the short term / through August.
