For now, it’s a tough time for the locals, and if you’re an owner with a big unit and are okay with “pale green” recycling, this is your market. As comedians say, “Destiny awaits, let’s just hope she’s pretty”.

headline: LIKE THE GANG!
body_text: Just like the rest of the industry, the Turkish Lira ended the week 18 basis points weaker at TRY 41.33 against the U.S. Dollar, all while a highly anticipated price cut in vessels prices remained safely amiss. Price cut?

headline: SPORADIC!
highlights: No equation. | Ratio of efforts. | Trump-o-nomics! | Election hopes.
body_text:
Demand, and subsequently local offerings from Bangladesh have turned even more sporadic over the last month, certainly since September transitioned in and this is surprising most in the industry given that post-monsoon trends in the ship-recycling industry have historically been on the up. As most units on offer have been smaller LDT vessels that have been increasingly less fancied by local recyclers and have simply not received any attention (let alone offers) whatsoever – and logically so.

Not only has the HKC turned import regulations and import control into a guaranteed session of rush hour traffic delays and headaches, but the Cirque Du Soleil of hoops that local recyclers now have to jump through (e.g., mandatory HKC yard / infrastructure upgrades) and continue to jump through (e.g., new documentary requirements and inward permissions) in order to simply import a vessel for recycling, has permeated a sense of disinterest towards smaller LDT units as the effort to import such small sizes doesn’t match the ratio of efforts for local recyclers at present .

As a result, most Chattogram Choppers (like the Gadani Gang) are electing to focus on larger LDT units that not only make sense to put their efforts into, but will also keep them pre-occupied longer than they would otherwise have to with smaller units, before they have to return to the bidding tables and repeat the frustrating process of fresh permissions on the next unit, all over again. Juicy LNGs have meanwhile been receiving a flurry of local interest and competitive offers, but with the limited number of units making the rounds has left such interest on the selective and subdued side - primarily depending on the availability of a local recycler.

Problems also persist with recycled ship’s steel failing to shift from end buyer yards due to an ailing economy and lack of any infrastructure projects emanating from the thralls of the interim regime that seems to have driven the country further down the stability ladder - although inflation has steadily retreated over preceding months as it ended August at 8.29% down from 9.8% just a few months ago).

Trump-o-nomics has also not spared the Taka from dithering across the year as after declining in segments across various quarters, it ended the week subdued at BDT 121.74, while local steel plate prices flatlined (or remained steady, depending on if your glass is half full or half empty) at a healthy USD 519/Ton. Local port position meanwhile escaped isolation as another fresh candidate greeted the waterfront, with the arrival of a decent LDT tanker.

Overall, as all eyes and all hopes remain posted on the upcoming elections in February 2026 when a change in leadership could bring with it renewed optimism and momentum following a dull and damp last year or so for the country, in the interim, this market seems destined to go through an extended period on the sidelines.

headline: SEPTEMBER SERENE?
highlights: Stability returns. | Market focus. | LNGs steady. | Average older. | Volatile still.
body_text:
After what seemed like months of unstoppable volatility, a modicum of stability seemed to enter the global trading markets this week as oil climbed marginally (0.17%) before the week ended, yet this remains a near 1.4% drop just this month and a 10.8% overall decline from the same time last year. On the flip side, trading markets continue to edge on as they surged another 3.6% this week, but the Baltic Exchange Dry Index reported both Panamax and Supramax indices dipping nearly 2% and 3% respectively, while the Cape index, which has been carrying the bulk of the dry index sector, climbed nearly 1% this week.

With minimal news emanating from the White House over the last couple of weeks and an ongoing status quo on state of warring nations, the mild serenity of the international markets found itself trickling down to the Indian sub-continent ship recycling locations as well this week, after what has been months of negative spirals that most destinations have endured over these summer / monsoon / recent months. Not only did local steel plate prices continue to flatline (remain optimistically steady?) across most locations, but even the U.S. Dollar seemed to weaken against key currencies this week, except for Turkey’s perennial landslide where its Lira is concerned. Supply too seems to have firmed a touch at the bidding tables of late, as recycling destinations continue to demonstrate the inflow of tonnage, while others languish in the obscurity on the availability of the types of units to bid on – and their subsequently willingness to engage on said units.

A majority of the slim collection of recent market sales remained focused on India, with Pakistan and (especially) Bangladesh still struggling to summon any coherent offerings or a clear buying at present, even for those vessels that are literally positioned in their backyard or sailing in from Far East locations. India meanwhile has cornered virtually all of the year’s LNG recycling sales, which have remained sporadically, yet mercifully steady over the last quarters (and indeed for much of the year), as other categories have clearly remained tied up in their respective trading lanes - given the performance of various indices over all of 2025.

As such, the average age of operating vessels has gradually increased with the draw of the Dollar from re-employment, with bulkers, containers and certain categories of tankers now often passing 30 years of age again. And while local market fundamentals do remain volatile, regulatory (HKC implementation) struggles continue to challenge a Pakistan market that desperately needs to catch up with yard infrastructure work. Turkey at the far end remains stranded in recycling oblivion out of necessity, then choice.

headline: SUSPECT IMPORTS!
highlights: Listed arrivals. | Sanctions raised. | Historical decline.
body_text:
Alang’s port report remains the busiest of all sub-continent ship recycling destinations, thanks in small part to the recent arrival of a few OFAC listed / sanctioned units that were otherwise turned away by competing locations who did chose not to violate international sanctions or regulations. And all of this comes at a time PM Modi is planning a visit to Bhavnagar this week, leading to all in the region turning busy to welcome the nation’s leader in his home State of Gujarat, resulting in a partial shutdown across much of the state and even Alang.

This alleged activity in the trade of sanctioned vessels by cash buyers has landed India in trouble with the U.S. and Trump in particular, who has raised all manner of sanctions and tariffs against India in order to try and deter their business dealings with perceived rogue regimes, over and above Trump’s distaste of India’s decades long oil trade with Russia, who he is clearly unable to control given the mounting pressure from Western States.

All of this has culminated into an India Rupee that has crashed all across August and more notably in September as it broke past prior records against the US. Dollar while mercifully (and finally) firming 21 basis points to end this week at Rs. 88.09. Local steel plate prices also started to mirror neighbouring competitors as they flatlined for the consecutive 3rd week in a row, at the sub-continent’s lowest levels at USD 448/Ton.

Yet, this has not deterred local interest to the extent otherwise feared and with HKC wings already primed for afterburner given Alang’s decade long expertise in the game, local anchorage has continued to outperform competitors for nearly two months now and even this week, with a healthy batch of arrivals and nearly 84K LDT of tonnage idling at anchorage / delivered locally. And while larger LDT favoured LNGs rich in nonferrous have been the juiciest flavour of the year, they have also been able to command a significant premium for their owners, a blessing considering the state of declining prices since January 2024.

Overall, despite the recent historical and concerning decline in the Indian Rupee, demand and purchases have certainly steadied / stabilised in Alang of late and especially this week.

headline: CURIOUSLY CONFUSED!
highlights: Heading elsewhere. | Shunning small LDT. | Work to do. | Watch this space.
body_text:
It is curious to see the leading ship recycling market (pricewise) in the world celebrate an empty port report for the third straight week in a row, given that much of the nonferrous and larger LDT LNG / LPG tonnage remains focused on India (including clearly OFAC listed / sanctioned tankers as well, several of which reportedly remain arrested outside Alang).

Moreover, and as highlighted in the Bangladesh section above, Pakistani ship recyclers have not been keen to import small(er) LDT units on account of their exclusive (and painful) issuances of DASR certificates that permit them to import vessels. But in Pakistan, their problems is magnitudes greater as not a single ship recycling yard is HKC certified as yet, while DASR issuances are reportedly being made to only those yard owners who continue to demonstrate ongoing upgrades and improvements at their respective yards.

As a result, even to merely get a “provisional” DASR certificate to continue operating in Gadani has left the Gadani Gang focusing primarily on importing larger LDT vessels that may come around. Unfortunately for them and as has been evident from ongoing port reports, most large LDT units have primarily been LNGs / non-ferrous vessels that have perennially remained an “India only” domain for nearly 2 decades – and the fact that Pakistan banned LNGs circa 2007.

In Gadani nevertheless, HKC yard upgrades are ongoing and reportedly at pace. And if their fundamentals continue to support their ongoing price levels – the PKR firming 18 basis points against the U.S. Dollar closing the week out at PKR 283.44 and local steel plate prices stagnating at the highest levels in the industry at USD 623/Ton (despite declining a comparatively marginal USD 4/Ton and still closing the week out USD 619/Ton) - Pakistan remains geared to be an industry leader, so as long as levels hold and HKC yards start to come online.

Work remains to be done, but with weeks of empty port reports and ongoing progress at local yards, Pakistan may just take off before the end of the year – watch this space.

headline: SILENT SLIDE!
highlights: Ruptured.
body_text:
Turkey has remained silent and sliding for over 24 months now and this week, import steel plate prices fell for the 2nd week in a row, the Lira slid 15 basis points to end the week at TRY 41.41 against the U.S. Dollar, and local port position reportedly remained famished.

All of the red-tape and regulations meant for good cause has only ruptured the fate of an entire industry.

headline: BYPASSED!
highlights: Quietest. | Failing to secure. | 18 yards HKC. | Lucky one.
body_text:
Bangladesh remains the quietest sub-continent ship recycling destination for yet another week and there are few signs that the pervading situation is likely to improve any time soon given that the overall state of affairs (as reported over recent weeks) has simply not changed an iota. Minimal recycled ship’s steel continues failing to shift from local yards due to the lack of development stimuli implemented by the interim regime (ahead of upcoming elections scheduled for February 2026).

Fundamentals too have stifled on the side of misalignment as not only did local steel plate prices fail to move - indicating that local recyclers are steadfast at current levels and refusing to buckle to the pressures of cheaper international steel imports, but the currency also started to groan like a retiree in hospice as the Taka ended the week on a lower note at BDT 122.04 against the U.S. Dollar.

And while tonnage availability has not been as big of an issue as it has been for much of the year, the state of the chartering markets has left nothing more than a healthy collection of small(er) LDT units being proposed at the bidding tables, which have remained beyond the grasps of local interests as most local buyers remain on the lookout for larger LDT units such as Capes / Panamax bulkers, which remain few and far between. Even worse? The rare few that are being proposed are being diverted towards competing India and likely even Pakistan (this week), so poor is the Bangladeshi sentiment at present.

HKC status too remains unchanged for the most part as from the last week’s count, there are still only 18 HKC compliant local facilities that are in operation, with a handful still struggling to complete their accreditation journeys. Reportedly, another 3 are set to be approved in October as Bangladesh continues to make meaningful progress with infrastructure upgrades, following the landmark entry of the Hong Kong Convention into force on June 26th.

At the local waterfront, at least one decent 7K LDT tanker made it into the hands of a local recycler as Chattogram’s waterfront continues to suffer week after week, virtually mirroring Pakistan’s recent performance. As advised in recent reports, unless you’re a lucky one with a large unit or simply don’t want to head further West, then only then is Chattogram your best bet.

headline: DISCONNECT?
highlights: INR spiral. | Steel decline. | Pak bright. | Future hopes.
body_text:
Global markets seem to be going through quite a disconnect of late as on the one hand, the last couple of months has seen a multitude of directions that stock markets, trading markets, charter rates, financial and FX markets, and even the ship recycling markets have been greeted by versions of unfolding realities that seem to conflict with what’s been transpiring at the bidding tables of late. On the one hand, various reports have been consistently confirming positive movements in dry / trading markets, oil up and down (with more down expected), financial markets wreaking havoc on the global ship recycling industry, and ship recycling volumes seemingly improving over recent weeks (primarily in India). And this week was another roller coaster of confusion.

The Baltic Exchange Dry Bulk Index fell nearly 7 points on Friday as Capes, Panamax, and Supramax indices all slipped 14, 3, and 4 points respectively. Yet, the overall benchmark reported a net 2.5% positive gain for the entire sector, driven primarily by the strength of Capes that reportedly firmed another 5.5%. On the flip side, WTI crude slipped 1% down to USD 65 / barrel as Iraq’s Kurdistan region reportedly resuming crude oil exports after a 2.5-year hiatus, adding a near 190K barrel / day output that is expected to climb to 230K bpd. The restart pushed by U.S. pressure comes as OPEC+ eyes further outputs while risks to Russian supplies linger amidst their war of attrition.

The net trickledown effect of the above coupled with a quick stop at sanctions stations has seen ship recycling nation currencies unexpectedly take a royal hammering this week as Bangladesh, India and Turkey all reported declines in their currencies once again, while local steel plate prices flatlined across the board, expect in India. Ongoing macro market movements have also seen a degree of sporadic buying return to the ship recycling markets from certain needlessly optimistic cash buyers, which has punctuated what has been an overall gloomy 2025 for the ship recycling scene where supply, demand, and pricing have all suffered tragically.

In Bangladesh, recycled product is simply refusing to shift from frustrated end buyer yards (much as we have seen for a majority of the year), leaving the overall ship recycling scene in Chattogram lost at high seas. Pakistan, and surprisingly even India, appear to be the only bright spots over recent times with an increased demand and higher indicative pricing of late, even though there is still much in terms of HKC infrastructure upgrades left to accomplish in Gadani, given that not a single ship recycling facility is HKC ready here. And Gadani buyers have been left relying on provisional DASR certificates issued by local authorities in order to continue doing business.

As Fall gets fully under way with September 2025 entering its forever slumber next week, dimly lit hopes lie in wait for brighter times ahead, for a beleaguered ship recycling industry.

headline: TURBULENT TIMES!
highlights: Vessels diverted. | Container sold. | Fundamentals fail.
body_text:
India has remained on the turbulent side of economic uncertainties over the last few weeks as Rupee woes and steel declines marred Alang’s ship recycling landscape over recent weeks, delivering a collection of gut punches to an already fragile sentiment. Not only has the Indian Rupee started its descent towards glooming uncertainty, but it also backed it up by declining a massive 55 basis points against the U.S. Dollar this week, ending it at INR 88.62. Of note, this was an improved ending to the Rupee’s performance as it briefly broke all time historical records this week approaching dangerously close to INR 89.

On the other side of the fundamental’s coin, after weeks of flatlining like its neighbours, Indian steel plate prices slid a whopping USD 15/Ton and end the week it at USD 409.20/Ton, well below recent offerings and even fixtures. Given that at a time some cash buyers are feeding off a misguided interpretation by relating the recent inflow of tonnage to the possibility of an upcoming market improvement, it is simply not the case. Moreover, while some recent sales have also tickled the limits of prevailing levels, it may be that the owners of these units could well face problems upon arrival at Alang should the Rupee’s and steel’s performance continue migrating South for the winter months.

Resultingly, it was of little surprise to see active negotiations on several vessels slow down amidst the disastrous decline in fundamentals this week, with reports of some working vessels being potentially diverted to competing markets (i.e. Pakistan), so terribly has the local situation deteriorated in India. In fact, there were two dry bulk sales into Pakistan to report and only one small tanker and one container into India, and that too at a curiously high and speculative level from the concerned cash buyer as Sinokor sold their 1997 Netherlands built (with steel propeller) NIIGATA TRADER (4,810 LDT) at USD 480/LT LDT with 120 Tons of bunkers ROB – certainly not a viable or realistic price today based on local fundamentals.

As the INR continues down this disastrous and historical spiral since President Trump launched his traction-less sanction action on the world along with maddening 50% tariffs on India for their tolerance of and business dealings with Russia on energy trade, Q4 might just turn into a Pakistan only game. This week, however, Alang simultaneously surprised with fresh tonnage at the waterfront and another cape arriving locally.

headline: BAGGING BULK!
highlights: Over the line. | Hmax sales. | Working hard.
body_text:
After nearly a month on the sidelines with empty port positions by the week, deals finally appear to have been concluded into a resurgent (and hungry) Gadani market this week, with several bulkers being reportedly sold to local recyclers including a unit likely inbound all the way from Indonesia, bypassing the traditionally hungrier Bangladesh and even Indian markets.

To start, the RISING HARRIER 8,600 LDT) was concluded for a decent USD 445/LT LDT from Middle East owners (with 150 Tons of bunkers included in the sale), whilst the PUTERI KIRANA (8,082 LDT) managed to fetch a fine USD 390/LT LDT basis an ‘as is’ Surabaya delivery and likely Gadani resale, wrapping up the two handy sales for the week.

Local port position also surprised the industry with at least one (but small LDT) handy finding its destination to a local recycler’s yard. Clearly, these DASR certifications are coming in at a hefty cost as this sub 3K LDT fixture highlights the growing desperation of local recyclers.

Fundamentals meanwhile continue to support the local mindset as not only have local steel plate prices continued to dominate the competing sub-continent steel charts for several months now, but they also remain flatlined at levels strong enough that seem determined to trudge through Trump’s uneducated business moves. The Pakistani Rupee also firmed a healthy 30 basis points against the U.S. Dollar this week to end it at PKR 282.50.

At the macro end, Pakistan is also idling with tariffs at a far lower 20% compared to Bangladesh’s 30% and 50% on India, making it increasingly seem as though the lack of HKC fervor was joined by local inaction towards a timely initiation of upgrades that have ended up partying hard into the night and created the tonnage hangover that the Gadani Gang continues to endure. And while the local buyers continue to work hard at getting their facilities up to HKC standards, the number of recyclers willing to negotiate on a majority of the market offerings, remains in the air.

headline: SNOOZE!
body_text: Lira drops 46 basis points to end the week at TRY 41.58 while steel continues to face a marginal dithering with every passing week. Not much else to report. Dithering.

headline: SCORCHED EARTH!
highlights: Most inactive. | Empty yards. | Time will come.
body_text:
As the lowest placed and most inactive global ship recycling market by far, it was no surprise to see Bangladeshi buyers swerving towards any hints of meaningful business this week, especially as local port position should’ve essentially marked itself empty had it not been for the lone wolf that’s been idling outside for about 2 months now.

Unfortunately, for the domestic ship recycling community, the feeling that the extent of the hard work, pressure, and investments expended towards yard upgrades in order to get in line with the standards of the HKC that resulted in them otherwise missing out on units during a time when the supply of vessels itself has been marginalized by Trump’s tariff trainwrecks that have been hammering the nation state of late. Add to it the probability of an inflationary hike and thereby more expensive financing could just cripple a market that is also battling funky fundamentals and aggressive pricing from regional competition, Chattogram Choppers seem like they’re walking into scorched earth territory for Q4 2025.

Local steel plate prices meanwhile remain stranded at a comparatively stronger USD 520/Ton, likely due to local recyclers holding pricing firm on their stockpile resales until steel mills buckle, which really remains to be seen now that domestic steel factories have now gotten a taste of cheaper steel imports. The currency too continues to dance on week after week as it loses another 5 basis points this week and end it at BDT 121.70. The silver lining to the currency woes? They’ve managed to remain within a BDT 3 limit for the last couple of months.

With no infrastructure projects announced as yet (going on over 12 months since the collapse of the last regime) and the future of the country hanging under the fragile control of the interim government for the next 4+ months, Bangladesh’s ship recycling fraternity seems as though it could cripple under the weight of its own HKC adventures, especially as more local yards come online and competition seeps in from the macro to the micro.

Of note, while the rains have seemingly ended and a resumption of daily activities ensues, local chop shops conversely find themselves amidst declining sentiments. Nevertheless, the time will come for Bangladesh to get back to buying and all of the HKC approved yards will be rewarded with tonnage as the quantum of the industry’s increasingly aging fleet comes knocking. Until then, it remains a wish and a prayer. A wish and a prayer.

headline: HALLOWEEN ALREADY?!
highlights: Still not over! | HKC hopes. | Upgrades ongoing. | Indian woes.
body_text:
As we enter October, global markets are ready registering spooks across the board, marking a drastic debut into Week 41. While inflationary numbers from the various locations pertinent to this Newsletter are still incoming, reports from both Turkey and Pakistan suggest they climbed through September, likely laying out the groundwork for a spooky October at both locations. Currencies too are back on the scary charts as oil finds itself slipping on its own spills and trading markets recorded the worst drop since January 2025 as the entire index declined nearly 16% for the week. Oil, on the other hand, tripped towards USD 60 / barrel and is nearly 20% lower than the same time last year as capes, panamax and even supramax indices saw the lower side of last week.

And expectedly, steel plate prices at the various recycling destinations also reflected last week’s positions with India still the only one going down the water slide.

Decidedly slipping into the micro, Indian sub-continent ship recycling destinations did not escape the incoming dark of the month as nearly all markets reported dithering numbers of arrivals at respective anchorages while recyclers continue to look for a “lift me” moment, after what has been an unexpectedly woeful 2025 of declining fundamentals, supply, prices, and sentiment. Indeed, this has turned out to be one of the slowest years for ship recycling in over a decade – and it’s still not over!

Markets have resumed a tonnage scarcity that that is struggling to keep ailing yards active, which themselves remain burdened by HKC requirements, delays, and regulatory changes. Ship recyclers must truly wonder whether all of the HKC upgrades and requirements were in vain when in the years prior, the operation of ship recycling was a fantastically well-oiled machine. Moreover, while a limited tonnage supply has been the flavor of the fruit of late, the combined present where the average age of vessels is creeping past 30 years old and new vessels continue to hit the water from newbuilding yards will see a phase out of vintage vessels in the years ahead. But the year(s) ahead has been a festering situation that’s only been getting worse since 2022. So, 2027 now?

With 18 HKC approved yards in Bangladesh and another 3 set to follow this month, Pakistan remains absent on its HKC scoreboard as the Gadani Gang continues to work hard upgrading their facilities after a slow pre-HKC start, all while Alang yards are all dressed up with nowhere to go. Pricing remains in Pakistan’s favor with provisional DASR certs playing referee on the state of incoming tonnage. India’s tough times don’t seem to end as currency and steel woes continue to sink the ‘sentiment ship’ across September. Turkey has turned into an absentee landlord, having local yards open for tonnage from Western ports but absent for the rest of the world. Oh, and the reported possibility of over 300 containers being earmarked for a ‘grey fleet’ designation? Spicy!

headline: WOEFUL SLIDE!
highlights: Under pressure. | Noise to LDT ratio. | Chem tanker sold.
body_text:
It has been a tumultuous time for the perennially nervy Alang market, with a drastically depreciating Indian Rupee that has been stealing the limelight as well as ship recycler’s peace of mind for weeks on end given that the Rupee has broken past all historical records and seemingly settled in the high Rs. 88s against the U.S. Dollar. In fact, even this week, The US$ gained 12 basis points against the Rupee, winding the week down at Rs. 88.74, inching back towards the increasingly dreaded Rs. 89 mark.

Constantly sliding steel plate prices that fell another USD 6/Ton and end the week at USD 402/Ton (well below current offerings) are also placing increasing pressure on current offerings as tabled levels are being reversed across active negotiations. Moreover, the fate of recent high-priced fixtures from ever-exuberant cash buyers also stand to strain upcoming deliveries and thereby, subsequent negotiations, especially if prices do fall and owners and cash buyers with inventory on hand start to chase prices down at a time Bangladesh is already a mere USD 10/Ton below and Pakistani recyclers noise to LDT ratio remains misaligned.

As a result, Alang sentiments remain under severe pressure despite being the most active sub-continent recycling destination. Moreover, with most of the 100+ operating yards in Alang already HKC approved and also celebrating another week as the most active waterfront across recent weeks, it has been a curious few months watching competitors get up to speed with HKC infrastructure upgrades, whilst supply suffers and Alang buyers are yet to take full advantage of their HKC status.

One sale was however recorded for the week as the BOW CEDAR (11,043 LDT) from Norwegian owners Odfjell managed to fetch a decent USD 940/LT LDT, thanks to the prevalence of 2,300 tons of solid stainless steel on board and 700 tons of bunkers on delivery, to a select HKC yard, the second such sale from the group in the last month.

As it stands, with both Bangladesh and Pakistan likely down and out for October, Alang retains the “go to” spot for ship recycling – and will likely be over the next upcoming weeks.

headline: FLIPPANT!
highlights: Limited higher LDT. | Still top. | No go for small LDT.
body_text:
Despite securing several handymax bulkers for recycling over the last month, domestic demand has yet to reach anywhere near satiated levels in Pakistan - and certainly for the preferred yet absent, large(r) LDT units (such as capes and even panamax bulkers) that have somehow managed to evade Pakistani shores over recent times and end up in Indian hands, despite Gadani being the highest placed market for pricing across all ship recycling locations.

Ongoing yard upgrades meanwhile highlight just how much remains to be done here and get domestic ship recycling facilities fully HKC ratified / approved, despite the temporary issuance of provisional DASR certificates continuing to assist local recyclers with their buying endeavors whilst they continue to demonstrate progress infrastructure upgrades, which curiously has yet to translate into Pakistan’s first internationally recognized HKC faclitily.

In the interim, small(er) LDT are receiving the same treatment as out of Bangladesh while even India is starting to price-cut their offerings on such tonnage due to the same issues that have been hampering sub-continent ship recycling destinations i.e. longer government and bank approvals as for larger LDT vessels, sanctioned units checks, and greater chances of steel wastage / loss during the recycling process of smaller vessels when compared to their larger brethren, expensive financing, and currency woes amidst flippant global fundamentals.

While local steel plate prices have managed to stay steady above USD 600/Ton (currently USD 100/ ton higher than Bangladesh at USD 620/Ton) for a healthy part of 2025, not much is there to write home about from this market. The PKR, like the INR, has been hemorrhaging value for a majority of the year as it finds itself devaluing from the highs of region PKR 276 down to PKR 283 against the U.S. Dollar at the end of the week. But skyrocketing inflation is what will hit Pakistan in the economic belly as it nearly doubled from 3% in August to 5.4% as September closed.

What lies ahead in October is the same as what Bangladesh will likely to face i.e. a tight 4 weeks, which in of itself seems to forecast a tonnage full month (if that is even such a thing anymore) for India.

headline: STUFFY!
highlights: Silent Q4? | Silent Q4?
body_text:
Like the Gadani Gang, Aliaga recyclers find themselves not only facing a currency that has been on a mission to eventually cross the TRY 50 mark as it lost a whopping 27 basis points against the U.S. Dollar this week and closed it out at TRY 41.70, but it was also domestic inflation that resulted in a meerkat moment for local recyclers as it reportedly went up from 32.95% to nearly 33.30%.

While the rise in of itself may not seem as drastic, but to an already stagnant and stuffy ship recycling environment, the possibility of more expensive loans on marginally available tonnage is certainly a double-gut punch.

headline: HKC COMA!
highlights: Interim inertia. | Some sales finally. | Election hopes.
body_text:
After nearly two full quarters of an HKC induced coma spent on the sidelines watching other markets acquire tonnage whilst Chattogram buyers scrambled to upgrade their facilities to HKC standards while concurrently watching their political economic state fall into disarray thanks to the inertia of the interim regime, signs of life seem to finally be emerging from local shores as several well-priced sales from existing cash buyer inventories (including one capesize bulker) were reportedly concluded to hungry local recyclers with empty plots and available credit facilities with their banks that has now helped them get active over these eerily quiet months.

Although it still is 4 months away, a degree of local momentum seems to be building ahead of the upcoming elections scheduled for February 2026, as this inexperienced and clearly inactive regime looks destined to be ousted with a potential return of the opposition BNP frontrunner - Tarique Rahman - who reportedly spent about two decades overseas. Until such time, the Bangladesh economy seems destined to traverse through its share of brewing local tumult and this destination will limp through the occasional high priced fixture(s) on the occasional large LDT unit that may sporadically appear on the scenes, especially as both the Taka and local steel plate prices have been in on the sentiment shaking wagon, week after week.

And this week was certainly no different as not only did the Taka fall 12 basis points to end it at BDT 121.55 against the U.S. Dollar, the industry has also kept one eye on local steel plate prices of the market leaders (where offers are concerned, provided you see one tabled) and has remained suspended at USD 519/ton, a USD 100/ton lower than Pakistan. However, as mentioned in the weekly, that was last week and the difference is (marginally) smaller now.

As such, despite gloomy post monsoon clouds that are still floating over the local ship recycling seascape, Chattogram does seem to be going through a potential upturn in vessel offerings as demand from dormant yards finally starts to tell and most recycling chop shops in Bangladesh are keeping an eye out on the upcoming elections as a potential turning point for their market.

A staggeringly uncertain time for this market lies ahead in the interim. Staggering uncertainty

headline: WHOANANZA?!
highlights: Rotten times. | HKC Fumble. | Rich clueless man. | India holds the fort.
body_text:
In ship recycling, where even a day can make an incredible difference (the summer of circa 2006 when India lost about USD 100/Ton overnight due to a collapse in steel prices, for example), a week can certainly make a dramatic difference especially given the turbulent nature of current times that global markets are enduring. Not only did the international markets ride through a rude awakening as a series of events and another proposed Peace Agreement in the Middle East between Hamas and Israel via the release of the all the hostages on the one hand, was met with the heads of states of Pakistan and the Taliban regime in Afghanistan pick up Russia’s old bad habits in Ukraine as all nations reportedly engaged in aggressions pursuant to a collapse in prior peace talks.

This will certainly affect the future of shipping / trade in the region and in turn, feed through to the global ship recycling markets via incoming tonnage, as change certainly seems as though it’s in the air this week.

Going through the checklist of key economic factors affecting the state of global ship recycling today, while the world awaits inflation reports from India and the U.S. (where the government is currently shut down), the Baltic Exchange Dry Index reported a marginal increase as it climbed a mere 13 points by close of Friday on the back of Capesize & Panamax indices both reporting a 13 and 34 point bump in their values, as the small vessel index fell to its lowest level since late August, resulting in the overall index still reporting a near 2% climb this week. Moreover, despite the rising trade rates, oil continues to take a hammering closing at a lowly USD 59.81 / barrel, a number that today stands 18% lower than the same time last year.

And tonnage, it sure seems as though it’s coming given this week’s result as both Indian and Bangladeshi waterfronts suddenly saw tonnage emerge at their respective anchorage horizons this week, especially in India - the nation most brutally hit by Trump’s cluelessness over failing of Reagan-era policies of “strength through peace”, where a 2025 rich man only knows how to dictate terms and temperament. Eroding fundamentals in the form of declining steel plate prices and fluctuating FTX values across the ship recycling board continue to see weekly disagreements as levels in some locations continue to devolve without end, while others display false hopes via marginal weekly improvements that disappear in subsequent ones. Turkey at the far end remains fashionably late with no progress in volumes, other than the occasional private fixture making the rounds.

As week 41 of 2025 / week 2 of October passes, a spook and a whoa later, the market remains just as devolved and unpredictable as ever, with India still holding the lowest placed highest value market to go to.

headline: FUNDAMENTALS FLOUNDER!
highlights: Miserable weeks. | Rs. 90? | What’s next? Rs. 90? | Torrid cycle. | Coattails.
body_text:
The Indian market has, and continues to endure the most miserable of times of all global ship recycling destinations as the ongoing Trumpian saga of knee-jerking into global economic crises has sunk this market to the bottom of the ship recycling pricing board, with most Alang recyclers now opting to remain completely quiet, fearful of further market declines or what Jack-in-the-Box uncertainty this White House administration might just spook them around the next turn with, given that Indian fundamentals have been clearly floundering over the recent past.

While local steel prices have lost over USD 34/LDT over the last 3 weeks alone and managed to fall another catastrophic USD 7/Ton (down from the high of USD 424/Ton end of September to USD 391.21/Ton this week), severely undermining the viability of tabled offer levels and the safety of upcoming deliveries), the currency remains is the one that taking the local ship recycling community for the longest joy ride on shortest highway as it lost another 4-basis point against the U.S. Dollar and ended the week at a disastrous Rs. 88.75 – inching ever closer to the paranoia of hitting Rs. 89.

If history can be a view into the future, this would turn out to be disastrous for the Indian ship recycling sector as the markets would certainly see the Alang end of the bidding tables vanish for the short term, which would spell trouble for recycling volumes given the spate of ongoing deliveries and units that have been arriving at Alang’s shoreline over recent weeks (months perhaps?). On the flip side, owners of seriously old assets who have no other route for their vintage units than recycling, will probably see the worse end of the currency fluctuation / price index in comparison. Torrid cycle of events stands to unfold.

Until such time, India will continue to be the lowest priced market dominator of the ship recycling world as was clearly demonstrated by the voluminous number and total LDT of arrivals and beachings that exceeded 10 vessels hit nearly 120K LDT at the nations waterfront just this week. Alang’s ride on the coattails of its HKC implementations until the Rupee crashes or competing neighbours’ inch up on their HKC status, is likely to continue unimpeded despite its receding offerings – with owners and cash buyers chasing them down.

headline: WAR = 2 / HKC = 0
highlights: Truce hopes. | Global turmoil. | Spicy. | Uncertainty index.
body_text:
In the last 6 months, the state of Pakistan has managed to enter into its 2nd armed conflicts with its neighbors on both side, yet in even more time (8.5 months and counting just this year) and ever since the Pakistani government announced the adoption of the HKC, not a single yard has managed to attain its accreditation as yet. And while the Pakistani Air Force dropped bombs on alleged Taliban terror camps in Afghanistan, the real progress that the rest of the business world is waiting for, remains dreadfully out of site.

While provisional DASR approvals have kept local deliveries primed for survival until yards tidy and gear up to be fully accredited, the absence of news pertaining to potential international class authorities visiting Pakistan to confirm progress / issue certifications remain suspiciously amiss – granted not too many in the industry would be keen to visit an active war zone.

And as global markets continue to react negatively to Trump’s chain reaction of ill-advised economic moves that are once again ratcheting up tariff threats against China (reportedly another 100% hike) and USTR (amongst another delayed U.S. tariffs) that come into effect, are leading to a host of Chinese reciprocal measures that stand to throw the shipping industry into disarray, should these tariffs come to pass. Pakistan’s 30% tariff rate has also done little to ease the hot plastic summer slide that’s been burning through Pakistan’s inflation rate ever since they were announced back in August, with inflation nearly doubled over the last month.

Adding to the spiciness of the present is the perennial problem of trying to snag a juicy large LDT dry unit, which remains far from the interests of respective owners or cash buyers who are wary of moving large units to an HKC uncertain Pakistan. Moreover, with an utter lack of local arrivals (not a single fresh unit arrived this week and the only one at anchorage is a problem child from September), domestic steel mills have reportedly resorted to sourcing competing steel product from Iran resulting in the otherwise rock steady local steel plate price tumbling about USD 3/Ton and down to USD 616.80/Ton by the time the week ended. The PKR wasn’t enjoying much of a “Prom Queen” moment either, losing about 18 basis points against the U.S. Dollar as the week ended and closed it out at PKR 283.20)

Overall, Pakistan’s uncertainty index seems shakier than Bangladesh’s and this remains clearly evident from the local mood and resulting number of deliveries week after week. Short term forecast? This is a market where you could go big or go home.

headline: JUST KEEP GOING!
highlights: Strugglingly and | ironic.
body_text:
Like the jingle from “Finding Nemo”, the Lira “just keeps going” down and down as it lost another 30 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and slumped even lower to end the week at a disastrous and record-breaking TRY 41.82. And while this has still not been the “INR 90” moment for the Lira (given that local recyclers are expecting to see levels cross TRY 50), the proportionate drop in local offerings in comparison to those from India, remain far more stable.

Yet, at what cost? When tonnage during these weakening financial times is certainly heading towards sub-continent shores vs. engaging with EUSRR rules and regulations. Struggling, yet ironic times indeed.

headline: INDELIBLY INDECISIVE.
highlights: Unexpected boon. | Timed out. | Inflation station.
body_text:
Over the last couple of weeks, after a seemingly unexpected “upturn” (if you can even call it one) in the fluctuating intentions of the Bangladeshi market saw a couple of decent priced sales finally take place to hungry local recyclers, including a cape and an MR sized tanker from existing cash buyer inventories. However, by the time the week ended, Chattogram was back in a slump with the few open buyers having booked tonnage and the local market seemingly retreating back to being indecisive – an indelible signature of their 2025 performance.

And this week of course, was no different. Even though Bangladesh was the only sub-continent ship recycling destination to report no declines to their local steel plate prices, they remain stranded at USD 519/Ton with ongoing news of recycled steel inventories just stockpiling at domestic yards, which justifies the sporadic extent of purchases from local ship recyclers. And the distaste is in the pudding as other than oldies idling for weeks on end at local anchorage, not a single new vessel has arrived Chattogram this week.

The Taka meanwhile delivered the brunt of the market hit this week as it dell nearly 0.5% and clocked the week out at over BDT 122 against the U.S. Dollar once again, leaving local recyclers with expensive purchases, unsold inventory, and no yard space all blended into a curdled milk shake as this market desperately awaits a new government to spearhead the direction of the nation, which is pulling up to inflation station once again.

Overall, even though the last couple of quarters had seen some constant price declined and reduced demand HKC yard upgrades came front and center whilst local authorities themselves scrambled to layout the new requirements, documentary procedures, and standards to be kept, the market has found itself without a synchromesh gearbox. With many yards lying dormant and LC / bank limits left to satisfy, certain end buyers have seen it fit to pick up some of the admittedly meagre supply of vessels at some of the best (spelled lowest) rates seen in the sub-continent for some months.

We can only hope some of this purchasing activity continues until February 2026 and this nation returns to the forefront of the buying, despite having only (likely) having 21 approved yards by that time. Forefront/

headline: CERTAINLY UNCERTAIN!
highlights: Baltic climbs | Post-Covid lows. | Gift wrap. | Shadow fears.
body_text:
Global markets continue in turmoil leaving the shipping industry in a true state of disarray as one segment of shipping has remained alarmingly / surprisingly busy over the last few years while the other opposite end of the segment has been dropped off to an empty pool. Trading markets continue to firm as the Baltic Shipping Dry Index inched up just over 1% this week, backed by the perennial firming of capes, panamax and dry indices, all of which reported gains of 2.1%, 1%, and 2% respectively.

And as charter rates climb and the industry continues to raise the bar of the overall age group of the world’s floating sector, oil decidedly continued its Lira-like descent into the high USD 50s/barrel as it clocked the week out at USD 57.38 / barrel – a whopping 8% decline over the last month alone and an 18% drop since the same time last year.

As cheaper oil and firmer rates help ship owners net wider margins, the ship recycling end of the industry (the empty pool end) has been and continues being deprived of tonnage as year after year, it has been the same story post-covid i.e. next year. And 4+ years into it, things have only gotten worse now that prices seem intent to slip back into the high-USD 300’s/ton, especially in India where an alarming few weeks have passed with Rupee drops, steel declines, and sentiments drowning.

In fact, as we zoom out to the macro of the micro, the overall Indian sub-continent ship recycling market seems intent on withdrawing their levels at the bidding tables this week as even Bangladesh and Pakistan boarded India’s financial roller-coaster, seemingly benchmarking themselves at lower (than their last) levels, all while an air of uncertainty seems ready to gift wrap the upcoming season even though a sudden spike in incoming tonnage over recent weeks at the various anchorages would seem to paint a rather different picture than what is actually playing out on the ground.

Finally, while the conflict in Gaza appears to have actually set a ceasefire rolling, it remains to be seen just how smoothly Red Sea routes open up again with Houthi activity having gone quiet (not silenced) for the time being. And while a resumption of traffic could certainly see global prices start to decline over the long run, for the short term, the impact on the supply of recycling units remains uncertain at this juncture, especially as prices are about break past the USD 200/Ton price-gram from the highs of just 22 months ago.

headline: ALL OUT OF BUBBLEGUM!
highlights: Turkish fever. | USD 40/LDT gone. | Massive influx? | Happy Diwali.
body_text:
As the phrase goes, reality is here to kick butt and chew bubble gum, and markets are all out of bubble gum for India who has sunk firmly to the bottom of the sub-continent rankings for nearly 3 months now, after what has been a woeful time of consistently collapsing steel prices and a currency that seems to be suffering from a Turkish Fever.

The Rupee remained the “Amazon Prime” of depressing mindsets, delivering negative sentiments as promptly as the Rupee kept slipping and nearly hit Rs. 89, but managed to miraculously recover a whopping 85 basis points and tap the week out at Rs. 88.02 against the U.S. Dollar, a level still lingering in the “record highs” territory from yesteryear. And local steel plate prices? They unplugged the bottom of the pool and dried another USD 5/Ton to clock out at USD 389/Ton, well below recent purchases and certainly devoid of any aggressive offerings.

Yet, local anchorage remained a sight to behold with over 120K LDT and 11 vessels in the midst of arrivals, renegotiations, and deliveries – including an armada of wet carriers of all types and sizes including small LDT ones that clearly did not make the cut into Pakistan (more on that below). Dry cargo units have been hit or miss of late given that the dry index has been on the rise again and Pakistani recyclers are reaching the tipping point of securing a unit or now incur losses on their fixed costs.

Indian recyclers on the other hand have cancelled their tickets to their bidding tables and abstained from any serious negotiating, as cash buyers caught with India only vessels (nonferrous rich / specialist units such as MOSS type LNGs, stainless steel tankers or even fishing vessels with SS) and / or strict green HKC units intended for an India only redelivery are now having to suffer as a result of the lack of participation from the local recycling community.

Indeed, the recent decline seems to have knocked nearly USD 40/LDT off keel and any available levels, especially dry bulk units on offer, are now being played the ”well below USD 400/LDT” card, thereby ruling Alang out of any imminent market purchases. Diwali holidays have ironically (for sellers) yet mercifully (for local recyclers thanks to the distracted time away from business and family) seems to have come at an ideal!

TO ALL OUR FRIENDS AND THEIR FAMILIES, WE WISH YOU A VERY HAPPY DIWALI AND

headline: RUNNING TO STAND STILL!
highlights: Iranian steel woes. | Some yards booked. | HKC focus. | Trade tragedy.
body_text:
Pakistan is the one market likely to race to the bottom of rankings before the year’s end with the latest batch of hurdles coming their way across October.

Inflation has nearly doubled in September, the PKR has lost 38 basis points against the U.S. Dollar just this week at PKR 283.62 and cheaper incoming Iranian steel / raw material has been realigning the focus of domestic steel mills away from the local ship recycling community for 2 weeks leaving local steel plate prices declining USD 5/Ton this week, down to USD 614/Ton - a grand total trip of USD 15/Ton in just over 2 weeks.

Ensuing local offerings along with sentiments and demand have understandably suffered, leaving end buyers spooked and largely resuming their coveted wait-and-watch mode when tabling offers on the few pieces of tonnage making the rounds basis a potential Pakistan re-delivery, which have remained amiss from the most part.

Notwithstanding, several dry bulk units were reportedly committed basis a Pakistan redelivery in the USD 420s/LDT (and above) over recent weeks and it seemed as though Pakistan was back in spades, especially given that a 22K LDT tanker and a 9K LDT bulker arrived locally just this week, leaving Gadani recyclers with nearly 33K LDT of tonnage via 3 ships.

But this week’s setbacks aren’t the only ones leaving the local ship recycling community with an overdose of pain killers as their HKC nightmare has not even started, let alone any accreditations being granted to the first yard. This is clearly in the back of ship owners and cash buyers’ minds given the heat around sanctioned vessels of late and the possibility of now running afoul of HKC regulations in a post HKC world.

As such, the current situation has once again left this this market marginally above a woeful India and it is likely to slip past the Alang market, which itself seems to be in freefall at present. Moreover, with not a single yard yet HKC approved, it is clear where the local focus must lie, now that their ability to secure tonnage is clearly being undermined by the tragedies of global trade.

headline: SURREAL RIDE!
highlights: Not nice.
body_text:
Turkey’s slippage has been the hallmark of this market’s performance for 2 years now and it continues performing unrestrictedly in the worst way imaginable. Lira is down another 35 basis points to clock the week out at TRY 41.97, just pennies away from the dreaded TRY 42 mark, local and import steel have been seeing jitters, local offerings are barely hanging on at last indications, and while this market has the hallmarks of one that’s under duress, local offerings have managed to cling on at the same overall levels.

Yet, the end of the year cuold certainly change things up (and not in a nice way). Like years prior, 2025 has been a surreal ride for this market, much in anticipation of a similar 2026.

headline: DEPRESSINGLY SELECTIVE!
highlights: Looking for large. | Beacon of hope. | Hmax sold.
body_text:
As the Chattogram ship recycling sector continues trying to balance itself on stilts in the middle of an earthquake, surprisingly decent levels have been tabled from some of the hungry / premium buyers on some of the select large(r) LDT vessels proposed into Bangladesh - capesize bulkers and Membrane type LNG carriers including some of the recent sales (mentioned below). However, the supply of those units has been transient traffic with smaller LDT vessels making up the bulk of the inward recycling rotation and is now seeing almost no interest from local buyers.

As the economic situation remains confounded with inflation rising marginally last month, 30% tariffs on the nation’s most vital exports (Readymade Garments), the Taka losing nearly 30 basis points against the Dollar this week (closing it out at BDT 122.35), and a local steel plate price that made a surprise opening at levels far higher than last week’s closing, but still declining about USD 3/Ton is certainly a sign of impending times for this market.

All eyes are therefore glued to the upcoming elections that have been tentatively scheduled for February 2026 and loom like a beacon of hope (or an axe swinging on a rope) as locally, the drive to oust an ineffective interim regime that has failed to stimulate the economy via any new infrastructure / development projects since June 2024, is being attributed as the key reason behind the nation’s economic decline. Notwithstanding, HKC yard upgrades have at least made decent progress with almost 20 yards now fully HKC ready, having made the relevant infrastructure upgrades to keep on the right side of the latest regulations.

On the sales front, the recycling LNG clear-out continued this week as after an agonizing wait, it has been confirmed that two 1995 built Membrane units PUTERI NILAM (26,915 LDT) and PUTERI DELIMA (26,915) have been committed on an enbloc basis to a buyer on private terms. One other sale was confirmed this week as the handymax bulk carrier from Waruna MONICA P (7,779 LDT) was fixed for a decent USD 380/LT LDT basis an ‘as is’ Belawan delivery, earmarking in the only sale of the week with a likely intended resale into Bangladesh.

Overall, dealing with Bangladesh in the present times is much like playing the lottery, until the elections seal a win. Lottery.

headline: WOEFULLY SLOW!
highlights: India down. | Bangla sporadic. | Confusion reigns. | Little to show.
body_text:
Global markets seemed to take a breather this week as things turned slow across the board once again, not only on the shipping side but even the ship recycling side of things. Currencies fluctuated in moderate tandem, local steel plate prices made surprisingly marginal moves, all while the Baltic Exchange Dry Index slipped and oil steadied itself. The BDI reported a declining week that shaved off about 3.2% by CoB Friday, dropping to its lowest levels since early October as the Cape index took the lead shaving off over 6% of its value, while Supramaxes dipped a comparatively milder 9 points and the Panamax index remained steady for the week even though the overall index is nearly 4% down.

As inflation rose marginally in the U.S. (climbing to 3% by the end of the September), oil managed to gain some traction this week, firming to USD 62.14/barrel – a 1% climb on the back of anticipations on a possible China – U.S. trade deal, all while Trump threatens Putin with further escalations as sweeping sanctions take effect, not only on Russian oil trade (particularly with India), but even the EU now hopping on the wagon, reportedly blacklisting hundreds of container vessels this week.

And as the global dark / shadow fleets start to grow, the woeful performance of the Indian sub- continent ship recycling markets continues on and there are few emerging signs of light at the end of the tunnel (more like an oncoming freight train) for the remainder of this year. Prices have fallen so low over recent weeks that constant discussions of prices below USD 400/LDT are comfortably prevalent and it seems increasingly certain that any viable recovery has still not bought a ticket to the sub-continent recycling sector.

India has endured the roughest times over the last several weeks with levels plummeting on the back of rapidly deteriorating local steel prices and a drastically depreciating currency that continues to suffer on the back of 50% tariffs amidst the U.S. – India – Russia love triangle. Pakistan has not been too far behind the recent falls with plunging demand due to an influx of cheaper steel imports, all while Bangladesh shows moderate signs of life with a couple of local arrivals. The occasional and aggressive offerings on larger LDT units have been so sporadic, it has left ship owners and cash buyers confused as to where levels on the ground really stand. And as India celebrates a quieter time thanks to Diwali Holidays, Turkey remains seemingly absent regardless of work or play.

headline: TIERED TRIBULATIONS!
highlights: Little Diwali joy. | Market struggles. | Shadow shame. | Pricing apple.
body_text:
Diwali holidays have come and gone without much respite or signs of stability for Alang and even the Indian market overall. It is therefore unsurprising to see any market sales being concluded to many of the 100+ ship recycling yards that remain empty, for yet another week. It must certainly be frustrating for ship recyclers in Alang to see global and even the domestic markets struggling so much, with tariffs, oil pressures, sanctions, blacklists, and even the formalization of the Hong Kong Convention that has been in force since June 26th, 2025.

And despite all 100+ yards in India being HKC certified even before the HKC came into force, market driven scarcity of viable tonnage that has been stalking the ship recycling industry for years now, has left the Alang buyers with no real tonnage to work on as prices fade from the highs of USD 600/Ton down to below USD 400/Ton once again, leaving them at a greater disadvantage (as compared to the neighbouring competition) in terms of putting their HKC accreditations to use whilst competing markets are still getting up to speed.

Part of the problem has been the supply of dark / shadow vessels into India and the willingness of certain end buyers to acquire these units cheaply despite the international regulations and sanctions being in place), meaning there is now a two-tiered market that is killing prices for clean vessels being proposed.

And sanctioned vessels aren’t the only price hunters while they remain under the umbrella of India’s fundamentals that have been taking a brutal beating of late even though the Rupee gained a minor 20 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and end the week at INR 87.54 while local steel plate prices waddled out of the bar at sunrise with a USD 1/Ton improvement, yet leaning against the pillars of USD 389/Ton – a number far lower than the current value of ships.

Notwithstanding the widow’s tales, India continues to hold on to the mantle of the safest “go to” ship recycling destination regardless of tonnage type or size, as long as you’re willing to take a bite of their pricing apple.

headline: PAYING THE PRICE!
highlights: Cheap steel influx. | Refrain. | Above 400, just.
body_text:
Just as the Gadani market had seemingly gotten back on its feet over the last couple of weeks with fresh tonnage incoming on the back of the highest ongoing offerings in the Indian sub-continent ship recycling sector with some decent LDT dry tonnage palliating the local appetite, a sudden and recent influx of cheap Iranian scrap steel has local offerings and prevailing sentiments nosediving into the abyss this week.

Whilst not quite as low as the miserable state of the Indian market at present, Pakistani ship recyclers are becoming feverishly concerned by this recent undercutting of their local inventories and have refrained from tabling offers on any of the slim pickings of vessels that maybe making the rounds.

As it stands, Gadani is still positioned just above USD 400/LDT and as is the case with their Bangladeshi counterparts, Pakistani ship recyclers are looking mostly for larger LDT units (specifically dry vessels) if they are able to get their hands on any. This change in in the local flavor is primarily due to the difficulty and time needed to get provisional DASR certifications from the relevant authorities whilst HKC yards are still ongoing and upgrades taking place, thereby rendering small LDT units increasingly less favorable (for the effort needed to import them and the shorter times to recycle them).

Fundamentals too have been chocking as not only has inflation nearly doubled across September on the back of U.S. sanctions and a fresh new war with the Afghani Taliban, but the Pakistan Rupee doubled back 20 basis points this week just like their Indian counterparts and closed the week out at PKR 283.50. Local steel plate prices also resumed flatlining at USD 614/Ton, after falling over USD 15/Ton over recent weeks.

This is only adding to local frustrations as their ability to compete is being hampered by geography and the opening of Bangladesh viable tonnage of late, leaving Pakistan as the market to keep an eye out, especially if you have a dry unit opening in the area and a Gadani buyer gets up to grab a bite.

headline: SURREAL RIDE!
body_text: No change other than marginal steel movements and Lira down another 17 basis points against the U.S.$, wrapping up the week breaching past TRY 42, at TRY 42.08. Slow times ahead. Breach.

headline: FAILING TO IGNITE!
highlights: Active on sales. | Price gauge. | Encouraging HKC. | Prompt deals.
body_text:
Several sales to hungry Chattogram ship recyclers seemed have to sparked the market this week. Yet, it really is a very few select end buyers who have been on the hunt for units and that too at surprisingly decent levels (when compared to prevailing local offerings), in order to keep their emptying yards active, and L/C & bank limits satisfied. But the overall trajectory and sentiments have been unchanged for the most part as prices have otherwise been on a downward flight over the last few months, primarily due to recycled ship’s steel failing to shift from local recycling yards due to a festering demand as domestic steel mills reportedly continue to outsource raw material.

And while this has clearly stalled local resales and left prices of recycled steel stranded - including a deliberation in maintaining resale prices on part of ship recyclers so as not to lose their collective shirts amidst the ongoing decline – finally saw steel levels slip USD 3/ton this week and end it at USD 529.50/Ton. The U.S. Dollar was even less unforgiving as it slipped another 45 basis points and ended the week at a healthily worrying BDT 122.37.

Coupled with the crippling uncertainties of the political and economic directions of the country under the current regime, domestic businesses remain on edge even though upcoming elections scheduled for February 2026 could potentially repave renewed economic pathways for the nation. Marginally increasing inflation in September and the possibility of another increase through October also leaves little for the local ship recycling fraternity (and the industry at large) to remain optimistic about either.

On the plus side, HKC progress and issuance of accreditations continues at pace with a few more yards set to get confirmed by the end of the year, taking the total number of HKC certified ship recycling facilities in the country to 21 – encouraging given that there were only a handful of HKC approved facilities at the start of the year!

For now, if you’re coming in from the Far East, be sure to check with your favorite Cash Buyer on pricing and good / prompt deals.

headline: HALLOWEEN NOVEMBER?
highlights: Stultifying. | Few sales. | Listed woes. | Trade warming. | Harrowing 2025.
body_text:
A spooky end to October delivered its share of unending surprises not only across the ship recycling arena, but even global markets at large. At the onset, Trump wraps up his Southeast Asian glamour tour touting deals made, especially one with China where an embargo on retaliatory trade sanctions and set offs between the two nations was set for at least a year, bringing a sigh of relief to embattled vessels enroute to discharge in Chinese waters and even global consumers at large. With September inflationary numbers on the rise and U.S. figures being released only a couple of weeks back (due to the ongoing government shutdown), November seems on track to deliver another set of surprises for ship recycling markets. Oil meanwhile slipped nearly 1% during the week as it lingered around USD 60.67, with OPEC+ announcing further cutbacks in the supply of oil in upcoming Q1 2026 (adieu 2025), leaving lingering expectations of increasing gas prices.

Supply side was no different as the Baltic Exchange’s Dry Index also reported a noteworthy fall as the overall index fell nearly 1.3% for the week (on the back of all sub-segments reporting losses), down nearly 8% for the month of October and further marking its first monthly decline since April 2025. And this slowdown is increasingly presenting itself via tonnages of various sizes and types across the Indian sub-continent ship recycling landscape, especially in India where despite the lowest prices in the region, Alang continues to report an eye-popping number of occasional arrivals. And yet, the glut of tonnage sailing the high seas remains disproportionately ratioed against the number of units recycled over the last several years, leaving a potential surge of incoming tonnage on the horizon.

As a result, the ship recycling industry has continued to endure a stultifying and sluggish Q4 (in line with the numerous quarters spanning the last few years) with declines evident across all sectors and sales (barring the occasional stunners) occurring at ever deteriorating levels. An eye-catching duo of LNGs sold last week (as a clear-out from this beleaguered sector continues) were just such a highlight, including a seemingly steady trickle of older dissolute handymax sized bulk carriers sold in recent weeks as well (as confirmed by the various port reports). Sales of sanctioned vessels have also shaken the industry with fixtures being reported at well below market pricing into a dithering Alang, establishing a two-tiered price system that is causing confusion and consternation in the industry.

headline: LITTLE HOPE!
highlights: Diwali downer. | Cheap dumping. | Steel decline. | Bite?
body_text:
The title reads just as the reader would interpret it i.e. based on your use case. But in India’s case under the present circumstances, it delivers a sign of hope despite being the lowest placed sub-continent ship recycling destination - and too by some distance.

Accordingly, although on the one hand, there has been little in Alang to encourage or excite ship owners and cash buyers holding previously acquired expensive inventory, on the other hand, the present also offers hope to those ship owners and cash buyers who are more in agreement with prevailing market conditions and are ready to accept the lowest recycling levels of the moment, in exchange of a far more secure re-delivery that is devoid of theatrics, despite the rolling state of market fundamentals and sentiments (subject of course all MoA terms being aligned).

And rolling fundamentals are certainly the sign of the times with Indian steel plate prices putting on quite the show of movement, yet ending up where they began at the start of the week. The U.S. Dollar and Indian Rupee divorce has also hit peak momentum as the Rupee lost a massive 1.25% this week, wrapping it up at Rs. 88.70 and striking ever harder that at the foundations that have been keeping local levels precariously balanced during this financial earthquake. Worse yet, post-September pre- November monsoon thunderstorms seem far from over just yet as Trump further threatens Putin with additional economic retaliations should the Ukrainian aggression not curtail – the beneficiary of which has been the Indian market of late.

Moreover, a great part of the problem has been a two-tiered market that has emerged, due to the dumping of cheap sanctioned tonnage (OFAC and EU / UK listed vessels) that have been concluded at prices well below market levels, thereby collapsing collective local expectations of where offer levels on conventional tonnage should stand at the bidding tables. And local port positions highlight just how far tonnage inflow continues to confound as most are missing the fact these are likely underpriced units with no valid destination to arrive, with India being the only sub-continent market willing / able to accept these dark / shadow ships – but to what end?

Overall, even though inflation has dropped far below the Reserve Bank of India’s 2% (stable) level and currently at 1.54%, there is clearly room for cheaper financial instruments and loans for ship recyclers. Question remains, how many will bite?

headline: IMPORTS IRE!
highlights: Steel worries. | Yards must upgrade. | No go low LDT.
body_text:
Whilst not quite as negative as a price-inert India at present, Pakistan has endured its own flavor of hurdles this year and even this week, with the ongoing dumping of cheap Iranian steel causing a reversal in vessel pricing even though local steel plate prices reman well above the entire industry and a whopping USD +230/Ton above those currently from India, local buyers have been unable to fully exploit the potential of such wide margins. Yet, recent odd maneuvers of readjusting local offerings in order to align themselves with India is more business as usual for the Gadani Gang, who have miraculously managed to retain 1st place on the market rankings for a healthy portion of the year – with nothing to show for it.

Similar to Bangladesh, both markets have seen a scattering of incoming tonnage over time and although Bangladeshi buyers’ revel in the afterglow of geographically suited tonnage with no other competition on that side of the seaways, Pakistani recyclers have to compete with India, which is proving to be a double-edged sword for this market. Moreover, despite having the highest offers at the bidding tables, local recyclers cannot escape the fact that nearly 4 months after the HKC coming into force, the focus to align all HKC yard upgrades towards fruition remains amiss as not a single yards is HKC certified yet (2026?).

This is causing consternation for those owners and cash buyers who are considering options on a non-India only re-delivery. The cost of considering? Problems upon delivery as both local recyclers and authorities aren’t entirely grounded on the new format of arrival procedures and are thereby facing hiccups. Case and point, the single straggler at anchorage that’s been there since late September despite mediocre arrivals deliveries ongoing into his market – including this week.

Notwithstanding, provisional DASR certificates have at least ensured some of the incoming tonnage is going through its share of evaluation and safer recycling practices. But how long will this continue with plate prices flatlining and the PKR itself hitting 283.17 against the U.S. Dollar while Iranian steel pulls the rug from underneath local steel plate prices. It seems as though until HKC accreditations come firmly into play, this destination will likely fester at the top spot in isolation. And not because they are able to offer the highest, but because competing markets continue to slide.

headline: SUPPLY PINCH!
highlights: 4 years.
body_text:
As the utter lack of supply continues to hammer Aliaga for several years now thanks to the red tape of bureaucracy and coupled with a near absence of Turkey-only market tonnage for nearly 4 years now, it wasn’t unexpected to see local recyclers raise their offers in order to tempt owners who may only be in the deliberation stages of recycling their units at this time.

But fundamentals remain far from their side as although local steel plate prices have made marginal improvements, the TRY (ending the week at 42.06 against the U.S.$) has done more damage to keep local business operating at usual speeds.

And while inflation (at a whopping +33%) may have countered some of the resale potential of recycled ship’s steel, it’s a matter of time until Turkey’s government makes appropriate fiscal changes to balance the cost of living, while simultaneously squeezing the pace of the domestic ship recycling sector, especially as lending rates remain unattainable for tier-B (and below) recyclers.

headline: DIM & DOUR!
highlights: Nothing viable. | Continue trading. | Quieter end. | Trump Cola.
body_text:
As the top placed market in terms of demand and pricing, it remains disappointing for Chattogram Choppers to have no viable market candidates to work on for yet another week as most owners of smaller-than-large-ldt units seem far more disappointed with the declined level of local offerings at the bidding tables and are happier to either engage competing markets or continue trading their units instead, eking out the final earnings for even overaged vessels lurking in the global fleets, rather than face the dour state of Bangladesh’s ship recycling reality today.

And that even goes for the better placed local open buyers who continue to pay well-above local market levels just to fill empty plots, utilize dormant L/C limits, and minimize operational and fixed losses in the interim.

But given Bangladesh’s economic reality? Rightly so, with the Taka having collapsed from a high of BDT 106 back in June 2024, down to BDT 121.93 against the U.S. Dollar as of this week. Moreover, after lackluster resales of recycled ships steel onto domestic steel mills and competing cheaper imports ongoing, local steel plate prices that consistently seemed to defy gravity and remain suspended at surprising levels, all but fell off a Bangladeshi cliff as the week ended with no trading reported. Next week will certainly present a clearer picture.

Inflation meanwhile has been see-sawing month after month as it fell to 8.48% in June, rose to 8.55% in July, back down to 8.29% in August, back up in September to 8.39% and now 8.17% as October ended. This is tumultuous for any nation’s economy as there is no resounding direction for the country and a clear failure of governance policy, which itself is due for a resurrection in February 2026 as riots and political instability are back in the headlines once again. And after a brief spell of marginal conclusions, the nation’s waterfront is back down to a stranded lone wolf with no fresh arrivals this week.

As such, it is set to be a much quieter end to 2025 than previously perceived – especially in a giant market like Bangladesh and especially after a promising start to the year, but an uncertain mid- year HKC + Trump-cola cocktail with an election cherry on top will ensure the end of the year for the Chattogram Choppers will be a messy one.

headline: TRADING DAY?
highlights: Defunct market. | Below 400. | Supply low. | HKC works. | Limping.
body_text:
Some other day, just not today, or this week, or this month, or this year, or the last few for that matter. As president economic turmoil tears down the White House back home and economies around the world, his actions are directly leading to a meltdown that has consistently been affecting international markets month after month, including the advent of November 2025 as inflation is still rising at key ship recycling destinations, global steel prices are collapsing, currencies devaluing like it’s an overdue assignment, and a disjointed ratio of trading units vs recycling volumes, all wrapped up in a 2025 burrito of unnecessary bombastic.

To start, inflation is on the rise again in Pakistan with Turkey and Bangladesh reporting barely noticeable corrections – all while India and USA figures are still lampooning with pending updates at their ends. The Baltic Exchange also rose to the tune of nearly 2% in just about a month with Capes, Panamax, and smaller segment indices all clocking the week out with 3.1%, 09%, and 0.5% respective gains and the overall index firming 7% just this week. As sanctions and bans increasingly strike at the world’s trading units and the balance of the legally trading group seems increasingly burdened with shouldering the load of missing tonnage, which itself cannot even be recycled anywhere, it is certainly starting to show at the waterfront once again. And for the world of ship recycling, is a disastrous turn of events as 2026 is already at attention on the horizon.
