Oil is likely to see similar performance hiccups as it declined nearly 20 basis points to end the week at levels barely above USD 60/barrel thank to global supply being on cue to outpace demand as the U.S. ramps up domestic production and investors continue to monitor the effects of Washington’s pressure-tactics on Moscow via pending sanctions on their top oil majors, including Rosneft PJSC and LukOil PJSC (LukOil even rumored to be filing for bankruptcy this week) and purchasing nations such as China and India now facing further economic pressures of their own. And all this while Dollars and lack of diplomacy are steering currencies into neverland.

headline: QUANTUM ENTANGLED!
highlights: Stranded. | Harrowed. | Mini-VLs. | Adept.
body_text:
One of the quirks of quantum mechanics is the ability a particle to be in two places at the same time in the micro-word, and Alang has managed to display a similar position in the real world where on the one hand, it has been and remains stranded at the bottom of the market rankings for what seems like an eternity now, and yet, it has been the top spot for incoming tonnage and deliveries week after, taking in a comparative plethora of tonnage while sailing through a drought of unavailability and being hit by financial storms and economic uncertainties.

And while a healthy majority of Alang recyclers have been forced to remain in a perennial wait and watch mode, Alang overall continues to surprisingly impress despite its poor market levels and a harrowing period of declines in steel and currency values.

Over USD 50/LDT has been wiped clean from domestic steel plate prices over the last few months including this week, where it fell a couple of Dollars to wind the week at USD 388.95/Ton – a clear indication of local recyclers destined to battling inevitable losses on upcoming deliveries. The currency meanwhile held on to the other end of the buckling stallions fraying economic reigns as it has declined to historical record-highs against U.S. Dollar of late – including this week winding it down at Rs. 88.67.

But Alang’s HKC prowess has certainly come through for this market as Alang has been the flourishing yet miserably priced destination that continues to report incoming units week after week, including this one where a couple of mini-VLCCs slid into local anchorage (one isn’t on the report as its still at outer anchorage and officially unreported).

As such, whether we see India get back to any reasonable level of buying before the end of the year or not, this market seems to be the puzzling and untold champion of 2025 and remains the “go to” destination, despite India and even the industry juggles economic meltdowns and fresh HKC hurdles – both of which nervy Alang recyclers seem clearly adept at handling.

headline: DEAD CANARY!
highlights: Steel worries. | Yards must upgrade. | No go low LDT.
body_text:
Despite a fire brewing in Gadani’s ship recycling sector, the “canary in the coal mine” remains dead silent in the fiery face of severely degraded levels of inactivity over the last few months, as the Pakistani market sinks to new lows across recent weeks with levels across the offer board now well below USD 400/LDT - largely due to the ongoing dumping of cheaper Iranian steel imports that keep undercutting local steel plate prices, which themselves have puzzlingly managed to stay nailed at USD 614/Ton, a massive margin over competing markets - especially India.

And the PKR? Like its neighbors, down 5 basis points to close the week out as PKR 282.50 against the U.S. Dollar.

Moreover, while Pakistan was celebrating a lower-than-its-neighbors 20% tariff quota, reality has strung an entirely different chord for the nation’s economy as inflation has skyrocketed from 3% back in August to 6.2% last month, further adding to Gadani’s perennially confusing vessel pricing strategies.

HKC hurdles meanwhile remain the primary contributors to the afflictions of this market amidst a reality that has ship owners and cash buyers spoked about the possibility of international prosecution outcomes – and a Gadani market that is still twiddling on temporary DASR approvals just to keep the domestic sector alive as despite news of ongoing local infrastructure upgrades, not a single yard has received its accreditation, far from officially entering the HKC arena.

Local deliveries too have dried up with Pakistan and Bangladesh twinning their anchorages as no fresh arrivals were reported for this week in Gadani as well.

As such, quiet has mostly descended on the waterfront with little for end buyers to chirp about and like ongoing interactions at the bidding tables, ship owners and cash buyer options are invariably funneled down to a stable Alang. Go figure!

headline: SILENT AS SHE STOWS!
highlights: 2026 door.
body_text: Lira plummeted nearly 40 basis points this week to close it out at a historically whopping TRY 42.23 against the U.S. Dollar while local levels have improved firmly in a beleaguered effort to entice a vessel (or two) into local port limits. Not many thus far and we’re knocking on 2026’s door.

headline: BARREN, YET BOLD?
highlights: Influx. | Barren 2025. | New Twilight. | Unchallenged.
body_text:
Despite all their efforts and firmer offers emanating out of Chattogram, very few market sales have been realized of late. Yet, it does seem as though several private units including those idling in cash buyer inventories that were likely awaiting a positive market movement without much luck, have clearly helped local recyclers this week as Chattogram’s waterfront reported an influx of tonnage that saw 7 vessels and nearly 66K LDT suddenly arrive the nation’s recycling anchorage just this week, including at least one large 21K LDT dry bulk unit.

An anemic yet growing demand from an increasingly hungry / desperate set of local recyclers of late has likely attributed to this outcome since Bangladesh has suffered a nearly barren 2025 ever since the HKC came into effect - save for a promising start to the year that essentially banked primarily on large LDT dry bulk / LNG units, we have seen very few vessels heading to Bangladeshi shores since June.

30% tariffs, overly paralyzing monsoons, political instability and unrest over the upcoming February 2026 elections, economic downturns, volatile inflationary figures, a collapsing Taka, and recently retreating local steel plate prices have all been delivering a death of a thousand cuts to the local ship recycling mindset over the last 2 quarters. In fact, just this week, we saw the Taka plunge nearly 40 basis points down to BDT 122.35 against the U.S. Dollar, whilst local steel plate prices took up the challenge and fell a meager USD 1/Ton after flatlining for the entire week.

With political violence now being reported, even day-to-day life in Chattogram seems to be coming under stress as daily headlines news on security lapses make the rounds as economic activity in the nation continues to take a hit. And with a healthy level of incoming units this week, it is very likely that we see the Bangladeshi ship recycling market enter a new twilight of absence at the bidding tables.

For now, the forecast for Bangladesh’s 2025 end remains unchallenged and otherwise expectedly barren for the most part, unless some of the better numbers for select tonnage seen over recent times continue to hold, especially as the industry moves towards the crucial local elections ahead.

headline: DESPERATE DOWNERS?!
highlights: Precarious. | Activity rises. | Price lull. | HKC diligence. | Socially busy.
body_text:
With the last 6 weeks of 2025 now firmly on the horizon, the final stretch of the year continues to demonstrate its sheer unwillingness to compromise as global economies are still reporting volatile movements of commodity prices and oil futures that are still unfolding with each passing week. But the ship recycling market economies are the ones generating even more confounding results amid an increasingly precariously posture at just how this momentum has been unravelling over the last 3 – 4 years and is now expected (feared) to likely continue deep into 2026.

While the Baltic Exchange Dry Index reported gains once again this week on the back of virtually all inclusive sub-sectors reporting improvements of their own through the week, oil futures on the other hand seem to be taking a beating after levels clocked the week out at USD 59.50/barrel after Ukraine successfully carried out a massive drone attack against Russia’s largest oil refinery located at Novorossiysk. The U.S. Dollar meanwhile continues its carnage across the globe as it firmed at nearly all locations across the board while local steel plate prices in the two steady recycling destinations retreated in varying degrees.

This double gut-punch targeted at the purchasing prowess of the ship recycling fraternity has driven demand and vessel offerings even further down this week as vintage tonnage starts to unexpectedly arrive at anchorages i.e. Bangladesh, which healthily beat India’s beaching quota for this week. Moreover, with freight rates continually rising / yielding profitable results for relevant stakeholders, recycling sales have been slow for the most part of the year even though sales activity has comparatively picked up a touch since the barren summer slump. Worse yet, many of the transactions concluded are at levels far below expectations and in the low USD 400s/LDT, with several reportedly in the high USD 300s/LDT on less preferred / small LDT tonnage.

Meanwhile, the poorer placed India and Pakistan continue struggling to register any worthwhile levels for owners / cash buyers despite the supply of older dry bulk units – particularly vintage handymax and panamax units including small -to medium- sized-tankers – registering an increase in the number of candidates being proposed for recycling. Yet, just how many are actually being concluded amidst a sea of boring offers remains inconclusive even though several end-of-life MR tankers, smaller product tankers, and a steady stream of occasional LNGs have kept ship recycling markets from dozing off completely in the latter part of this year.

headline: VIEW FROM BELOW!
highlights: Silence descends. | USD 600/Ton? | Hopes ahead. | Unexpceted.
body_text:
Alang’s slide down the foothills of the price rankings mountain has seen an increasing silence descend across the industry, given that India has been the only worthwhile destination to seriously consider of late, with a far more capable set of local recyclers and a strongly established HKC base. And as clearly evident from this week’s port position, this still seems to be the case given that a bunch of smaller LDT units, which more than likely did not find a retirement spot on the beaches of Gadani, have happily ended up in Alang instead.

And with little demand and minimal offers emanating from the largest and most HKC approved destination in the world today, such a reticence and disillusionment over the ongoing performance of industry is a worrying factor and for what has been an overall declining and lethargic market over the course of 2025 and even back in 2024, where levels not-since-seen the highs of USD 600/LDT has turned the business of ship recycling into a struggle for survival for the 100 HKC approved yards that still stand in operation today.

The crushing decline in supply has maintained posture and the sporadic flurry of incoming units certainly deceives the number of deliveries the entire sub-continent has otherwise been acclimatized to and left even ship owners and cash buyers worrying where their end-of-life assets will eventually price out on the books, especially as fundamentals continue taking a hammering. The Rupee lost 11 basis points to end the week at Rs. 88.70, local steel plate prices were the only ones to make an unexpected turnaround by about USD 4/Ton, though it remains far from stable territory to where acceptable offerings on smaller LDT dry units could scrape past USD 400/Ton.

Seems 2026 is gearing up to be a playback of 2025 with its own flavour of unexpected coming the industry’s way – especially given how things are playing out worldwide.

headline: REDUCED OUTPUT!
highlights: Under performing. | Lowly does it. | Pressure needed.
body_text:
After an altogether (comparatively) healthier few months of deliveries and reported yard upgrades that have yet to deliver the nation’s first HKC approved ship recycling yard, the Pakistani market’s performance continues to leave an unimpressive mark on the industry with lackluster offerings at the bidding tables, assurances of compliance via provisional DASR certificates, poorly performing economy, an inflation that has more than doubled in the span of a couple of months, and a local ship recycling mindset that is being hammered by the inflow of far cheaper Iranian product that continues undercutting local steel plate prices.

In fact, we finally saw the first signs of this hitting the domestic ship recycling community where it hurts most, in local steel plate prices that not only opened the week lower than last, but remarkably, managed to even decline a whopping USD 13/Ton and below the USD 600/Ton mark for the first in a few quarters. Not to be outdone, the PKR too fell about 11 basis points and closed the week out at levels approaching PKR 283 against the U.S. Dollar, at PKR 282.80.

This has left Gadani positioned just above a lackluster Alang and leaving not much else on the table in terms of safe redeliveries. Case-and-point, if a tiny 1400 Ton straggler can manage to remain stranded at anchorage for nearly 2 months, it certainly leaves no room for owners / cash buyers of larger LDT units to risk the Pakistani market, especially amidst this ongoing decline.

HKC hurdles have certainly left this market stranded in the face of the competition as no new vessels have arrived Gadani this week and authorities will ultimately have to fuel progress at yards in order to remain relevant. Even with incoming cheaper steel product, higher tariffs on imported steel need to be imposed so that the state of affairs doesn’t cannibalize local business viability.

The big question remains, when and how soon will any of this come into effect as it is clear that Pakistan will likely spend the rest of the year (like India) in a disheveled state. Worse yet? Much like the last 2 years and especially 2023 have turned out, where a meager 16 vessels were delivered locally over the entire year, to snap that figure into perspective, this is the number of vessels across all anchorages just this week.

A truly disappointing turnaround for such a big market.

headline: SO, WHAT ELSE IS NEW?
highlights: High-stakes.
body_text:
Can’t talk about the weather in here but there’s just little to discuss about Aliaga. And sadly, there’s nothing other than the perennial decline of the Lira to first highlight as it declined a healthy 25 basis points into neverland and passed TRY 42.30 against the U.S. Dollar, making the recent price hike in the face of declining fundamentals that much more confounding.

The price of hoping to remain in business is certainly high stakes.

headline: TWENTY UP!
highlights: Anorexia | Some units sold. | 20 HKC. | SSORP in action.
body_text:
Bangladeshi pricing and demand continue to lead the way across global ship recycling markets, even though there have been very few workable candidates to placate increasingly hungry end users. Although a series of older tankers managed to find their way to end buyers at decent levels over recent weeks and larger LNGs have remained the flavor of late, it has been a far quieter week at the waterfront, much more than many had been expecting, and frustrating given the fact that by this point of the year, the volume of units delivered has been abysmal as the nation continues battling economic anorexia for much of the year.

With inflation yoyoing around the 8%–9% mark for much of the year and the Bangladeshi Taka (like India) struggling to stabilize itself since June 2024, this week saw the Taka declining over 20 basis points to close the week out at BDT 122.53 against the U.S. Dollar – gradually approaching BDT 123. Local steel plate prices also seem to have hit an oil patch on the road and started declining over recent weeks, including this week, where they fell again, albeit by a marginal USD 1/Ton, as they closed the week out at USD 525.93/Ton.

Clearly, the unsold volumes of recycled steel that have been piling up at local recycling yards since the summer months have left Chattogram chop shops scrambling to make domestic deals with steel mills even at breakeven levels, unfortunately without much success thus far as, like Pakistan, cheaper imported scrap steel continues to take the limelight. And with the upcoming elections of February 2026 heating up the nation, domestic peace has taken a hit as well, with sporadic reports of political violence sprinkling the national headlines.

Meanwhile, another HKC approval has come through this week as the remaining unapproved yards endure infrastructure upgrades, taking the total to 20 approved HKC yards by various bodies (NK, BV, IRS, etc.), and several more are set to follow in the month ahead before year end. In fact, GMS is pleased to report that its Sustainable Ship and Offshore Recycling Program (SSORP) has certainly helped, as free safety and training sessions for workers across India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan have been going on at pace. As of October 2025, the program successfully completed 766 training sessions and reached 11,730 workers on 69 safety and environmental topics.

Overall, it seems 2025 is destined to end just like 2024 – hammered by availability and collapsing prices but with an HKC medal in Chattogram’s back pocket.

headline: FORUMS AND FRICTIONS!
highlights: Annual event. | Dark challenges. | Pak HKC. | More muted. | Busy times ahead.
body_text:
This has been a disastrous week for nearly all the key indicators tracked in this newsletter, including the state of oil futures, freight rates, local steel plate prices, and disastrous currency devaluations (especially in India). To start, oil found itself slipping rather shockingly as it fell to USD 57.68/barrel – a total drop of over 6% in the last month and over 16% lower than the same time last year. As oil slipped, freight rates continued to climb throughout the week, recording a near 9% decline over the course of 30 days and over 48% as compared to November 2024.

At the same time, governments in the U.S. continue their sanctions and blacklist wave as EU members too are reportedly preparing the 20th batch of sanctions against Russia that could authorize member-state navies and coast guards to board shadow-fleet vessels suspected of carrying sanctioned cargoes. The proposal also considers granting third-country flag administrations permission to deregister such vessels and further tighten flag-state cooperation to curb evasive shipping activities. Moreover, the U.S. continues to tighten Iran’s economic activities and levy further sanctions that have now wrapped a reported 170 ships in the tangle of global blacklists.

All of this has trickled down to the ship-recycling industry, as not only is supply getting increasingly restricted (as evident from the quantum of the week’s deliveries at the various sub-continent waterfronts), but steel plate prices also fell in both Bangladesh and Pakistan, all while Bangladeshi and (especially) Indian currencies staged a late-Thanksgiving horror show this week. As the trading tables went comparatively quiet, much of the industry remained distracted as many gathered in Hong Kong for the annual Tradewinds Ship Recycling Forum. Among the many topics that were hot points of debate were future trends, supply, HKC developments, the dark-fleet problems plaguing the industry, and what possible solutions (if any) lie ahead. It is apparent that what happens with the dark/shadow fleet is of utmost importance given that over 900 vessels are now on the list with no viable exit or strategy for when they come of recyclable age.

Unlike forums of yesteryear, where plenty of trading and recycling deals were concluded on the conference floor, this year was far more muted in terms of deal flow, supply of vessels, and the dampened pricing and demand. The event was well attended by end users, cash buyers, insurers, and lawyers, all expecting (more like hoping, after the performance of the last few years) that vessels across the whole trading spectrum that are approaching 30 years of age and older should see a busy few years of activity in 2026.

headline: LOSING BIG-LY!
highlights: Failing to transact. | HKC advantage lost. | Arrowing down. | Quivering.
body_text:
An anxious and increasingly fraught Indian market has once again failed to successfully transact any serious tonnage this week as recyclers remain reticent to offer, with markets so weak and fundamentals entering a performance comatose on the back of a declining Rupee that fell nearly 1.10% in just five days, closing the week out deep into Rs. 89 territory against the U.S. Dollar at Rs. 89.61. As the currency teeters on the edge of a massive Rs. 90, perennially nervy Alang recyclers have clearly spoken out loud in silence via no meaningful offerings at the bidding tables.

Local steel plate prices too remain stranded under USD 400/Ton, even though they marked a healthy USD 5/Ton improvement this week, clocking in at USD 398/Ton and further cementing offers for smaller LDT / less-preferred tonnage at well under USD 400/Ton. But even this improvement in steel plate prices remains “too little too late” as the Rupee continues to decimate the sentiments and expectations of delivering deals into Alang that would remain in the green for the ship recycler by the time the vessel(s) arrive(s) and are eventually recycled. The nation’s overall economic state too is slipping into stagflation territory, as inflation fell to just 0.25% through October – down from 1.44% in September and well below the 2%–2.5% that the government was hoping to stabilize it at.

Meanwhile, adding fuel to the competitive fire are both Pakistan and Bangladesh, who are now at the early stages of catching up with Indian HKC yards. Although Pakistan remains some ways away, it is certainly a matter of time in 2026 when India will start losing its HKC edge. Moreover, in tandem with global stock markets, Indian offerings continue on a downward trajectory and have done so with determination over the last month, as end recyclers grapple with a two-tiered market due to the thorny issue of cheaper-priced dark fleet tonnage being imported, cheap steel from abroad, and even dithering steel prices that are contributing to the local quivering.

With Alang’s port position turning bare after a spate of local deliveries this week – down to just one vessel idling at anchorage and no market fixtures reported – the writing is on the wall for Alang as December slowly creeps in.

headline: MAKEOVER!
highlights: Landmark news! | Mexican stand-off | Momentum shifting.
body_text:
Landmark and encouraging news has emerged from Pakistan this week, with the first domestic ship recycling yard set to be HKC-approved and due for an announcement in the coming week(s) after all audits are signed off and HKC infrastructure upgrade works are reportedly completed. This is certainly revelatory news for a market that led the sub-continent price rankings for a healthy few months in the summer, but has unfortunately fallen behind its sub-continent counterparts ever since the Hong Kong Convention finally came into force on June 26th, 2025.

While several more yards are set to follow with HKC approvals within the next 3–6 months to keep the local momentum moving, another handful are expected to join the fray by the summer of next year as the industry in Pakistan gets the makeover it has been urging for many a year. Yet, this promising news will unlikely deviate any tonnage towards Gadani shores on the back of provisional DASR certifications and approvals.

Moreover, adding to the local negative temperament are the ongoing inflictions from last week that continued into this week as well, with weakening fundamentals and competing (cheaper) steel imports from Iran dragging local steel plate prices down by the week — including this one, where they fell a massive USD 11/Ton to USD 586/Ton — even though they remain the highest in the sub- continent ship recycling industry. The Pakistani Rupee somehow managed to evade a Mexican stand-off against the U.S. Dollar as it recovered nearly 5 basis points and ended the week at a still- high PKR 282.58.

This is also the third week of no fresh arrivals at the waterfront, with the only local delivery being that of a distraught vessel that had been idling for over a month at Gadani’s waterfront. And like India, Pakistani recyclers are watching India’s pricing movements closely to determine where their next pricing index will land for the coming week(s), resulting in another no-sale week for this market where the Gadani Gang also refrained from offering.

With the overall macro situation on the freight index not helping ship recycling by way of a sustained supply, it is likely Gadani will traverse December much like Alang — waiting for some stability to rein in the maddening state of affairs.

headline: NOTHING NEW!!
highlights: Supply pillow.
body_text: Lira’s down another 30+ basis points against the U.S.$. this week and past TRY 42.40 against the U.S. Dollar, steel plate prices are stagnating, demand is suffocating by the supply pillow and there’s simply nothing new to talk about right now.

headline: IN VOGUE!
highlights: HKC focus. | Dollars and Cents | Work ongoing. | Uncomfortable.
body_text:
The focus in Bangladesh over the last five months has been clearly targeted at bringing domestic ship-recycling yards up to speed, with tremendous progress having been made on HKC infrastructure upgrade work. Twenty-one yards are now approved (under NK, IR, BV classes), and another yard has reportedly reached completion, taking the total to 22 set to follow shortly. While this is certainly encouraging news for the industry as a whole, on an individual basis the fractured state of supply continues to make ship recyclers at these yards wonder if such gratuitous expenses during a four-year spell of tonnage drought have been financially worth it, because at the end of the day, it’s all dollars and cents.

And deservedly so. The last four years have brought massive instability to the nation via skyrocketing and volatile inflation, a Bangladeshi Taka that has dragged local pricing down— collapsing from the highs of USD 600/Ton to USD 400/Ton since January 2024—political instability, national riots, uncontrollable monsoons, cheaper steel imports that have, for the first time, hammered local sentiments in unexpected ways, and local steel plate prices that are escaping down a chute like a bad dinner.

Speaking of local steel plate prices, they fell even further this week (as they have for several weeks now), dropping USD 11/Ton and closing the week at USD 506/Ton—a massive fall from above USD 600/Ton and now potentially approaching sub-USD 500/Ton through December. The Taka, on the contrary, managed to escape last week’s fate, firming nearly 30 basis points and ending the week at BDT 122.08 against the U.S. Dollar.

The nation’s prevailing sentiments also continue to remain fragile as the interim government stays in a paralytic state, and tensions and bursts of local political violence remain scattered across the nation as the upcoming elections of February 2026 linger on the collective minds of the populace. Steel imports also continue to affect the resale values of recycled ships’ steel that remains at local yards, even though incoming imports over the last couple of weeks indicate local resale movements and emptying plots that have respective yard owners eager to take in units. This week’s anchorage certainly reflected that sentiment as a collection of various sub-10K units earmarked the waterfront.

Pricing meanwhile has managed to remain the most impressive in the sub-continent (although that isn’t saying much given the quantum of declining levels across the industry), while levels over USD 400/LDT are regularly available for larger LDT, good-condition units, with smaller vessels generally taking the pricing brunt well below USD 400/LDT—if any interest were to arise at all. As such, the next quarter is certainly of interest to those with tonnage to sell

headline: STUMPED, YET PRIMED!
highlights: First Pak HKC. | 21 up in Bangla. | Lowly markets. | Few ships. | Focus firm.
body_text:
Global market chaos continues post-Thanksgiving like a bad stomach after too much turkey. Steel plate prices were the highlight of the entire sub-continent—and even China—where they unanimously retreated in unison this week, while the U.S. Dollar also decided to join in on the fun as it too retreated at all sub-continent locations (except—no surprise—Turkey!). Making matters worse are the rising freight markets that continue to surprise the industry, as the Baltic Exchange’s Dry Index climbed another 3.2% through the course of the week, hitting a new high since December 2023 as practically every segment assisted in with the rising rates. Oil, meanwhile, remains at 21st- century lows, idling with marginal fluctuations, yet it closed the week out at USD 59.16/Ton—a near 14% drop over the last 12 months.

As supply continues to be restricted by the widening net of sanctions and blacklists in addition to rising freight rates, it was still a kind gesture by the gods of tonnage that both Bangladesh and India mercifully reported fresh arrivals and deliveries at the waterfront, all while Pakistan’s dithering local anchorage returned zilch this week. Prices too remain fragile amidst dreadful fundamentals that haven’t gotten a chance to get off their respective trampolines, as most of the tonnage introduced to the markets is either an off-market questionably sourced unit or smaller LDT units that are regularly seeing sub-USD 400/Ton from key locations, creating a dual-priced reality for the markets.

Yet in the midst of uncertainty, a momentous development unraveled this week with the first Pakistani ship-recycling yard to be awarded HKC compliance, as Prime Green Recyclers became the first in the nation to join the array of international yards—bringing Pakistan into the new league. Prime Recyclers attained Bureau Veritas (BV) blessings after the requisite investment and infrastructure upgrades spanning this past year bore fruit, and the matter became critical after the Hong Kong Convention came into force on June 26th. This follows on the heels of 21 Bangladeshi yards receiving their HKC accreditations and a 22nd yard set to reportedly follow imminently, as compliance is firmly underway at both locations to revolutionize and improve domestic standards and catch up to Alang, where over 100 yards have been HKC compliant—some practically for over a decade now.

headline: LOSING HOPE!
highlights: Below 400. | Diversions. | Culprits.
body_text:
A lowly Alang market remains positioned below USD 400/LDT on most tonnage and is thus out of the picture for the collection of competitive vessels that have been making the rounds of late. Making matters even more challenging is their inability to negotiate effectively on HKC tonnage for select local yards, as Bangladesh is clearly catching up with a larger fraction of HKC yards—and even Pakistan finally entering the ring.

Indeed, even favored LNG vessels rich in non-ferrous (if MOSS type) have found their retirement spots in Bangladesh in recent times, so poor have levels from Alang been recently. Local anchorage, however, mercifully managed to take in their regular share of questionable tankers, which have been finding India a convenient location to offload.

What has been really affecting the local purchasing mindset are the key fundamentals: not only did the Indian Rupee plummet into the high INR 89s—despite firming 28 basis points against the U.S. Dollar this week and closing out at INR 89.35—but local steel plate prices fell USD 5/Ton this week, clocking out at USD 390/Ton.

Yet the Indian economy has been generating positive results, as the nation’s GDP climbed 8.2% on the back of improvements in the construction and manufacturing sectors, prompting industry pundits to improve future growth prospects for the economy.

Even so, recycling remains in shambles as competing nations are comparatively higher placed and keep chipping into Alang’s HKC share, while fundamentals affecting the nation’s ship-recycling sector have clearly been the pricing culprits for this struggling market.

headline: FIRST HKC!
highlights: Big news! | Others to follow. | Status quo.
body_text:
This has truly been one of the most momentous weeks not only for Pakistan’s ship-recycling sector, but also for the nation’s ship-recycling future, as Prime Green Recyclers of Gadani have become the first HKC-approved facility in Pakistan, with BV announcing the momentous news this week.

This is a major milestone for the sector as it finally brings Gadani into the big leagues, and all it will take now is a willing group of shipowners and/or cash buyers to propose vessels locally and evaluate the efficacy of the upgrades and ensuing recycling processes. As several more yards are also undergoing HKC upgrades, it is likely we may see the next round of approvals come through reportedly within the next 3–4 months.

Yet, like India, the nation’s economy remains in a fragile state, as not only did local steel plate prices fall USD 7/Ton and wrap the week up at USD 579/Ton, but the Pakistani Rupee firmed a relatively minor 9 basis points and ended the week at PKR 282. While these numbers are certainly far better than those from competing India (helping the Gadani Gang maintain their position in the market rankings), the lack of HKC yards has punished Gadani’s anchorage by ending another week with an utterly empty waterfront.

As such, it has remained a quiet week in terms of sales and activity, and with the bulk of the tonnage delivered into Bangladesh clearly opening up in the Far East and India taking in units, the future for Gadani across December will likely maintain the status quo.

headline: CHANGING TACTICS!!
highlights: Unstoppable.
body_text:
The Lira’s decline continues unabated as it fell 15 basis points and breached TRY 42.50 against the U.S. Dollar, as the Turkish government finally decided to step in and announce economic measures to curtail this seemingly unstoppable decline. Surprisingly, amidst inflation nearing 33%, GDP posted nearly 5% growth in the second quarter, easing some financial stresses for its citizens.

For Aliaga’s citizens, however, the situation remains rather dim.

headline: WAIT CONTINUES!
highlights: Cooling off. | Demand ripe. | LNGs to arrive.
body_text:
After a fruitful month of HKC progress that included an impressive couple of weeks of tonnage deliveries, the Bangladeshi ship recycling market seemed to rapidly cool this week, ensuring that any of the slim pickings of units making the rounds at the bidding tables continued to see lower overall levels now that most Chattogram recycling yards had taken in at least one unit across November.

Adding to the disappearing flavor of the local purchasing mindset has been the curated collective of fundamentals that mercifully timed their arrival this week, after all local deliveries had been completed as not only did the BDT lose 35 basis points against the U.S. Dollar ending the week at BDT 122.35, but local steel plate prices also fell by about USD 5/Ton to end the week at USD 502/Ton. Clearly afflicted by the recent performance of fundamentals and other than a sea of deliveries of tonnage that in fact arrived last week, not a single fresh unit greeted Chattogram’s waterfront this week.

Through it all, and as stated in the Market Commentary above, HKC upgrades continue at pace locally as 22 ship recycling yards have now received their HKC accreditations since March this year and, as space slowly clears up on the back of declining plate levels that clearly suggest recycled material is now moving off local yards, local appetite seems to be getting its rumbles in what has historically been one of the busiest times of the year for businesses wanting to close their books.

Economically overall, inflation is expected to continue lingering around the high 8.x% range as an economic stagnation seems to fill the domestic environment, given that there have still not been any economic policies set in place to accelerate domestic growth by the interim government, which itself is aware of its impending dissolution come February 2026 on the back of the upcoming elections and a fresh new government finally taking the reins.

In the interim, local recyclers will likely keep themselves busy with several of the larger LDT LNGs that have ended up in Bangladesh over the last few months (including HKC select yards only from both Seapeak and MISC). It seems like it’s destined to be a silent Christmas after all. Silent Christmas.

headline: TURKEY, AND HAM…STRUNG!
highlights: Lacking. | HKC boon. | Upgrades work. | Pak advances. | Slowing supply.
body_text:
As we head into the traditionally quieter festive / Christmas season, ship recycling markets appear to be hamstrung on the back of a stubborn and persistent lack of meaningful tonnage, violently collapsing fundamentals that were promptly followed by declining offers, and all of this ongoing non-stop for nearly all of 2025 that has seen purchasing sentiment in a post-HKC world get crushed under the weight of it all.

To start, the onset of December brought with it a declining Baltic Exchange that saw the Dry Index fall by about 3%, this week, dragged down by mounting pressure across all segments that saw capes slipping 4.4%, panamax dropping 1.4%, and the smaller segments shedding 5 basis points, all while oil barely moved the needle as it closed another week at region USD 59.70/barrel (expected to breach USD 60/barrel in the coming week) and inflation reported minor improvements at a couple of key ship recycling destinations.

But it were financial currencies that really battered both India and Bangladesh, all while Turkey perennially decorated the top three of the declining currency marathon that it alone has been on. Not wanting to be left behind, local steel plate prices also fell by just under USD 5/ton across all sub- continent recycling destinations, leaving ship recyclers firmly holding off on further negotiations as the week ended.

As such, the lack of tonnage has delivered yet another characteristically low supply of vessels for a few weeks now, especially considering the lack of the occasional large LDT LNG vessels (with around 15 sold so far this year) drying up as freight rates continue to remain at elevated overall levels, thus depriving ship recyclers for yet another week. Further cementing this fact was the sheer lack of arrivals at every sub-continent ship recycling location – probably a true first in its own right.

Thankfully, compulsion has successfully driven remarkable developments across the Indian sub- continent ship recycling sector, with HKC infrastructure upgrades still ongoing and a confirmed 23 HKC-certified ship recycling yards now added to the existing sub-continent fleet of HKC certified yards – including Pakistan’s first HKC approval that was announced just last week. Ever since the Hong Kong Convention came into force on June 26th earlier in the year, it has been encouraging to see increased investments and upgrades taking place at these new locations, ensuring a better and safer set of standards for responsible recycling.

Overall, 2025 will probably be the cherry-year of the last four and 2026 hopefully brings more tonnage and stability across the globe.

headline: SET ADRIFT!
highlights: Little hope. | Poleaxed. | No advantage.
body_text:
India has been set adrift at the bottom of the Indian subcontinent ship recycling price board as Alang recyclers seem to be losing hope of securing any standard, competitive ships any time soon – and rightly so, given that freight markets continue to soar at impressive highs.

Buckled tighter by the increasing number of vessels being added to the list of international sanctions and blacklists as governments globally battle for economic attrition against embattled nations, Alang’s waterfront highlighted the situation incredibly well this week, with not a single fresh arrival reported.

Fundamentals have also been dragging the sentiment canoe down level 1 rapids as not only has the Indian Rupee depreciated against the U.S. Dollar once again by a massive 70 basis points and clock the week out at a deathly Rs. 89.96, but local steel plate prices also retreated a milder USD 4/Ton and end the week at nearly USD 387/Ton – clearly highlighting the upcoming levels of local offerings in the coming weeks.

Unlike their competing neighbours, most Alang yards have been HKC-approved for nearly a decade now, but the state of fundamentals has driven prices so low that local recyclers have simply been unable to hammer home the HKC advantage while competing markets are still having their yards upgraded and infrastructure brought up to HKC standards. Notwithstanding, Alang yards have been comparatively busier than their regional competition would seem to suggest.

Overall, until the supply of tonnage increases, there remains nothing to really report from these markets – other than the unfolding state of fundamentals.

headline: TAILGATING!
highlights: Primetime! | Brief spurt. | Taking stock.
body_text:
Prime Green Recyclers has become the first ever HKC-approved ship recycling yard not only in Gadani, but also the first facility to bring Pakistan into the international playground within 2025. And while progress reportedly continues locally at pace along with infrastructure upgrades, the rest of the sector remains in shambles as prices have largely tailgated India’s (no surprise there), even though they remain higher on the market rankings.

But the double whammy brought on by both an overall scarcity of tonnage along with a prevailing scarcity of HKC-approved yards has left Gadani’s anchorage empty once again this week – and that too for nearly a month now.

After a brief spurt of activity in September backed by comparatively decent levels of DASR assisted local deliveries, local fixtures have all but flatlined over recent weeks as end buyers continue their HKC development work and take stock of where the market may be heading next.

And rightly so, given that local steel plate prices continue to slip by the week as they fell nearly USD 5/Ton again and drifted further down to USD 575/Ton (from the highs of USD 650/Ton), as cheap Iranian imports continue to influence prevailing resale prices of recycled stock. Furthermore, the Pakistani Rupee miraculously firmed despite its depressed overall state as it gained an impressive 45 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and end the week at PKR 280.42.

Overall, a lot of work still lies ahead for Pakistan’s ship-recycling sector and the next batch of yards to achieve HKC approvals will probably be in Q1 2026, whilst several more yards in Bangladesh have infrastructure works underway and are expected to reach HKC status in the months ahead as well.

headline: FIRMING?
highlights: Russian Roulette.
body_text:
A surprising couple of weeks not only saw import steel prices but even local steel plate prices firm by about USD 10/Ton, which in turn promptly transitioned to firmer levels from Aliaga recyclers that jumped by about USD 10/Ton as well.

What jumped as well was the value of the U.S. Dollar against the Turkish Lira, which slipped another 20 basis points and end the week at a disastrous TRY 42.55. Just how soon and effective will the government’s intended economic measures to assist the Lira’s value be, remains to be seen. Until then, it seems like Russian roulette with pricing, just to tempt in more tonnage.

headline: POST-FOREFRONT!
highlights: HKC green sales. | Prices suffer. | Waiting to reconcile. | Promising
body_text:
Chattogram has certainly been at the forefront of recent sales and deliveries, given how busy its waterfront has been throughout November, including a raft of green, HKC-only LNGs to select yards (four in total), a mini cape, and an MR tanker.

And although Bangladesh has remained the highest-priced destination in the market rankings for at least two months now, local recyclers found it pointless to their offerings when their currency was being frayed at the ends week-after-week and local steel plate prices regularly started to see the south side of last week’s levels, compelling recyclers to lower their offerings – especially in the face of declining competitors. As such, the recent sales of these units at below-market prices sent overall vessel pricing across the entire Indian sub-continent reeling, as levels on conventional vessels across the board are increasingly seeing offers at or below USD 400/ton.

With freight rates still high overall, and vintage ’90s bulkers — and even some tankers — still sailing the high seas far longer than expected, it may well be a quieter Christmas/festive period in Bangladesh as end buyers digest some of the recent deliveries and reconcile not only where vessel prices will go, but where the nation overall will head in a post-election era. February 12, 2026, has now been confirmed as the next General Election Day, which will certainly oust this dysfunctional interim government and hopefully induce an economic resurgence that has been sorely lacking in Bangladesh since June 2024.

But anticipation of the upcoming election has also brought with it growing instances of political violence and instability that could make everyday life a hassle as we get closer to the election date — a not-so-uncommon feature of Bangladeshi politics.

As logical/meaningful indications all but disappear off the Bangladeshi end of the bidding tables, local anchorage continues to reflect the state of affairs with only one mid-sized LDT bulker greeting the waterfront this week. And while the currency — which only lost 1 basis point against the U.S. Dollar — could have offered “some” encouragement to the local mindset, it was collapsing local steel plate prices that essentially dictated the tone for local offerings, as they fell a massive USD 9/ton dropping below USD 502/ton from last week’s close to the high USD 493s/ton this week.

Where the market goes from here as we wait for demand and levels to pick up again heading into the new year, remains to be seen- but Bangladesh is not a promising destination in the short run.

headline: DECEMBER DOWNERS!
highlights: Festive decline. | Cheap Green. | Supply boost. | Bangla takes. | HKC continues.
body_text:
Markets across the board seem to be getting hit by the tragedies of 2025 as December firmly stamps its footprints across the 2025 ship-recycling timeline, ensuring the situation doesn’t get a chance to improve just yet! Inflation is on the rise again, plate prices are collapsing in the wrong places, all while the U.S. Dollar continues to rummage through the wreckage of 2025 for whatever it can suck out of ship-recycling currencies and both freight rates & oil futures tumble in unison — just within the span of week 50.

To start, the Baltic Exchange Dry Index reportedly fell nearly 4%, down to its lowest level in nearly a month, dragged by capes that fell 5.6%. Panamax followed suit with a 2.1% drop, and smaller vessels wrapped up the cold blanket with a 16-basis-point drop as the cherry on top. And, surprising many industry traders, oil futures failed to hit the much-anticipated USD 60/barrel mark, instead retreating over 3% to USD 57.61/barrel as the week clocked out — amidst global fears primarily brought on by forecasts predicting an overproduction of oil. The International Energy Agency reaffirming its forecast for a “record supply glut.”

Local steel plate prices seemed to slip on the spilling oil figures as they, too, followed suit with noteworthy drops of their own, compounded by slipping currencies as the U.S. Dollar continues to rattle major trading economies.

As the occasional introduction of a market vessel remains the carrot dangling at the end of a drying supply stick, Indian sub-continent ship-recycling markets were already declining, ensuring that the upcoming festive time may perhaps be the perfect moment to reflect and reset after an altogether inadequate and underwhelming few years of horrid supply and ever-declining levels. USD 600/ton was breached back in January 2024, and for a great majority—standing at the doorstep of 2026, and across all sub-continent locations—prices have dipped below the USD 400/ton mark.

While several green vessels have been sold cheaply into Bangladesh over recent weeks, prices here seem to have slipped off the back of a spate of recent deliveries pulling local levels down. Domestic turbulence is unfortunately on the rise in the small nation once again as the final election dates get announced. And although a healthy majority of the recent supply was squarely focused on a Bangladesh redelivery that has now slipped into the background—joining Indian and Pakistani recycling markets on their downward decline once again—evidence was across all the waterfronts this week, including a surprise.

headline: DISCOURAGING!
highlights: Lowest again. | Unable to acquire. | Currency woes.
body_text:
As the lowest-placed Indian sub-continent ship-recycling destination for yet another week, it has been discouraging for Alang recyclers to see usually favoured green vessels heading to Bangladeshi shores rather than India over recent weeks, even while some above-market (for India) offers failed to swing certain vessels further West, despite local demand being relatively firm in the growing impossibility of securing any tonnage at all — so slow has the introduction of vessels been of late.

And given the pitiful levels being tabled from Alang buyers, the number of local arrivals this week certainly highlighted the ongoing diet of tonnage that Alang recyclers are being forcefully fed, while being simultaneously tempted by the fact that far lower-priced, but questionable background units remain omnipresent and able for a quick pick-me.

The state of ongoing offer levels is clearly being dominated by local fundamentals that are in a seriously woeful state, as the already depressed level of local steel prices suffered another brutal hit, losing over USD 7/ton and pulling overall steel trading levels to USD 377/ton. But it has been the Indian Rupee that has been the apostle of misery for the local mindset, as it lost a massive (by recent standards) 65 basis points against the U.S. Dollar once again, closing the week out at a record-breaking INR 90.50.

Stagflation territory, however, seems to be on a diet as inflation levels rose from 0.25% to 0.71% as November wrapped up, even though inflation remains at record-low levels and well below the Reserve Bank of India’s tolerance threshold of 2%. With the Rupee getting ever weaker and local steel plate prices in the middle of a typhoon spin, perhaps this tonnage shortage is what this market needs to stabilize before profitable (for all) deals become the norm rather than the exception.

headline: BREATHTAKINGLY INERT!
highlights: Non serious. | Vessels diverted. | Iranian imports.
body_text:
Despite the recent announcement that Prime Green Recyclers became Pakistan’s first HKC-ratified ship recycling yard, it has been an absolutely inert time for new (any?) business in Gadani as local recycling yards struggle to offer anywhere near acceptable levels for any of the sporadic candidates being offered locally. As a result, anything proposed at the bidding tables almost never greets the local waterfront, given this market’s shortage of HKC yards and prevailing DASR approvals introducing their own set of hula-hoops to wiggle around in.

Surprisingly, however, Gadani ended up being the donor of the surprise anchorage of the week, as—similar to all of its regional competition—local recyclers welcomed at least one smallish LDT unit that likely opened up in regional waters and decidedly wound up in Pakistan, as it would have received lower levels from India, along with a longer voyage and more expensive inward clearance to boot.

Fundamentals here, just like the overall state of global affairs, continue to decimate the ship recycling landscape. Even though an already high inflation improved slightly to 6.1% from 6.2% back in October, local steel plate prices (as in India) have been the deadweight dragging sentiments down of late. After weeks of relentless declines as the market continued to compete against cheaper Iranian imports, levels flatlined at a still-low USD 575/ton. The Pakistani Rupee too found stable footing as ended the week where it started, at PKR 280.35 against the U.S. Dollar.

As vigilance on ship recycling gains increasing global attention and Pakistan suffers its unfortunate fate of lagging behind on the HKC spectrum—and as shipowners worldwide grow increasingly cognizant of their final recycling destinations—even an increase in tonnage supply in 2026 might not alleviate Pakistan’s depressed state.

headline: SLOW END?
highlights: Viva 2026!.
body_text: Lira slipped another 26 basis against the U.S. Dollar and end the week at TRY 42.70 against the U.S. Dollar, all while import and local steel plate prices stabilized this week and the higher levels reportedly bought in no market tonnage this week. Viva 2026!

headline: WILD YEAR!
highlights: 22 yards approved. | Price decline. | LNGs find home. | Shopping Bonanza.
body_text:
While some might see that Bangladesh has endured an positive overall year where ship recycling is concerned — given the progress toward HKC-certified recycling, with 22 domestic ship recycling yards now HKC-accredited by various international bodies and work continuing in the background on a couple more yards — and given that it has enjoyed more time atop the market rankings than its regional neighbors for a majority of the year, offering regionally opening tonnage that extra USD/ton in the bank for all parties involved, that’s about where the parade of pride would likely end.

On the flip side? Literally everything has declined in Bangladesh in 2025. To start, after breaching the USD 600/ton mark back in January 2024, local offerings have now declined by almost USD 200/LDT down to the low USD 400s/LDT, and certainly lower now that a recent surge of tonnage has local bellies full for the time being. Tariffs, the taka, steel plate prices, and a dearth in the supply of tonnage has left this market frustrated and deprived of any regular flow of business sense amid exasperating yard upgrades and infrastructure work, thanks to unexpectedly firm freight trading rates across the board.

And this week was probably 2025’s cherry for Bangladeshi recyclers, as not only did the U.S. Dollar gain 20 basis points — pulling the taka up to BDT 122.30 once again — but local steel plate prices truly stole the spotlight, plummeting a massive USD 12/ton in just five days and closing the week out at USD 485/ton. To remind you, they stood at just over USD 600/ton not 45 days ago, which makes this an instrumental decline behind the ongoing strength of local offerings. And amid the HKC celebrations, we lost track of the fact that Bangladesh has now gone from a market of about 35 ship recycling yards to only 22 (even though a few more are reportedly still in the plans).

For the nation at large, it’s been even worse: 30% tariffs from Trump; the interim government doing its best to redefine lethargy; a monsoon that betrayed local yard-upgrade operations; interim confusion around inward-delivery procedural formalities causing massive delays during August to October across the waterfront — all gift-wrapped in recently resurging political violence that even saw the untimely death of a local electoral candidate, with riots re-erupting at key locations across the nation and business closures once again seemingly imminent as the date of the upcoming elections draws nearer.

Overall, although we can recognize that a large number of LNGs — even for select HKC-only yards for green recycling — were concluded to select end buyers in Bangladesh this year and the nation has now started to feasibly compete with India on these specialist units, it is 2026 that remains pivotal for the nation overall as not only does a hopeful inflow of tonnage likely lie in wait, but the upcoming elections should hopefully jolt the nation’s economy back into gear, just in time for the pre-monsoon shopping bonanza to take on a new meaning.

headline: WT…DECEMBER!
highlights: Landmark year. | Upgrades continue. | Reduced supply. | Freight firm. | Average age up.
body_text:
This year doesn’t cease to surprise, as December just showed what true volatility can be — in a mere two consecutive weeks at that. What a week this has certainly been, where freight rates continue to fall, the U.S. Dollar forgets which way is up, oil rises yet remains low, local steel plate prices slip oddly across the board at the various destinations, all while Turkey enjoys a forced retirement from the sidelines, watching its currency values fall ever deeper into the abyss.

To start, inflation figures that were never released in the U.S. for October due to the government shutdown did come out for November. In Trump’s “hottest country in the world,” his regime reported inflation back down to 2.7% last month. India and Bangladesh were both up, but share the same reasons to celebrate, and Turkey was mercifully down as well. The Baltic Exchange Dry Index reported an overall drop of 2.3% this week, brought on by capes, panamax, and smaller vessels collectively dragging the Baltic down by 1.4%, nearly 5%, and 36 basis points, respectively.

This could likely be brought on by the mixed signals out of the U.S. economic inflation figures, along with oil futures that barely rose 73 basis points and close the week out at a globally welcome low of USD 56.86/barrel. As freight rates continue to fall, a collection of market and private fixtures started to announce their arrivals across sub-continent beaches as famished recyclers await upcoming deliveries. And the U.S. Dollar? I’ll let the rest of the report speak for itself.

Meanwhile, with Christmas just around the corner, we can reflect on what a disastrous yet pivotal year of upgrades and change across the Indian sub-continent ship recycling markets (and even the ship recycling industry writ large) it has been, with the Hong Kong Convention for safe and responsible recycling finally coming into force on June 26 this year. With this landmark set of initiatives and guidelines finally in force, it is encouraging to see most of the previously 100+ yards HKC-certified by various classification bodies in Alang, 22 yards now in Bangladesh, and only one in Gadani (the rest clearly have some catching up to do) fully operational to a set of globally approved standards.

And just like the previous year, we have seen even lower levels of supply this year, following a 2024 that saw decade-low levels of supply. Although the performance of freight markets across all sectors has been largely responsible for the ongoing starvation in the supply of tonnage, could recent declines indicate a positive change for the ship recycling industry come 2026? Perhaps the timing in the shortage of supply was apt, as HKC upgrades and adapting to the new rules and regulations — not only for recyclers, but even local authorities to come to grips with — certainly helped everyone.

headline: TAKING THE PRIZE!
highlights: Dipping below 400. | Vanguard market. | Bootleg paint. | 2026 Workout.
body_text:
India has certainly taken the 2025 prize for having the most torrid year of declines experienced by a ship-recycling destination in recent memory, so drastic has the overall drop over the last quarter been. And it’s not just prices — like Bangladesh, a smorgasbord of tail-spinning events colluded to drag Alang down across nearly all of 2025, and the fact that this market somehow managed to take in the most tonnage and/or HKC units of any ship recycling destination across 2025 while still retaining the title of epicenter of the recycling world across late Q3/early Q4 — and that too in the face of declining local offerings — is a stellar retelling of the convolutions of the ship recycling world.

Levels have certainly dipped below USD 400/LDT for many competitive, and even green, units that have consequently found their way to competing markets in Bangladesh and even Pakistan at different points this year. Worse yet? As the previous leading vanguard market in terms of creating the path on HKC development work, it was certainly frustrating to not see Alang use that to its full potential at any point this year (despite the ongoing shortage of tonnage), or that it will likely ever use it to its full potential again — especially as Pakistani yards start stacking the competitive odds across the entirety of the Indian sub-continent as well.

Fundamentals, fundamentals — where do we even start? The Rupee has turned into the bootleg paint- huffing cousin that everyone somehow aware of, suffering several drops, recoveries, relapses, and recurrent recoveries since Q3 2025, and it took on a whole new energy spike this week as it jumped against the U.S. Dollar by 1.07%, regaining territory back into the INR 89s once again and closing the week out at INR 89.57. Local steel plate prices, especially, seemed to have forgotten what gravity is, reportedly firming a massive USD 10/ton across five days, nearly wiping out recent losses and bringing an added layer of optimism about the next few weeks.

Moreover, some market/private deals seemed to mercifully slip into Alang’s waterfront this week and should keep local recyclers distracted in the face of ongoing sufferance(s), with nearly 26K LT worth of deliveries to look forward to — including a couple of decent LDT tankers.

With a hopeful 202X (another in the series of declining years) coming up, and the outlook being backed by declining freight rates and ever-aging units facing imminent surveys, let’s hope the industry gives the HKC world a true 2026 workout.

headline: ONLY WAY IS UP!
highlights: Encouraging. | Back to buying. | Next approvals due.
body_text:
And for Pakistan, standing on the precipice of 2026, that remains a fact. Not only is it fantastically encouraging to see the first ship recycling yard gain HKC certification last month, but with more reportedly set to join the ranks within Q1 2026 and 2026 hopefully finally shaping up to be a healthier year in terms of supply, Gadani has certainly lined itself up to put a serious dent in the global ship recycling post-HKC era, where redistribution of recyclable tonnage is concerned.

Unfortunately, given Pakistan’s ongoing and serious HKC handicap and despite being placed 2nd

on the market rankings (in terms of pricing), DASR approvals have done their utmost to ensure regular business remains a nightmare. With incoming tonnage being regularly subjected to delays, it is no surprise that the industry remains wary of a Pakistan redelivery.

Case in point: despite being the only recycling destination in the Indian sub-continent that is not tide-reliant and has the least restrictive inward requirements, vessels in a post-HKC era seem to be regularly facing delivery delays, as evidenced by the currently idling mini-VL that has been sitting at anchorage for nearly 20 days now.

Domestic fundamentals too have notably done more to help than hurt Gadani of late, as local steel plate prices jumped by over USD 4/ton and closed the week out near USD 580/ton — an industry- leading margin at present. Moreover, the recently firming PKR — which found itself back down around PKR 280 (from PKR 283) — lost 13 basis points but still closed the week out at PKR 280.30.

Overall, as work continues locally and more yards are set to join the global HKC fray, and as long as fundamentals hold their ground, Gadani is certainly set to have a busy year ahead — especially for the HKC-certified crew.

headline: ENJOYING THE VIEW?
highlights: Russian Roulette.
body_text:
Aliaga recyclers seem to have relegated themselves to a forced holiday, as prevailing government restrictions fine-tuned the madness of the ongoing shortage of tonnage and pushed this market further away from industry attention across all of 2025. And with little else to report beyond the lira’s ongoing ballet as it lost another 27 basis points against the U.S. Dollar this week and closed it out at TRY 42.81, edging ever closer to an imminent breach of TRY 43.

Inflation last month, however, took a notable drop, falling nearly 2% down to TRY 31% (from 32.87% in October) and marking its lowest reading since November 2021. As domestic prices for virtually everything pivot south for the winter, this should also help Aliaga recyclers manage their operational margins a little better — especially in the face of an ever-declining Lira.

With 2026 showing signs of promise, let’s hope Turkey’s current pricing trajectory holds long enough for local recyclers to step back into the game once again.

headline: SLIGHT STAIN!
highlights: Positive fourth | quarter. | Yards filling. | Cheap green affects. | Cheap way is up.
body_text:
The decline in sentiment and pricing that accelerated toward the end of the year has left a slight stain on what has otherwise been a comparatively healthier (for what it’s worth) fourth quarter. Prices have indeed cooled off noticeably from the Bangladeshi corner of the bidding table, and as many of the open and capable yards took in a good bit of tonnage during November’s buffet storm, a shortage of “locally available” reselling options for shipowners and cash buyers looking to fix tonnage has come under severe strain this month.

Notwithstanding, throughout the year, we have seen a collection of larger LDT vessels sold into Bangladesh, including LNGs, mini capes, a collection of large(r) tankers, and several comparatively cheaper green units for recycling. As this has significantly affected December sentiments around how conventional vessels should be priced, it seems the net effect will now be to drag down local offerings even further once the market is eventually back in play.

What is dragging down the local ship recycling fraternity are domestic fundamentals, which continue to display unexpected movements week after week. This week, the Bangladeshi taka managed to firm a mere five basis points against the U.S. Dollar and close at BDT 122.22. But it was local steel plate prices that won the fancy-dress competition as, reportedly, there was a dead halt in local trading, resulting in levels being truly flat on the floor.

Another surprise was local anchorage, which reported a healthy number of arrivals / deliveries, marking the end of the final beaching tide of the year and the closing of books for some buyers. It also clearly highlighted improving performance and speed of inward-clearance formalities at Chattogram anchorage, as some units arrived and were even delivered within days.

Yet, with the nearing of Election Day on February 14, 2026, political violence continues to mar the streets of the nation’s capital, as growing instability is being reported across key political jurisdictions not only in Chattogram, but reportedly across the nation.

Overall, for 2026, Bangladesh seems more optimistically placed on the ship recycling front — and should the political cards fall in favor of the populace, then hopefully the wider economy as well. It seems that for Bangladesh, as a nation, the only way from here is up.

headline: AU REVOIR, 2025!
highlights: Turbulent year. | Scarce supply. | Freight still high? | HKC catch up. | Season’s Wishes!
body_text:
A turbulent 2025 — not only for the ship recycling industry, but for global economies churning under the weight of tariffs, tantrums, and tumultuous international situations — finally comes to a close, there were certainly some positive highlights to note as remarkable progress on HKC infrastructure upgrades has been carried out across the entire Indian sub-continent ship recycling industry right before the year-end — a leaving a positive mark for the ship recycling industry and certainly a welcome sign for 2026.

Yet, the glaring fact remains that prices are far poorer than the USD 600/ton highs of January 2024, driven by consistently declining steel plate prices across the Indian sub-continent markets, coupled with incredible volatility in global currencies/foreign exchange trading, never-ending political events, and a touch of monsoon rainstorms that even brought the weather into the mix. As such, markets continue to shift and slide, while the ongoing scarcity in vessel supply remains ever consistent. It has also been a quiet week at the bidding tables (Christmas mood notwithstanding) and another largely uneventful — and eerily quiet — year on the recycling waterfront, punctuated occasionally by the odd large LDT LNG and older bulker.

But that we hope will change going into 2026, as the Baltic Exchange continued reporting downward trajectory for the dry sectors, falling another 0.8% this week to its lowest levels since October. The decline was driven by an overall retreat in capes (down 0.5%) and the smaller segments that shed 18 basis points. Oil on the other hand, managed to climb to USD 57.21/barrel — a 0.82% increase this week — yet it registered an overall 3.56% drop across December, and a 19.2% overall decline compared to the same time last year. Local steel plate prices, too, surprisingly donned new hats this week, shifting from rising, to falling, to flat-out lack of trading.

As 2026 rolls around next week, and with many expecting freight markets to continue performing into the first half of 2026, the introduction of vessels for recycling could therefore be potentially delayed even further — at least until surveys and dry dockings start kicking in. Hopefully, this delay should create the opportunity for both Pakistan and Bangladesh to make meaningful progress on their HKC journeys, as more yards are expected to be approved by then and ready to take on fresh units in 2026, in line with the Hong Kong Convention.

As 2026 looms and a quiet week ensues, we at GMS wish all our readers and friends, a Happy Christmas and a Happy, Healthy, and Prosperous New Year ahead!

headline: UNTAPPED POTENTIAL!
highlights: Planted at foot. | Missed opportunity. | 2026 hopes.
body_text:
India remains planted firmly at the foot of the global ship recycling market rankings for yet another week/month, capping off an overall miserable year of declining rates, a frighteningly depreciating currency, and collapsing local steel prices that seem to have lost track of time and space.

As competing sub-continent markets continue to catch up on the number of HKC-accredited yards in their respective corners, Alang recyclers seem to have missed their opportunity to use their HKC status to their advantage this year, despite the overall dearth of tonnage that has still managed to produce sporadic phases of inflow of tonnage into competing nations – including HKC units.

But what a year it has truly been for Indian fundamentals — both local steel plate prices and the Indian Rupee, and especially the Rupee over the last two quarters. While local steel plate prices started the year around USD 462/ton and ended the final week of 2026 at a noteworthy USD 393/ton (a USD 70/ton drop), it was the Rupee’s rapid descent that stole the show, with levels across the year declining from a low of Rs. 85.30 to above Rs. 91, and clocking week 52 out at Rs. 89.80 against the U.S. Dollar.

Yet, the nation overall remains in a better economic posture than before, as inflation rises to gradually scoop the country out of stagflation territory. And while economic talks with the White House are reportedly still ongoing, 2025 has been a strong economic year for India, with GDP expanding over 8% in key quarters where projections hovered around 6.5%–7%.

Overall, there are still reasons to be hopeful going into 2026, as more vessels are expected to come for recycling (eventually), which may finally help Alang plots begin to fill their quotas once again.

headline: STARVED PRIDE!
highlights: First HKC. | Serious work. | Back to buying.
body_text:
As 2025 draws to a close, Pakistan can only look back with pride as the nation’s first HKC-approved ship recycling yard joined the international fray — not only for Pakistan, but as a first step onto the global stage.

While earlier in the year, it seemed like an impossibility for Pakistan to catch up with HKC yard- upgrade requirements within 2025 (given how far behind local progress staggered), serious investments and infrastructure updates have taken place in the interim to speed up the process. And with many more yards reportedly on the way scheduled for Q1 2026 approvals, Pakistan may become the one market capable of putting a serious dent into India’s HKC prowess west of Bangladesh.

Adding to Gadani’s favor, and unlike its neighboring competition, are Pakistan’s fundamentals that have remained comparatively tame and stronger. The PKR gained four basis points to close a year that started at PKR 278.30 against the U.S. Dollar, at PKR 280.13. And despite a USD 80/ton drop, local steel plate prices remained flatlined through the week at around USD 580/ton (well ahead of the competition), having started the year near USD 640/ton.

While Gadani buyers did get back to buying with a mid-year spree, thanks to firmer fundamentals and timing, this was not at sustained throughput as imports of cheap Iranian steel products started to hammer local sentiment — and local offer levels for tonnage as a result.

Yet, like Chattogram, with inflation now declining last month, relatively stable fundamentals, and only additions to the number of HKC-accredited ship recycling yards, the only way for the Gadani Gang in 2026 is up.

headline: QUIET!
highlights: Lethargy.
body_text:
The Turkish Lira lost 24 basis points against the U.S. Dollar to close the week out at TRY 42.92, having started the year at TRY 35.08 — a near 15% decline for the currency. Beyond that, it was a quiet overall year; and, like Pakistan, the sporadic inflow of tonnage was meted out to local recyclers like mercy through a drought.

Beyond that, we can only hope that with a hopefully increased inflow of tonnage, volumes will help Aliaga recyclers beat the lethargy odds.

headline: PRICE PLUNGE!
highlights: USD 50/LDT decline. | Violent protests. | Violent protests. | Appealing
body_text:
Ever since the tonnage engorgement back in November 2025, the Bangladeshi ship recycling market has been on a consistent nosedive, leaving recyclers in Chattogram largely uncompetitive when it comes to offering on the limited number of units currently paraded at the bidding tables. Levels have shockingly come off by about USD 50/LDT since the highs of Q4 2025 — an uncharacteristically rapid, drastic, and unexpected deterioration that has left local demand and overall industry sentiment toward Chattogram on voicemail mode.

Moreover, with significant uncertainty building ahead of the February elections, violent protests followed the death of youth leader Sharif Osman Hadi, who was shot by masked gunmen while leaving a mosque in Dhaka back in December. The death of Bangladesh’s first female PM, Khaleda Zia, last week at the age of 80 also sent much of the country into mourning, as these uncertain and dark times become headline news nationwide.

Dripping down into the ship recycling sector, the situation clearly remains ever worse, albeit with a lemon-twist surprise at the waterfront, as Chattogram was the only sub-continent destination to report any arrivals — including the nation’s first prompt delivery — this week. But on the fundamentals side, things remain scattered: local steel plate prices recorded their usual weekly volatility, while the BDT lost six basis points against the U.S. Dollar and closed the week out at BDT 122.30.

Overall, the trajectory of this market over the next couple of months does not seem appealing to the industry, as with price, tonnage follows suit. And it would not be an impossibility to see Far Eastern tonnage heading to shores west of Bangladesh.

headline: NEW YEAR, W.T. FEARS!
highlights: India improves. | Maduro capture. | Decisive times. | Price plunge. | Upheaval.
body_text:
After what only seemed like a calm period while Donald Trump was flailing in the polls amid ongoing scandals and investigations, he ramped it up and brought 2026 in with a literal BANG via his latest incursion into — and seizure of — President Nicolas Maduro and his wife from their Presidential Home in Venezuela, in a pre-dawn raid by special-forces. Trump even posted a Polaroid of the handcuffed Maduro, blindfolded, as they landed at a secure / undisclosed facility.

While Trump’s true intentions remain unclear (just yet), it’s only a matter of time before we see how global / oil / shipping markets react in the coming week(s) to this globally dictatorial move that has most certainly violated a long list of international laws pertaining to sitting presidents and prisoners of war. Moreover, major news outlets are now reporting confusion over who maintains control. Although major news sources report that the U.S. is claiming to hold power over the country, Trump claims the current Venezuelan government (albeit with the President missing and all) will hold interim power while the U.S. administers the nation until such time that a new administration capable of resuming duties is in place to lead the country. Hard to reread that and not think that a prominent three-letter agency was missing some South American sun this frigid time of the year; and after all the geopolitical craziness that gripped — and impacted — us through 2025, I don’t know how many were ready to see Trump Theatre & Co. deliver a cake factory to celebrate his madness this soon in 2026.

In the meantime, global economies delivered mixed signals as U.S. stocks maintained a steady decline over the tail-end of December, China’s industrial growth slowed, and EU stocks reportedly surged. The U.S. Dollar started the year off-balance against ship recycling currencies, shipowners started to rejoice as the Baltic Exchange Dry Index showed signs of a resurgence, oil continued to slip on its way to USD 60/barrel even though it climbed to USD 57.17/barrel this week, local steel plate prices made no jarring moves beyond the recent trend, and beaching tides delivered twins in both India and Pakistan. At least it was encouraging to see the Indian market display some signs of improvement over the first week of 2026, as busier and less challenging times hopefully lie ahead.

In the ship recycling markets overall, increasingly decisive times lie ahead for Bangladesh as a nation given that impending elections are nearing by the week and the country is being increasingly submerged by political protests, rioting, and instances of violence. Bangladesh levels and demand have plummeted as a result and now lie at the foot of the sub-continent price rankings board, given that Pakistan and India both made improvements as December 2025 ended, and they moved up the ladder.
