With more upheaval now expected across the world, continued economic and geopolitical shocks may temporarily prop up shipping markets and deprive recycling locations of vintage tonnage for a while longer — it seems as though 2026 is taking on the mantle from 2025!

headline: STEEL SURGE!
highlights: Encouraging signs. | Back top. | Currency woes. | DASR dance.
body_text:
The Indian market surged by nearly USD 30/LDT over the last week, sending Alang soaring to the top of the price rankings board for the first time in over a quarter, as 2026 began on a far cheerier note than the end of 2025 would otherwise seem to suggest.

Surprisingly, despite the U.S. Dollar gaining 20 basis points against the Indian Rupee and closing the week at Rs. 90.28 – breaching into the dread Rs. 90s once again, demand still managed to improve and, after a fairly woeful 2025, Alang recyclers can be a touch more optimistic heading into what many are hoping will be a far busier year ahead — the perennial prayer of the recycling ports over the last five years that has yet to be answered.

Yet, the biggest surprise of the week was local anchorage, which, for the first time in a very long time, reported a deserted theatre — a first for this market. Although in fairness, there are units idling at outer awaiting entry onto the port report so it’s only a matter of time before their scoreboard for 2026 starts all over again.

Overall, India is once again the best-placed market to take in tonnage. It seems odd not to mention HKC or “otherwise” anymore, since every vessel has naturally been subject to the Convention since June 26, 2025, when it formally kicked into gear. With Bangladesh overstuffed and facing a clear shortage of available HKC yards, and with shipowners/cash buyers staying away from the DASR dance, Alang anchorage might be the one to keep an eye on — at least until Bangladesh’s elections formalize, a modicum of stability starts to reign, and positive economic measures are implemented.

headline: HOT WHEELS!
highlights: Waiting to pounce. | Below 400. | Indignity.
body_text:
Pakistan remains hot on the heels of its Indian neighbors/competitors, and as Bangladesh currently takes a breather, now could be the pivotal time for Gadani recyclers to step into the breach with some opportunistic vessel purchases. But will they?

Local offerings are still positioned below USD 400/LDT on a majority of the tonnage being presented locally, and it has been a fairly inert December 2025/first week of January 2026, after a promising few months in 2025 that briefly saw Gadani top the price board and have a flush anchorage to match.

Proof of this is the state of local anchorage, which has resumed its time in solitary — mirroring India. It certainly is an eclipse moment for the ship recycling world when regional recycling anchorages west of Chattogram sit completely empty.

In the meantime, yards remain busy upgrading and improving infrastructure to fall in line with HKC standards (with one yard already approved), with the HKC now fully in force as of June last year. But this remains a major limitation for the market, especially with an expected influx of tonnage and Bangladesh largely out of the running.

Fundamentals, meanwhile, continue on their merry way, with local steel plate prices maintaining the status quo and the PKR losing 20 basis points, though it still managed to stay within PKR 280 territory as it wound the week down at PKR 280.62. Domestically, there was good news for the nation’s economy as well with inflation reporting a sharp drop down to 5.6%, its lowest level since August 2025.

Overall, it seems this market will suffer the indignity of an HKC-short beachfront, which will more than likely see India consume most of the tonnage in the near term. New year and empty anchorages aren’t how Gadani recyclers anticipated the start of 2026.

headline: ZZZZZ!
highlights: TRY troubles.
body_text: Aliaga recyclers seems to be chilling on an extended 2025 holiday on the sidelines, with nothing more than the Lira sinking further by another 26 basis points and locking itself in firmly into TRY 43 territory, as it closes the week out at TRY 43.03.

headline: TAILS UP!
highlights: Price return. | Political problems. | LC hold up. | Full stomach.
body_text:
After the stark declines towards the tail-end of Q4 2025 followed by vanishing demand and collapsing local offerings that saw Chattogram choppers land at the bottom of the market rankings just last week, signs of life and recovery emerged locally this week

However, with the wild performance of India’s fundamentals and dithering local sentiments there, demand in Bangladesh started to firm, despite political uncertainty reportedly reaching a feverous pitch amidst tensions and outbreaks of violence continue, with the nation’s critical elections now just about a month away. Moreover, following the recent death of the first female PM to run the country and the assassination of a youth leader — both within weeks — episodes of violent protest engulfed Bangladesh in the aftermath, leaving many hoping for a more serene and orderly election process ahead.

Locally, the still-deflated level of supply saw just one fresh vessel arrive and make its way to delivery, alongside all of the units that arrived the week prior, leaving Chattogram’s anchorage dead as the week ended. This cross-border see-saw — which saw empty anchorages in Alang and Gadani just last week — may soon see Chattogram tie the competition with a likely empty anchorage of its own in the coming week(s).

Several L/Cs were meanwhile held up over the recent tide due to a change in personnel at the Central Bank in Dhaka, with additional documentary requirements introduced since the change to push these L/Cs through. For the most part, however, the fact that Chattogram’s anchorage is now empty, indicates that local deliveries did manage to pull through.

Fundamentals meanwhile remain frail, as the Taka gained a mere nine basis points against the U.S. Dollar and walked out the Friday door at BDT 122.26. Local steel plate prices, on the other hand, finally started trading once again and opened mid-week around USD 500/ton — not the best place to be, but still not as grim as India, which is nearly USD 100/ton lower and yet continues to outbid Bangladesh at the tables.

Clearly, no one locally wants to eat on a full stomach.

If local recyclers don’t make it back into the fray by end of Monday, it seems all will be quiet locally — at least until elections conclude.

headline: TAUT WITH TENSIONS!
highlights: Constant shocks. | US threats. | India volatile. | Pre CNY buying. | Around 400.
body_text:
If 2026 continues as it has started, we are more than likely in for another roller-coaster year full of geopolitical risks, tensions, aggravations, and increasingly frequent shocks that could affect the shipping and ship recycling industries in numerous — and as yet untold — ways.

Trump’s kidnapping (let’s call it what it is) of President Maduro and his wife from Venezuela — followed by U.S. claims that it will “run” the country when Trump can’t even handle the U.S. — has already set the tone for the madness we can expect in 2026. Amping up the octogenarian crankiness, he also threatened to take Greenland as a U.S. territory this week, drawing swift condemnation from Russia, China, and even senior Congressional Republicans on Capitol Hill, who confirmed that Congress would never agree to such overtly aggressive actions on behalf of the U.S. The subsequent capture of a Russian-controlled oil tanker carrying Venezuelan oil sent further shocks through the industry, raising the question of which other wild move this administration is willing to inflict on the world.

Markets reacted as they always do i.e. with chaos and volatility. The Baltic Exchange reported another bleak week of declines for the fifth straight Friday, falling about 1.7%, dragged down by capes (down 3%) and supramaxes (down 9 points), while panamaxes jumped about 0.7% by Friday’s close. Oil meanwhile managed to rise just about USD 59.50/barrel, extending its gain for a third consecutive session.

Currencies went on a tear once again, with the U.S. Dollar inflicting pain in Turkey and India (once again), while retreating in the Pakistani and Bangladeshi markets. Last week’s reported increase in local steel plate prices was also met with declining levels, even though the weekly moves might suggest otherwise — as current pricing remains lower than where it stood two weeks ago.

Trickling down to the ship recycling sector, while India has enjoyed a resurgent start to the year on the back of local steel plate prices that jumped nearly USD 30/Ton, this week saw local sentiment turning negative again as plate levels retreated just as rapidly. Pakistan and Bangladesh meanwhile responded in kind with improved demand and pricing of their own as activity starts to seemingly heat up ahead of the inevitable slowdown for Chinese New Year at the end of January into February and Far Eastern tonnage typically takes another break from Bangla waters. Local deliveries also showed marginal improvement, with just a couple of candidates making it to sub-continent anchorages this week.

headline: QUICK REVERSE!
highlights: Steel slide. | Weakened. | v needed. | Short nap.
body_text:
After what seemed to be some serious improvements in local steel plate prices post-New Year in India — with levels jumping nearly USD 30/ton last week, this week, they opened USD 6/ton lower than last and ended up wiping out all of the recent gains, sliding back down to USD 400/ton once again. Not wanting to be outdone, the Rupee chased the U.S. Dollar as it lost another 20 basis points this week and closed at Rs. 90.21.

Given that Alang buyers tend to be a nervy bunch, sentiment has weakened, and end buyers have become more cautious about being boisterous with their offers, for fear of further falls ahead — particularly amid the global political and economic uncertainty besetting markets at present. At the same time, a USD 30/ton swing in the core pricing mechanism of recycling vessels is not something to be scoffed at.

Mercifully, tonnage supply remains weak, so these expectedly lower indications are unlikely to lead anywhere in the interim. But even as supply remains thin, India did manage to crawl out of “empty anchorage” syndrome as at least one 2,500 LDT vessel greeted the waterfront last week, with another two reportedly waiting to come in.

Notwithstanding, sustained performance — and a bit of courage — will be needed in Alang for recyclers to secure their share of any market tonnage that becomes available, especially as Pakistan and Bangladesh warm up to negotiating at the tables again, albeit with Bangladesh potentially in for a short nap until election day.

headline: INTO THE BREACH!
highlights: Seeking to buy. | DASR stopgap. | Supply hopes.
body_text:
Pakistan has been looking to get back into the action since the start of the year, with enquiries emerging from buyers whose yards are in the process of being upgraded to HKC standards. However, local offerings have (as has been the trend over the last 2.5 decades from this market) remained just behind those of India, and more aggressive posturing will be needed to secure tonnage and fill local plots again — especially given that local fundamentals remain a breath of fresh air compared to the competition, with both the PKR and local steel plate prices displaying far more stability across the region.

Not only did local steel plate prices firm by about USD 6/ton this week, they also closed the week out at USD 585/ton — USD 185/ton higher than India and an USD 85/ton margin over Bangladesh. It certainly seems as though Iranian imports may have eased off the brakes for now, given Iran’s own domestic upheaval at present. At the same time, the Pakistani Rupee gained seven basis points against the U.S. Dollar and closed the week at PKR 280.12 — inching its way back toward the PKR 279s.

With so much financial artillery in Gadani’s possession, it was shocking to see the market end last year with just 202 total vessel s delivered locally. Seemingly this year — this poor waterfront performance seems likely to continue especially as HKC yards remain scarce and provisional DASR certifications (issued while HKC upgrade work continues) remain a barrier to fresh inflows. This has left the market barren at the waterfront, and for the second week in a row in 2026, Gadani’s anchorage ended the week on an empty note.

Speaking of inflow, with the supply of tonnage expected to increase in 2026, Pakistan ship recyclers need to be ready — and willing — to step into the breach at meaningful numbers, with certified yards in place, in order to fill plots and secure their share of the recycling action.

headline: MORE ZZZZZ!
highlights: Need some logic.
body_text:
Aliaga’s ship recycling sector seems to have gone into winter hibernation, with little noteworthy news emerging other than the ever-degrading Turkish lira, which lost another 23 basis points this week and closed at TRY 43.14 against the U.S. Dollar.

While local deliveries have remained lower than those seen in Pakistan, it is not for a want of tonnage, but rather the need for a more logical application of EU laws so businesses do not suffocate under media pressure and NGO scrutiny. However, with the sub-continent now formally operating under the HKC, it remains to be seen whether any knock-on changes will be forthcoming for Aliaga in 2026.

If the last five years are any indication — and especially if the lira continues to slip — local offers will continue to fall, and EOL vessel values will ultimately fetch even less for the banks who have mortgaged assets out. What happens then?

headline: GOING BIG!
highlights: Buyers looking. | Reluctant for small. | Elections loom. | On the heels
body_text:
For as satiated as the Chattogram market has been of late - given its healthy set of deliveries in late November and even the last couple of weeks, including this one, where at least one decent LDT tanker arrived locally – local ship recyclers are clearly becoming available for the right kind of tonnage - and that too at the best levels in the industry. However, this recent interest is deviating towards mostly larger LDT units like LNGs, tankers, and dry vessels such as capes (if any do come available).

With prices to match and as determined as tier-1 local buyers tend to be, indications surfacing this week have helped push Bangladesh into the top spot of the market rankings yet again. So, now you know, if you’ve got a large LDT hulker regardless of type, now’s as good a time as any to get in on it.

Notwithstanding the limited spectrum of resurging optimism, this improvement has puzzlingly arrived at a peculiar time when inflation has risen from 8.29% in November to 8.49% in December and prices across the board (food, housing, utilities, furnishings, etc.) have risen of late. This was followed on by a local steel plate price that tanked USD 12/Ton this week and end at about USD 487/ton, which was accompanied by a declining Bangladeshi Taka that lost also 12 basis points to the U.S. Dollar and conclude the week at BDT 122.40 – one of the higher levels we have seen of late.

Moreover, as violence continues to mar the streets of the capital city Dhaka, amid escalating attacks that saw two newspaper offices become the latest victims, election fever has clearly been ramping up along with local agitation and its effects on day-to-day life. Blended into the mix is the domestic economy, making it a commendable feat to witness the resilience of the Chattogram Choppers at the bidding tables, week after week.

Overall, while this market stands open and willing to engage in serious discussions on tonnage, there remains an overall reluctance to engage in small(er) LDT units, which have been increasingly diverted Westward. Smaller, poor(er) condition bulkers are also seeing lower rates here, as well as the entire sub-continent, as a few recent fixtures well below USD 400/LDT come to light.

With the critical election looming on the horizon on February 12th, Bangladeshi buyers need to remain alert enough to snap up their share of any of the slim pickings of the right vessels that may make an appearance before the elections, especially if the wrong choice of leader is elected (any recent elections affecting the world grab attention?), and as Pakistan and India still remain on their heels.

headline: REVERBERATIONS!
highlights: Marble-chasing. | Turbulent times. | VL market firing. | Price wobbles. | Demand rising.
body_text:
Post–New Year developments and shocking events have continued to send reverberations across the markets, directly and indirectly, following the surreal extrication of President Maduro and his wife from Venezuela under Trump’s orders — with clear intentions around the country’s oil riches — followed by his marble-chasing claims over Greenland that are based on similarly wet-spaghetti logic, which has since sparked a serious fallout with several European and even Canadian leaders to match. What a time to be a witness.

In the meantime, S&P markets saw at least one buyer in particular, who has been making some major plays on VLCC assets as secondhand values show few signs of deterioration — and the Baltic Exchange Dry Index echoed just that this week as it halted a nine-session slide to mark a 2.3% U- turn, climbing to 1,567 points. This was driven by gains across segments: Capes (up 2.3%), Panamax (up 4.3%), and the smaller segments adding four points by week’s end. Notably, the overall benchmark index still finished the week down 7.2%. Oil too continued to trip on itself and stayed below the coveted USD 60/barrel mark despite a 0.4% increase, closing the week out at USD 59.44/barrel.

The U.S. Dollar meanwhile dominated all ship recycling currencies this week, while local steel plate prices across destinations dissolved into a mixed bag of opposing moves — both competitively and historically (i.e., versus last week).

As such, ship recycling markets may be continue to deprived of tonnage as hopes for a brighter start to 2026 — indicated by the tapering indices back in November – December 2025 — begin to fade once again. Prices across the Indian sub-continent have meanwhile continued their own song and dance on a downward path over the last month, with dry bulk indications at the bidding tables regularly below USD 400/LDT and several sales reportedly even being concluded in the USD 370s– USD 380s/LDT range.

Across destinations, India briefly surged by about USD 30/LDT before losing the full move the very next week as fundamentals softened. Pakistan’s demand has begun to show, with end buyers now increasingly hungry to fill plots as empty anchorages become more of the norm than the exception. Bangladeshi recyclers have largely been on the lookout for particular units based on their recent appetites as local offerings have helped them bounce back to the top of the market rankings again. And Turkey? A bevy of European RoRos finally arrived Aliaga this week, delivering much-needed sustenance to an ailing local industry.

Overall, the interim / near-future still looks like a quiet one – maybe not for Turkey? That’d a switch.

headline: CURIOUS WEEKS!
highlights: Back down. | Rupee woes. | HKC up. | Take it for what it | is.
body_text:
It has been a curious 2026 in India thus far, with steel plate prices and local offerings surging by nearly USD 30/LDT at the start of the year, only to find themselves tumbling down the very next week by nearly the same number and spectacularly lose any gains that may have otherwise been realized, leaving owners and cash buyers with little chance to gauge the way of the pricing winds from Alang in the coming week(s).

And domestic fundamentals have certainly been to blame as they have been on an absolute bender of late, given that local steel plate prices reclaimed USD 11/ton this week (having lost USD 24/ton just the week prior) and clock out at USD 410/Ton. The Indian Rupee meanwhile lost over 0.55% and welcomed the weekend at Rs. 90.72 – approaching the psychological boundary of Rs. 91 once again. Should that come to fruition, ever-nervy local recyclers will find themselves promptly reassessing their offerings,

The only rainbow on the otherwise grey horizon was the arrival of 3 new vessels at Alang’s waterfront this week, including an over 16K LDT tanker. Hopefully, all were concluded at levels safe enough to keep their deals in the green (or out of the red at the very least).

Domestic inflation has meanwhile managed to climb out of stagflation territory from 0.71% back in November and ring the New Year in at 1.33%, clearly inching into healthier zones once again. And if this trend continues over the next couple of weeks, we may see fundamentals stabilize and bring prices up enough to grab some attention again, especially as the pivotal month of March (and businesses closing their books for their year) comes around.

Overall, Alang recyclers certainly seem ready to engage in discussions at current levels and on any tonnage – as and when it may be tabled. For now, it’s clearly a “take it for what it is” situation.

headline: SLAP HAPPY!
highlights: Stable offerings. | Slow rolling. | Rarely proposed.
body_text:
Right alongside India, Pakistan has registered a strange start to the year with hungry end buyers finding themselves shifting from 3rd place on the market rankings to the 2nd without really having changed their offer levels at all, thanks to comparatively stable offerings than what neighboring India’s pricing trajectory has been of late. And while firmer levels are always welcome on the supply side of things, this has unfortunately not translated into any fresh arrivals at Gadani’s waterfront so far this year.

Clearly, several items have colluded to deliver this effect viz. a lack of supply, a lack of HKC yards to engage in local competition and ensure a fair price target is achieved, and an unwillingness on part of the selling community to engage in DASR procedures, which generally result in delays at anchorage and potential loss of delivery time on what should otherwise be prompt deliveries, all while slow-rolling formalities are completed. Gadani recyclers, it would seem, are destined to enter an unintendedly slap happy phase this January 2026.

And with fundamentals playing the funk again, that local steel plate prices have resumed flatlining at USD 600/Ton, indicating a lack of local trading on account of virtually no local deliveries or generated recycled ship steel. The PKR also added to current stresses, as it too lost nearly 0.5% against the U.S. Dollar (like their Indian brethren) entering the weekend at PKR 280.

Yet some positivity remains: Pakistan’s first HKC approved yard has been welcomed into the international fraternity, and several more are reportedly set to follow in the coming month(s). Hopefully, Gadani starts to catch up to the international stage with HKC infrastructure upgrades and accreditations soon.

For now, despite its firmer offerings, we do not foresee too many (if any) of the rarely proposed units heading to local shores.

headline: I SEE MOVEMENT…
highlights: Smart move.
body_text:
Aliaga’s ship recycling sector woke up like Bigfoot in the woods, appearing out of nowhere with several sales registered to local recyclers, leaving Aliaga’s anchorage earmarked over the last couple of weeks with a bunch of European RoRo’s that were in the process of being delivered to their respective recyclers.

Even though import steel plate prices climbed and the Turkish Lira dropped another 31 basis points against the U.S. Dollar to close the week at TRY 43.27, local offerings are holding steady — a smart move given the possibility of a busier Q1 ahead.

headline: SLIPPAGE!
highlights: Underwhelming. | Missing out. | Overall pause. | Gear up, grind down.
body_text:
Like a roller coaster without brakes, Bangladesh zoomed to the bottom of the Indian sub-continent ship recycling market rankings this week, delivering an entirely new flavor of underwhelming performance at the bidding tables, with almost no offers coming forth on any of the marginal units that are being paraded for a potential recycling sale. What’s worse? Any indications that did emerge were at levels that lingered even below those from Pakistan and India.

As a result, a healthy majority of recent fixtures have slipped through the hands of the Chattogram Choppers and on to neighboring India and Pakistan — as clearly highlighted by the emergence of an empty port position this week, certainly for the first time in a very long time for the Bangladeshi ship recycling market. Moreover, seeing even geographically positioned Far Eastern tonnage heading Westward to the better-placed Gadani and Alang markets speaks volumes about the growing disinterest emanating from Chattogram of late (given the volume of recent deliveries here), coupled with severely lacking levels to match — a Frankenstein of their own making.

Critically, the observant among us may have caught on to the ongoing performance of local fundamentals, which seem to be settling into a violent pattern of abnormal normality as the Taka continues to climb and deteriorate beyond marginally acceptable trade/economic volumes. This week, it gained a healthy 40 basis points against the U.S. Dollar yet closed at BDT 122.02. Local steel plate prices found the bottom of the pool and simply lay there throughout the week, at last week’s closing level of USD 487/ton, as resale prices of ships steel are being severely undercut by competing product and local recyclers remain unable to move recycled product off their yards.

Election fever meanwhile continues to ramp up as voting holidays were officially announced for both February 11 and 12, as the populace prepares to vote and either gear up (or grind down) the future of the nation based on the impending performance of the incoming administration next month.

For now, with February looming large and spurts of violence still being reported regularly, we do not expect much from Chattogram beyond the odd delivery that simply could not make it further west.

headline: MUSICAL CHAIRS!
highlights: Reflecting. | Bangla sinks. | Gadani back. | Demand ripe. | India specialist.
body_text:
Indian sub-continent ship recycling markets have been reflecting on what has been escalating on the international stage of late, with extremely turbulent effects emanating week after week from these markets — meaning it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify what price can be obtained for which type / LDT of unit and, most importantly, which buyer in which market would be willing to jump for the unit in question. Certainly, a game of where is Carmen San Diego seems to be unfolding but before we go on the hunt, let’s look at the internationals, shall we?

As we await January’s inflation figures from the various destinations, the Baltic Exchange Dry Index managed to edge up a little more on Friday, helped by the smaller segments, while capes fell 0.2% and the panamax index declined by about 0.1%. Meanwhile, crude oil finally breached the awaited USD 60/barrel barrier and wrapped up the week at USD 60.92/barrel, rising nearly 7.3% over the last month but still dangling 16.81% lower than the same time a year ago.

Meanwhile, the U.S. Dollar and local steel plate prices were on missions of their own this week as on the one hand, both India and Turkey continued to take in their share of the battering against the Dollar while on the other, local steel plate prices decided that staying horizontal for the week was better than the tiring weekly fluctuations - and a majority of them seemed to take a break in unison. As a result, pricing continues to surprise the entire industry, which itself seems to be running around playing third grade musical chairs with glee.

From the top of the price rankings board, Bangladesh has now managed to sink itself to the bottom of the sub-continent charts, with no discernible pre-election optimism radiating through the country just yet. It now seems to be Pakistan’s turn to enjoy a moment in the sun, with improved demand and even pricing (although this will always remain questionable given the ongoing volatility of neighboring competitors), reportedly even diverting vessels from the East into the hands of eager Gadani recyclers this week. Much of this renewed optimism in Gadani can be put down to a slow down / pause in the import of cheaper Iranian steel product into the local market. Yet the dejecting and ongoing scarcity of supply has left a plethora of Gadani yards, open and available for the most part, with provisional DASR certs and ready L/C limits to take in tonnage — and the hunt remains.

India remains sandwiched between the two, ready and available to take specialist tonnage (LNGs rich in non-ferrous, stainless-steel tankers, and reefers, for example), but at clearly shaky rates amid worrying depreciations of the Indian Rupee and still-fluctuating steel prices that have persisted as a terrifying theme since much of last year. Finally, Turkey at the far end remains busy (for what it’s worth) with its sudden ingestion of RoRos — but what next? More silence and Lira depreciations.

headline: WRIGGLES!
highlights: Sealing sales. | Marathon moves. | On edge.
body_text:
India has found itself wriggling its way back into the recycling conversation once again and Alang recyclers reportedly even managed to pick up some interesting specialist vessels from various cash buyer inventories this week, including another LNG, snatching the unit away from the frequently more aggressive Bangladeshi market. This was certainly expected, given Bangladesh’s breathtaking performance at the bidding tables this week, which helped India inadvertently unable to deny themselves the ability of slipping into second place on the market rankings as a result.

Of note, neither India’s pricing volatility nor its market ranking has seemed to affect the inflow of tonnage, as Alang’s anchorage reported the arrival of a healthy array of smaller LDT units and types of tonnage at the waterfront, contributing to an impressive collection (given the current environment) of over 23K LDT waiting to be delivered to their respective owners.

But how much longer can this “performance” be sustained, especially given not only how volatile the Indian Rupee has been of late, but also how much it affects local pricing — in addition to the degree of permeation and effect that steel trade has on recycled steel, which affects all recycling markets. Of these, India has by far been the apostle of misfortune, as not only did the Rupee collapse by over 1% in just five days, it also closed the week breaching Rs. 91 by a wide margin (nearly hitting Rs. 92) and wrapping its roller coast ride at Rs. 91.65.

Pepper that in with a dash of perennially nervy sentiment à la Alang recyclers, and we have another price-drop soup-brew moment just waiting to appear at any time. Maybe Far Eastern tonnage stops flowing further out west; maybe it gets extended on account of what’s happening with Bangladesh’s election cycle; maybe Chinese New Year Holidays drop the anchor anyways? We’ll have to wait and see — but we certainly know now what to expect.

As it stands, with Bangladesh expectedly out of the running until election day, India will remain the go-to spot further west, with Pakistan taking in a few for its share as well.

headline: STEELY!
highlights: Picking up. | Proudly top. | Supply worries.
body_text:
With the inflow of Iranian steel product into Pakistan slowing/ceasing of late, both sentiment and pricing have predictably picked up, resulting in some much needed and well-priced purchases being reported for Gadani’s corner.

Alas, this buying spree has come too little, too late, and has not yet helped the destitute state of Gadani’s anchorage, which has sat empty throughout 2026 (and then some), and despite Pakistan sitting proudly atop the sub-continent pricing board on account of Bangladesh’s recent slippage. Mercifully, this move into first place has helped local recyclers divert some tonnage away from the usually eager — and geographically better-positioned — Alang market.

Moreover, given the ongoing trend of minimal supply, it seems likely we will see more favored dry-bulk sales arrive at this market in the weeks ahead. And with Bangladesh now exiting the building, the timing could not have been better for Gadani recyclers to steer their share of tonnage toward local shores in the immediate future — so keep an eye out.

Meanwhile, ongoing concerns around the availability of tonnage, coupled with incoming Chinese New Year holidays on February 17 — a traditionally quieter time for sale-and-purchase activity in the Far East — may further fuel the ongoing shortage and keep local anchorage(s) suffocated just that much longer.

Either way, local fundamentals seem steady enough and have held their ground at decent levels over recent weeks, with the Pakistani Rupee even gaining an impressive 70 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and log in a healthy PKR 278.19 at the time of close — levels not seen since circa Q1 2025. Local steel plate prices too , after improving to current levels over recent weeks, have helplessly flatlined at an industry-leading USD 587/ton.

For now, we should see Gadani’s anchorage light up with the few recent fixtures reported into this market — and there is certainly room for more.

headline: NOW WHAT?!?
highlights: Stream.
body_text:
Aliaga’s anchorage is certainly having its moment in the sunshine, as a fleet of EU-owned RoRos has streamed into anchorage over the last few weeks. But we have seen this before haven’t we? During the Pax surge of 2022 / 2023 that saw Aliaga’s anchorage littered with cruise ships / luxury liners across the landscape.

And while this surge will come to an end, then what? Is it back to business as usual? Only reporting that the Lira lost another 30 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and closing the week out atr another record breaking TRY 43.97 and already a foot into TRY 44?

We can only hope that with nations and government organizations increasingly chasing after afflicted / sanctioned tonnage, what becomes of these units is the next big question — especially those that are of recycling age (and there are a lot of them). Let’s pray , this becomes a saner stream of exit for these assets, not only for Turkey, but for the rest of the industry as well.

headline: BACK TO BIZ?
highlights: Securing cape. | 22 HKC yards. | Landmark elections. | Tick tock.
body_text:
After missing out on several vessels to sub-continent rivals (including an LNG to India and several panamax sized bulkers seemingly into Pakistan), it was certainly good to see Bangladeshi buyers get back in on the action at the bidding tables with the only reported capesize bulker acquisition of the week, and that reportedly too at decent levels, an oddity considering Bangladesh’s overstuffed and digestive state just last week.

And as purchases were grabbing the headlines at the waterfront, political headlines continue to grab the news inlands across the country, especially now with January passed and the nation’s landmark elections - the first in 2 years - standing just 2 weeks away. It has certainly been a long time coming for the country to finally find a modicum of political and economic stability, even if it potentially stands to be short-lived (just as the last election was), and given how much the nation has clearly struggled under the currently dysfunctional regime over the last 20 months, they are hopefully on their collective way out.

What has also been short-lived is Chattogram’s dance with an empty port position as clearly this week, several tankers of varying LDTs greeted the waterfront with one even being promptly delivered to its respective new owner already. News of the lowly local resale prices on some of the smaller tankers are emerging as well, with one reportedly achieving a meager USD 330/LT, hence the surprise at the reportedly firm price on this week’s reported acquisition.

Fundamentally, things look like they make solid pricing moves (at least in early February) a near uncertainty given the ongoing performance of local steel plate prices (currently dead on the floor for at least 2 weeks running), which are stranded at USD 487.24/ton. Add into the pricing cocktail, some spicy Tabasco of Bangladeshi Taka, which fell 1% this week and closed it out at BDT 122.95 against the U.S. Dollar, it seems like next week might be back to the pricing board for local buyers, before making any rash purchases in the immediate future.

Overall, with 22 yards (and counting) that now stand HKC approved, it has been encouraging to see some fierce bidding on HKC only tonnage (particularly LNGs) being offered to approved Chattogram yards. And his becomes even critical whenever the supply of green tonnage ramps up (tick tock reality, its 2026 already).

headline: AND JUST LIKE THAT…
highlights: Debbie Downer. | India secures. | Supply slow. | Challenges. | HKC gains.
body_text:
… January 2026 joins the pages of history as being the purveyors of ongoing misery for the global ship recycling world as despite the odd wave of tonnage that has made us numb to the conflicting signals of the markets based on supply trends across the last 5 years, something eye-catching did change this week. And it would seem that the rising ripples from Trump’s train wreck of activity has posed global markets to setup a serious “Debbie Downer” for February 2026, especially if the current trends persist.

To start, we have noteworthy surges to report this week. Across the board, for most of the major fundamentals, except sub-continent steel plate prices that have become the perennial party poopers of the recycling world of late, the momentum was definitely beyond noticeable. The Baltic Exchange Dry Index, oil futures, and the U.S. Dollar collectively soared this week, creating ripples that would certainly be felt within the next 4 weeks. While the dry index soared 7.3% on the back of Capes pole- vaulting 12%, Panamaxes tripping up 1.6% in comparison, and Supras having a comparatively minor hiccup gain of 0.5%, oil futures impressively slid past USD 65/barrel and close the week out at USD 65.10 – a near 1% jump from last week.

And the U.S. Dollar’s performance across the ship recycling markets was reminiscent of Marilyn Monroe’s infamous wavy skirt subway photo, the wavy lines capturing just how volatile Trump has made global financial markets on the back of further tariff threats against Canada, nation states in Europe including France and Denmark, and even striking into the hearts of global ship recycling markets with Pakistan (surprisingly) taking the biggest of hits this week. Speaking of the ship recycling markets, they certainly seem to be having a global “up” moment, with India, Pakistan Bangladesh and Turkey all reportedly picking up some long overdue tonnage, although only India Bangladesh and Turkish anchorages are delivering the receipts to confirm these fixtures. India managed to even secure an LNG for strictly HKC recycling only and Turkey with its bevy of roros and “buffet-full bellies” confirming that all of the major ship recycling destinations collectively secured their share of available market vessels since the start of January 2026 (and in a long time).

headline: RABID RUPEE!
highlights: Belly jiggle. | Damp demand. | Cannot compete. | Triangular seesaw.
body_text:
The Indian Rupee has had a fundamental (pun intended) earthquake on an economic scale as it plummeted another 25 basis points by week’s end, and after briefly surging to Rs. 92.18 against the U.S. Dollar – currently still in excess of Rs. 93 for non-regulatory Dollar purchases (i.e. for regular people) – it closed shop for the weekend at Rs. 91.82.

Local steel plate prices added their own belly jiggle to this week’s entertainment as it fell to nearly USD 398/Ton before recovering to a – still lower than last week - level of about USD 401/Ton, dictating the destiny of upcoming offer levels in the coming week. And as is typical of the nervy Indian sentiment, amidst the perplexing historical lows seen in the performance of INR, of course we saw fears that the currency may even breach Rs. 100 against U.S. Dollar, ensuring future acquisitions get ever so dicier!

Ironically however, while on the one hand, this clearly placed a dampener on prevailing sentiments and demand, manifesting itself into the current state of local offerings that have ensured India remains at the bottom of the sub-continent pricing board, on the other hand, Alang was and has been the busiest of all anchorages as nearly 47K LDT via 6 vessels (including another large LDT tanker) earmarked the nation’s ship recycling waterfront this week.

But, as recycling nation currencies across the board have reacted negatively and in unison to the U.S. Dollar this week, could we see the same level of pullback from competing markets in the coming week(s) now that as Pakistan and Bangladesh have had their chance to stay notably ahead over these last couple of weeks? Crystall ball moment.

What is however certain, is that with another Pakistani yard not snagging a Class NK pedigree HKC approval in Gadani, the triangular see-saw of sub-continent ship recycling is about to get really interesting in the months and years ahead.

headline: SECOND HKC UP!
highlights: Iranian halt. | Importing dry. | Right time.
body_text:
That’s not a “second hiccup” folks and you read that right. Gadani’s HKC recycling momentum has now welcomed a Class NK approved HKC certified ship recycling yard to its gradually growing collection, with Salams International now becoming the nation’s second ship recycling yard to earn this prestigious certification.

And while this will certainly challenge neighboring Alang’s purchasing prowess as time progresses, it truly welcomes Gadani’s infrastructure into the international arena and will hopefully generate greater confidence towards the nation’s industry.

Meanwhile, local steel plate prices, like those in Bangladesh, seem to be experiencing their own lights-out moment as they remained horizontal for the week, albeit at an industry-leading USD 587/ton. But after weeks of flaunting its stabilizing (and even firming) ability, it was the Pakistani Rupee that took home the attention of the industry, declining by about 1.4% and wrapping up the week at nearly PKR 282 once again.

In the interim (and reportedly), several decent sized bulker sales (largely handymax and panamax sized) have taken place to local buyers, as a result of Pakistan’s comparatively firmer offerings than India, and there is still a growing desire to import more vessels – particularly evident this week during a bidding contest over a capesize bulker for recycling.

Overall, slow and steady gains mixed in with better late than never is what the Gadani Gang seems to be prodigiously on, and with the timing of supply, the clock might just show the right time for Gadani soon enough.

headline: DEMAND AND LIRA…
highlights: Merrily.
body_text:
After the recent entry of a batch of roros into Aliaga of late, demand (and hunger) for tonnage is on the rise, including the rise of the U.S. Dollar against the Turkish Lira that too ended the week 26 basis points weaker, at TRY 43.50, merrily on their way to greet TRY 44.

Moderate fluctuations in import steel levels aside, there really isn’t much to report from Turkey this week.

headline: ELECTION SPECULATION?
highlights: Back in the picture. | Critical event. | More progressive? | Land of no return.
body_text:
After a worrying start to the year that saw local offerings placed firmly below the psychological barrier of USD 400/LDT—and Bangladesh even slipping to the bottom of the market rankings for a week—Chattogram seems to have slipped back into the picture this week, not only through local discussions but also with a local anchorage that remained busy, including local deliveries from last week that were promptly delivered when the tide broke this week, as well as the welcome arrival of a rare large LDT tanker.

The performance of domestic fundamentals certainly played its part with the Taka spiking 0.65% against the U.S. dollar this week and venturing off into the weekend at BDT 122.05. Local steel plate prices also shockingly woke up after two horizontal weeks (with no local trading being reported) and jumped nearly USD 9/ton clock out at almost USD 494/ton, giving local recyclers that much more of a buffer on the state of current purchases—because for the upcoming units? Who knows where the markets might stand then.

Meanwhile, shades of pre-election speculation are starting to take grip the nation as the critical election day is due to take place by mid-February, and the usual flurry of lobbying, rallying, and breakout instances of political violence continue to mar headlines across the nation. If, as is being hoped for, a more progressive pro-business party is elected to power, we could see a surge in local markets off the back of long-delayed infrastructure projects being resumed, with optimism finally returning to the nation as a result.

For now, however, as Chattogram continues to confuse with its weekly performance—where last week it felt like a “land of no return”—this week feels like a whole new personality breaking through the seams yet again. Seems like Mr. Hyde is out and about once again.

headline: SEARCH OF LIFE!
highlights: Gravitational drop. | Still shortage. | Older handies. | Steel settle. | Concerns afoot.
body_text:
The weekly roller coaster that has become the global marketplace went through its regular gravitational drop this week, with the U.S. dollar taking the “cement-footed diving approach” in all ship-recycling destinations… except—you guessed it—Turkey!

The Baltic Exchange Dry Bulk Index fell 0.7% down to a two-week low, dragged by the Capesize index, which fell a massive 1.1% over the week. The Panamax index slipped a comparatively more acceptable 0.4%, while the Supramax index rose a modest 0.2% to even things out. Meanwhile, easing tensions between the U.S. and Iran alleviated concerns over potential supply disruptions erupting out of the Middle East (thanks, Donnie), resulting in oil falling below USD 62/barrel, yet it managed to crawl ahead and close Friday at USD 63.15/barrel.

As we slip past oil discussions and into the Indian sub-continent ship-recycling destinations, faint signs of life have certainly started to show (at least at the waterfronts) as we head further into February, after an inert start to the year produced some worrying reversals that seemed like the visiting mother-in-law who wasn’t planning on leaving (still feels like that way somehow). Local steel prices surged this week with all sub-continent destinations reporting major jumps across the week.

The shortage of recycling candidates meanwhile continues to flirt with a starving industry that is seeing stars and demand ramp up once again, following what has been a general theme over the years, accompanied by record-low sales due to continually firm freight markets on the back of some new global crisis that somehow never misses a beat to arrive for a paycheck. Older handy bulkers and LNGs have certainly been sold at the start of this year, and at some firming levels too, but tankers (for the most part) and containers have been absent over the last few years.

Bangladeshi elections are also on the horizon and the government has widened the local holiday period to ensure everyone has time to register their vote. All sub-continent recycling destinations meanwhile have had their own unique port positions to report for the week, with Chattogram leading the way once again. That can’t be happening, right? Turkey at the far end remains relatively quiet again, with no news of freshly proposed market units of late.

As Fun February breaks in, it’s looking set to be another quiet 2026, especially as geopolitical shocks continue to keep trading markets propped up —be it by men in suits or in traditional clothing.

headline: SECURE ME SOME!
highlights: LNGs still. | Rupee concerns. | HKC advantage. | Week after week.
body_text:
Alang buyers have reportedly managed to secure some interesting market / private units of late (and this week), including another high-profile LNG and several smaller LDT units positioned in the region, whilst Pakistan and Bangladesh went for the larger dry bulk units in the parade.

Moreover, even though there was another arrival of a rare large LDT tanker, most of the deliveries (just like in Chattogram) were those from last week, taking the total LDT at Alang to just over 36K, for what has been a terrible few weeks thus far.

And while local steel plate prices have primarily been the driving force behind the disaster that has been Alang’s constant re-positioning on the market rankings of late, this week saw a whole new face as not only did local steel plate prices jump USD 14/ton to nearly USD 415/ton, but the U.S. dollar also lost a massive 1.32% against the Indian Rupee and closed shop for the week at INR 90.08, looking ready to break back into Rs. 89.X territory (hopefully next week).

On the HKC front, with nearly all recycling yards in Alang being HKC-certified—23 in Chattogram and two in Gadani (with more on the way)—India will still hold the advantage in this regard, even if (and whenever) competitors catch up and an abundance of tonnage forces sellers toward Alang. Only one of these will sadly be true for the foreseeable future.

For now, regardless of the performance of the competition and where India lands on the market rankings week after week, Alang will always be a home for a unit being proposed on the bidding tables.

headline: LEADING WAY?
highlights: Stunning reversal. | Dry bulk sales. | Good HKC news.
body_text:
After what can only be described as a stunning reversal of fortunes since the start of this year, Pakistan has surprisingly been leading the way in the sub-continent ship-recycling sector over the last few weeks, including this one, where several Panamax and handy bulker sales have reportedly taken place to hungry local recyclers. And from the looks of it, there is still further demand from a hungry few to import vessels at decent levels, still exceeding USD 400/LDT.

Like the rest of the industry, domestic fundamentals have been the trampoline bounce that Gadani recyclers have been desperately looking for, as local steel plate prices finally broke through their cemented coffins and surged nearly USD 8/ton, closing the week out at an industry leading USD 597/ton. Not wanting to be left behind, the Pakistani Rupee also seized the moment this week and surged 1% against the U.S. Dollar, registering a closing bell of PKR 279.14.

And what really snapped the camel’s back this week was the arrival of a near 7K LDT unit at Gadani’s anchorage, breaking what has been a tediously deserted 2026 for the nation’s waterfront thus far. Moreover, with so many rumors of private and market fixtures to the Gadani Gang over the last couple of weeks, the immediate future remains an exciting one to keep an eye on.

Finally, further good news enveloped the market at the start of this year, as the second HKC yard was approved in Gadani and announced in recent weeks. We are finally starting to see the requisite infrastructure being laid out across the shores of Gadani to ensure the survival of this industry in the decades ahead.

With Chattogram decidedly out of the running during election time and tonnage seemingly squeaking its way onto the bidding tables, it’s certainly an exciting time for the Gadani Gang after what feels like an eternity on the sidelines.

headline: STILL LIFE
highlights: UAP.
body_text:
Other than a stage of momentum for Aliaga recyclers with roro deliveries over recent weeks, it seems as though its back to basics for this market, with nothing new to report other than a Lira that was the only ship recycling destination to lose 20 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and clock out at TRY 43.58, merrily on its way to breach TRY 44.

Seems like some serious anti-gravity UAP like performance from the Lira.

headline: BNP IN!
highlights: Election decided. | Infrastructure hopes. | IRRC needed. | Loose belts.
body_text:
After what has seemed like an eternity (and then some) of a wait, encouraging political news finally emerged through from the beleaguered Bangladeshi market this week, as the interim student-led regime finally made way for the country’s second largest party, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), into the leadership seat with more than a 2/3 majority win during the nation’s recent General Elections.

This (hopefully) means that the long-awaited (and quite frankly, desperately needed) domestic infrastructure projects can finally get off the drawing board and into the national eye, which should ignite domestic construction projects and resume demand for steel once again. While there is likely (more like hopefully, with Trump still at the helm of the global economic reins) to be some increased optimism in the market now that a far more progressive, business-friendly, and locally popular party is finally in charge, reality may have its own say on the matter. Time will tell, eh?

Meanwhile, following a request by the government to follow all international HKC regulations, this week also saw the BSBRA adopt the provisions of the International Ready for Recycling Certificate (IRRC), as is also the case now in Pakistan and India. This would mean that once the mandatory IHM Parts I, II, and III have been provided to the ship recycling yard by the Sellers, the relevant recycling yard must then produce a Ship Recycling Plan (SRP), which will then be presented to the class / flag state authorities (once available), in order to produce an IRRC — a fresh requirement for any vessels now arriving any sub-continent ship recycling destination.

On the fundamentals side, all was not rosy, especially given that the Taka lost 17 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and closed the week out at BDT 122.25, on a trajectory that seems to indicate even more falls next week. Local steel plate prices have, meanwhile refused to leave their hammocks as they continue to flatline at nearly USD 494/ton for nearly 3 weeks now, indicating an utter lack of trade with local steel mills, which itself presents a massive problem for Chattogram yards if they are unable to sell any of the recycled ship’s steel.

But that certainly hasn’t stopped them from keeping an eye out for the right “type” of unit, as not only did local recyclers manage to reel in another collection of smaller LDT units including a 7K LDT bulker, it was the arrival of a 24K LDT unit that confirmed why Chattogram choppers willingly loosen their belts at the recycling buffets.

As such, despite what has happened/might happen in the nation, the right type/LDT combination of unit will bring a Bangladeshi buyer out of the woodwork and strike a deal.

headline: CONFUSING VALENTINES!
highlights: Bizarre performance | Ain’t that a switch | Bacteria brewing. | CNY hols. | Election boo.
body_text:
The second week of February brought on a really confusing spin to the markets, with fundamentals across the board performing bizarrely (compared to last week’s performance), as after a volatile beginning to the month, the Baltic Exchange Dry Index and even oil futures found steady ground this week, while even the U.S. Dollar firmed against all ship recycling nation currencies except India (ain’t that a switch), as did local steel plate prices, which also saw India slip the car into reverse and backpedal nearly all of its recent gains.

In an expanded view, the Baltic Exchange’s Dry Bulk Index fell 0.6% this week, pressured primarily by the larger-sized segments, as Capes fell nearly 2% and the Panamax index slipped a matching 0.6%, Supras marched (improved) an impressive 1.8% of their own. Sliding into the barrel, we see WTI crude oil futures pull a drone maneuver and hover around (a lower) USD 62.8/barrel, as markets, investors, and traders collectively worry about the bacteria brewing under the U.S./Iranian nuclear peace carpet once again, and fears over ongoing supply being drastically affected could have a devastating effect on oil prices the world over.

But for the ship recycling world, it’s likely to be even quieter as Chine enters its New Year holiday period, an already subdued (in terms of volumes, not price/demand) international ship recycling market is more than likely to be deprived of potential recycling candidates even further. The incoming Year of the Horse hopefully brings with it some better times for the industry, after what has been (and seemingly continues to be) a record low delivery of recycling tonnage over the last several years, and depreciating levels from the highs of USD 600/LDT down to well below USD 400/LDT, have been a jolt to end-of-life residual values of ships and the books of owners/operators.

Recycling markets do seem to have stabilized within the region of the turbulence and for the time being, events are conspiring in favor of sub-continent markets that paint a brighter picture moving forward. The much anticipated (and long overdue) Bangladeshi elections were finally settled this week with an expected victory for the second largest party in the country (behind disgraced and banned former PM Sheikh Hasina’s party), as the BNP claimed power with over a 2/3 majority. The Pakistani market remains the firmest for another week as the cheap flood of Iranian imports has ceased for the time being, and Gadani steel plate prices continue to dominate industry levels.

And with currency concerns consuming India’s sanity since the start of the year having stabilized this week as well (even showing signs of improvement) and Turkey on the far side slipping back into obscurity after a brief binge of RoRos, overall, it does seem that things couldn’t get any worse than they have, and levels may have reached a state of equilibrium for the year (unless something happens). The only thing left is for supply to deliver on its side of the bargain.

headline: CLIFF HANGER!
highlights: Gravity of hope. | Steel respite. | Election hopes.
body_text:
The Alang market continues to leave the industry on a cliff-hanger, week after week, with vessel prices moving, fundamentals violently shaking the sanity of everyone’s innards, and a hungry landscape of ship recyclers who remain on the lookout for tonnage fueled by nothing more than a hefty serving of nervy sentiments and the gravity of hope.

And even though India may be at the bottom of the ship recycling ranking board for yet another week, Alang recyclers have managed to remain quizzically competitive with their neighbors on any of the slim pickings of vessels that do sail onto the bidding tables, as is amply evident by the state of Alang’s anchorage this week, where well over 47K LDT is idling / has been delivered to its new owners, including 2 rare large LDT tankers — certainly a sight for hungry eyes.

From Alang’s performance at the bidding tables to the reality on the beaches, one thing is for certain: the ongoing lack of tonnage is seeing the ship recycling fraternity (regardless of destination) reacting rather unexpectedly as they’re now seemingly making a dash for the winning line when the right type of unit is tabled. And it’s easy to see why.

Fundamentals, meanwhile, continue to rubber-band the local mindset into frenzies after immediate declines, where even this week, we saw local steel plate prices systematically fell nearly USD 10/ton and reversed a majority of its recent gains, all while the Indian Rupee decided heading north was a better option and reclaimed another 15 basis points against the U.S. Dollar, to end the week at Rs. 90.6.

Overall, the election victory for the BNP in Bangladesh may ease some of the tensions between India and Bangladesh, as a settled and elected party finally takes control, and former disgraced PM Sheikh Hasina, who has been sentenced to death in absentia, continues to live in exile in Delhi despite demands from the Bangladeshi government for her return to face the consequences of her trial, having fled Bangladesh in August 2024.

headline: PAPA’S HUNGRY!
highlights: Stranger things. | HKC works. | Trends
body_text:
Gadani continues to lead the way for yet another week despite an improving Bangladesh narrowing the gap (in the wake of the election victory for the BNP). Yet, the Gadani gang remained comfortable negotiating on (critically) few workable fresh candidates in order to satisfy what has been a corrosive demand fueled by the acidic lack of supply that is only expected to get worse now that the traditionally quieter Chinese New Year holidays are under way. Truth be told, it would have to be a cold day in Lucifer’s bathtub for a Chinese-owned unit to be delivered into Gadani, but stranger things have happened, as reality is weirder than fiction.

And other than leading the recycling ranking charts, Pakistan has also been dominating sub- continent currency and steel plate price performances over the last couple of quarters, given that not only has the Pakistani Rupee firmed to below PKR 280, but local steel plate prices even rose recently and have remained atop the industry numbers.

Moreover, this week’s performance wrench that affected all markets, managed to keep Pakistan more or less in the clear, as it ended the week just a few basis points weaker at a still healthy PKR 279.59. Local steel plate prices, too, remain even-keeled at an industry-fantastic PKR 594/ton — USD 100/ton more than those from Bangladesh and about USD 190/ton above those from Alang.

And these improvements, backed by news of numerous local market and private fixtures, saw Gadani’s waterfront light up with a series of decent LDT bulk carriers that collectively carried the total volume of tonnage at anchorage to nearly 30K LDT via 4 vessels this week. A massive upgrade for local buyers compared to their silent operating mode over the last several months, where the occasional small LDT vessel would arrive locally, be delayed, and eventually beach.

Finally, HKC infrastructure works also continue at pace in Gadani, with two ship recycling yards now having received their HKC accreditations and upgrades on remaining yards still ongoing and reportedly even making significant progress, as Pakistan may continue to dominate the rankings should the current trends persist.

headline: OH, ALIAGA!
highlights: Lingering.
body_text: Give more than just a weakening Lira and the occasional batch of ships that seem to emerge after years. And since Lira is all there ever is, it’s down another 24 basis points this week and scratching at the knees of TRY 44, having closed the week at TRY 43.71 against the U.S. Dollar. Local offerings and demand, like the sub-continent, remains lingering and omni-present.

headline: JACK-IN-THE-BOX!
highlights: BNP victory. | Leapfrog. | Larger LDT pref. | Spring and sunshine.
body_text:
Like a jack-in-the-box springing back to life, this week Bangladesh worked its way back to the top of the market rankings board — an impressive move given the state of local fundamentals, the economy, and the nation overall. Ever since the election victory for the country’s second-largest political party, the BNP, was declared last week with a two-thirds majority, the bounce in the step certainly seems to be back as Chattogram Choppers started offering some really strong numbers on decent LDT and well-conditioned market/private tonnage that made it to the tables this week.

Taking a step back to truly appreciate the scenario: leapfrogging a bullish Pakistan has been no easy feat for Bangladeshi recyclers, especially with ongoing HKC yard accreditations in Gadani — which now has two domestic yards on the roster and growing international interest once again — alongside an improving Pakistani economy and demand in Gadani that has built up over the last four months amid a near-zero number of local arrivals. Chattogram recyclers had to really drop the hammer and are now seeing the best levels across the Indian sub-continent ship recycling sector once again.

While the preference-backed pricing has primarily been for good/decent-condition larger LDT units, the attractive pricing certainly helped reel in the second Cape bulker of the year, which was delivered locally this week. In fact, speaking of local deliveries, the anchorage itself was impressive — not only was a collection of larger LDT bulkers delivered, but they were topped by a near 27K LDT LNG unit that remains idling outside awaiting delivery. Impressively, local market news also reports that several LNG units are still working toward onward sale into Chattogram in the weeks ahead. Well timed, considering reports highlight Bangladeshi inflation climbing from 8.49% in December 2025 to 8.58% in January 2026 — not an entirely alarming rise by any stretch of the imagination, but just enough to add pressure on local costs.

And with the rear-view mirror presenting a darker period for Chattogram Choppers, a freshly elected and popular government, a Taka that firmed a healthy 0.31% against the U.S. Dollar, and local steel plate prices that posted a massive USD 16/ton jump this week suggest that March might just deliver spring and sunshine.

headline: RAGING HANGOVER!
highlights: CNY pause. | Price push. | Doc clarity. | Ramadan ensues. | Freight flying.
body_text:
International market turmoil from the direct / indirect imposition of global tariffs and related actions by Donnie Dementia saw a crazy Week 8 wind up in 2026, as freight rates and oil prices both moved up and subsequently reconsidered their moves, retracing their steps before the week ended. The U.S. Dollar and local steel plate prices reformulated their individual strategies as they returned mixed results of their own across the various sub-continent destinations — all in the midst of rising inflation in a confusion-laden ship recycling industry. To start, let’s paint a clearer picture of the international state of affairs as of January 2026, with key inflation figures from Trump’s wrap-up of his year one “presidency.” U.S. inflationary figures (un?)surprisingly fell to 2.4% (from 2.7% in both of the preceding months), even as the cost of living rises and the populace responsible for the performance of the economy collectively tightens their purse strings. Turkey’s figures for last month followed suit in the path of U.S. numbers, while Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi figures all rose in unison.

As oil rose above USD 63/barrel from last week to well over USD 66/barrel this week, it retreated back down to USD 65.93/barrel by week’s end, amid investors and forecasters increasingly weighing the deranged possibility of Donnie Silver Spoon launching another confounding attack against Iran, in an ongoing effort to distract from the JE files (having failed with his bid involving President Maduro’s kidnapping just last month), and still failing. The Baltic Exchange’s Dry Bulk Index, meanwhile, snapped a three-day losing streak by the end of the week and climbed a healthy 1.2% on the back of Capes (which rebounded a healthy 1.7%) and Panamaxes (which rose 1.2%), despite Supras easing by 1 point. All of the above showed a different face in the ship recycling markets, as local anchorages were relatively stacked this week, with a collective 151K LDT via 16 vessels that arrived and were delivered across India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan — a truly welcome change for the industry.

headline: HAVE MY CAKE& EAT IT!
highlights: Smattering. | Hide-and-go-seek. | Select edge. | Get stuffed.
body_text:
Amid the smattering of sanctioned vessels that continue to arrive into India, Alang buyers are still taking in their fair share of specialist vessels and geographically positioned units of all LDTs and types. Local port positioning demonstrates not only the type and distribution of LDTs on the board, but also highlights a fairly even share of vessels between all sub-continent markets (with Bangladesh well ahead in terms of total LDT, as expected).

With the fundamentals still playing hide-and-seek with stability in the minds of local recyclers, encouraging signs finally seem to be emerging in Alang despite the ongoing chaos and a rocky end to 2025. Highlighting the turbulence, the Indian Rupee lost 0.15% against the U.S. Dollar and ended the week at Rs. 90.76. Meanwhile, local steel plate prices also took a carnival ride, losing nearly USD 4/ton and ending the week below the dreaded USD 400/ton mark (at USD 399).

On the economic front, India’s inflation jumped to 2.75% in January, well above domestic market expectations of landing near 2.4%. What is particularly noteworthy is that, from a low of 0.25% (firm stagflation territory) back in October 2025, India’s inflation has risen steadily each month — 0.71% in November, 1.33% in December, and now 2.75% in January.

Coupled with domestic growth, this heated rise also carries a heavy dose of Trumpian “Victory Dressing.” Speaking of which, the fact that the Supreme Court of the United States reversed all of Donnie’s unbridled global tariffs on Friday reportedly sent him into a rage on Saturday, tweeting out policy declaring that the U.S. would levy an additional 15% tariff on the world under a 1970s law that does not support his justification. As such, India (and the world) can certainly expect rough waters sailing into March.

Overall, even though Alang buyers are unable to compete on favored larger LDT units with the likes of Pakistan and Bangladesh, India will always hold the advantage in taking in specialist non-ferrous units and offshore vessels. It retains the edge with the most — and some of the highest-standard — HKC yards available, and remains the one destination that will not run out of space, even when the competition gets stuffed.

headline: QUICK RELINQUISH!
highlights: Missing out. | Good run. | Cessation.
body_text:
Pakistan has already relinquished the top spot to a resurgent Bangladesh this week, in the wake of the welcome victory for the BNP party there (which should hopefully lead to further stability in Chattogram as renewed impetus on critical infrastructure projects takes hold).

Nevertheless, it has certainly been an encouraging run for Gadani so far this year. With several larger units (particularly on the dry bulk side) having been concluded to hungry Gadani buyers at some of the best rates on show across the sub-continent, local anchorage has finally started to spill the beans on the state of recent fixtures, with a healthy collection beginning to gather at the waterfront.

In fact, it has truly been a sight for sore eyes to witness five vessels at Gadani’s waterfront this week (some delivered and some in the process of delivery). The variety in type and variance in LDT is also a welcome break from the mundane for local recyclers who, as the types of units confirm, tend to stay on the straight and narrow.

Despite local fundamentals performing comparatively healthier than the competition and doing their best to support Gadani buyers — with local steel plate prices still flatlining at the highest in the industry at USD 594/ton, and the Pakistan Rupee snaring a healthy 0.40% against the U.S. Dollar to close the week at PKR 278.49 — what remains confounding is the incredible volatility behind the purchasing mindset and trends arising out of Pakistan since last year.

While the cessation of Iranian steel dumping has, for the time being, given end buyers added confidence to fill dormant plots again, what about the prior months — and much of 2025 — when the situation was fairly similar, yet Gadani yards languished in isolation? Perhaps inflationary trends are responsible for this performance: inflation fell as low as 0.3% back in April 2025, rose to 4.1% by August, crossed over 6.2% by October, wrapped up 2025 at 5.6%, and rose again in January to 5.8%.

This kind of volatility, backed by Trump’s 30% tariffs on various nations, could well be contributing to the overall fragility of local offerings at the bidding tables. But with local yards now becoming HKC-certified and a decent supply of incoming tonnage, let’s hope 2026 is the year Pakistan finally breaks past 25 ships in a year.

headline: SAVING GRACE!
highlights: Stomach full.
body_text:
Other than the monotony of the ailing Lira (which lost another 0.26% against the U.S. Dollar and wrapped the week up at TRY 43.84) and the occasional sprinkle of cheer via a sudden surge of tonnage, Aliaga yards have been stuck at the extreme ends of an overstretched rubber band, with inflation filling in the middle.

Released figures indicate Turkey’s annual inflation eased marginally from 30.89% in December 2025 to 30.65% in January. However, it remained notably above market expectations of 20%. Moreover, with rising costs of food and consumables, consumer prices reportedly surged to a one-year high of 4.84%.

With rising costs, steady inflation, and muted supply, local recyclers have little more than a stomach full of desperation to keep them fueled.

headline: DISPARATE!
highlights: Atop. | Chief focus. | Newly elected. | Tough March.
body_text:
Bangladesh sits atop the Indian sub-continent ship recycling rankings for yet another week, amid fresh sales that have been hard to come by as trading markets endure another week of poking volatility that is continuing to deprive recycling markets of any meaningful tonnage.

The situation unfolding across the Middle East will be the chief focus of the world in the weeks ahead, and it is nearly assured that rising freight and oil rates will, in turn, see recycling markets forcibly face another spell of tonnage absence at the local waterfront, spelling trouble for the recyclers who are yet to receive their share of recompensate for all the yard expenses ensured during the HKC upgrade and accreditations phases.

Speaking of tonnage absence at the bidding tables, all anchorages still have units arriving across the various locations, including Chattogram, which saw the arrival of a near 20K LDT bulker and a handful of smaller dry units, all while last week’s large LDT LNG was delivered to her new owners for recycling. But with a major conflict now underway and Far Eastern markets still in a holiday mood, the coming weeks are likely to be a pinching affair for this market.

Fundamentals, meanwhile, have taken hits to varying degrees, as not only did local steel plate prices slide a couple of dollars to end the week at USD 507.81/ton, but the Taka also lost 0.20% and wound the week down at BDT 122.71 against the U.S. Dollar.

Despite the globally brewing chaos, things domestically seem to be in a better state for the nation, as optimism lingers in the air on the back of the newly elected governing body in Bangladesh. They certainly have a job on their hands, deciphering where they sit on the international spectrum and with whom to form strategic alliances in this fractured and disparate world we now live in.

As tonnage at the bidding tables dries up once again and Far Eastern owners are still not fully back in business after the Chinese New Year holidays, Chattogram Choppers at least have a month of fasting and celebrations to keep them busy.

headline: W.A.R.
highlights: On edge. | Shipping halt. | Oil flies? | Recycling deprived. | Disruption.
body_text:
Whackos Attacking Reality — WAR — is literally the definition of the weekend as the Middle East descended into all-out chaos between the U.S. & Israel on one side and Iran on the other, leaving regional and international markets bracing for the inevitable whirlpool of global insanity that is about to suck the entire world into short-term (at the very least) tumult.

Oil was already on its way up during the week, but as the weekend came around, it spiked over 10%, jumping from around USD 63/barrel last week to nearly USD 71.90/barrel at the time of writing. The Baltic Exchange was also on its way up (rising 1.1%) but remained comparatively subdued in comparison to oil futures…yet. The Cape, Panamax, and Supra indices all climbed 0.2%, 1.4%, and 3% respectively. Currencies, too, took a hammering, as all of the major ship recycling destinations registered declines across the board. Local steel plate prices also declined across the board, albeit marginally, likely waiting for Monday to turn around before deciding whether to join the ranks of rising rates.

The news immediately worsens for the maritime industry as insurance premiums, bunkers, voyage insurance, blockages, delays, and charters running afoul are just the tip of this ballooning iceberg while the dust settles amid a still inexplicable war campaign that is reportedly set to continue for at least another four weeks — which clearly means buckle up, folks.

Especially as calls for calm and de-escalation intensify but are reportedly falling on deaf ears on the Iranian side following the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader in his compound and over 60 others, including children at a local school, according to U.S. sources.

The resulting backlash and retaliation from the pariah state have seen several major Middle Eastern states (Qatar, UAE (Dubai, Abu Dhabi), Oman and many more) come under direct Iranian fire across much of the last 36 hours. Iran has also reportedly halted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while the cancellation of thousands of regional and international flights to and from the region is another immediate knock-on effect to trade and commerce — not only in the region, but globally — as the rest of us wait with bated breath to see how the coming week unfolds.

headline: STALLED SUCCESSFULLY!
highlights: Fair share. | Conundrum. | Slim pickings. | Hell or high water.
body_text:
As the lowest-placed sub-continent market, India has been — and continues to — face hardships in the current environment, having to make do with strictly Alang-only HKC vessels in recent times, along with the usual distribution of specialist units such as LNGs, reefers, and offshore vessels. Local port positions indeed show that all sub-continent recycling destinations have had their fair share of arrivals in recent times, including this week, with India taking the largest slice of the sub-continent anchorage pie.

And the irony? Despite being the lowest-placed ship recycling destination in the sub-continent, Alang recyclers were busy taking in nearly three times the number of vessels as their Chattogram counterparts / 1.5 times the LDT, but they took in nearly four times the number / about 20 times the LDT of the Gadani Gang. A juicy near-30K LDT LNG, a +25K LDT container was mixed in with a bevy of small LDT reefers, bulkers, and general cargo units that rounded off the arrivals list.

And through it all, even with the lowest prices on show, geography was busy baking its cookies on the shores of Western India, where Alang had been stalled on pricing but still managed to successfully beat out the competition on acquisitions and arrivals this week. Moreover, India’s stance on the global stage will once again face scrutiny amid the latest Middle East madness, as was the case when it previously remained a neutral party between Russia and the West — a move that saw an enraged Trump levy the most tariffs against India in the sub-continent.
