The real kicker remains the state of local fundamentals, which have left India stranded in third and facing many of the same hurdles competing markets faced this week — namely, marginally declining local steel plate prices that fell about USD 1/ton and closed the week at USD 400/ton, while the Indian Rupee aimlessly followed suit, slipping 0.31% and wrapping up the week at a high Rs. 91.02 once again.

Overall, and as previously stated, come hell or high water, Alang’s torches always seem to have power.

headline: INCOMING ALERT!
highlights: Deprived. | Overtaken. | Unstable.
body_text:
While Pakistan has been alert to any available larger LDT dry vessels coming its way over the last few months, elevated freight markets continue to perform, keeping global ship recycling starved of any significant tonnage — a trend that has persisted for several years now. Despite holding the top spot for a short while and delivering Aliaga-like bursts of performance across various quarters, including this most recent one, it seems Gadani may be starting to slip off the port reports once again.

Last week saw four arrivals. This week, two of those were delivered, leaving just two on the port report — and no fresh arrivals. Other than the one vessel that has been idling at the waterfront for the last two weeks.

Moreover, just like its regional competition, Gadani’s fundamentals — which have been among the strongest in the sub-continent ship recycling community — also saw their share of jitters. Local steel plate prices lost nearly USD 2/ton, closing the week at around USD 507/ton. The Pakistani Rupee also slipped 0.10%, ending the week at PKR 279.26.

Making matters worse for Gadani is not only its proximity to Iran amid the ongoing war in the region, but also the escalating tensions between the Afghan Taliban and the Pakistani government, which are now reportedly engaging in open conflict of their own, adding further instability across the region. While this may further curtail the flow of Iranian steel into Pakistan — potentially supporting local steel plate prices — the future inflow of regional tonnage into Gadani waters remains a toss-up at this time.

Overall, even though Bangladesh overtook Pakistan for the top spot on the sub-continent price board just a couple of weeks ago, the unfolding events across the Middle East, coupled with the political situation inside Pakistan — which remains unstable, with several deaths reported during pro-Khomeini rallies over the weekend — suggest that political stresses may be shifting westward. We may well see empty anchorages all over again.

Probably why the beaches in Alang will continue to remain busy.

headline: FIERY NEIGHBORHOOD!
highlights: Darn close.
body_text:
Having close ties with the Ayatollah certainly won’t help Turkey’s political situation in the short term. Not only are America and Iran at odds in Turkey’s front yard, but with Turkey declining U.S. use of its bases for Trump’s latest catfight, the Turkish government is now expecting an influx of displaced Iranian refugees — a development that is sure to strain the state in the near term.

With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz already marginalizing supply chains for ships, Aliaga buyers are likely to get hit even harder in the short term, especially as the Lira lost another 0.32% over the last week and closed out at TRY 43.97 against the U.S. Dollar — darn close to breaking into TRY 44 next week.

headline: PRIORITIES!
highlights: Interesting initiation. | Alliances. | Rising levels. | ETTD!
body_text:
It has been an interesting initiation for the new BNP regime in Bangladesh after the recent election victory for its party on February 2 (weeks ago), with the outbreak of war across the Middle East occurring soon after. The chief priority for this newly elected body will be ensuring that its alliances remain secure in the face of such belligerent forces at play that are claiming to remove rogue regimes across the world in the name of peace and stability, all while destabilizing the world before any form of nobility behind their intentions/actions was even born to justify the reported deaths of 1100 Iranian citizens (and counting).

Moreover, the prolonged de-stabilizing marathon that Bangladesh suffered since the violent coup that ousted the unpopular Sheikh Hasina and her ruling party back in June 2024, only left the fate of the nation in the hands of a useless regime that drove its economy into a tailspin for the subsequent 20 months (until February 14, 2026), which also saw some catastrophic economic decisions being delivered that resulted in the Taka tail-spinning to its current highs.

In fact, even this week, the Bangladeshi Taka lost 10 basis points against the U.S. Dollar and clocked out at BDT 122.18, with extreme volatility coming through toward the end of the week as the war intensified. Local steel plate prices also dipped their heads back into the scene, dropping a far more moderate USD 1/Ton and down to nearly USD 507/ton. The war has also delivered a cessation of workable tonnage across the last two weeks, in addition to a gradually slimming Chattogram waterfront that has only seen action in the form of local redeliveries of prior arrivals from the week before, with no fresh arrivals reported this week.

All this is rearing its head at a time the domestic ship recycling community was seemingly poised for a return on the back of firming local steel prices, coupled with demand from most of the 22+ HKC-approved buyers that had been improving on the back of the hope that this new government would make an urgent and renewed push on domestic and infrastructure projects, resulting in economic stimulus for the country.

But Everything Trump Touches Dies! — so here we are.

headline: WHAT DID ANYONE EXPECT?
highlights: War spreads. | Hormuz closure. | Ships sunk. | Rising fuel. | Operating costs.
body_text:
As the un-announced and Congress unapproved U.S. / Israeli war against Iran enters its second week, the assassination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in a join air operation by the nation continues to see earthquakes reverberate across vast regions in the nation that are under control by various Iranian religious groups that served the Ayatollah, are now breaking away at their “free will” into smaller groups controlling massive non-intersecting regions of Iran and retaliating Willy Nilly, with no clear control and / or coordination between the groups, resulting in Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian apologizing to neighboring Arab nations for the bombings from his country on day and rebel groups bombed DXB Intl Airport and a government high-rise in Kuwait the very next day.

And as the epicenter of chaos remains uncontrolled and uncoordinated (as chaos during war tends to), the world is immediately suffering the economic devastation that generally follows war’s welcome party, with the immediate impacts being felt across the shipping world following the costly closures of the Strait of Hormuz and Houthis declaring war on passing vessels in the Red Sea, all while the Houthis in the South and Hezbollah in the North declare war against Israeli and American forces in the region. This not only saw fuel prices sky-rocketing – but also affected how, when, and where, vessels impacted by the war can freely trade under international laws.

The closure of the Straits of Hormuz, one of the busiest waterways in the world has been the most devastating blow to the world given that not only is it the busiest oil terminal in the world, but most vessels will also now be diverted from the region, likely seeing an increase in tankers at the bidding table. Escalating for those stuck in the region is getting out of it, without getting attacked or captured in the process of doing so. Insurance premiums for vessels stuck there is also rising exponentially, all while Diaper Don brags about sinking the entire Iranian nay, including an Iranian warship that had been notably sunk off of the coast of Sri Lanka by a U.S. submarine, in a conflict that continues to spread its circumference far beyond the epicenter of the Epstein Files, and is potentially endangering the safety of the world in the process.

headline: GAS GUZZLERS!
highlights: Shortage rumours. | Normal output. | Erring on positive. | Holdout?
body_text:
With global turmoil born out of another American Israeli / Middle East conflict brewing fresh on the pot, and the neighboring region suffering immediately its week that even saw its reverberations filter through to Alang’s ship recycling sector this week, rumors of a feared gas shortage that could lead to partial closures of local ship recycling facilities started to make the rounds. However, the word on the ground is that these fears are exaggerated and that Alang ship recycling yards are operating at normal output — unsurprising, perhaps, given the overall shortage of tonnage imported to local plots over recent years.

Yet, India’s problem with the war circles primarily around the import of oil, with Russia and Iran being its primary sources of oil supply. But Trump’s recent sanctions against India’s trading of oil with Russia saw even more needles added to India’s balloon party after its second source of supply, Iran, shut down the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in oil and gas products becoming extremely expensive for the common man in the Indian subcontinent.

And given how nervy overall Indian sentiments tend to be, markets saw the Indian Rupee fumble nearly 1% (0.95% to be precise) and wrap up the week at Rs. 91.94 against the U.S. Dollar. It was local steel plate prices, however, that turned the week into a Formula 1 racetrack as they whizzed by industry players from USD 396.83/ton at the start of the week to USD 414.53/ton by the time the week ended — a near USD 28/ton meteoric rise, likely resulting from fears of import shortages of steel scrap from the region.

The waterfront, however, continued to impress, even though it was only a handful of small-LDT arrivals that graced Alang’s anchorage this week (likely units being displaced because of the regional conflict), taking the total number of units at anchorage to 6 and in excess of 44K LDT. A strong number, given the state of the times.

So, what lies ahead? It seems tonnage inflow might just become real as more and more units start getting displaced because of the war, routing patterns change, voyages become expensive, inflation starts to rise in the short term before demand starts to incrementally decline to where supply starts to diminish, and vessels (especially the old(er) ones still making the rounds, and that too hopefully in abundance) return to the bidding tables eventually. Just how soon is anyone’s guess.

Most educated minds will tell you catastrophic changes to global supply chains and resulting economic equilibriums generally takes 6–9 months to reach. Can we the industry hold out another year again?

headline: SHORTAGE?
highlights: Pricing good. | Could change? | Regional violence
body_text:
Despite a rising shortage of recent arrivals into Pakistan last week, demand and pricing remain good and positioned not too far from their Bangladeshi counterparts, even though a few recent candidates have reportedly been heading their way from the region, including this week, that saw the arrival of a small LDT general cargo unit late last week.

That may be set to change however as the conflict in the Middle East rages on and the operating cost of vessels starts to soar once again (with freight in certain sectors, mainly tankers, also expected to fly off the charts), we may see even more regional tankers start to arrive Gadani’s waterfront in the coming weeks.

Especially geographically positioned tonnage from regional owners who are more interested in wrapping up a quick deal with a yet to be certified yard, saving whatever little they can in documentary formalities during these trying times. Violence has also started to beset the country, with factions opposed to the U.S. and Israel interventions in Iran causing aggression and attacks against U.S. embassies across the latitude, in what is expectedly to be a violent time country as it is, being engaged in a full-frontal war with the Afghani Taliban from their side.

The cumulative effect of all this fighting has seen domestic fundamentals reacting strangely as local steel plate prices froze in their tracks at USD 590.54/ton for the entirety of the week, all while the Pakistani Rupee surprisingly firmed 35 basis points and ended the week at a healthier PKT 278.08 against the U.S. Dollar.

What happens with Gadani in the coming week(s) remains to be seen, but one thing is for certain. If local offer levels hold higher than those of India, Gadani will become the destination for regional owners of units displaced by the war, to find a final resting place for their steel beauties.

headline: EGE ÇELİK GETS THE BOOT?
highlights: Darn close. | Interesting times in Gadani.
body_text:
The week's standout headline out of Aliağa had nothing to do with steel prices — it was a regulatory hammer landing on one of Turkey's best-known recycling names. Ege Çelik has been stripped of its EU certification, vanishing from the approved list if facilities that was published on February 27th. Inspectors flagged insufficient pre-cleaning before main cutting and no impermeable surface at the shoreline — both high-risk on pollution and worker safety grounds. One of the five deficiencies cited had already been flagged in a prior audit. Corrective reports were submitted; they delisted the yard anyway.

Meanwhile, a surprising turn of events has seen fresh tonnage arriving Alaiga’s shoreline — as Romanian-detained vessel Lily-Ha was reportedly sold to Aliağa on March 7th as the Lira’s unplugged drain continued to tank the value of its currency, riddling it down another 27 basis points, blowing past TRY 44 against the U.S. Dollar this week, and wiping out at TRY 40.10.

headline: STUNNING HAUL AS MARKETS FALL!
highlights: Main market. | Barren recently. | Sales glut. | Just stay home?
body_text:
Bangladesh has been the market of the moment as Chattogram Choppers take in a stunning haul of vessels at the bidding tables this week, including three LNGs, and several handymax bulkers at the best market levels available at the moment, which also stand well above the regional competition and well ahead of expectations from the Chattogram market even in just the last week. After a barren few weeks at the empty bidding tables and near empty port reports on several occasions, the recent past and moreover, this week was compellingly more productive for the local market as MISC committed three more LNGs to local buyers as the PUTERI MUTIARA SATU (28,804 LDT), the PUTERI ZAMRUD SATU (28,858 LDT), and the PUTERI FIRU SATU (28,805 LDT) all were committed at over USD 11 million each, basis an ‘as is’ Malaysia delivery. In other sales, two handymax bulkers were committed to local buyers as the OCEAN AMAZING (7,075 LDT) was fixed for USD 300/LT LDT, also on an ‘as is’ Jakarta basis, but under tow. Finally, the WANTONG SUMMER (8,196 LDT) was finalized for an appreciably firm USD 443/LT LDT.

And as ship owners and ship recyclers were just about fed-up with the overall state of the ship industry since 2022, Donnie delivered madness and surprising movements in the sub-continent that even helped local recyclers take delivery of a new 27K LDT LNG, despite an Ozempic anchorage this week. A thinning anchorage wasn’t the only surprise awaiting local recyclers through the course of the week as Taka plummeted a massive 0.56% against the U.S. Dollar and ended the week at BDT 122.73. Local steel plate prices further tightened local margins by declining USD 4/Ton on their end and registered a still decent USD 502/ton.

Economically however, the effects of war are starting to hit the nation as the local government has started rationing fuel delivery at local gas stations that is now leading to long lines and panic at the pumps. Schools, colleges, and universities have all been reportedly shut down for the time being. Fertilizer factories have ceased operations as electric load shedding (resulting in power losses) has become a regular cycle, on that’s going to wreak havoc with incoming summer months. The effects on domestic ship recycling yards are reportedly even more dire as fuel quantities needed to operate yard machineries and motor-driven equipment have reduced operating hours. Local trucking delays in shifting recycled ship’s steels out of yards has resulted in a 50% decline of output as trucking companies themselves are restricting their fleets from traveling longer distances. Inflation is back up on the rise as it wrapped February up at 9.13% (up from 8.58 in Jan). Seem only thing left when the monsoons arrive is for people to just stay home.

headline: Turbulent Tides!
highlights: Tensions lift oil. | Freight follows oil. | Shipping routes | Markets turn
body_text:
Escalating tensions in the Middle East ran through global markets again this week, as military activity near Iran’s Kharg Island, the country’s primary oil export terminal that can host up to 10 supertankers at a time, unsettled already fragile energy markets and pushed oil prices that currently linger around USD 100/ton even higher. Developments around the terminal quickly drew market attention as traders reacted to potential disruptions in regional supply flows, while movements in oil prices began to ripple across shipping markets and broader economic indicators. As oil started to climb, freight followed suit, continuing to feed the already rising global inflation picture, while the U.S. Dollar wore the crown jewel of the week, rising notably against all of the major international ship recycling markets. At the same time, local steel plate prices saw another volatile week across several recycling destinations as currency fluctuations and domestic demand influenced pricing levels across the Subcontinent.

As the situation developed, additional maritime security measures were introduced across key transit routes in the region to help ensure the safe passage of commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Given that this corridor remains one of the most critical shipping arteries for global crude flows, even the perception of instability quickly translates into stronger oil prices, firmer freight sentiment, and renewed uncertainty across shipping markets.

International markets overall are expected to remain unsettled while tensions continue across the Middle East. Surging fuel prices across most regions are already beginning to lower freight incomes on a wide range of vessels, while security concerns have also increased following reported incidents involving commercial ships this past week, alongside continued warnings directed at vessels operating nearby. Quick stats before we run out of space? Oil closed roughly 3% higher than last week at USD 98/barrel and is expected to remain volatile should tensions escalate further, while the Baltic Exchange Dry Index rose nearly 3% as well, fueled by the Cape (up 5.8%), Panas (up 0.2%), while smaller indices moved lower (down 0.5%).

Behind the broader market volatility lies a challenging reality: assets under pressure, currencies depreciating, and businesses across several sectors facing tighter operating margins as higher energy costs ripple through the global economy. Trickling down, recycling markets are again facing fluctuating currency rates and unsettled recyclers, while rumors of anticipated shortages of fuel and gas continue to add to industry uncertainty.

headline: LONG WALKS ON SHORT BRIDGES!
highlights: Losing green. | Gas worries. | Prolonged shortage. | Predicament.
body_text:
The Indian market remains price-positioned a long way away from its Bangladeshi competition (who unsurprisingly secured all of the sales of the week, including several Class NK-only HKC green units that are usually reserved for India), and is even behind its eager Pakistani counterparts for the last few weeks now. And unlike the competing regional economies in the ship-recycling space, India has generally weathered international storms and events with comparative ease, given, logically, its far greater economy.

Yet, all is far from well, with a sprinkle of good news thrown into the mix. To start, the rumored shortage of fuel and gas availability that was supposed to hit the local market over the last couple of weeks has yet to surface, and will likely even fail to do so, given Trump is now attempting to back- pedal his brain from his own catastrophic, and inherently consequentially devoid, decision-making standards by lifting India’s sanctions against Russian oil that should help India’s rapidly rising inflation over recent months.

Speaking of which, inflation has now climbed from 0.25% in October to over 3.2% in March, highlighting probably the fastest pace of inflation, for better or for worse, over the last 11 months. And the performance of the Indian Rupee (which fell another 0.70%, down to Rs. 92.56 against the U.S. Dollar), along with local steel plate prices (which also fell a comparatively massive USD 10/Ton, down to USD 410/Ton), have likely been contributors to the degrading state of inflation and have also done little to help Alang’s purchasing prowess, even though local anchorage has been far and away from facing as many near-empty reports as competing neighbors have during the same time.

And while the ease of completing an Alang re-delivery has historically helped this market see more tonnage come in than Bangladesh and Pakistan, the current state of Alang’s pricing and the sudden improvements from Bangladesh this week, at a time when the world looks like it’s on fire (just for fun), actually saw Alang-favored specialist units such as LNGs (rich in non-ferrous) likely heading to competing markets.

Long walks during short, trying times is certainly what seems to be Alang’s current predicament.

headline: MORE THAN JUST THE MUSIC!
highlights: Empty handed. | Regional upheaval. | Demand good.
body_text:
Pakistan as a nation is facing up to more than just the music over the last few weeks as economically, politically, and from a ship-recycling standpoint, it’s all gone a bit Willy Wonky. To start, on the international arena, Pakistani intelligence, ISI, is in a full public conflict against the Afghani Taliban, who it claims are being funded by India to engage in terrorism against Pakistan.

While that is ongoing, the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran is seeing some fallout in Pakistan, given that the nations are neighbors, and violent pro-Iranian factions in Pakistan have been targeting U.S. facilities in the country, with deaths being reported as a result.

On the ship-recycling front, things continue a la Ozempic as another empty-handed week at the bidding tables for Gadani was instead spent witnessing all of the market tonnage heading to Chattogram shores, at rates far beyond the reach of offers tabled by the Gadani Gang, and despite demand still being ripe for the time being, having taken several larger LDT bulkers so far this year.

But like its sub-continent brethren, local fundamentals here remained in a pickle as, on the one hand, the Pakistani Rupee slid 0.48% and called it a week at a still-strong PKR 279.20 against the U.S.$, whilst local steel plate prices were the only rebels of the fundamentals as they climbed over USD 6.50/ton and wrapped things up at nearly USD 599/Ton – the highest margins of the industry. The logical cessation of inflow of steel scrap from Iran during these trying times will likely help this key fundamental deliver fair winds in the short term and help local pricing.

But with a war-riddled geographic region and an HKC development chart-sheet that’s still teething at best, Gadani’s waterfront will continue to see tonnage arrive in squirts every other month – and with the way 2025, and even 2024, has been for this market, it seems 2026 will likely be no different, especially as domestic inflation itself surged to 7% last month (up from 5.8% in January).

Like a handicapped father’s unwitting dance at his daughter’s wedding, Gadani’s delivery schedule seems trapped in a similar fate.

headline: STUGNATED?
highlights: Life support.
body_text:
Stuck next to the warring nations and stagnated by degrading and dead fundamentals, Aliaga seems to be returning to vacation mode after what turned out to be one of the busiest starts to a year Aliaga has seen in recent times. Yet, making its presence felt week after week has been the U.S. Dollar, which has been painfully and consistently reminding Aliaga recyclers how much tighter their belts will continue to get as they hold on to their vessel prices in the face of a Lira that fell another 0.25% this week and wrapped things up at TRY 44.20.

If there is one thing that has remained consistent for Aliaga, it is just how fundamentals and international politics will be the ones to leave Aliaga’s ship-recycling industry on life support before anything else does.

headline: PRICE ADVANTAGE!
highlights: Market leaders. | Taka losing ground. | No OFAC. | Supply issues.
body_text:
Bangladesh enters this Eid holiday in an unenviable position, leading the sub-continent price board, yet unable to convert that pricing leadership into meaningful transaction volume. The holiday has effectively shuttered negotiations for the week, with Chattogram's waterfront operating at ceremonial pace and no new arrivals of note reported as buyers observe the three-day festival.

The Bangladeshi Taka continued to lose ground against the U.S. Dollar this week, slipping a further 8 basis points to close at BDT 122.26, its weakest level against the Dollar in 2026. For recyclers buying tonnage in dollars and selling recycled steel in Taka, this persistent currency erosion is a structural headache that holiday cheer does little to address. Local steel plate prices nudged upward marginally, finishing the week at approximately USD 511/ton, though this modest improvement was largely driven by supply anxiety rather than genuine demand strength, as the war's impact on regional steel flows continues to introduce unpredictability into procurement chains.

The two OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs that have been idling at OPL Chattogram continue to attract considerable industry attention, though not of the productive variety. Neither vessel has yet received the No Objection Certificate required for entry into port limits, and the BSBRA has made clear it will not facilitate their delivery. The episode serves as a pointed reminder of the risks that some cash buyers appear willing to accept in pursuit of margin, and of the reputational damage that can flow to the wider market when international sanctions are visibly flouted at the anchorage.

Looking ahead, the post-Eid period will be the true test. If Bangladesh can couple its pricing advantage with faster central bank approvals on Letters of Credit, a bottleneck that has frustrated Sellers and buyers alike for weeks, the market may yet see a modest pre-monsoon flurry of activity. The HKC certification pipeline at Chattogram is also progressing, with several yards now reportedly within weeks of completing their documentation. A cleaner, more compliant Bangladeshi market is on the horizon. Whether tonnage arrives in sufficient quantity to fill those upgraded yards before the June rains is the more pressing question.

headline: EID PAUSE!
highlights: Eid hols. | War ongoing. | Recycling ruse. | Sales slow. | USD woes.
body_text:
Eid al-Fitr has arrived to greet the world's ship recycling markets this week, and as is tradition, it came bearing the gift of silence. From Chattogram to Gadani, Alang to Aliağa, the holy festival has pressed pause on an industry that was already beginning to feel the compounding weight of war, currency volatility, and a stubborn absence of fresh tonnage offerings.

The backdrop to this year's Eid break is, to put it charitably, anything but restful. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has now stretched into its third week following the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, continues to send tremors through global energy and freight markets in equal measure. Brent crude briefly pierced USD 119/barrel on Thursday following Iranian retaliatory strikes on Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG facility, before retreating to settle at USD 108.65/barrel after Netanyahu signalled Israel was helping reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The week's close above USD 100/barrel for the sixth consecutive session shows just how embedded this new price floor has become.

For ship recyclers, the arithmetic of this war continues to deliver perverse outcomes. Higher oil prices logically translate into higher freight earnings for trading vessels, which in turn means owners are less inclined to sell tonnage for recycling when their ageing units are suddenly pulling respectable income. The Baltic Dry Index closed at 2,057 today, down 7 points on the session but still firm relative to the sub-1,600 lows seen in January, another nail in the coffin for those hoping for a surge of demolition candidates before the monsoon season arrives in June.

The U.S. Dollar continued its reign across all ship recycling destination currencies this week. The Indian Rupee, Pakistani Rupee, Bangladeshi Taka, and Turkish Lira all weakened against the USD, adding inflationary pressure to domestic steel pricing that is already under strain from disrupted supply chains. For recyclers whose revenues are denominated in USD but whose cost bases run in local currency, this would ordinarily be welcome news. Instead, the combination of reduced tonnage supply and unsettled buyer sentiment has meant that the currency advantage has delivered little in the way of increased appetite.

If there is any comfort to be found this week, it is that the Eid holiday provides a natural pause during which yards in both Bangladesh and Pakistan can press forward on their Hong Kong Convention compliance upgrades. With the HKC now in force and inspections increasingly rigorous, any time away from active purchasing is time that can be redirected toward certification.

headline: OBSERVANT!
highlights: Crises unfold. | Gas shortage? | Rupee worries. | HKC gains.
body_text:
Alang's yards observed Eid with a quiet that belied the underlying anxiety of the week. India's ship recycling community finds itself watching two crises unfold simultaneously, one external, one domestic, and neither is particularly conducive to bold purchasing decisions.

On the external front, the war in the Middle East has now directly disrupted India's two primary crude oil supply relationships. Iranian supplies are effectively suspended for the foreseeable future following the closure of Hormuz to unchaperoned transit, while Russian oil, already subject to the price cap architecture, faces fresh U.S. secondary sanctions pressure that has made Indian refiners increasingly cautious about their exposure. The practical result has been a sharp rise in the landed cost of energy across India's industrial base, with gas shortage rumours at Alang, though firmly denied by the BSBRA's Indian equivalent, adding a layer of operational uncertainty that recyclers could do without.

Domestically, the Indian Rupee extended its weakening trend against the U.S. Dollar, closing the week at approximately Rs. 92.40, a new low for 2026 and a level that has rattled sentiment among Alang's more cautious buyers. Local steel plate prices remained volatile, trading in a range between USD 418 and USD 422/ton through the week before settling at approximately USD 422/ton by Thursday. The intra-week swings, driven in part by speculation about steel scrap import disruption from war-affected regions, are making it difficult for Alang recyclers to set offer levels with any confidence, as the underlying cost basis shifts beneath their feet.

The HKC picture at Alang remains India's strongest competitive asset. With the overwhelming majority of Alang yards now holding valid SoC certifications, India is uniquely positioned to receive compliant green tonnage from owners who are under regulatory pressure to demonstrate responsible end-of-life practices. Several such units are understood to be in the pipeline, though formal sales have not yet been announced.

Alang's anchorage remains relatively thin, with only a handful of small LDT units observed this week, largely regional general cargo vessels displaced from war-affected trading routes. The bigger question, when the wave of war-displaced tankers and bulkers that many expect to eventually head for recycling will actually materialise, remains stubbornly unanswered.

headline: MAKING PROGRESS!
highlights: Eid break. | Geopolitics. | Al Hamza BV HKC!
body_text:
Pakistan's waterfront observed Eid with three days of official holiday, March 21 through 23, and the week's reduced activity was therefore entirely expected rather than concerning. What is more notable is the underlying sentiment heading into the break, which is one of cautious optimism that represents a meaningful improvement from the despair that gripped Gadani for much of the past eighteen months.

Local steel plate prices held firm at USD 591.50/ton through the week, a remarkable steadiness in the context of regional turbulence, while the Pakistani Rupee held stable at PKR 279.15 against the U.S. Dollar, effectively flat week-on-week and representing a rare island of currency calm in a sea of depreciation across the sub-continent. For recyclers buying tonnage in dollars, this stability is a meaningful operational advantage.

The geopolitical dimension of the current conflict has, counterintuitively, presented Gadani with a modest opportunity. Regional tonnage owners, particularly those with tankers that were trading in Gulf waters and now find themselves either displaced or facing prohibitive war risk insurance, are beginning to consider Gadani as a potential end destination. Pakistan's geographic proximity to the Gulf, combined with yard availability and competitive pricing relative to Bangladesh, makes Gadani a plausible landing point for some of this stranded tonnage.

Prime Green Recyclers, Pakistan's first HKC-certified yard along with Salams International and now this week, in further encouraging news, Al Hamza Commodities as the first BV Class Certified HKC yard in Gadani, continues to attract serious interest from owners who need a compliant South Asian alternative to Alang facilities. Additional Gadani yards are reportedly within two to three months of completing their own HKC upgrade journeys, a development that, when it materialises, will meaningfully expand Pakistan's addressable market for green demolition work.

Factions opposed to U.S. and Israeli actions in Iran have continued to demonstrate in major Pakistani cities, and isolated incidents near diplomatic facilities have been reported. These tensions add a layer of country risk that some international owners remain sensitive to, even where recycling yard operations themselves are unaffected. The situation bears monitoring as the conflict develops.

headline: QUEITISH!
highlights: TRY challenges.
body_text:
Turkey had a brief/busy run, and now it is quiet again. After a period of surprising activity in the opening weeks of 2026, Aliağa has returned to a state of dormancy that has become familiar. Eid al- Fitr holidays, running from March 19 through 23, have provided convenient cover for what was already shaping up to be a subdued week, and no sales or significant enquiries were reported across the entirety of the period. The Turkish Lira continued its seemingly inexorable slide against the U.S. Dollar, trading at TRY 44.32 per Dollar this week, a fresh record low. While a weaker Lira theoretically makes Turkish steel more competitive in export markets, the domestic recycling sector operates primarily on local scrap economics, and a depreciating currency simply inflates the input costs that Aliağa yards face when bidding for international tonnage priced in dollars.

The Ege Çelik delisting from the EU's approved ship recycling facility register, which saw the yard removed following an inspection that cited insufficient pre-cleaning and the absence of an impermeable shoreline surface, continues to cast a shadow over Aliağa's regulatory credibility. While Ege Çelik has submitted corrective plans to the relevant authorities, the reputational damage of a public delisting is not easily repaired, and European owners considering Turkish yards for their EU- flagged vessels will need to satisfy themselves that alternatives on the approved list can absorb their requirements. Import steel prices at Aliağa continued their modest weekly corrections, with HMS 1&2 scrap edging lower by approximately USD 4/ton, reflecting both the holiday slowdown in purchasing activity and the broader uncertainty about steel demand in the construction sector that has been weighing on Turkish scrap economics since the start of Q1.

headline: BANGLA BOON!
highlights: Appetite good. | VLs linger. | Steel flat. | Yearning supply.
body_text:
Bangladesh enters the post-Eid period with an appetite that has caught more than a few observers off guard. After weeks of cautious, holiday-dampened sentiment, Chattogram's recyclers appear to have used the festival break to clear inventory, settle financing, and sharpen their pencils for the fresh tonnage hunt that typically follows the Eid pause. The mood at the waterfront is meaningfully more engaged than it was heading into the holiday, with reports of several buyers actively seeking units in the days following the resumption of normal operations.

The two OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs that have been idling at OPL Chattogram since before the Eid break remain unresolved. As highlighted in last week's edition, both vessels fell afoul of USDN rules and have become victims of OFAC sanctions, with no prospects of a final resting place on the immediate horizon. The episode has sharpened due diligence practices among cash buyers and recyclers, who are now increasingly vigilant in their vetting of proposed tonnage, particularly units that may have changed hands through channels connected to sanctioned parties. Reports suggest there are still a handful of similarly suspect units in cash buyer hands awaiting introduction to the market. Given the fate of the Chattogram duo, how these pending and future dealings will eventually transpire remains very much to be seen.

Bangladeshi and Chinese steel levels continued to flatline this week, providing little fundamental support for any dramatic upward repricing of recycling offers. The Letter of Credit bottleneck that has frustrated transactions in recent weeks has not yet fully resolved, though there are indications that central bank approvals are beginning to move more smoothly in the post-holiday environment. If that pipeline clears, and if the tonnage that Bangladesh's hungry recyclers are seeking actually materialises, the market could yet see a pre-monsoon burst of activity before the June rains close the window. Whether tonnage availability will cooperate remains the unanswered question.

headline: WAIT GOES ON!
highlights: Post hols mood. | Currency woes. | Supply slow. | Bangla bullish. | Conflict reigns.
body_text:
As the world's ship recycling markets emerge from the Eid al-Fitr holidays, they do so into an environment that continues to generate more questions than answers. The post-holiday reopening, always anticipated as a potential catalyst for pent-up activity, has instead delivered something more characteristic of the broader 2026 narrative: confusion. Steel plate prices played opposite roles in Pakistan and India this week, as Indian levels recorded an impressive jump while Pakistani levels continued to bleed, declining non-stop over the course of the last month now. Bangladeshi and Chinese levels continued to flatline at the bottom of the pool, offering little directional signal to a market already starved of pricing clarity.

Even the U.S. Dollar, which has otherwise been a reliable source of sub-continent pressure this year, chose this week to remain undecided, making firm improvements against some recycling currencies while losing ground against others. The mixed signals have left buyers and sellers alike struggling to anchor their negotiating positions, and the result has been another week in which market activity remained well below the levels needed to make meaningful inroads into the tonnage backlog that has been building throughout Q1.

Bangladesh has emerged from the Eid break in a surprisingly bullish frame of mind, likely on the back of a few hungry recyclers whose yards have cleared sufficient space to welcome fresh tonnage. This is a noteworthy shift from the cautious posture that defined the Chattogram market through the holiday period. India and Pakistan, by contrast, struggled to keep pace despite the end of the holy month, hampered by the persistent absence of workable tonnage and the ongoing uncertainty around steel economics that has made confident bidding difficult to sustain.

The broader macro context remains unchanged and unresolved. The Middle East conflict continues to keep freight earnings elevated, discouraging owners from sending ageing tonnage for recycling. The Baltic Dry Index has yet to give meaningful ground. Oil remains firmly above USD 100/barrel, reinforcing the perverse arithmetic of a market where higher energy prices translate into longer trading lives for the very vessels that ship recyclers need. As Week 13 closes and Q2 begins, the industry finds itself asking the same question it has asked for most of the past year: when will the tonnage arrive in sufficient quantity to match the appetite that recyclers, particularly in Bangladesh, are beginning to demonstrate?

headline: ON THE LOOKOUT!
highlights: Steel firms. | Lacking tonnage. | Over 100 HKC. | EU questions.
body_text:
India delivered one of the more surprising data points of the week in the form of a sharp upward move in local steel plate prices, an impressive jump that has provided Alang's recyclers with at least a temporary boost to their pricing confidence. The move is a welcome reversal from the prolonged softness that has characterised Indian steel economics for much of Q1, though veterans of the Alang market will be cautious about extrapolating too much from a single week's movement in a market that has demonstrated a pronounced tendency to give back gains almost as quickly as it makes them.

The deeper structural challenge at Alang remains unchanged: there is simply not enough workable tonnage arriving at the waterfront. Strong freight earnings, elevated oil prices, and owners' continued preference for keeping aging vessels in service rather than sending them for recycling have combined to leave Alang's anchorage thin and its yards underutilised. The arrival of a handful of smaller regional general cargo vessels, largely units displaced from war-affected trading routes, has provided some activity, but the larger LDT units that Alang's recyclers need to generate meaningful revenue remain stubbornly absent from the demolition pipeline.

India's strongest competitive position continues to be its HKC compliance infrastructure. With more than 110 yards now holding valid Statements of Compliance, Alang is the only sub-continent destination capable of absorbing significant volumes of regulated European and Japanese tonnage at scale. GMS has continued its public advocacy for the inclusion of qualified Indian yards on the EU's approved recycling facility register, noting that continued exclusion appears driven by political considerations rather than compliance standards. Whether that advocacy translates into regulatory progress in Brussels before the next wave of EU-flagged vessels reaches end-of-life will be a defining question for India's medium-term recycling volumes.

headline: STILL KEEN!
highlights: Seeking tonnage. | HKC gains. | Rupee steady.
body_text:
Pakistan produced something of a surprise this week, taking in more vessels than India despite a clear overall decline in the number of arrivals and deliveries across the sub-continent board, and despite the ongoing deterioration in local steel plate prices that has become Gadani's most persistent structural headache. Pakistani steel levels have declined non-stop over the last month, a trend that sits in stark contrast to the sharp upward move recorded in India this week and that continues to compress the margin available to Gadani's recyclers on each unit they acquire.

The tonnage arrivals, modest as they are in absolute terms, nonetheless represent a meaningful signal of continued buyer engagement at Gadani, a market that was effectively written off by much of the industry as recently as twelve months ago. The combination of three new HKC certified yards, the geographic advantage of proximity to Gulf tonnage displaced by the ongoing conflict, and the relative availability of yard space has made Gadani a viable landing point for owners who need a compliant, accessible South Asian alternative to Alang.

The Pakistani Rupee's recent steadiness, holding broadly flat after weeks of depreciation pressure, provides at least a temporary floor under Gadani's economics. Should steel prices stabilise and additional HKC certifications materialise in the coming weeks, Pakistan's improved position in the regional competitive landscape could translate into a more sustained flow of tonnage. For now, the market remains a work in progress, better than it was, not yet where it needs to be.

headline: STEADY BUT SILENT!
highlights: Disadvantaged.
body_text:
Turkey ends Week 13 in much the same position it has occupied for the better part of the year: structurally disadvantaged on price, watching the sub-continent capture what little tonnage is available, and waiting for a market shift that shows no sign of arriving on the immediate horizon. Aliaga’s yards continued to operate at subdued levels through the post-Eid week, with no significant sales or major new enquiries reported across the period.

The Turkish Lira's continuing depreciation against the U.S. Dollar remains the defining constraint on Turkish recycling economics. At indicative levels of USD 265-285/LDT depending on vessel type, Aliaga cannot realistically compete with sub-continent pricing for mainstream commercial tonnage. The domestic steel scrap market, which ultimately sets the ceiling on what Turkish recyclers can offer, continues to reflect sluggish demand from the construction sector and the broader uncertainty that has characterised the Turkish economic environment through Q1.

Turkey's structural advantage in the specialist segment, EU-approved yards able to receive EU- flagged vessels under the Ship Recycling Regulation, continues to provide a thin but durable revenue stream for the handful of facilities that hold approved status. The Ege Çelik delisting and the reputational overhang it created for Aliaga’s regulatory credibility has not helped, and European owners considering Turkish yards for their regulated tonnage will continue to apply careful scrutiny. For the broader Turkish market, the question of when it next becomes genuinely competitive for international recycling tonnage remains open, and the answer, for now, does not appear to be this week.

headline: HUNGRY AFTER THE HOLIDAY
highlights: Momentum holds. | Compliance tightens. | Clock ticking.
body_text:
The bullishness that characterised Chattogram's return from the Eid break shows no sign of fading as Week 14 opens. Bangladesh's recyclers remain among the most actively engaged in the region, with yard space continuing to clear and appetite for fresh tonnage undiminished. The mood at the waterfront is more constructive than it has been at any point in Q1, and the Letter of Credit pipeline, which has been a persistent drag on transaction velocity, is beginning to move more smoothly as post-holiday central bank approvals gather pace. Bangladesh continues to hold firmer ground in terms of prices offered for recycling candidates than India, maintaining the competitive edge that has defined the sub-continent's pricing hierarchy through the opening quarter.

The two OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs idling at OPL Chattogram remain unresolved and are now entering their third week of limbo. No pathway to a final resting place has emerged, and the heightened due diligence culture they have prompted across the cash buyer community shows no sign of easing. Reports continue to suggest a small number of similarly suspect units remain in cash buyer hands awaiting introduction to the market. Each week that passes without resolution of the Chattogram duo reinforces the caution that buyers and recyclers are now applying to any tonnage with opaque ownership or transaction history. It is a compliance hangover that will outlast the specific vessels that caused it.

Bangladeshi steel levels edged fractionally higher to BDT 61,500 this week, a modest but directionally positive move for recyclers whose offers have been anchored by flat local pricing throughout Q1. The USD/BDT rate closed the week at 122.91, barely changed from last week's 122.81, providing minimal FX headwind. The pre-monsoon window is narrowing, the June rains are roughly eight weeks away, and the pressure to convert appetite into executed transactions is beginning to intensify. If the LC pipeline continues to clear and owners begin to release the medium-sized dry bulk and LPG units currently circulating as recycling candidates, Bangladesh has both the will and the financial positioning to absorb them. The clock, however, is ticking.

headline: Q2 OPENS UNDER PRESSURE!
highlights: War premium. | Rupee rebound. | Mixed signals. | Bangla leads.
body_text:
Week 14 opens the second quarter of 2026 under the same structural pressures that defined Q1, and then some. The Iran war continues to dominate the macro agenda, with Brent crude holding above USD 109/barrel for a seventh consecutive week and the Strait of Hormuz remaining effectively constrained. Geopolitical risk has overtaken supply-demand fundamentals as the primary price driver in energy markets, and ship recycling is feeling the impact from both sides, as higher oil keeps aging vessels trading while a volatile USD makes confident bidding difficult to sustain.

India delivered the week’s most notable currency development, as the rupee rebounded sharply from its record low of 94.42 to 92.73 following intervention measures by the Reserve Bank of India, including curbs on forward transactions, limits on banks’ FX positions, and restrictions on corporate rebooking of cancelled contracts. Pakistan and Bangladesh saw only marginal currency movement, while the Turkish lira weakened further to a fresh record low of 44.59, continuing a prolonged depreciation trend that is steadily eroding Aliağa’s competitiveness for international tonnage.

Even the U.S. Dollar, which has otherwise been a consistent source of pressure on sub-continent markets this year, sent mixed signals again this week, strengthening against the Turkish lira while easing against the Indian rupee. The INR’s recovery offers some support to Alang by improving USD-denominated bidding capacity, though the sustainability of this move remains uncertain if oil prices continue to rise and capital outflows resume. These mixed signals continue to cloud price discovery, leaving buyers and sellers struggling to anchor positions and keeping overall market activity subdued, with little progress made on clearing the tonnage backlog that has built up over the course of Q1.

Bangladesh remains the standout positive in the region. The post-Eid momentum seen last week has carried into Week 14, with Chattogram recyclers actively seeking tonnage and maintaining the most engaged sentiment across the sub-continent. India and Pakistan, by contrast, continue to operate cautiously, constrained by limited supply and ongoing uncertainty in steel fundamentals that continues to weigh on bidding confidence.

headline: STEEL JUMPS, BUT TONNAGE ABSENT
highlights: Rupee rebound. | Energy drag. | No supply. | HKC strength.
body_text:
India’s most consequential development in Week 14 emerged not from steel prices, but from the foreign exchange market. The Indian Rupee staged a sharp recovery from last week’s record low of 94.42, firming to 92.73 against the U.S. Dollar by April 3 following a series of intervention measures by the Reserve Bank of India. These included curbs on forward transactions, tighter limits on banks’ foreign exchange positions, and restrictions on corporates rebooking cancelled contracts.

For Alang’s recyclers, a stronger INR provides structural support, as vessels are acquired in USD while recycled steel is sold in rupees. This shift marginally improves bidding economics. Local steel plate prices also edged higher to INR 38,500 per ton, lifting the USD equivalent towards USD 415 per ton and offering modest support compared to the previous week.

This improvement, however, is being offset by emerging pressure on the energy side. LPG supply disruptions are now affecting steel mills in Alang, slowing production and weakening underlying demand for recycled steel. While partial relief has been announced, the extent to which this will translate into improved yard economics remains uncertain. Market indications continue to show that Indian recyclers are offering the lowest price levels in the sub-continent, highlighting how quickly operational constraints can offset gains from currency and steel movements. India’s core challenge remains unchanged. Tonnage availability continues to fall short of what is required to sustain meaningful yard activity. Alang has the infrastructure, compliance credentials, and capacity, but without sufficient inflow of vessels, these advantages remain underutilised.

Structurally, India retains its strongest edge in HKC compliance. With more than 110 yards holding valid Statements of Compliance, Alang remains the most capable destination in the region for handling regulated European and Japanese tonnage at scale. The Good Friday bank holiday on April 3 provided only a temporary pause and does not alter the broader outlook. Until freight markets soften and geopolitical pressures ease, the flow of recycling candidates is likely to remain constrained. The infrastructure is ready. The supply is not.

headline: FIRMER GROUND
highlights: Firm footing. | Back in play. | Supply decides.
body_text:
Pakistan enters Week 14 on firmer commercial footing than at any point during Q1. The steel plate jump recorded at the end of March, rising from PKR 168,000 to PKR 175,000 per ton, has held into the new quarter, with pricing consolidating near PKR 175,000 and the USD equivalent settling around USD 627 per ton. The Pakistani Rupee has remained broadly stable at 279.07, reinforcing this improvement and marking a clear shift from the prolonged weakness that weighed on Gadani’s economics through much of March. Market indications now place Pakistan ahead of India in pricing terms, reestablishing Gadani as the sub-continent’s second most competitive recycling destination.

Structural improvements are also becoming more visible. Three HKC-certified yards are now operational, with further certifications expected in the coming weeks. Combined with proximity to Gulf-sourced tonnage influenced by ongoing regional tensions, Gadani is increasingly positioning itself as a practical alternative when Alang faces limited inflow. The current pool of recycling candidates, including medium-sized dry bulk, LPG, and offshore units, aligns well with Gadani’s available yard capacity and improving compliance profile.

At current levels, the gap between indicative sentiment and executable pricing appears narrower than it has been in recent months. With steel holding firm and the PKR stable, recyclers are operating on a more predictable cost base than earlier in the year. The key variable now is supply. Whether owners choose to release tonnage at prevailing levels, and whether regional dynamics continue to direct units toward Pakistan, will determine how sustainable this improvement proves to be. The market is clearly stronger than it was. Whether it can build on that momentum remains the open question.

headline: STILL ALONE AT THE BOTTOM TABLE
highlights: Lira slides. | Outpriced again. | Niche only.
body_text:
Turkey enters Q2 with the Turkish Lira weakening further to a record low of 44.59 against the U.S. Dollar, extending a depreciation trend that has now run for most of the past year and reflects a decline of over 17% during that period. The Central Bank of Turkey has intervened heavily, reportedly selling more than USD 8 billion in reserves during March, while also halting its rate- cutting cycle in response to inflationary pressures driven by rising energy costs. These measures, however, have provided little relief to Aliaga’s recyclers. The continued weakening of the lira directly compresses the USD value of local steel prices, widening the gap between Turkish offers and sub- continent levels.

At current indications of USD 265-285 per LDT depending on vessel type, down from last week’s USD 270-290 range, Aliaga remains uncompetitive for mainstream recycling tonnage. The domestic steel scrap market continues to reflect weak demand from the construction sector, while inflation, running at 31.53% as of February, keeps operating conditions challenging. Broader geopolitical uncertainty and elevated energy prices continue to weigh on the domestic economy, and activity levels reflect this pressure, with no significant sales or major new enquiries reported during the week.

Turkey’s relevance continues to rest in its specialist segment. EU-approved yards remain capable of receiving EU-flagged vessels under the Ship Recycling Regulation, providing a limited but consistent flow of compliant tonnage. This segment operates independently of sub-continent pricing dynamics, as European owners prioritise regulatory compliance over commercial returns. Outside of this niche, however, Turkey remains structurally constrained. The question of when Aliaga can re-enter the market as a competitive destination for mainstream recycling tonnage remains unresolved, and nothing in Week 14 suggests that shift is imminent.

headline: THE WINDOW NARROWS
highlights: Steel spikes. | LC flow improves. | Pre-monsoon urgency.
body_text:
Bangladesh enters Week 15 with the sharpest improvement in steel economics seen in the quarter. Local steel plate prices jumped to BDT 71,000 per ton, the most significant single-week move of Q1–Q2, translating to a USD equivalent near USD 578/ton at current exchange rates. With the USD/BDT rate holding steady at 122.70–122.85, barely changed from 122.81–122.91 at the close of Week 14, the steel price improvement flows directly into offer capacity without the FX offset that has blunted similar gains in Alang and Aliağa. Bangladesh continues to hold its position as the sub- continent's highest bidder and its most actively engaged recycling market.

The Letter of Credit pipeline, which served as a persistent friction point on transaction velocity through Q1, continues to clear at an accelerating pace. Post-Eid central bank approvals are gathering momentum, and the structural transaction bottleneck that defined the opening quarter is meaningfully less acute entering Week 15. The two OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs at OPL Chattogram enter their fourth week unresolved. The heightened due diligence culture they have embedded across the cash buyer community shows no sign of easing, and the compliance shadow they cast over any tonnage with opaque documentation continues to slow the introduction of otherwise qualified recycling candidates to the market. A small number of similarly classified units reportedly remain in cash buyer hands.

Bangladesh's March 2026 CPI eased to 8.71%, down from 9.13% in February, which had been the highest reading since May 2025. The moderation was driven by food price declines in the post-Eid period, while non-food inflation edged higher to 9.09%. The relative macro stability provides continued central bank flexibility on LC approvals. However, the pre-monsoon window is now the dominant operational constraint. With the June rains approximately seven weeks away, the pressure to convert appetite into executed transactions is intensifying. The oil pullback, if it signals even a partial and sustained release of the Q1 tonnage overhang, arrives at precisely the right moment. Bangladesh has both the financial positioning and the urgency to absorb tonnage rapidly. The question remains one of supply, not demand.

highlights: Premium cracks. | Freight firms. | Dollar eases. | Supply waits.
body_text:
The single most consequential development of Week 15 came out of Washington, not the recycling yards. President Trump’s decision to delay planned strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure by five days, alongside comments describing talks with Iran as “productive,” triggered the sharpest oil reversal since the conflict began. Brent, which had held above USD 109/barrel through Q1 and into early Q2, fell to near USD 101/barrel by week’s end, an almost 8% drop in a matter of hours. WTI followed, settling around USD 90/barrel. Tehran denied any negotiations even as Washington insisted talks were ongoing, highlighting just how fragile the situation remains. The Strait of Hormuz is still constrained, but markets are now pricing in the possibility of reopening, and that alone has begun to erode the war premium in energy markets.

The Baltic Dry Index rose to 2,139 by April 8th, continuing a recovery that began from the March trough and extending to its highest level since early March. Capesize earnings improved as a Brazil- to-China iron ore window opened, with the BCI C3 Brazil-to-Qingdao route briefly breaking above USD 30/metric ton for the first time since July 2024. Panamax and supramax both held gains. The improvement in freight sentiment is notable against the backdrop of the oil move. It suggests that some operators are reading the diplomatic pause as a stabilization signal rather than a durable resolution and are positioning freight accordingly. For ship recycling, a firming BDI is a headwind on the supply side. Vessel earnings continue to provide incentive to trade, not recycle.

Currency markets remained largely stable. The Indian Rupee softened slightly to 93.21, reversing part of last week’s recovery, while Pakistan and Bangladesh currencies held steady. The Turkish Lira improved modestly from recent lows but remains structurally weak. A softer Dollar, with the DXY near 99.3, offers some support to sub-continent buyers heading into Q2.

For recyclers, the oil correction is important but not decisive. Lower fuel costs may eventually undermine trading economics for older vessels, but the move is still too recent to trigger immediate recycling flows. Owners are unlikely to react to a single week’s volatility. The Q1 backlog of tonnage remains in place, with conditions improving but not yet compelling.

headline: RUPEE GIVES BACK, SUPPLY STILL ABSENT
highlights: Rupee reversal. | Energy drag lingers. | HKC strength.
body_text:
India's Week 15 was defined by the partial reversal of the currency gains that had been Week 14's most positive domestic development. The USD/INR rate moved back to approximately 93.21, retracing a portion of the RBI-engineered recovery from the record low of 94.42 recorded in the prior week. The move aligns with the risk outlined in Week 14, that the INR recovery's durability was conditional on both oil price behavior and capital flow dynamics, neither of which has been resolved. The oil pullback is directionally positive for India's import bill, with approximately 70% of crude and 90% of LPG transiting outside the current Hormuz constraint, but the market is treating the diplomatic pause with appropriate caution. The rupee has accordingly given back a portion of the intervention-driven gains.

LPG supply disruptions at Alang's steel mills have shown only partial easing. Local steel plate prices reached INR 41,000 during the week before settling back near INR 40,600, a mid-week improvement that was not fully sustained, reflecting the uneven recovery in yard-level energy supply. At a USD equivalent of approximately USD 436/ton, India remains the lowest-priced destination in the sub- continent. This position reflects neither a lack of appetite nor infrastructure capacity, but a combination of energy disruption, unfavorable exchange rate dynamics, and the continued absence of adequate recycling tonnage flow. India's February 2026 CPI of 3.21% confirms that inflation remains well within the RBI's target band, but the LPG dependency on the Strait of Hormuz remains the key operational vulnerability. The oil pullback's long-term benefit to Alang hinges on whether the Hormuz situation resolves in a durable manner.

Structurally, India's strongest differentiator heading into Q2 remains its HKC compliance infrastructure. With more than 110 yards holding valid Statements of Compliance, Alang retains unmatched capacity to process regulated European and Japanese tonnage at scale. The India CPI for March 2026 is due for release on April 13, and the RBI has formally reaffirmed its 4% inflation target with a 2–6% tolerance band for the 2026–2031 period. The broader supply challenge, insufficient inflow of recycling candidates to sustain meaningful yard activity, remains the defining constraint. Alang's readiness is not in question. Until freight markets soften and geopolitical pressures ease, the supply side will remain the story.

headline: STABILITY IS THE STORY
highlights: Firm footing. | Gulf proximity. | Oil risk noted.
body_text:
Pakistan's Week 15 is characterized by one quality that has been notably scarce in the sub-continent through Q1: stability. The Pakistani Rupee has held in a narrow 278.58–279.00 range through the week, essentially unchanged from the 279.07 recorded at the close of Week 14, and local steel plate prices at PKR 177,000, with a USD equivalent of approximately USD 634/ton, have remained firm without the volatility seen in India and Bangladesh. The gap between Pakistan and India in pricing terms, approximately USD 200/ton at current levels, reaffirms Gadani's position as the sub- continent's second most competitive recycling destination. March 2026 CPI at 7.3% represents a move above the State Bank's 5–7% target, driven primarily by transport, which rose 12.5% on the month, and housing costs. This remains structurally manageable for yard economics given the stable PKR base.

Gadani's structural positioning in a Gulf-disrupted environment continues to provide a meaningful tailwind. Ongoing regional tensions have maintained a proximity advantage for Gulf- sourced tonnage that aligns well with Gadani's yard configuration. Three HKC-certified yards are now operational, with further certifications in the pipeline, expanding Pakistan's compliance credentials and attracting growing interest from owners seeking alternatives to Alang when Indian inflow is constrained. The circulating pool of recycling candidates, including medium-sized dry bulk, LPG, and offshore units, continues to align with Gadani's available capacity and improving compliance profile.

The one ambiguity introduced by the Week 15 oil move is the potential moderation of Gadani's Gulf proximity advantage. If a broader de-escalation of the Iran conflict takes hold, the regional dynamics that have been directing tonnage toward Pakistan may ease. For now, this remains a speculative risk rather than an immediate market reality. Pakistan enters the second half of Q2's pre-monsoon window on its firmest footing of the year, with predictable cost inputs and a competitive pricing position. The key variable, supply, is shared equally by all four destinations. Whether the oil pullback becomes the catalyst that finally releases the Q1 backlog will be the defining question of the coming weeks.

headline: BREATHING ROOM, NOT RECOVERY
highlights: Lira firms modestly. | Inflation cools slightly. | Niche only.
body_text:
Turkey enters Week 15 with its first modestly positive week of Q2. The Turkish lira edged from its Week 14 record low of 44.59 to approximately 44.34 against the U.S. Dollar, supported by the oil price reversal and a softer Dollar. The Central Bank of Turkey continues to operate with limited room for maneuver, having sold more than USD 8 billion in reserves during March and halting its rate-cutting cycle amid inflation pressures. These dynamics remain unchanged, and the lira has paused its slide rather than reversed it.

March 2026 CPI eased to 30.87%, below both 31.53% previously and expectations of 31.4%. The softer reading was driven by slower price growth in food, housing, and education, while transport costs accelerated sharply, rising 34.35% annually and 4.52% on the month as fuel costs filtered through. Independent estimates remain significantly higher, with ENAG at 54.62% and Istanbul Chamber data at 37.68%. The central bank maintains its 16% year-end target, though this remains difficult to achieve.

At USD 265–285/LDT, improving marginally to about USD 268–288 on the firmer lira, Aliağa remains structurally uncompetitive for mainstream tonnage. The gap to Pakistan, at roughly USD 445– 475/LDT, remains too wide to bridge. Turkey’s relevance is confined to its EU-approved yards handling regulated tonnage, where compliance overrides price. Outside this segment, nothing in Week 15 suggests any meaningful shift in positioning.

headline: SIX WEEKS TO MONSOON
highlights: Window narrows. | Compliance lingers. | Supply decides.
body_text:
Bangladesh enters Week 16 with its structural pricing advantage intact and its pre-monsoon clock loudest. Local steel plate prices have held at BDT 71,000 per ton, sustaining the USD 578 to USD 584 per ton USD equivalent established the previous week. The USD/BDT rate has remained steady in the 122.70 to 122.85 range, unchanged from the close of Week 14 and Week 15, preserving the direct flow-through of steel strength into offer capacity that continues to distinguish Bangladesh from Alang and Aliaga. Chattogram holds its position as the sub-continent's highest bidder and the most actively engaged recycling market heading into what is now a narrowing operational window. The June rains sit approximately six weeks away. Every week of continued supply hesitation by owners is now a week subtracted from the practical time available to convert appetite into executed transactions before yards are forced to slow beaching cycles.

The Letter of Credit pipeline that defined Q1 friction continues to clear at an accelerating pace. Post-Eid central bank approvals are gathering further momentum entering Week 16, and the structural transaction bottleneck that characterised the opening quarter is now meaningfully less acute. The two OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs at OPL Chattogram enter their fifth week unresolved, and the heightened due diligence culture they have embedded across the cash buyer community remains firmly in place. The compliance shadow over tonnage with opaque documentation continues to slow the introduction of otherwise qualified recycling candidates, and there is no operational development this week that suggests relief. A small number of similarly classified units are reported to remain in cash buyer hands. The LC situation has improved. The compliance situation has not.

Bangladesh's March 2026 CPI at 8.71% provides continued central bank flexibility on LC approvals without introducing fresh macro concerns. Non-food inflation at 9.09% remains elevated, but the relative macro stability is sufficient to sustain the current transaction environment. The pre- monsoon window is now the dominant operational constraint, and the week-over-week firming of the Baltic Dry Index to 2,523 points has made the supply side harder, not easier. The oil softening of the past ten days has not released the Q1 overhang because owners are no longer treating it as a stabilisation signal. Bangladesh has the financial positioning, the compliance pathway, the urgency, and the pricing. What it does not have, and what it cannot create, is the tonnage. The demand is real. The supply is the problem.

highlights: Risk resets. | Demand bites. | Freight runs. | Owners hold.
body_text:
The Week 15 thesis that the war premium was cracking has not held. What looked like a diplomatic off-ramp has narrowed into a less convincing outcome. Washington and Tehran are considering a two-week ceasefire extension, but talks are now focused on a temporary memorandum to avoid renewed conflict, not the broader agreement and Hormuz reopening markets had priced in.

Risk remains elevated. The U.S. has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports, while Tehran continues to restrict the Strait of Hormuz to non-Iranian traffic. The Department of Defense is deploying 6,000 additional troops, with a further 4,200 expected by month-end. A ten-day Israel– Lebanon ceasefire offers only limited relief. Markets are not stabilising. They are adjusting to a higher plateau of risk.

Brent traded between USD 94.89 and USD 97.06 per barrel, settling near USD 95, down from Week 15’s USD 101 close. The driver has shifted from de-escalation hopes to demand concerns after the IEA cut its 2026 consumption forecast. At the same time, U.S. crude inventories posted a 9.13 million barrel draw against expectations of a 154,000-barrel build, the first draw after seven consecutive weekly increases. The physical market is tight, but sentiment remains uncertain, offering no support for a reopening of supply corridors or a shift in recycling dynamics.

Freight is clearer. The Baltic Dry Index extended its rally to nine consecutive sessions, closing at 2,523 on April 16, up 39 points and at its highest level since early December. Capesize rates moved above 3,100 points to a four-month high on Brazil to China iron ore flows, with Panamax and Supramax also gaining. Improving earnings are keeping older bulkers trading, and the expected Q1 tonnage overhang remains withheld.

Currencies and steel are not the drivers. The USD/INR is around 93.46, Pakistan and Bangladesh remain steady, the Turkish Lira has held its recovery, and the Dollar Index remains near 99. Bangladesh steel holds Week 15 gains, while Pakistan edges higher.

With roughly six weeks before the monsoon window closes, sub-continent fundamentals are supportive. Bangladesh leads on pricing and improving LC flows, Pakistan offers stability, and India retains its HKC advantage. Yet across all three, yards are waiting for ships that owners are choosing not to sell.

headline: HORMUZ STILL SHUT, RUPEE DRIFTS
highlights: Currency tells. | Oil misleads. | Supply lacking.
body_text:
India's Week 16 is characterised by the continuation of the currency slide that began at the close of Week 15. The USD/INR rate has drifted to approximately 93.46, extending the partial reversal of the RBI-engineered recovery from the Week 14 record low of 94.42. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed with the US naval blockade in place, which directly undermines the directional benefit that the Week 15 oil pullback was supposed to deliver to India's import bill. Approximately 90% of India's LPG continues to transit routes impacted by the Hormuz constraint and approximately 70% of crude is similarly exposed. The intervention capacity of the RBI has not been exhausted, but the appetite to deploy it further in a market where the underlying geopolitical driver has not been resolved is visibly diminished. The currency is telling the truth that the oil market is only hinting at.

LPG supply disruptions at Alang's steel mills continue to show only partial easing. Local steel plate prices have oscillated through the week between INR 40,800 and INR 41,900, settling around INR 40,900 at the time of writing, a mid-week pattern that mirrors Week 15's uneven recovery in yard-level energy supply. At a USD equivalent of approximately USD 437 per ton, India remains the lowest-priced destination in the sub-continent, with the gap to Pakistan holding near USD 200 per LDT. This position is not a function of insufficient appetite or insufficient infrastructure. It is a direct consequence of the Hormuz situation's refusal to resolve and the INR's ongoing drift. The oil correction's medium-term benefit to Alang remains conditional on a durable opening of the strait, which the current ceasefire extension does not contemplate, and the US blockade does not permit.

India's structural differentiator entering Q2 remains its Hong Kong Convention compliance footprint. More than 110 yards at Alang hold valid Statements of Compliance, a capacity that no other sub- continent destination can match for regulated European and Japanese tonnage at scale. The India CPI for March 2026 was released on April 13, with the RBI reaffirming its 4% inflation target and 2% to 6% tolerance band for the 2026 to 2031 period. The macro foundation for Alang is durable. The supply challenge, the insufficient inflow of recycling candidates to sustain meaningful yard activity, remains the defining constraint and has, if anything, worsened over the past ten days as freight markets have firmed. Alang's readiness is not the question. The question is whether any of the tonnage that owners are currently holding will arrive before the monsoon season closes the beaching window in the Bay of Bengal.

headline: STABILITY BECOMES ADVANTAGE
highlights: Stability holds. | Advantage builds. | Timing risk.
body_text:
Pakistan's Week 16 extends and arguably intensifies the stability theme that defined Week 15. The Pakistani Rupee has held in a narrow range near 278.90 through the week, essentially unchanged from the close of Week 14 and Week 15, and local steel plate prices at PKR 188,000 per ton have pushed further above the Week 14 level, translating to a USD equivalent near USD 671 per ton. This places Gadani at its firmest absolute USD pricing position of the year. The gap to India has widened modestly to approximately USD 230 per ton at current levels, reaffirming Pakistan's position as the sub-continent's second-most competitive destination with accelerating momentum. March 2026 CPI at 7.3% sits above the State Bank's 5% to 7% target, driven primarily by transport at plus 12.5% on the month and housing, but the trajectory remains manageable for yard economics given the stable PKR base.

The continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports are, on balance, reinforcing Gadani's structural positioning rather than eroding it. The speculative risk noted in Week 15, that a broader de-escalation might moderate Pakistan's Gulf proximity advantage, has receded with the narrowing of the US-Iran talks from full settlement to a temporary memorandum. Three HKC-certified yards are now operational with further certifications in the pipeline, and the pool of recycling candidates consisting of medium-sized dry bulk, LPG, and offshore units continues to align well with Gadani's available capacity. The compliance profile is improving. The pricing position is firming. The Gulf logistics advantage is holding. All three reinforcements are operating simultaneously, which is unusual.

The one remaining unknown for Pakistan is whether the structural position translates into executed transactions before the regional dynamic shifts.
