headline: CPI CLIMBS, RUPEE SHRUGS
highlights: CPI climbs. | Rupee shrugs. | Clock starts.
body_text:
Pakistan’s May CPI printed at 11.7% year-on-year, up from 10.9% in April and the highest reading since June 2024, with transport at plus 36.8% (versus 29.9%) and housing and utilities elevated at 16.8%. The headline is the war shock’s full accumulation in the annual series. The composition tells the more important story: monthly inflation collapsed to 0.5% from April’s 2.5%, the Sensitive Price Indicator’s month-on-month pace eased to 0.7%, and the Wholesale Price Index declined 0.8% on the month. The annual rate is climbing on base effects while the underlying shock decelerates sharply. The smoke alarm rings loudest after the fire has begun to go out.

USD/PKR held at approximately 278.39 through the print, sustaining its strongest level of 2026 and extending the rupee’s standing as the only sub-continent currency to have appreciated against the dollar across the entire conflict. The FX market has looked through the 11.7% headline to the 0.5 % monthly pace and the Brent collapse that will feed the June print, and has concluded the State Bank’s 100 basis point hike to 11.5% has the trajectory contained. With the weekly oil import bill that Prime Minister Sharif quantified at USD 800 million now deflating alongside Brent, the external account stress that defined the April shock is unwinding at its source. The currency’s verdict on the inflation print was to ignore it.

Local steel plate prices at PKR 195,000 per ton held, with the USD equivalent near USD 700 per ton on the firm rupee. Gadani’s absolute pricing remains the firmest of the year, the gap to India is near USD 295 per LDT, and the arrival of the Ron at 21,502 LDT marks the largest unit Gadani has received since the war opened. The strategic clock, flagged last week, is now visibly running: each tanker that transits Hormuz under US coordination erodes a little more of the Gulf proximity premium that anchored Gadani’s wartime advantage. A signed deal with a 30-day de-mining clause would set that erosion on a schedule. Pakistan consolidated the war quarter better than any destination in the basin. The peace quarter will test how much of that consolidation was structural and how much was circumstantial.

headline: INFLATION CREEPS, LIRA WAITS
highlights: Inflation creeps. | Framework strained. | Niche persists.
body_text:
Turkey’s May CPI printed at 32.61% year-on-year, up from 32.37% in April and slightly above expectations of 32.5%, the highest reading since October 2025. As in Pakistan, the monthly composition softened materially: consumer prices rose 1.71% on the month, down sharply from April’s 4.18% and the weakest monthly increase since December. Food and non-alcoholic beverages rose to 34.86% annually, while housing eased slightly to 45.59% and transport to 34.29%. The Istanbul Chamber’s parallel series for the city printed 36.8%. The annual rate creeps higher on arithmetic. The monthly pulse, for the first time since the war opened, is fading.

The Central Bank of Turkey has suspended its year-end inflation forecast range outright, citing “a period of high uncertainty,” while maintaining a 24% year-end target and tightening liquidity by shifting funding to the 40% overnight lending rate. The suspension of the forecast range is the institution’s most candid admission of the year: the controlled-disinflation framework that the war’s energy shock overran in April cannot yet be re-anchored. USD/TRY steadied near 45.85, just off the 45.90 record, as the broad dollar eased. The Brent collapse toward USD 89, if sustained through a signed deal, is the disinflation tailwind the TCMB has waited for all year. The bank has stopped forecasting whether it will arrive. It is waiting, like everyone else, on the pen.

At USD 268 to USD 290 per LDT across vessel types, Aliaga remains structurally uncompetitive for mainstream tonnage, with the gaps to Pakistan and Bangladesh unbridgeable and the gap to India steady on the rupee’s consolidation. Turkey’s relevance remains confined to the EU-regulated tonnage segment, where Basel Convention compliance overrides price. The prospective flood of post- war tonnage, when it comes, will route overwhelmingly to the sub-continent on the price differential, and Aliaga’s share of it will be set by regulation rather than by markets. That was true through the war. It will remain true through the peace.

headline: PEACE LANDS, RAINS HOLD
highlights: Band holds. | Peace lands. | Rains hold.
body_text:
Bangladesh enters Week 25 with USD/BDT near the floor of its band at approximately 122.75, the level at which the Taka has now closed the entire war chapter without a single breach of the 122.74 to 123.18 range. The collapse in Brent toward USD 78, the broad easing of the dollar on the peace agreement, and the rupee’s rally have all reinforced the band rather than tested it. Foreign exchange reserves near USD 34.12 billion remain ample, and with the global risk premium now draining out of every market, the central bank’s management burden has fallen to its lightest since before February. Local steel plate prices held the BDT 65,000 level, with the USD equivalent near USD 530 per ton, the mill complex awaiting direction from the post-war scrap and billet markets rather than setting it.

The end of the war reshapes Bangladesh’s second-half setup more favourably than any single event of the year. The reopening of Hormuz and the collapse of the bunker-cost floor remove the central reason owners held ageing tonnage at sea through the conflict, which means the candidate pool that starved Chattogram for eleven weeks is now being primed to release. The interim peace agreement, the lifting of the US blockade, and the removal of sanctions on Iranian oil collectively point to a normalising freight and fuel environment through July and August. Chattogram enters that environment with the basin’s strongest demand position intact: full plot capacity, a cleared Letter of Credit pipeline, and the region’s most stable currency.

The obstacle is now, simply, the sky. The Bay of Bengal monsoon governs the beaching calendar through August, regardless of how favourable the macro setup becomes, and the deferred tonnage wave, when it sails, will arrive at a coast that cannot beach at full capacity until the rains lift. The sequencing matters: if the candidates release through July as the war premium evaporates, and the monsoon eases into September, Chattogram could face the strongest post-monsoon demand-and- supply alignment in several years. The war that closed the strait could not fill the beach. The peace that reopened it cannot, for now, fill it either. But the reason has changed from a blockade to a season, and a season, unlike a war, keeps a schedule.

headline: PEACE SIGNED, RAINS REIGN
highlights: Peace signed. | Brent collapses. | Premium | Rains reign.
body_text:
The war is over. The United States and Iran digitally signed an interim peace agreement this week, a US official confirming the memorandum has taken effect, with a formal signing in Switzerland set for Friday and the Strait of Hormuz reopening after more than one hundred days closed. President Trump announced the breakthrough from Air Force One en route to the G7 summit at Evian, authorising the strait to open and the US naval blockade to lift, and telling the world’s shipowners, “Ships of the World, start your engines.” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council confirmed that all military operations, on all fronts, including Lebanon, would cease immediately and permanently. The sub-continent, which spent the entire quarter praying for exactly these ships, must now ask them to keep their engines idling until the monsoon lifts.

Brent crude has collapsed to approximately USD 78 per barrel, its lowest since late February and effectively the level at which the war began, erasing the entire premium that carried it to USD 126.41 on April 30. WTI trades near USD 75. The agreement removes sanctions on Iranian oil exports and clears the way for Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Iraq to restart millions of barrels of halted output. The International Energy Agency, which in Week 18 called the Hormuz closure “the largest supply disruption in history,” now warns of a coming glut, projecting global supply to rise eight million barrels per day by 2027 against demand growth of two million. The forecast has travelled further than the oil.

Freight has continued to cool as the war premium drains from the dry bulk market. The Baltic Dry Index eased to 2,653 on June 17 from the June 1 peak of 3,222, with daily Capesize earnings falling to USD 35,162 from the USD 49,511 high of late May as the disrupted long-haul trades that inflated Capesize demand begin to normalise. Notably, Supramax and Handysize both firmed through the week, the geared segments most relevant to recycling candidate flow holding even as the headline index falls. The bunker-cost floor and the Capesize premium, the twin forces that kept older tonnage profitably trading through the war, are now deflating together and in earnest.

The currency response divided precisely along the fault line the conflict drew. The three Hormuz-exposed importers all strengthened or held: the Indian Rupee rallied to a five-week high near 94.60 as the collapse in oil prices improved its external balances, the Pakistani Rupee held its 2026 best near 278.28, and the Bangladeshi Taka held the floor of its band near 122.70. The Turkish Lira, alone, broke through 46 per dollar to a fresh record near 46.15, its slide driven by domestic structural inflation that the peace does nothing to address. The deal rescued the oil importers. It had nothing to say to Ankara.

And so the arc closes. Brent climbed past USD 126 and has returned to USD 78, roughly where it began; the barrel toured the war and came home. The strait the war closed has reopened, the blockade has lifted, and the premium that kept the world’s ageing tonnage profitably at sea is evaporating from the fuel side and the freight side at once, which means the deferred wave of recycling candidates that eleven weeks of war held back is now, finally, being primed to break. It will break onto a sub-continent in the deep monsoon. The ships are free to sail toward a beach where the weather has just closed. Peace is signed. The rains reign. For the first time since February, the only thing standing between the yards and the tonnage is the sky.

headline: RUPEE RALLIES, MONSOON RULES
highlights: Rupee rallies. | Inflows return. | Monsoon rules.
body_text:
India is the single largest currency beneficiary of the peace. USD/INR rallied to a five-week high near 94.60, appreciating sharply from the 96.97 record of May 21 as Brent’s collapse toward USD 78 fed directly into the external-account arithmetic of an economy that imports more than 80% of its crude. The MoU’s finalisation over the weekend, the reopening of Hormuz, and the prospect of restored capital inflows combined to take the conflict premium out of the rupee in a way that seven weeks of intervention could not. India’s May trade deficit had already narrowed slightly to USD 28.21 billion even as petroleum imports surged to USD 22.7 billion; the June figures, struck against USD 78 Brent rather than USD 107, will tell a materially better story.

The rupee’s rally is the cleanest expression yet of the war’s end, but it is not unconditional. Foreign institutional investors were still net sellers in places through the week as global growth uncertainty lingered and as reports cautioned that shipping and energy flows may take weeks to fully normalise. The interim deal leaves the nuclear question and the durability of the Lebanon ceasefire unresolved, and a five-week-high rupee carries embedded expectations that the implementation must now meet. The Reserve Bank of India’s June 5 inflow measures, the bond capital-gains tax removal among them, are now operating into a tailwind rather than a headwind. The currency has repriced the war’s end. It now waits on the war’s end to be delivered.

Local steel plate prices at Alang softened through the week, moving from INR 38,000 at the start of the reporting period to INR 37,500 by June 19, after briefly firming to INR 38,300 mid-week. The USD equivalent eased from approximately USD 400 per ton to just under USD 397 per ton, as the post-war collapse in energy and scrap sentiment outweighed the support from a firmer rupee. India remains the lowest-priced sub-continent destination. The operational reality is unchanged by the diplomacy: the monsoon governs Alang’s beaching calendar through August, and the candidate wave that the war’s end is priming will arrive at a coast in the depths of the rains. Alang enters the post-war period with the basin’s deepest yard capacity, a compliance footprint exceeding 110 valid Statements of Compliance, and, for the first time since February, a recovering currency and a deflating bunker floor working in its favour. The rains rule the third quarter’s opening. The recovery rules what follows them.

headline: RUPEE HOLDS, PREMIUM FADES
highlights: Rupee holds. | Premium fades. | Position transitions.
body_text:
Pakistan closes the war chapter as it spent it, as the basin’s currency anchor. USD/PKR held near 278.28, sustaining the strongest level of 2026 and finishing the conflict as the only sub-continent currency to have appreciated against the dollar across its entire span. The State Bank’s 100 basis point hike to 11.5%, disciplined reserve management, and resilient remittance inflows delivered a rupee that not only survived the most volatile quarter in years but strengthened through it. With Brent now near USD 78, the weekly oil import bill that Prime Minister Sharif quantified at USD 800 million at the height of the war is collapsing toward its pre-conflict level, removing the external-account pressure that drove the April CPI shock at its source.

The peace, however, begins immediately to dismantle the specific advantage that made Gadani the basin’s firmest market during the war. The Gulf proximity premium, which compounded structurally while Hormuz was closed and Gulf-region tonnage reassessed its positioning, now faces direct erosion as the strait reopens and routing economics normalise. The strategic clock that the Weekly first flagged three weeks ago is now running at full speed: each tanker that transits a reopened Hormuz, each barrel of restarted Gulf production, returns the maritime geography to its pre-war shape, in which Gadani competes on price and compliance like everyone else rather than on a wartime locational edge. The advantage was real. It was also, as the Weekly noted, circumstantial. The circumstance has just ended.

Local steel plate prices at PKR 195,000 per ton held, with the USD equivalent near USD 700 per ton on the firm rupee, Gadani retaining the firmest absolute pricing in the basin for now. Three HKC- certified yards remain operational with further certifications in the pipeline, and the Ron at 21,502 LDT continues to work through the yard. Pakistan enters the post-war period from the strongest position any destination held during the conflict, but it enters a different competition: the wartime premium that lifted Gadani is fading, the deferred tonnage wave will route on price and compliance once the monsoon lifts, and the basin’s competitive order will reset to its structural fundamentals. Pakistan consolidated the war better than anyone. The peace will measure what that consolidation is worth at normal tide.

headline: LIRA BREAKS 46, NICHE HOLDS
highlights: Fresh record. | Inflation governs. | Niche persists.
body_text:
Turkey enters Week 25 with USD/TRY having broken through 46 per dollar to a fresh record near 46.15, having touched 46.44 intraday, the lira down approximately 17.2% over the past 12 months and roughly 7% year-to-date. The break is the clearest possible demonstration of the conflict’s asymmetry: in the very week the war ended and every Hormuz-exposed currency in the basin firmed, the lira made a new low. Turkey’s pressures are domestic and structural, the product of an inflation problem that long predates the war and that the peace does nothing to resolve. The Central Bank of Turkey’s managed-depreciation framework continues to function as designed, the slide orderly, the level steadily worse.

The May CPI at 32.61%, with the year-end forecast range suspended and the official target held at 24%, remains the operative read, and the central bank’s policy rate stays at 37% against an effective 40% overnight lending rate. The one channel through which the peace genuinely helps Turkey is energy: a Brent price near USD 78 rather than USD 107 lowers the imported-inflation pulse that drove the April acceleration, and a sustained post-war oil environment is the most plausible disinflation tailwind the TCMB has had all year. It arrives, however, into an inflation structure so entrenched that even the largest favourable oil moves in a decade register as a marginal improvement rather than a turn.

At USD 268 to USD 290 per LDT across vessel types, Aliaga remains structurally uncompetitive for mainstream tonnage, and the post-war landscape sharpens rather than softens that reality. The deferred wave of recycling candidates that the war’s end is priming will route overwhelmingly to the sub-continent on the price differential once the monsoon lifts, and Aliaga’s share of it will continue to be set by EU regulation and Basel Convention compliance rather than by price. Turkey occupied a different market throughout the entire war. It will occupy the same market throughout the peace. The conflict changed everything in the basin except Aliaga’s position, which is precisely where it began.

headline: TAKA HOLDS, WAVE FORMS
highlights: Taka holds. | Wave forms. | Holiday slows.
body_text:
Bangladesh enters Week 26 with USD/BDT near the floor of its band at approximately 122.70, the Taka having now held the 122.74 to 123.18 range intact through the war and into the peace without a single breach. The collapse in Brent below USD 74, down more than 20% on the month, removes the imported-energy pressure that was the band’s principal external risk, and the broad strengthening of the dollar on US rate expectations has been absorbed without strain. Foreign exchange reserves near USD 34.12 billion remain the operative buffer. Local steel plate prices moved from BDT 65,000 to BDT 67,000 through the week, with the USD equivalent rising from approximately USD 535 to USD 551 per ton, the mill complex still taking direction from a post-war scrap market that is searching for its floor rather than setting one.

The first concrete evidence of the deferred tonnage wave has arrived. The Andhika Paramesti, a 9,369 LDT bulker, was sold to Bangladesh at USD 460 per LDT on an as-is Sambu basis, the first reported sale into the basin since the strait reopened and a marker that the candidate pool the war held back is beginning to release. It is one vessel, not a flood, and it lands in a week shortened by Ashura and constrained by the monsoon, but the direction is established: with the bunker-cost floor and the Capesize premium both deflating, owners who held ageing tonnage at sea through the conflict now have materially less reason to keep holding it. Chattogram is positioned to absorb the wave when it builds, the question being one of timing rather than appetite.

Ashura, observed June 26, has brought Chattogram’s cash-buyer activity to its customary holiday pause, layered atop the monsoon’s seasonal reduction in beaching cycles. The Letter of Credit pipeline remains in its most permissive posture of the year, full plot capacity is available, and the currency is the most stable in the basin, which means the only binding constraint on Bangladesh converting the incoming wave into beached tonnage is the calendar. The structural setup for the third quarter is the strongest the market has carried since before February: strong demand, cleared financing, a stable Taka, a reopening supply pipeline, and a monsoon that, unlike the war, has a known end date. The wave forms offshore. The beach waits for the sky.

headline: TRAFFIC DOUBLES, YARDS WAIT
highlights: Strait fills. | Oil sinks. | Queue builds. | Yards wait.
body_text:
The war is over; the paperwork is taking longer than the peace. The formal signing of the US-Iran agreement at Bürgenstock in Switzerland was abruptly postponed last Friday, with Vice President Vance turning his plane around over what the White House called unresolved logistical issues, even as the interim memorandum remained in effect and implementation accelerated on the water. Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz doubled in 24 hours to its highest level since late February, with at least 34 ships exiting into the Gulf of Oman against a pre-war daily average of 110. The Vice President noted that Iran had, for a second consecutive night, declined to fire on any vessel. The ships, having no plane to turn around, simply kept sailing.

Brent crude has fallen below USD 74 per barrel, its lowest since before the war began and now only about 7% above its pre-conflict level, having shed more than 20% in June alone. WTI trades below USD 70. The IEA estimates the UAE is already exporting at roughly 85% of pre-war volumes and warns of a coming glut; OPEC’s secretary general rejects both the glut and the notion of a demand peak, leaving the two agencies agreed on nothing except that the other is mistaken. Beneath the collapse sits an oddity: US crude inventories have fallen to their lowest since 1984, with Cushing below operational minimums, a tightness the price has chosen to ignore in favour of the reopening.

Freight has continued its orderly descent from the war peak. The Baltic Dry Index eased to 2,634 on June 24 from the June 1 high of 3,222, with daily Capesize earnings settling near USD 35,800 as the disrupted long-haul trades that inflated demand through the conflict normalise. The geared segments most relevant to recycling held firm, with Supramax near USD 21,400 and Handysize near USD 17,000 per day. The Capesize premium that kept the largest ageing tonnage trading has now fully unwound, and the freight side of the equation that held candidates at sea through the war has, like the fuel side, returned toward its pre-war shape.

The currency picture has acquired a second force. The Indian Rupee firmed to a six-week high near 94.30 on the oil collapse and improving capital inflows, the Pakistani Rupee strengthened to a fresh 2026 best near 278.10, and the Bangladeshi Taka held the floor of its band near 122.70. But the dollar itself is now strengthening: the Dollar Index has reached its highest in more than a year as US inflation climbed to 4.2%, a three-year high, and markets price roughly a 75% chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase by September. The Turkish Lira, domestic to its core, slid past 46 toward 46.40, a fresh record. The energy shock that drove inflation across the sub-continent has ended; America’s inflation, meanwhile, has reached a three-year high. The fire did not go out. It changed address. Detailed country reads follow on pages 2 through 5.

headline: RUPEE FIRMS, DOLLAR RESISTS
highlights: Rupee firms. | Dollar resists. | Alang resumes.

Improving capital flows have reinforced the move: investment into Indian debt has strengthened and the one-sided dollar demand that pressured the rupee through the war has eased, with traders willing for the first time in months to take positions on both sides.

The rupee’s advance is now meeting a genuine counterforce. The Dollar Index has climbed to its highest in more than 1 year as US inflation reached 4.2%, a three-year high, and markets moved to price roughly a 75% probability of a Federal Reserve rate increase by September under the new chair. Foreign institutional investors remained net sellers of Indian equities through the week even as bond inflows improved, capping the rupee’s gains. The oil tailwind that should, in isolation, drive the rupee well through 94 is being met by a dollar strengthening on America’s own inflation problem. The rupee is winning the argument it can control and being held back by the one it cannot.

highlights: Rupee leads. | Premium gone. | Position resets.

Pakistan opens the post-war period as the basin’s strongest currency. The Gulf proximity premium, which compounded while Hormuz was closed and Gulf-region tonnage reassessed its routing, has eroded in real time as the strait reopens: with vessel traffic through Hormuz doubling in a day and the UAE exporting at 85% of pre-war volumes, the maritime geography that handed Gadani a wartime locational edge has returned to its ordinary shape. The strategic clock the Weekly began flagging a month ago has, in effect, run out. Gadani now competes where it always competes in peacetime, on price and on compliance, and the wartime premium that lifted its position is no longer a factor in the basin’s pricing.

Local steel plate prices at PKR 195,000 per ton held, with the USD equivalent near USD 701 per ton on the firm rupee, Gadani retaining the firmest absolute pricing in the basin for the moment. Pakistan won the war quarter. The peace quarter will be a different contest, played on different ground.

headline: LIRA SLIDES PAST 46, NICHE HOLDS
highlights: Lira slides. | Energy helps, barely. | Niche persists.

Turkey enters Week 26 with USD/TRY having extended its slide past 46 toward approximately 46.40, deeper into record territory, the lira down roughly 17% over the past 12 months. The peace and the oil collapse that lifted every Hormuz-exposed currency in the basin have done almost nothing for the lira, whose pressures remain domestic and structural. The Central Bank of Turkey’s managed- depreciation framework continues to function as designed, the slide orderly and the level steadily worse, against a strengthening global dollar that compounds the local weakness. The lira made new lows through the war, through the ceasefire, and now through the peace, indifferent to all 3.

The single channel through which the war’s end genuinely assists Turkey is energy. Brent below USD 74, against the USD 107 of mid-May and the USD 126 peak, materially lowers the imported- inflation pulse that drove the April and May CPI acceleration, and a sustained post-war oil environment is the most plausible disinflation tailwind the TCMB has had all year. With the May CPI at 32.61%, the year-end forecast range suspended, and the policy rate held at an effective 40% overnight, the oil relief is welcome but marginal against an inflation structure measured in the thirties. The fire that the sub-continent has now escaped still burns in Ankara, and cheaper oil lowers the flame without putting it out.

At USD 266 to USD 288 per LDT across vessel types, Aliaga remains structurally uncompetitive for mainstream tonnage, and the post-war landscape only sharpens the point. The deferred wave of recycling candidates that the war’s end is releasing will route overwhelmingly to the sub-continent on the price differential once the monsoon lifts, and Aliaga’s share of it will continue to be set by EU regulation and Basel Convention compliance rather than by price. Turkey occupied a separate market through the entire conflict and occupies the same separate market in its aftermath. Of everything the war changed in the basin, Aliaga’s position is the one variable it left exactly where it found it.

headline: BAND BREAKS, WAVE NEARS
highlights: Band breaks. | Wave nears. | Setup holds.
body_text:
The band that survived one hundred days of war broke up in the third week of peace, to the dollar. USD/BDT eased off the 122.70 floor where it spent the conflict and moved through the upper bound of its long-held 122.74 to 123.18 range, trading toward approximately 123.2 to 123.3 this week, the first breach of the band in either direction since the war opened. The driver is not Chattogram and not Hormuz: it is the broad dollar, with the Dollar Index at its highest in more than a year, US inflation at 4.2%, and markets pricing roughly a 75% chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase by September. The pressure the Taka absorbed from a war next door is now being taken from a central bank an ocean away. Foreign exchange reserves near USD 34.12 billion remain the operative buffer, and the move remains orderly, measured in tenths rather than whole figures. Local steel plate prices eased from the firmer BDT 67,000 level reached late last week to BDT 66,000 by July 3, with the USD equivalent holding near USD 543 per ton on the softer Taka.

The deferred tonnage wave now has a census. Lloyd’s List estimates roughly 550 merchant vessels are preparing to exit the Gulf as the strait normalises, including approximately 200 bulk carriers, 160 tankers, 60 container ships and 10 vehicle carriers, and every unit of ageing tonnage in that queue exits into a freight market whose Capesize premium has unwound and a bunker market priced off USD 71 Brent rather than USD 126. Chattogram’s anchorage and delivery list are already showing the early arrivals converting, with the Zamrud and ERGY gas carriers at 28,858 and 31,341 LDT among the largest units delivered during the window, and the Andhika Paramesti sale at USD 460 per LDT two weeks ago still the wave’s first executed marker. The Letter of Credit pipeline remains fully permissive, plot capacity is available, and the June 30 to July 3 tide window is running as this issue publishes, with the next window July 14 to 17. The wave is no longer a thesis. It is a list.

Bangladesh’s June CPI from BBS is the operative watch item in the coming days; the April print of 9.04% remains the reference, and the Pakistan June read, which turned lower on the oil collapse, suggests the Taka basket’s energy pass-through should begin unwinding on the same mechanics. The structural setup for the second half is unchanged and remains the basin’s strongest: full demand, cleared financing, pricing that holds Chattogram at the top of the rankings, and a monsoon that lifts into September just as the counted queue converts into candidates. The band’s break at the top costs the mills a few dollars per ton on the import side and hands the breakers a marginally better Taka realisation per dollar of steel. The season still governs the next eight weeks. The list now governs everything after.

highlights: Fleet exits. | Oil settles. | CPI turns. | Dollar enters.
body_text:
The war is over, and the fleet is finally moving. Crude flows through Hormuz exceeded 10 million barrels per day this week under US military coordination, while Lloyd’s List counts roughly 550 merchant vessels preparing to exit the Gulf, including some 200 bulk carriers. The central channel remains constrained by an estimated 80 mines, keeping traffic to the northern and southern routes for now, but the direction of travel is no longer theoretical. Tehran continues to decline face-to-face talks with the Americans in Doha. Its cargoes carry no such reservations.

Brent has settled near USD 71 per barrel, effectively back at its pre-war level, closing the quarter with its sharpest fall since 2020 after touching USD 126.41 on April 30. Analysts have cut their 2026 forecasts for the first time since the war began, after five consecutive months of raising them, even as US crude inventories have now drawn for twelve straight weeks. The barrel has completed the round trip. The inventory shortage remains. The price has chosen the reopening.

Freight has adjusted, but not collapsed. The Baltic Dry Index bounced late to approximately 2,650 on iron ore strength, with Capesize earnings near USD 32,060 per day. The index gained 25% for the quarter and lost 22% for the month, which is the cleanest measure yet of the conflict’s afterlife in freight. The war’s freight premium outlived the war by exactly one month. It is now fading into a market where the ships that stayed trading through the conflict have fewer reasons to keep doing so.

The dollar has taken the war’s place as the basin’s moving force. The Indian Rupee gave back part of its recovery to near 95.1, the Bangladeshi Taka eased through the top of its long-held band toward 123.2, and the Turkish Lira set another record low near 46.70. The Pakistani Rupee alone strengthened, breaking below 278, while Pakistan’s June CPI turned lower to 11.1%, with prices falling outright on the month. Islamabad’s July 1 tax and duty SROs have also quietly shifted the ground beneath Gadani, introducing a local-policy variable just as the external war premium disappears.

The yards now face two queues. One is the visible line of vessels exiting the Gulf. The other is the deferred recycling wave that the war held offshore and the monsoon is still holding from the beaches. The exit queue and the deflating premium govern what will come. The rains and the tide calendar govern when it can land. The ships are moving. The beaches are waiting. The war deferred the wave; the weather now decides its arrival.

headline: RUPEE RETREATS, DOLLAR RULES
highlights: Rupee retreats. | Dollar rules. | Alang holds.
body_text:
The rupee has given back its recovery. USD/INR weakened from the six-week best of approximately 94.26 on June 25 to trade near 95.1 to 95.2 this week, surrendering most of the ground gained since the peace was signed, even as Brent held at its pre-war level near USD 71. The Week 26 configuration, in which the rupee was winning the argument it could control and being held back by the one it could not, has resolved in the dollar’s favour: the Dollar Index at a more-than-one-year high, US inflation at 4.2%, and roughly 75% odds of a September Federal Reserve hike have overpowered the oil tailwind that should, in isolation, have carried the rupee through 94. The war’s pressure on the rupee came through the import bill. The peace’s pressure comes through the Fed. The bill was easier to model.

The transmission now runs almost entirely through the capital account. Foreign institutional flows remained mixed through the week, with debt inflows supported by the Reserve Bank of India’s bond capital-gains tax removal but equity flows capped by the global rate repricing, and the rupee’s June range of roughly 94.3 to 95.3 maps almost precisely onto the dollar’s own moves rather than anything domestic. India’s June CPI, due mid-month, will be struck against pre-war oil for the first time since February and should extend the 3.48% April calm; the June trade figures, priced off USD 71 Brent rather than USD 107, should materially narrow the petroleum bill. The fundamentals are turning supportive on schedule. The currency is waiting on Washington’s inflation problem, not Delhi’s.

Local steel plate prices at Alang softened from INR 37,200 mid-week to INR 36,700 by July 3, with the USD equivalent easing to approximately USD 385 per ton. India remains the lowest-priced sub- continent destination, with the gap to Pakistan now near USD 310 per LDT at the ton level, the widest of the year, as Gadani’s plate holds near USD 700 while Alang’s sits below USD 385. The monsoon caps beaching through August, the June 27 to July 5 tide window runs as this issue publishes, and the compliance footprint of more than 110 valid Statements of Compliance positions Alang for the post- monsoon routing of the counted Gulf exit queue. The deferred wave will route on price and compliance. On compliance, Alang leads the basin. On the offered price, it remains the basin’s floor. The post-monsoon quarter will price that tension vessel by vessel.

headline: DUTIES SHIFT, CPI TURNS
highlights: Duties shift. | Competition firms. | CPI turns.
body_text:
The Federal Budget, which at announcement appeared to leave the metal sector untouched, has clarified itself. With the issuance and implementation of the SROs from July 1, the actual duty changes are now visible: Regulatory Duty on re-rollable and melting scrap has been reduced by 1%, worth approximately PKR 1,000 to 1,500 per metric ton, or roughly USD 3.5 to USD 5.5 at prevailing rates. The larger moves sit in prime products. RD on HR prime imports has been cut by 2.5%, worth approximately PKR 3,500 per ton, or USD 12.5, while the reduction on wire rod imports delivers a saving near PKR 6,000 per ton, or approximately USD 21.50. The ship recycling sector itself received no direct changes. The budget, at announcement, appeared to leave the metals market alone. The SROs, at implementation, confirmed that it had not.

The transmission to Gadani runs through the product rather than the plot. Cheaper imported scrap applies moderate pressure, with buyers positioned to press for relatively cheaper local material, but the more consequential moves are HR prime and wire rod: at USD 12.5 and USD 21.50 per ton of new duty relief, imported prime product becomes materially more competitive against locally recycled and re-rolled material, sharpening the ceiling over what Gadani’s output can command. The sector that received no direct changes in the budget is the one now expecting the pressure. The effect is assessed as moderate rather than significant on the scrap side and more noticeable through the prime channel, and it arrives in the first fiscal week after the wartime Gulf premium finished eroding, making it the opening structural test of Gadani’s post-war pricing.

Pakistan’s June CPI eased to 11.1% year-on-year from May’s 11.7%, the first annual deceleration since the war opened, and consumer prices fell outright by 0.3% on the month, the first monthly decline of the conflict era, as the Brent collapse fed directly into the domestic fuel complex. Prices in Pakistan fell in the month; the smoke alarm has finally heard about the fire. The Wholesale Price Index slowed to 10.7%, with a 1.2% monthly decline, urban core eased to 8.7%, and the full fiscal year closed at an average of 7.05%, under the government’s 7.5% target despite petrol printing a record PKR 458.40 per litre in April. USD/PKR broke below 278 to trade near 277.7 to 278.0, a fresh 2026 best, stronger by roughly 2.1% over twelve months and still the basin’s only appreciating currency. Local steel plate held at PKR 195,000 per ton, near USD 696 on the firm rupee, with the Jenny Lucky and Ladonna bulkers the newest arrivals at Gadani. The macro turn is in. The duty structure beneath the plate quote has just moved, and July will measure which force the breakers feel first.

headline: LIRA NEARS 47, PRINT LOOMS
highlights: Record extends. | Print looms. | Niche persists.
body_text:
Turkey enters Week 27 with USD/TRY at approximately 46.70, a fresh record extending the slide past the 46.40 reference of last week and touching toward 47 at the intraday extreme, with the lira down roughly 17.3% over twelve months and about 7% year-to-date. The strengthening global dollar that pushed the Rupee back through 95 and the Taka through its band top now compounds a depreciation that was already running on domestic fuel alone. The Central Bank of Turkey held its policy rate at 37% for a third consecutive meeting in June, encouraged by the May monthly inflation print easing to 1.71%, while the effective 40% overnight funding rate continues to tighten. The framework functions. The level, as it has all year, worsens on schedule.

Turkey’s June CPI prints July 3, the day this issue publishes, and it is the first reading struck substantially against post-war oil. The May print of 32.61% annual and 1.71% monthly remains the operative read, the year-end forecast range remains suspended with the 24% target nominally intact, and independent estimates continue to track materially above the official series. Brent near USD 71, against USD 107 in mid-May and the USD 126 peak, is the genuine disinflation tailwind the TCMB has waited for all year, and the June and July prints will show whether it can bend an inflation structure still measured in the thirties. The bank stopped forecasting in May. The data resumes speaking tomorrow.

At USD 266 to USD 288 per LDT across vessel types, Aliaga remains structurally uncompetitive for mainstream tonnage, and the counted Gulf exit queue sharpens the point: the roughly 200 bulk carriers preparing to leave the Gulf will route overwhelmingly to the sub-continent on the price differential once the monsoon lifts, while Aliaga’s share of the wave will continue to be set by EU regulation and Basel Convention compliance rather than by price. The lira’s slide toward 47 firms Turkish offers marginally in dollar terms without bridging a gap measured in hundreds. Turkey occupied a separate market through the war, occupies it through the peace, and will occupy it through the wave.

headline: RIVERS RISE, YARDS STALL
highlights: Rivers rise. | CPI eases. | Wave waits.
body_text:
The monsoon has turned from a calendar constraint into an operational one. Constant flooding across the Chattogram region is hampering production at the yards, with market reports confirming limited cash buyer demand as plot operators contend with the weather rather than the pipeline. Chattogram Division recorded extremely heavy rainfall within a single 24-hour period this week. The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre has placed at least seventeen districts under short-term flood warnings, while the Halda, Sangu, Matamuhuri, Feni, and Gomti rivers are running at or above danger levels across Chattogram, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, and Feni. Landslide risk remains elevated across the hill districts, with heavy to very heavy rainfall forecast for several more days under a monsoon low over the northwestern Bay of Bengal. Beaching cycles have slowed beyond the ordinary seasonal pattern. This is no longer the monsoon merely closing a window. It is the monsoon standing in the yard.

The macro backdrop, by contrast, improved on schedule. Bangladesh's June CPI eased to 9.16%, with lower food prices slowing overall inflation as the fiscal year closed, while the IMF moved to release USD 1.3 billion following a reform breakthrough, reinforcing the external position alongside reserves near USD 34.12 billion. USD/BDT held above its former band ceiling near 123.2 to 123.3, with the dollar-driven break of Week 27 consolidating rather than extending. The renewed conflict has so far placed less pressure on the Taka than on the Rupee, with the energy pass-through reflected in Bangladesh's 9.16% inflation rather than the double-digit levels Pakistan carried through much of the conflict. The latest available local steel indication remained near BDT 66,000 per ton, equivalent to approximately USD 535 at the prevailing exchange rate. No trading was reported during the latter part of the week as heavy rainfall and flooding disrupted activity across the yards and local steel market.

The 550-vessel Gulf exit census that gave the deferred wave its first hard number now carries an asterisk. Hormuz transits are declining again as the conflict resumes, visible traffic is concentrating on Iran-approved routes, and the owners who were moving closer to recycling decisions as the war premium eased are now watching that premium rebuild. Chattogram's July 14 to 17 tide window approaches with the yards flood hampered and demand limited, a combination that defers rather than destroys. The Letter of Credit pipeline remains permissive, plot capacity remains available, and the structural second-half setup survives intact beneath the water. The wave now waits on two skies, the one over the Bay of Bengal and the one over the strait, and neither is currently taking instructions from the market.

highlights: Truce breaks. | Brent jumps. | Rivers rise. | Yards stall.
body_text:
The peace lasted three weeks. After Iranian projectiles struck three tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on July 6 and 7, the United States hit more than 80 targets in one night and roughly 90 the next, from Qeshm Island and the approaches to Bandar Abbas to the Chabahar maritime control tower, and revoked the waiver permitting Iranian oil sales. Iran responded with attacks against U.S. military facilities in Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and Jordan. President Trump, attending the NATO summit, declared the ceasefire over in the morning and reported by evening that Iran wanted a deal “so badly.” The truce was over at breakfast and negotiable by dinner.

Brent jumped 5.2% to approximately USD 78 per barrel, its biggest daily gain since May, before easing toward USD 77 as traders weighed threats of a renewed blockade and possible strikes on the Kharg Island export terminal against a strait that has not, so far, fully closed. Hormuz transits are declining again, with visible traffic increasingly using Iran-approved routes. The barrel that toured the war and came home has packed again.

Freight chose an awkward week to rally. The Baltic Dry Index rose for a sixth consecutive session to 2,875, its highest since June 8, on firmer iron ore and coal demand, with the Capesize index reaching 4,514. The premium that peace spent a month deflating is now repricing from both the cargo side and the war side at once.

The currencies re-sorted along the old fault line within hours. The Indian Rupee slid to a one-month low near 95.5, with the Reserve Bank defending the level; the Taka held above its former band ceiling near 123.2; and the Lira remained in record territory near 46.7. The Pakistani Rupee alone held near its 2026 best around 278. The June inflation prints, struck during the peace, arrived just as it ended: Turkey eased to 32.11%, its first annual decline since the war opened, while Bangladesh slowed to 9.16%. The disinflation tailwind reached the data on July 3. The war reached back for it on July 7.

At the beaches, the sky has opened. Persistent flooding across Chattogram Division, with rivers above danger levels and warnings extending across seventeen districts, is hampering yard production and thinning demand, while the resumed conflict delivers its familiar knock-on hesitation to owners and the Gulf exit queue alike. The wave counted last week now waits beneath two skies: the weather over the Bay of Bengal and the ordnance over the strait. Detailed market briefs follow on pages 2 through 5.

headline: RUPEE SLIDES, OIL RETURNS
highlights: Rupee slides. | Oil returns. | Alang waits.
body_text:
The rupee has taken the war’s return harder than any currency in the basin. USD/INR slid to a one- month low near 95.50, falling 0.6% on Wednesday alone and more than 1% across six sessions, with the Reserve Bank of India reportedly selling dollars through state-run banks near the 95.50 level to slow the move. The stress spread across the asset complex: Indian equities fell 2% in their steepest session of the period, while the ten-year government bond yield rose seven basis points in its largest one-day move in more than three months. The oil-import vulnerability that the peace had pushed into the background is back in the foreground, and the rupee, which spent June trading the dollar’s moves, is spending July trading the war’s.

The arithmetic is unchanged from the spring; only the level differs. Brent near USD 77 to USD 78, against USD 71 a week ago, re-widens the import bill of an economy that buys more than 80% of its crude abroad, and it does so just as the Federal Reserve’s June minutes put roughly one-in-three odds on a July hike and two-in-three by September, with the U.S. ten-year yield at 4.565% and the Dollar Index above 101. The rupee is again fighting on two fronts, oil and the Fed, and this week both advanced. India’s June CPI, due mid-month, was struck against the peace-era oil environment of June and should still print calm; the July number will carry whatever the strait decides. The war’s first act taught the rupee’s range. The second act has opened at the weak end of it.

Local steel plate prices at Alang firmed from INR 36,500 to INR 37,000 during the week, with the USD equivalent rising from approximately USD 383 to USD 388 per ton. India remains the basin’s lowest- priced destination, with the gap to Pakistan above USD 310 per LDT. The July 11 to 20 tide window opens as this issue publishes into a market where the monsoon caps beaching, the resumed conflict has suspended the exit-queue mathematics of a week ago, and more than 110 valid Statements of Compliance wait on a routing decision the war has again deferred. Alang’s position is unchanged: deepest capacity, strongest compliance, weakest price. What changed this week is the timetable, which now belongs once more to the strait.

headline: RUPEE HOLDS, GULF SHAKES
highlights: Gulf shakes. | Rupee holds. | Duties digest.
body_text:
The war’s return arrived at Pakistan’s doorstep. Iran retaliated with missile and drone attacks against U.S. military facilities in Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and Jordan, bringing the conflict back to Gulf waters that frame Gadani’s routing lanes, while the Gulf Cooperation Council’s condemnation of the attacks confirmed the region’s re-entry into the conflict it had spent three weeks exiting. Analysis of Tehran’s posture suggests Iran values control of the strait above avoiding escalation, implying that the coming weeks may again be governed by the coercive mechanics that defined the spring: attacks on shipping, strikes in reply, and a waterway whose usability is decided daily. The Gulf proximity that was first a wartime premium and then a peacetime irrelevance is now a live variable again, and its direction has yet to declare itself.

Through all of it, the rupee simply held. USD/PKR remained near 278, at or close to its 2026 best, extending the currency’s standing as the only one in the basin to have appreciated through the war, the peace, and now the war’s resumption. The June CPI turn reported last week, 11.1% annually with an outright 0.3% monthly decline, remains the operative read, while the renewed oil spike retests the import bill from USD 77 rather than USD 126, a materially shallower starting point than the spring shock. The State Bank’s 11.5% policy stance, disciplined reserve management, and remittance resilience carried the rupee through the worst quarter in years. The market’s early verdict on the second act is that they may carry it again.

Gadani is spending the week digesting policy and war at once. The July 1 SROs remain the structural story beneath the plate quote: Regulatory Duty relief of roughly USD 12.50 per ton on HR prime and USD 21.50 on wire rod continues to sharpen the competitiveness of imported prime product against locally recycled material, while the scrap-side relief of USD 3.50 to USD 5.50 exerts more moderate pressure. July’s realizations will show which channel the breakers feel first. Local steel plate held at PKR 195,000 per ton, near USD 700 on the firm rupee, while the yards continue working through the Jenny Lucky and Ladonna intake. The resumed conflict cuts both ways for Pakistan: it revives the locational calculus that favoured Gadani in the spring, and it revives the shipping hesitation that starved every beach in the basin. Which force wins is the question July will answer.

headline: CPI TURNS, WAR RETURNS
highlights: CPI turns. | War returns. | Niche persists.
body_text:
Turkey finally got its number. June CPI printed at 32.11% year-on-year, down from 32.61% in May, marking the first annual decline since the war opened and the lowest reading since March. Monthly inflation eased to 0.99%, the smallest increase in six months. Housing slowed to 45.14% and transport to 31.15% as the post-war oil collapse fed through, while food inflation continued climbing to 35.45%. The print landed broadly in line with expectations and revived market discussion of the central bank resuming its easing cycle after months of emergency tightness. The disinflation tailwind the TCMB waited for all year reached the data on July 3. The war reached back for it on July 7.

The resumption carries a particular geography for Ankara. President Trump declared the ceasefire over while attending the NATO summit in Turkey, and Brent’s jump back toward USD 78 threatens the oil relief that produced June’s improvement before it could compound. USD/TRY held in record territory near 46.7, with the lira’s managed slide continuing against a dollar strengthened by Federal Reserve rate-hike expectations. The policy rate remains at 37%, while the effective 40% overnight rate continues to do the work. The June print gave the easing argument a hearing. The July print, struck against resumed hostilities and USD 77 oil, will decide whether that argument survives its first witness.

At USD 266 to USD 288 per LDT across vessel types, Aliaga remains structurally uncompetitive for mainstream tonnage, and neither the war’s end nor its resumption has changed that fact. The Gulf exit queue, whose routing was last week’s question, is this week’s suspended question, but its eventual answer remains unchanged: the tonnage will move to the sub-continent on price, while Aliaga’s share will continue to be determined by EU regulation and Basel Convention compliance. Turkey has now occupied its separate market through a war, a peace, and a second war, which is, at minimum, a demonstration of consistency.

headline: FLOODS DEEPEN, MARKET WAITS
highlights: The toll. | Markets pause. | Reserves hold.
body_text:
The confirmed death toll from this month’s flooding and landslides has reached at least 51, with 39 injured and more than one million people affected across seven districts, according to disaster- management officials. An embankment failure on the Khowai River flooded twenty-five villages in Habiganj, while a landslide inside a Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar killed sixteen residents, including children. The Chattogram Meteorological Office has recorded some of the heaviest rainfall totals in the region’s history over the past ten days, and forecasters continue to monitor several river basins for renewed short-term flooding. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has ordered all relevant agencies onto maximum alert, while emergency cash and rice allocations have been released to the worst-affected districts.

Against that human toll, the commercial picture remains what it has been for two weeks: paused, not broken. Beaching activity at Chattogram has slowed to a near-halt, cash-buyer enquiries remain thin, and the July 14 to 17 tide window closes with little to show for it. The next window with meaningful capacity opens July 29. Yards that had positioned for the deferred Gulf exit wave are, for now, waiting for dry ground, while the renewed blockade and firmer freight market give owners further reason to delay recycling decisions. The supply has not disappeared. Its arrival has simply been deferred again.

The macro backdrop continues to run separately from both the weather and the war. USD/BDT held near 123.30, comfortably within the range established after Week 27’s break, with reserves supported by the IMF’s confirmed USD 1.3 billion disbursement following June’s reform breakthrough. No new inflation print is due until early August, leaving June’s 9.16% as the operative read. The fiscal year closed with average inflation near 8.68%, above the government’s 7% target, but below the double-digit pressures seen elsewhere in the basin. Local steel trading remains effectively suspended, with no reliable fresh price direction emerging from mills or yards. The plot floor is, for the moment, underwater in more ways than one.

headline: BLOCKADE RETURNS, TOLL RISES
highlights: Blockade returns. | Brent climbs. | Flood toll rises. | Yards stall.
body_text:
The second act arrived with a name this time, and it was not “ceasefire.” Five consecutive days of American strikes through Wednesday hit Iranian positions from Bandar Abbas and Qeshm Island to Sirik, while Washington reinstated the naval blockade of Iranian ports lifted during June’s interim peace. The blockade found its first target within a day. A Curaçao-flagged tanker bound for Kharg Island ignored repeated warnings and was disabled by a Hellfire strike into its smokestack, stopping the vessel without spilling its cargo. Two others were redirected without incident. President Trump is reportedly weighing a broader campaign and has revived the idea of seizing Kharg Island outright, while abandoning the proposed 20% Hormuz transit fee. Nobody involved is using the word peace this week, which may be the most accurate statement anyone has made since February.

Oil has now made this climb three times since the conflict opened, and the muscle memory shows. Brent touched USD 84.77 and WTI USD 79.56 on Thursday, one-month highs that recovered roughly one-third of the ground surrendered during June’s interim peace. A reinstated blockade and open discussion of taking a major export terminal will do that. Yet the move remains smaller than the first shock, and the market’s patience is noticeably shorter. Traders are repricing a war whose script they can now recite from memory.

Freight, characteristically, is having a different week. The Baltic Dry Index closed Friday at 2,944, its highest since June 5, while the Capesize Index rose 1.9% to 4,655 on continued iron ore and coal demand. Dry bulk owners are pricing cargo fundamentals rather than Hormuz, and for another week, cargo fundamentals are winning the argument. The recycling implication remains familiar. Firmer earnings keep ageing tonnage trading, while renewed war risk interrupts the Gulf exit queue.

The data released this week was arguing with the news that overtook it. U.S. June inflation eased to 3.5% from 4.2%, its first decline in five months, with core inflation slowing to 2.6% as the energy relief delivered by the now-defunct ceasefire reached the figures. India’s June print moved the other way, rising to 4.38% from 3.93%, its highest since December 2024 and above expectations as the spring energy shock reached transport and food costs. The calm print anticipated last week did not arrive, and the Rupee noticed. USD/INR touched 96.40 on Thursday before easing toward 96.20. The Taka held near 123.30, the Turkish Lira reached another record near 47.10, and the Pakistani Rupee barely moved, the only basin currency that appears to have opted out of 2026. In Bangladesh, the numbers that matter most are not economic. Flooding and landslides across Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Habiganj, and neighbouring districts have killed at least 51 people and affected more than one million. A failed embankment on the Khowai River flooded twenty-five villages, while a landslide inside a Cox’s Bazar refugee camp killed sixteen Rohingya residents, including children. Against that human toll, disruption to Chattogram’s yards is secondary, but commercially real. Beaching has slowed to a near-halt for a second consecutive week, and the Gulf exit queue that was expected to test the port’s capacity this month now waits on a recovery that has not arrived.

The war has returned to the strait just as the weather has closed the beach. Firmer freight keeps candidates trading, the blockade delays the Gulf exit queue, and flooding prevents Chattogram from absorbing whatever reaches it. The market remains paused, not broken. The ships wait for passage. The yards wait for dry land.

headline: THE CALM THAT WASN’T
highlights: Rupee climbs. | The calm wasn’t. | Alang holds.
body_text:
USD/INR touched 96.40 on Thursday, its weakest level since May and within striking distance of the May 21 record of approximately 96.97, before a modest Friday recovery returned it toward 96.20. The Reserve Bank was again visible smoothing the move through state-run banks, though Governor Malhotra has consistently described such action as volatility management rather than defence of a particular level. The ten-year yield and equity markets both moved through a milder version of the Week 28 shock, suggesting that the second escalation has rattled fewer nerves than the first, even at a weaker exchange rate.

Last week’s edition previewed India’s June CPI as a reading struck largely during the peace-era oil window that “should still print calm.” It did not. Inflation rose to 4.38% from 3.93%, its highest since December 2024 and above every forecast on the board. Transport inflation rebounded to 4.31% as the spring energy shock cleared customs, while food inflation rose to 5.32%, helped by a 50% surge in ginger prices. The lesson is familiar: forecasting Indian inflation during a conflict that repeatedly stops and starts remains a dangerous game. July’s number, due next month, now has considerably more to explain.

Local steel plate at Alang firmed through the week from approximately INR 37,200 to INR 38,000, with the USD equivalent rising toward USD 394 as the local increase outweighed the weaker Rupee. The July 11 to 20 tide window enters its final days with the Gulf exit queue still suspended and monsoon conditions limiting beaching activity. Alang’s wider position remains unchanged for a third consecutive week: the basin’s deepest capacity, more than 115 valid Statements of Compliance, the strongest compliance profile, the weakest price, and little tonnage being offered.

headline: RUPEE HOLDS, BLOCKADE BITES
highlights: Blockade bites. | Rupee unbothered. | Duties unchanged.
body_text:
The reinstated U.S. naval blockade produced its first casualty within a day, with a tanker bound for Kharg Island disabled by Hellfire fire after ignoring repeated warnings and two further vessels redirected without incident. The enforcement sits closer to Gadani’s routing lanes than anything since April’s original blockade, reviving the locational calculus that briefly favoured Pakistan earlier this year. Brokers report renewed war-risk premiums for Gulf-transiting recycling candidates, though from a sufficiently low base that the increase is more notable than the absolute level.

USD/PKR spent the week inside a range of barely a quarter rupee, closing near 278.15 and remaining effectively unchanged through renewed conflict, a disabled tanker, and another round of American strikes. For the third escalation this year, the Pakistani Rupee remains the only basin currency that has simply declined to react. The State Bank’s 11.5% policy rate and disciplined reserve management continue to receive the credit, though the currency’s stability is beginning to look less like a policy outcome and more like a defining characteristic. No new CPI print is due until early August, leaving June’s 11.1% reading and rare outright monthly decline as the operative verdict.

Gadani’s plate quote held flat at PKR 195,000 per ton, near USD 700, for a second consecutive week, while the July 1 Regulatory Duty relief continues working through the market at its own pace. Yard demand remains steady but unspectacular. Pakistan closed Week 28 asking whether locational advantage or owner hesitation would dominate as the conflict resumed. One week later, the answer remains unchanged: the market has not finished deciding, and may not do so before the next headline arrives.

headline: STILL HELD, STILL DISPUTED
highlights: Rate held, third time. | The other number. | Niche unmoved.
body_text:
The TCMB kept its policy rate at 37% at its latest meeting, the third consecutive hold, citing renewed energy-price volatility in the inflation outlook. The committee’s language was unchanged, with rates set to remain restrictive until price stability is achieved. USD/TRY nevertheless moved into fresh record territory near 47.10, while the effective overnight rate near 40% continues to carry the policy burden without yet reversing the currency’s decline.

June’s official inflation reading of 32.11%, the lowest since March, remains the headline figure. Independent economists at the Inflation Research Group place the annual rate closer to 51.4%, a gap that has persisted for years and shows no sign of narrowing. Both measures agree on the direction, if not the scale. June benefited from easing oil prices. July is being struck against a renewed conflict and another rise in crude, making a repeat of that relief less likely.

Aliaga’s plate indications held at USD 263 to USD 285 per LDT across vessel types, leaving Turkey structurally uncompetitive against the sub-continent for a third consecutive week. The eventual routing of the Gulf exit queue remains secondary to Aliaga’s core market. Turkey’s share continues to be defined by EU regulation, Basel Convention compliance, and specialist tonnage rather than price. The war has changed the headlines. It has not changed the niche.

headline: WATERS RECEDE, WINDOW WAITS
highlights: The toll. | Recovery begins. | Compliance bites.
body_text:
The confirmed death toll from this month’s floods and landslides has reached 57, according to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, with three deaths added in the most recent daily reporting period. Cox’s Bazar accounts for 32 of the dead, including thirteen Rohingya refugees killed in camp landslides; Chattogram has recorded fifteen, Bandarban six, Rangamati three, and Moulvibazar one. More than a million people across seven districts were affected at the peak. The waters are now receding: 111 shelters remain open with roughly 4,000 people still in them, down from tens of thousands, and allocations of emergency cash and rice continue to reach the worst- affected areas. Forecasters are still monitoring the river basins, but the operative word this week, for the first time this month, is recovery.

The commercial thaw is visible. Chattogram port operations have largely normalised, with average vessel waiting back near a day and a half, and a threatened 48-hour prime mover and flatbed strike over an increased advance income tax was announced and then withdrawn inside the same week following talks, a dispute that resolved faster than the floodwater. Local steel trading, dormant through the deluge, has begun to pick up as yards reopen, and mills expect firmer demand once the monsoon passes. Beaching eyes now turn to the July 29 to August 1 tide window, the first with meaningful capacity since the rains began, with a second window to follow August 12 to 15. The deferred supply has not disappeared; the beach may finally be ready to receive it.

The week’s sharpest development was regulatory rather than meteorological. A tanker was sanctioned after its arrival at Chattogram and after clearances were completed, caught, in effect, between the anchorage and the beach, and the episode has sharpened caution across recyclers and cash buyers alike. Enquiry for tonnage remains healthy but increasingly selective, favouring bulkers and units free of compliance exposure. USD/BDT held near 123.35 at the top of its established band, and with no inflation print due until early August, June’s 9.16% remains the operative read. The plot floor is drying out. The paperwork, it turns out, can flood too.

headline: CRUDE CROSSES, WATERS RECEDE
highlights: Crude tops $100. | Second front opens. | Freight rolls over. | Waters recede.
body_text:
The thirteenth consecutive night of American strikes closed out the week, and for the first time since this conflict began, the map grew. Yemen’s Houthis struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea and threatened a blockade of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the route Saudi barrels had been taking around a shut Hormuz. Washington answered with threats of military punishment for further attacks on shipping and floated billing the damage to frozen Iranian assets, while both sides ruled out near-term talks. Asked about a ceasefire, President Trump said Iran needs “more of the same.” The war that spent months confined to one strait has developed ambitions.

Oil did what oil does when chokepoints multiply. Brent crossed USD 100 on Thursday for the first time since May before easing to USD 97.63 by Friday, with WTI near USD 89.77, still leaving crude up roughly ten percent on the week. A third front opened quietly in the Black Sea, where drone attacks on tankers loading at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal on July 17, 19, and 21 halted operations, forcing Kazakhstan, which routes some four-fifths of its exports through the terminal, to cut production. Asian buyers have begun pricing Saudi crude via the Suez Canal and around the Cape of Good Hope, itineraries last considered state-of-the-art in 1869 and during the Ever Given’s brief tenancy, respectively.

Freight, which spent last week ignoring the war, spent this week ignoring its own rally. The Baltic Dry Index fell more than six percent last week to 2,752 and kept going, touching 2,671 on Monday, its lowest since July 2, as the Capesize index dropped 5.6% and then another 5.1% to 3,889 on softer iron ore and coal enquiry and improving vessel availability. The Supramax index, contrary as ever, climbed to 1,738, its highest since August 2022. Last week’s edition noted that cargo fundamentals were winning the argument “for another week.” The market, rarely so punctual, took the deadline literally. Softer Capesize earnings are the first genuine nudge toward the beach in months; the problem now is not the intent to exit, but the routes out.

The data calendar offered no fresh inflation prints. June’s readings, from Washington’s 3.5% to Karachi’s 11.1%, remain operative until August, each now arguing in advance with an oil price that spent Thursday above USD 100. The TCMB filled the vacuum by holding at 37% for a fourth consecutive meeting. Currencies did the talking instead: USD/INR touched 96.88 on Thursday, near May’s 96.97 record, before recovering toward 96.50; the Taka held at 123.35; the Lira set fresh records near 47.35; and the Pakistani Rupee closed near 278.40, again inside a quarter-rupee range. At this point, it is less an exchange rate than a physical constant. In Bangladesh, the human toll from this month’s flooding has risen to 57 confirmed dead, most in Cox’s Bazar, including thirteen Rohingya refugees, with more than a million people affected at the peak. The waters are receding: shelters have consolidated to 111, relief allocations continue to move, and forecasters are watching river basins rather than the sky. Recovery, not rescue, is finally the operative word.

Commercially, Chattogram is stirring. Port operations have largely normalised, and a threatened 48-hour container transport strike was announced and withdrawn within the same week, resolved, unlike the weather, by conversation. The week’s sharpest lesson came from compliance: a tanker was sanctioned after arrival and after clearances were complete, caught between anchorage and beach, while appetite across the basin tilted firmly toward bulkers and clean-history units.

headline: TIGHT PLATES, FRESH RECORDS
highlights: Rupee at the door. | Plates firm. | The niche widens.
body_text:
USD/INR touched 96.88 on Thursday, its closest approach yet to the May 21 record of approximately 96.97, before a Friday recovery returned it toward 96.50. The Reserve Bank remained visible, smoothing the move through state-run banks, while equity and bond markets absorbed the year’s third escalation with notably less drama than the first two, a market that has, like everyone else, learned the script. With no CPI print due until mid-August, June’s 4.38% surprise stands as the operative number, and July’s reading is being struck against an oil price that visited three digits.

Local steel plate at Alang firmed through the week from approximately INR 38,200 toward INR 38,500, with the USD equivalent approaching USD 400 as monsoon-slowed cutting activity tightened plate supply faster than the weakening Rupee could offset it. The move is real but fragile: downstream steel demand remains tepid, several vessels remain away from shore, and the rebound owes more to scarcity than appetite. The July 11 to 20 tide window closed with little fanfare; the next opens Monday, July 27, and runs through August 4.

Alang’s structural position strengthened almost by accident this week. As compliance caution sweeps Chattogram following the sanctioned tanker episode, India’s status as the basin’s only market accepting dark fleet tonnage has quietly turned from footnote into commercial moat. The wider position is otherwise unchanged for a fourth consecutive week: the deepest capacity, more than 115 valid Statements of Compliance, the strongest compliance profile, the weakest price, and now, uniquely, the widest door.
